life|01-01||Άγιος Πέτρος ο Πελοποννήσιος||Saint Peter was a new martyr from Tripoli in the Peloponnese. He was martyred in Asia Minor by hanging, because he confessed his faith in Christ. // According to the text, his martyrdom had not yet been published.

life|01-02||Άγιος Βασίλειος ο Μάρτυρας εξ Αγκύρας||Saint Basil came from Ancyra and lived in the time of Julian the Apostate, around 361. He was arrested because he believed in Christ, and he confessed his faith boldly before the governor Saturninus, whereupon they flayed him mercilessly. // He was taken to Constantinople, where they tore him again and stretched him so much that the joints of his arms and shoulders were dislocated. They cut strips from his body and pierced his flesh with red-hot irons, but he endured everything with fortitude. According to the text, when they threw him into a furnace of fire, he was marvelously preserved unharmed through his prayer. // Afterwards, bound in Caesarea, he was condemned by the ruler to fight with beasts. After he prayed, a lioness struck him, and thus his martyrdom was completed. His relatives carefully gathered his relics, wrapped them with myrrh and linen sheets, and buried them in a notable place, where a church was later built in his name.

life|01-02||Άγιος Θεαγένης ο Ιερομάρτυρας||Saint Theagenes was bishop of the city of Parium, a colony of the Parians situated between Cyzicus and Lampsacus. He was denounced to the tribune Zelicindius and confessed Christ as the true God. // They beat him with clubs, bound him, and threw him into the depths of the sea. Thus he completed the course of martyrdom and received from the Lord the unfading crown.

life|01-02||Άγιος Κοσμάς ο Θαυματουργός Α’ Πατριάρχης Κωνσταντινουπόλεως||Saint Cosmas was a monk of the Chora Monastery and became Patriarch of Constantinople under Emperor Michael Doukas, in 1070. He was adorned with many virtues and was also cultivated in learning, which is why the emperor loved him. // By him was crowned the emperor Nikephoros Botaneiates, who reigned in 1078. His memory is honored at the Chora Monastery and in the Great Church.

life|01-02||Άγιος Γεώργιος (ή Ζώρζης) ο Νεομάρτυρας ο Γκιουρτζής||Saint George, also known as Zorzis, was a new martyr who was martyred in Mytilene. According to the text, he was perfected by hanging.

life|01-02||Αγία Θεοδότη||Saint Theodota was the mother of the first pair of the holy Unmercenaries. She passed from sickness to the other life and fell asleep in peace. // For the three pairs of Unmercenaries, the text refers to their commemoration on October 17.

life|01-03||Άγιος Γόρδιος||Saint Gordius lived in the time of Emperor Licinius, around 314, and came from Caesarea of Cappadocia. He was a military officer, a centurion over one hundred soldiers. // He could not bear to see the audacity of the idolaters and to hear their blasphemies against Christ, so he left the city and lived in the mountains among the wild beasts. There he was set aflame with longing for Christ and, strengthened by God, he rushed into the city like a mighty lion. In the marketplace and in the theater he proclaimed Christ, turned the crowd to his side, and astonished the ruler, who was enraged and beheaded him. // Saint Basil the Great wrote an encomium for the saint.

life|01-04||Άγιοι Ζώσιμος και Αθανάσιος||Saint Zosimus came from Cilicia and lived in the desert together with the wild beasts. The ruler Domitian arrested him and, because he confessed Christ as the true God, they burned his ears with red-hot irons, put him into a cauldron of boiling mud, and hung him upside down. According to the text, he was preserved unharmed through all of it, and in the theater a lion appeared that spoke with a human voice about the divinity of Christ. // Thus he drew Athanasius the Commentariensis to the faith. Zosimus, when he was set free, returned to the desert and the mountains where he had lived before, and catechized and baptized Athanasius. // While they were there, according to the text, a rock was marvelously split, both of them entered inside and gave up their souls to God.

life|01-04||Όσιος Ευθύμιος Ηγούμενος Μονής Βατοπαιδίου και οι συν αυτώ μαρτυρήσαντες 12 Μοναχοί||Venerable Euthymius was abbot of the Vatopedi Monastery. He rebuked the Latin-minded emperor Michael and the patriarch Beccus, and completed his martyrdom drowned in the sea. // Together with him twelve monks of Vatopedi were martyred, who likewise rebuked the Latin-minded and were perfected by hanging.

life|01-05||Όσιος Γρηγόριος ο εν Ακρίτα||Venerable Gregory came from Crete and was the son of pious parents, Theophanes and Julian. After he had studied for some time, his parents put him to tend sheep, but once, set aflame with divine zeal, he left his homeland for Seleucia, where he lived on a little bread and water. At the age of twenty-six he went to Jerusalem and suffered there for twelve whole years at the hands of Hagarenes and Jews. // Then he went to Rome, where he received the angelic schema and subdued his body with self-restraint. In the years of Patriarch Nikephoros, the confessor Michael, who had been sent to Rome, found him there and brought him to Constantinople, to the monastery of the place Akritas, near Chalcedon. There he lived barefoot, with only a single tunic, slept on a mat, and ate every two or three days a little bread and water. // He shut himself in a very deep pit and for many years mourned the turmoil of the Church caused by the rejection of the holy icons. Later he came out of the pit and shut himself in a very narrow cell, wearing a leather tunic. At night he would enter naked a large jar of water in the garden and read the whole Psalter, and when he finished he came out. He did this all the days of his life and gave up his soul to God.

life|01-05||Όσιος Φωστήριος||Venerable Phosterius came from the East to the western regions and went up a high and quiet mountain. There he prayed and afflicted his body with fasting, vigils, and sleeping on the ground. He kept his body pure and his soul clean and acquired the gift of miracles, so that he healed every illness of those who approached him with faith. // According to the text, he received bread from heaven through the mediation of an invisible angel, and as many brothers as visited him, so many loaves he found at the appointed place. But when he founded a monastery and gathered many monks, he no longer received bread from God, but provided what was necessary for himself and for many others by the labor of his hands, in order to teach his disciples by his example. // When a heresy appeared and a Synod was convened, Phosterius was also summoned, he was present, and by his words many heretics returned to Orthodoxy and many others became monks. Many miracles were worked through him, both while he lived and after his repose, which took place on the evening of January 5.
life|01-05||Άγιος Ρωμανός ο Οσιομάρτυρας||Saint Romanus was a new venerable martyr from Karpenisi. He was martyred in Byzantium, that is Constantinople, in 1694 and was perfected by the sword.

life|01-06||Άγιος Ρωμανός ο Λακεδαίμονας||Saint Romanus was a Lacedaemonian hieromonk and a new hieromartyr. He was martyred for Christ in Byzantium, that is Constantinople, in 1695, and was perfected by the sword. // For most details the text refers to the New Martyrologion.
life|01-07||Άγιος Αθανάσιος ο Νεομάρτυρας εξ Ατταλείας||Saint Athanasius was a new martyr, originating from Attalia. He was martyred in Smyrna in 1700.

life|01-08||Οσία Δομνίκη||Venerable Domnica lived in the time of Theodosius the Great, around 384, and came from Carthage in Africa. On some business she went up to Constantinople together with forty other virgins. Patriarch Nectarius, who was then in office, received them following a divine revelation and deemed them worthy of divine baptism. // Domnica became a nun and by manly struggles reached the summit of asceticism, so that she even worked miracles. After shining with these, she departed to the Lord.

life|01-08||Άγιοι Ιουλιανός, Βασίλισσα, Κέλσιος, Αναστάσιος και Αντώνιος οι Μάρτυρες||Saint Julian lived in the time of Diocletian and the governor Marcian, around 290, and came from Antinoöpolis in Egypt. He persuaded his lawful wife, Basilissa, to remain in chastity and virginity. She became a nun in one monastery and he in another, where he became abbot of twelve thousand monks. // When the governor arrested him, he did not deny Christ but mocked the idols. The governor sent men, and they burned the monastery together with the monks and with all the bishops and clergy of the region who had taken refuge there. Julian himself they beat and squeezed with iron chains, which crushed his bones. An executioner, blind in one eye, believed in Christ and was healed by the martyr, and Julian was finally beheaded. // Celsus, the governor's son, believed together with twenty soldiers, when he saw Julian raise a dead man by his prayer. They put him in prison and then threw him into red-hot cauldrons of boiling water, together with seven other sons of the governor, the priest Antony, and Anastasius, who had been raised from the dead. According to the text, all were preserved unharmed, many Greeks believed, as did the mother of Celsus, the governor's wife, and the idols of the temple fell and were shattered. Then they bound the hands and feet of the saints with bundles of papyrus soaked in oil and set them on fire, but they were not burned. They pulled off and removed the skin from the heads of Julian and Celsus, put out the eyes of the priest Antony with iron hooks, and hanged the mother of Celsus and gave her to the beasts, but again they were preserved. Finally all were beheaded and received the crowns of martyrdom. // Their synaxis is held in their martyrial church, near the Forum.

life|01-08||Άγιος Καρτέριος ο Ιερομάρτυρας||Saint Carterius lived in the time of Diocletian and of Urbanus, the governor of Caesarea of Cappadocia, around 298. He was a priest and a teacher of the Christians. He built a house of prayer, that is a small church, where he gathered the multitude of Christians and taught them to worship Christ alone. // He was denounced to the governor and hid, but the Lord appeared to him and told him to present himself. They imprisoned him and, when he was ordered to sacrifice to Serapis, according to the text he brought down the idol by his prayer. They beat him with clubs, pulled out his nails, tore his body with iron claws, pierced his ankles, and sat him on a red-hot iron stool. According to the text, an angel made him superior to the tortures and healed him, and during the night the Lord freed him and brought him out of the prison. Many unbelievers who saw him healthy ran and were baptized by him and were healed of their diseases. // They tortured him again with suspended stones, beating, lit torches, sulfur and pitch, and with boiling lead in his mouth, and they threw him into a fire, where he remained unharmed and hymned God. A Jew who was present pierced him in the side with a javelin, from which so much water came out that it put out the fire, and afterwards blood came out too. Thus he gave up his soul to God.

life|01-08||Άγιοι Θεόφιλος και Ελλάδιος οι Μάρτυρες||These saints were from Libya, Theophilus a deacon and Helladius a layman. They were arrested because they confessed Christ and were led to the proconsul and ruler of Libya. Because they persevered in the faith, they were torn, and after their hands and feet were bound, fire was set to their backs and they were pricked with sharp and pointed spits. Because the torture lasted many hours, the saints gave up their souls to God and ascended as victors to the heavens.

life|01-09||Όσιος Ευστράτιος ο Θαυματουργός||Venerable Eustratius came from Tarsium in the province of the Optimati and was count of the town of Vitziani. He was born in 808 of pious parents, George and Megethe. At the age of twenty divine love seized him, he left his parents for Olympus and went to the Monastery of Agauroi, where his maternal uncles, Basil and Gregory, were distinguished. There he became a monk and served all the brothers with humility, slept on haircloth and, as they say, never slept on his back nor on his left side in all the seventy-five years of his asceticism. When the previous abbots died, he accepted the abbacy at the request of the brothers. // In the years of Leo the Armenian, who renewed iconoclasm, all the Christians were leaving their homes. And Eustratius, urged by Venerable Joannicius the Great, left the monastery and went to his homeland, and when the Church recovered its adornment with the restoration of the icons, he returned to his monastery. // By day he labored with the brothers in bodily works, by night he kept all-night standings and prostrations, and at the services he stood in the sanctuary saying the Kyrie eleison. He worked many miracles and, before he died, he called the monks and urged them to keep the holy schema. He sealed them with the cross, raised his eyes to heaven, said "Into thy hands, O Lord, I commend my spirit," and fell asleep at the age of ninety-five.

life|01-10||Άγιος Μαρκιανός Πρεσβύτερος και Οικονόμος της Μεγάλης Εκκλησίας||Saint Marcian lived in the time of Emperor Marcian and Pulcheria, around 453. His ancestors came from old Rome and came to Constantinople. He built a church of Saint Irene near the sea, to which he joined the house of prayer of Saint Isidore, and a church of Saint Anastasia in the Embola of Domninus. // This church he saved from a great fire, when the flames were burning its upper parts, as he stood on the roof with raised hands and prayed. He received from God the gift of miracles and, although he was rich, he lived in cheap clothes, with a poor diet and strict asceticism. His synaxis is held in the church of the Prophet and Baptist John, near the Cistern of Mocius.

life|01-12||Άγιος Μέρτιος ο Μάρτυρας||Saint Mertius was a soldier in the unit of the Mauri, in the time of Diocletian, around 298. He was denounced as a Christian and, when he was led before the emperor and did not agree to sacrifice to the idols, they took off his belt, the sign of his military rank. // They beat him and tore his body with clubs. He endured with such courage that he did not utter even a small cry, and the astonished tyrant threw him into prison. After eight days much pus ran from his wounds, and the athlete of Christ gave up his soul to God.

life|01-13||Όσιος Ιάκωβος||Venerable James lived in the time of Constantine the Great and came from Nisibis in Mesopotamia. He loved stillness and went up to the high peaks of the mountains, where he endured the heat of summer and the cold of winter, fed on wild herbs, drank little water and wore poor clothes, while his soul was nourished by prayer and the reading of the Scriptures. // Through his virtues he received from the grace of the Holy Spirit the gift of working miracles and foreseeing the future. According to the text, he once saw young women behaving shamelessly at the spring, cursed the spring and dried it up, and turned the black hair of the women white, while the spring flowed again at the supplication of the Christians. As for a false beggar who pretended to be dead in order to receive burial expenses, his prayer made him truly die, and he raised him afterwards at the request of his companions. // For his virtues he became bishop of his homeland, Nisibis, and was present at the First Ecumenical Council of Nicaea, where the fathers anathematized Arius. When Shapur, king of the Persians, besieged Nisibis, the venerable one besought God and a cloud of gnats and mosquitoes was sent against the Persians, which drove the horses and elephants mad and made the king return in vain to Persia. He lived a long life, full of days, and died peacefully.

life|01-14||Όσιος Θεόδουλος υιός του Αγίου Νείλου του Σοφού||Venerable Theodulus was the son of the wise Nilus, who had first become prefect of Constantinople and then, leaving the glory of the world, went to Mount Sinai and became a monk together with his son. // While they were living in stillness there, barbarians suddenly fell upon them and began to slaughter the fathers. Nilus escaped, while Theodulus was taken captive together with another youth, and they dragged them bound. The barbarians wanted to sacrifice them to the star of Aphrodite, the morning star; the other youth managed to escape, and Theodulus was left alone. // The barbarians slept drunk until morning and, when they woke and did not see the morning star, they did not slay him but wanted to sell him. Because the buyers offered only two florins, a barbarian drew his sword to kill him, but a bishop who saw it bought him and set him free. Theodulus afterwards lived in virtue and died peacefully; the memory of the father and the son is celebrated in the church of the Apostle Paul at the orphanage.

life|01-14||Όσιος Στέφανος||Venerable Stephen was from the East, noble by birth like the righteous Job. From the beginning he loved the ascetic life and went around the monasteries and hermitages of the venerable ones at the Jordan and in the desert of Saint Euthymius, as well as of Saint Sabbas and of Theodosius, learning from each its way of life. // Later he went to Constantinople, in the years of the iconoclast Leo the Isaurian, and the then patriarch Germanus received him as a guest, and he stayed near him for some time and was benefited. Taking counsel on what good thing to do, he spent his life at the place where the monastery he founded stands, that of Chenolakkos. He gathered a multitude of monks and guided them in the training and admonition of the Lord, and after his conduct he died; some who were deemed worthy saw, according to the text, his soul ascending in glory to the heavens.

life|01-15||Άγιος Πανσόφιος ο Μάρτυρας||Saint Pansophius came from Alexandria, in the years of the emperor Decius. He turned away from earthly things in order to find the Lord and lived in the desert for twenty-seven whole years, devoted alone to God in stillness and prayer. // When he raised his mind to the heavens, he was denounced to Augustalius, the governor of Alexandria, who had taken from the emperor the war against the Christians, since so much virtue could not remain hidden. He presented himself before him, refuted the error of the idolaters by their own myths and put the tyrant to shame, and for this they beat him severely. Thus he received the unfading crown of martyrdom.

life|01-16||Αγία Νεονίλλη η Μάρτυς||Saint Neonilla came from Cappadocia and was the grandmother of the three holy brothers Speusippus, Eleusippus, and Meleusippus, who were triplets. When her grandsons were celebrating in their homeland a festival of Nemesian Zeus, they invited her to kiss her, and she, who had been taught the faith in Christ, told them of God's economy for us and mocked the idols. // Her account became for the young men an occasion of faith and salvation, for each one remembered what he had seen in his sleep. They then threw down the idols and openly confessed Christ, and their idolatrous masters threw them into the fire. According to the text, together with her grandsons Neonilla also was perfected in martyrdom and received the crowns.

life|01-16||Άγιοι Πεύσιππος, Ελάσιππος και Μέσιππος οι Μάρτυρες οι αυτάδελφοι||Saints Speusippus, Eleusippus, and Meleusippus came from Cappadocia and were triplet brothers, skilled at riding and taming young and wild horses and at racing with them on the plain. // In their homeland they were celebrating the festival of Nemesian Zeus and invited their grandmother Neonilla to kiss her. She, who knew the faith in Christ, spoke to them of God's economy and mocked the idols, and her account became an occasion of faith and salvation, for each one remembered what he had seen in his sleep. // The three immediately threw down the idols and boldly confessed Christ; their idolatrous masters threw them into the fire, and there they were perfected and received the crowns of martyrdom.

life|01-16||Άγιος Δάναξ ο Αναγνώστης||Saint Danax came from Illyricum, present-day Slavonia, from a place called Aulona, and was a cleric, a reader, of the church there. He took the vessels of the church to protect them from the raid of the unbelievers, but he was caught in a certain place. // They forced him to sacrifice to the idols and, because he was not persuaded, they put him to death with their knives, and thus he received the crown of martyrdom.

life|01-16||Προσκύνησις της Τιμίας αλύσεως του Αγίου και ενδόξου Αποστόλου Πέτρου||On this day is venerated the honorable chain which the chief apostle Peter received for Christ, by order of the tetrarch Herod, as Luke relates in the twelfth chapter of the Acts. From that apostolic body the chain received the sanctifying and wonder-working grace to sanctify those who venerate it with faith and to loose from the bonds of every evil and illness. // When it fell from the apostle at the appearance of the angel, some Christians found it and kept it, one after another in succession. Later the pious emperors brought it to Constantinople and placed it in the church of the Apostle Peter within the Great Church, where its synaxis and feast take place. According to the text, the wise Theodore Ptochoprodromos wrote, by a revelation of Peter, how the chain was transferred from Rome to Constantinople.

life|01-18||Αγία Θεοδούλη η Μάρτυς||Saint Theodula was martyred in the years of Diocletian and Maximian, at Anazarbus in Cilicia, where the governor Pelagius had been sent to punish the Christians. She was arrested as a Christian and confessed before all Christ as true God; they hung her by the hair from a cypress and wounded her breasts with red-hot spits. // When she asked to see the governor's gods, they sent her to the temple of the idol of Hadrian. According to the text, by her prayer and her mere breath the statue fell and was shattered, and when Pelagius, weeping, begged her and promised to believe, the statue by her prayer became whole again. The emperor then ordered that she be tortured and put to death; they drove five nails into her, in her ears, forehead, and breasts, but she prayed and endured the torments. // Helladius the Commentariensis, who had tortured her, became a Christian through her words and was beheaded, and the same happened to Boethus. Theodula was put into a lit furnace and was preserved unharmed, then onto a red-hot grill that scattered and burned many of those present, and finally they threw her into a great furnace, where with many other saints she completed her martyrdom.

life|01-18||Άγιοι Ελλάδιος, Θεόδουλος, Βοήθος, Ευάγριος και Μακάριος οι Μάρτυρες||These saints were martyred at Anazarbus in Cilicia, in the years of Diocletian and Maximian, near the holy martyr Theodula. Helladius the Commentariensis had driven the nails into Theodula, but, seeing her patience and hearing her teaching, he believed in Christ and confessed before the governor Pelagius, who ordered that his head be cut off and his body thrown into the sea. // Boethus, who had taken the saint into his house saying that he would not be persuaded as the Commentariensis was, changed as well and the next day confessed Christ before the governor, and they cut off his head. // Evagrius and Macarius believed in Christ through Saint Theodula and were perfected in the fire, when they were thrown together with the saint and many others into a great furnace.

life|01-19||Αγία Ευφρασία η Μάρτυς||Saint Euphrasia came from Nicomedia and lived in the years of the emperor Maximian, of a renowned family, with a prudent and pious mind. She was denounced as a Christian and, because she would not be persuaded to offer sacrifice to the demons, they beat her harshly. // Because she persisted in the confession of Christ, they handed her over to a barbarian to dishonor her. She deceived him wisely, promising that, if he did not molest her, she would give him a drug that would keep him unharmed from swords and arrows, and told him to test it on her neck. The barbarian, believing her words, struck hard with the sword and cut off her head, and thus she remained undefiled and received the incorruptible crown of martyrdom.

life|01-20||Άγιοι Βάσσος, Ευσέβιος, Ευτύχιος και Βασιλείδης οι Μάρτυρες||The four saints were martyred in the years of the emperor Diocletian and were wealthy men and members of the senate. They believed in Christ and were baptized when they saw Bishop Theopemptus endure with courage the tortures of the unbelievers and work miracles by the power of Christ. // They were denounced to the emperor and, after first having their belts removed, which they wore as a sign of their rank, each one met a different end. Bassus was thrown into a pit up to his thighs and they cut him on the hands and over his whole body. Eusebius was cut in his limbs, Eutychius was divided into three parts, and Basilides burst in the belly, and thus they were perfected.

life|01-20||Άγιος Ευσέβιος ο Μάρτυρας||Saint Eusebius was one of the four martyrs of the time of Diocletian, wealthy and a member of the senate. He believed in Christ and was baptized when he saw Bishop Theopemptus endure the tortures and work miracles. // He was denounced to the emperor together with Bassus, Eutychius, and Basilides and his belt was removed. He was martyred by the cutting of his limbs, remaining steadfast in the Orthodox faith.

life|01-20||Άγιοι Ιννάς, Πιννάς, Ριμμάς οι Μάρτυρες||The three saints came from the same village, in the northern part of their country. They were arrested by idolatrous barbarians and led to the ruler, who, as soon as he heard them confess Christ, condemned them to die of cold. They were bound to upright stakes, fixed in the middle of the river in the midst of winter, when the water was completely frozen. By this torture they gave up their souls to God and received the crowns of martyrdom.

life|01-20||Άγιος Πέτρος ο Τελώνης||According to the text he lived in the years of the emperor Justinian, was a patrician, and governed the whole of Africa. Because he was very harsh and merciless, everyone called him the miser. Once a poor man went to test him and begged persistently for alms. Peter became angry and threw at him like a stone a hot loaf, which his servant had just brought from the oven. In two days he fell gravely ill and saw in a vision that he was being called to give an account. He saw a scale, with the black ones placing his evil deeds on one side and those in white finding nothing good on the other except that loaf. When he recovered and rose, he distributed to the poor all his possessions, even the clothes he was wearing. Because in his dream he saw Christ wearing those clothes, he also sold himself and gave the price to the poor. A goldsmith master bought him. When he realized that he risked being recognized, he said to the doorkeeper, who was deaf and mute: In the name of Christ, hear me and open the door. Then the doorkeeper, according to the text, began to speak and hear, and Peter left. He went to Jerusalem and from there to Constantinople, where he fell asleep in the Lord and was buried.

life|01-21||Άγιος Νεόφυτος ο Μάρτυρας||He came from Nicaea of Bithynia, the son of Christian parents, Theodore and Florentia. From childhood he was full of the grace of God. When he was nine years old and was learning letters with the other children, he prayed, and a dove came to his bed and guarded it. Because the dove spoke with a human voice, his mother was frightened and died, but the saint raised her by his prayer. Later he went to Mount Olympus, entered a cave that the dove showed him, drove out the beast that was there, and remained, nourished, according to the text, by an angel. Guided by a divine revelation, he came down once to greet his parents, distributed their possessions to the poor, and returned to the mountain. At the age of fifteen, led by an angel, he presented himself to the emperor Decius. Because of his great boldness they struck him, put him into a lit oven and, after he remained unharmed by the grace of Christ, gave him to the beasts. He remained unharmed by them also, and finally was put to death by a barbarian who rushed at him with a sword, thus receiving the crown of martyrdom.

life|01-21||Όσιος Ζώσιμος||He came from Sicily, the son of pious parents who had an estate near the monastery of Saint Lucy the virgin. As soon as he was weaned, his parents dedicated him as a gift to Saint Lucy together with the estate, and he grew up in the monastery under the guidance of the abbot. He quickly acquired all the virtues, humility, meekness, obedience, and purity, and was entrusted with the care of the relics of Saint Lucy. According to tradition, once when he went to see his parents, they sent him back, and during the night Saint Lucy appeared to him and threatened him with a beating. Another glorious woman in royal purple, perhaps the Theotokos, defended him, and the saint struck him lightly and commanded him not to leave the monastery again, which he observed. It was also told that a sinful woman of a distinguished family, who went to the monastery at night, was called by Saint Lucy to be thrown out, and her maidservants found her dead. When the abbot died, the brothers went to Bishop John and he, knowing the worth of Zosimus, who had remained to guard the monastery, appointed him abbot and soon ordained him priest. He shepherded the flock for forty years with meekness, love, and sympathy. When the bishop of Syracuse died, he became bishop of Sicily, ordained by Pope Theodore of Rome, and governed for thirteen years in holiness. He worked many miracles and many sick were healed before and after his burial, the possessed were freed and the blind saw. Someone took a piece of his garment and, giving it to his wife who was hemorrhaging, healed her immediately.

life|01-21||Άγιοι Ευγένιος, Ουαλεριανός, Κάνδιδος και Ακύλας οι Μάρτυρες||They were martyred in the years of Diocletian and Maximian, under the duke Lysias, in Trebizond. They were hiding in the mountains of Trebizond, where the three were arrested as Christians by Lysias and, after confessing Christ, were exiled to a cramped fortress in the land of the Lazi, Pityus. Then they were brought to Trebizond, where they were struck with ox-hide whips, hung up, torn with iron claws, and burned with lit torches. Because the executioners fell prostrate on the ground, Lysias was troubled and imprisoned them. A few days later Eugenius was also arrested, confessed Christ, and was beaten mercilessly. In the temple of the idols he prayed and, according to the text, all the idols fell and became dust. They stretched him with ropes and struck him with rods, hung him up and tore his sides, burned him with torches and rubbed his wounds with salt and sharp vinegar. Then they put all four saints into a lit furnace, from which they came out unharmed, and for this they were beheaded and received the crowns of martyrdom.

life|01-22||Άγιοι Μανουήλ, Γεώργιος, Πέτρος, Λέων, Σιώνιος, Γαβριήλ, Ιωάννης, Λέων, Πάροδος και άλλοι τριακόσιοι εβδομήντα επτά Μάρτυρες||All these saints came from various provinces and lived in Adrianople. The Bulgarians came to fight the Romans, took captive the Christians of Thrace and Macedonia and, after they captured Adrianople, according to the text around 815, under the emperor Leo the Armenian, their ruler Krum brought out forty thousand Christians and the bishop of the city. Later the brutal ruler Ditzengos tore in the middle the archbishop Manuel, cut off his arms and shoulders and threw them to the beasts. He was succeeded by Mortagon, who put to death those Christians who would not agree to deny Christ, with tortures and inhuman punishments. Bishop George of Develtus and Bishop Peter he beat with rods and beheaded, and with the sword he put to death three hundred and seventy-seven others. He beheaded the generals of the Christians, Leo and John, tore open with a sword the belly of Bishop Leo of Nicaea, beheaded Gabriel and Sionius, and condemned the priest Parodos to stoning. And other successors of the Bulgarians put many Christians to death with various torments.

life|01-23||Όσιος Μαϋσιμάς ο Σύρος||He lived in the region of Cyrrhus, near Antioch, and spoke Syriac. He grew up in a rustic and peasant way of life, but was distinguished for his virtues. He had only one garment and, when it grew old, he did not throw it away, but sewed other patches onto the torn parts to cover his body. He cared for and hosted strangers and the poor with such readiness that he opened the doors of his cell to everyone. According to the text he had two jars, one full of wheat and the other of oil, and from them he gave to all who were in need, without them ever being emptied, as God did with the jar of the widow of Zarephath. After living well and in holiness, he fell asleep in the Lord. Theodoret of Cyrrhus wrote his life and records that the venerable one had received from God the gift of miracles.

life|01-23||Όσιος Σαλαμάνης ο Ησυχαστής||He came from the village of Capersana, on the western bank of the Euphrates. He loved the hesychastic life of the monks and, finding on the opposite bank of the river a small cell, shut himself in it without leaving either door or window. Once a year he dug beneath the ground, came out, and gathered the necessary food for the whole year. When the bishop of the region learned of his virtue, he went to give him the priesthood, dug through part of the cell, entered, put his hand on the head of the venerable one and read the prayer of ordination. He spoke much to the venerable one, but heard from him not a word, and left after commanding that they rebuild the part he had torn down. At another time the Christians of the neighboring village crossed the Euphrates by night, tore down his cell and carried him on their shoulders to their village, without his resisting or giving them any order. They had another cell ready for him, where they shut him in again, and the venerable one kept stillness in the same way, speaking to no one. A few days later the Christians of another village, on the opposite bank, came and took him in the same manner to their own village, and he neither objected nor was eager to follow them. Thus he put himself completely to death, saying with the apostle Paul that it is no longer he who lives, but Christ who lives in him, and he fell asleep in the Lord.

life|01-24||Άγιοι Παύλος, Παυσίριος και Θεοδοτίων οι Αυτάδελφοι Μάρτυρες||They lived in the years of Diocletian and Maximian, when the governor in Cleopatris in Egypt, present-day Suez, was Arrian. They were three brothers. Paul and Pausirius became monks from a young age, while Theodotion lived in the mountains with the robbers. Paul, thirty-seven years old, and Pausirius, twenty-five, were arrested by the governor and boldly confessed the faith of Christ. Theodotion, when he learned of it, left the mountains and the robbers and went to see them and bid them farewell. Seeing them on trial, he did not dare to approach, but pondered what glory his brothers would inherit. His heart was warmed by divine grace, he turned back, presented himself to the governor, confessed also that he was a Christian and, leaping upon the governor, threw him down from his throne. Immediately they pierced his sides and belly with red-hot nails and then beheaded him. Paul and Pausirius were thrown into a river, and thus their martyrdom was completed.

life|01-24||Όσιος Μακεδόνιος||This venerable one had as his place of asceticism and dwelling the peaks of the mountains, living in stillness now here and now there, in Phoenicia, Syria, and Cilicia, to avoid those who ran to him. He spent forty-five years without any roof or hut, standing in a deep pit. When he grew old, he yielded to entreaties and made a hut, and afterwards he stayed in cells that were not his own. He lived another twenty-five years, so that all the years of his life reached seventy. For forty years he fed only on barley and water, and later, when he fell ill, he lived on a little bread and plain water. The Lord granted him to work miracles, to cast out demons, and to heal illnesses. They brought to him a woman who, by the working of the devil, ate excessively, thirty hens a day, and was still hungry. Her relatives begged him and the venerable one prayed, put his right hand in water, sealed it with the sign of the cross and commanded the sick woman to drink it, and thus she began to eat normally and half a hen sufficed for her. After serving God genuinely for seventy years, he died.

life|01-25||Όσιος Πούπλιος||He came from the senatorial order and his homeland was Zeugma, a city on the Euphrates. He went up a high mountain, thirty stadia away from the city, and built there a small cell. Whatever possessions he inherited from his parents he distributed to the poor, and from then on he lived with much asceticism and virtue. Because his fame spread everywhere, many brothers ran to him and built cells, in which they lived in stillness. The venerable one often visited the brothers and checked whether anything superfluous was to be found in someone's cell. He weighed even the bread they ate on a scale, and whoever he found had more than the appointed measure he called a glutton and lover of flesh. Whoever he saw removing the bran from the flour he called luxurious, like the Sybarites. He went also by night to the door of each one: if he found him awake and praying, he left in silence, but if he perceived that he was sleeping, he knocked with his hand on the door of the cell and with his tongue rebuked the sleeper. Thus many brothers, like sponges, absorbed all his virtues. Among them were Theoteknos and Aphthonius, who after the death of the venerable one took over the care and abbacy of the brothers. After struggling so well, he gave up his soul into the hands of God.

life|01-25||Όσιος Μάρης||He was still young and living in the world, handsome and with a beautiful voice, and he adorned the feasts of Christ and of the saints with his sweet songs. He always loved God and eagerly kept his commandments, keeping his body pure and his soul spotless, although he was among the snares of pleasures and mingled with worldly people. When he wished to renounce the world, he went to a village called Homerou, built there a small cell and shut himself in it for thirty-seven years. The cell received much moisture from the neighboring mountain and harmed his health, but the venerable one would not change it and remained in it until the end of his life. He loved simplicity, detested cunning, and preferred poverty to wealth. He wore clothes of goat hair and was content with a very little bread, salt, and water. Because he had stayed in the desert for many years and had not seen the divine liturgy, he asked that a liturgy be held in his cell. Present was Theodoret of Cyrrhus, who also wrote his life, who received the request with joy and sent to the neighboring village to bring the holy vessels. Using the hands of the deacons instead of a holy Table, he offered on them the bloodless sacrifice before the venerable one. He was filled with such joy that he thought he saw heaven itself, and said that he had never before enjoyed such spiritual gladness. After spending his life thus, he ascended to the heavens.

life|01-25||Όσιος Καστίνος||He came from old Rome, was at first a pagan, a ruler of the imperial Senate and very wealthy. For many years, according to the text, the demon schooled him, so that he would turn away from Hellenic error, and Castinus tried every means to be healed of the demon, without success. He learned in Rome that Bishop Cyrillian of Argyropolis worked miracles in the regions near Constantinople, left at once, met the saint and, falling at his feet, was healed and immediately baptized. He sent to Rome and distributed to the poor all his possessions, while he himself remained with Cyrillian serving him like a humble servant. Cyrillian, who had the gift of foresight, taught him the whole state of the Church and before he died ordained him bishop of Argyropolis and Byzantium, commanding him to transfer the church of Argyropolis to the opposite land of Byzantium, which God had revealed to him long before. After Cyrillian's death Castinus built in the northern part of Byzantium a church in the name of Saint Euphemia, who had recently been martyred in Chalcedon, and transferred to it the see of Argyropolis. Thus Castinus is the eighteenth bishop of Argyropolis and the first, after the apostle Stachys, bishop of Byzantium. He shepherded the flock of Christ apostolically for seven years, ordained in Byzantium as his successor the most reverent Titus, and died in the Lord.

life|01-26||Όσιος Συμεών ο Παλαιός||Venerable Symeon, who was named the Elder, loved the desert life from childhood and dwelt in a cave on Mount Amanus. According to the text, he did not eat human food, not even bread, but only edible herbs. When he wished to go to Mount Sinai, he entered the cave where Moses hid, fell prostrate and remained fasting for seven days with tears and prayers, until he heard a divine voice commanding him to rise and eat the three apples that lay before him. Returning from there he built two monasteries and ended his life after working many extraordinary miracles. // According to the tradition preserved by Theodoret, when some lost Jews asked for a guide, two lions escorted them at the command of the venerable one to the place where they had lost their way, while to a farmer who had stolen sheaves and whose threshing floor was burned by lightning, the venerable one said that the fire would be put out if he returned what was stolen, and indeed it went out without water.

life|01-26||Άγιοι Ανανίας, Πέτρος και οι επτά στρατιώτες μάρτυρες||These saints lived in the time of the emperor Diocletian and of Maximus, the governor of Phoenicia, around 295. Ananias was arrested, confessed Christ and mocked the idols, and for this they struck him with rods, burned his sides with red-hot spits, and sprinkled his wounds with vinegar and salt. By his prayer, according to the text, the temple was shaken and the idols fell down, while in prison he was fed by God. By this miracle he brought to the faith the jailer Peter and seven soldiers. // By order of the governor Ananias, Peter, and the seven soldiers were thrown into the sea, and thus they received the crowns of martyrdom.

life|01-26||Όσιος Αμμωνάς||Venerable Ammonas was so gentle and good that, according to the text, not even the wild beasts resisted him. When a lion came and held the branch of a palm tree, the elder made a sign to it and it moved aside from the place. Then, when he commanded it, it brought the palm branches and, at a new command, went far away and slept like a rational man. Thus, according to the text, virtue makes even wild beasts submit. // The synaxarion preserves other traditions about Ammonas: that he was the bishop of whom the Great Anthony prophesied that he would advance in the fear of God and that he showed great forbearance, and that he was the ascetic whose life is found in the Lausaic History, who for fourteen years asked God night and day to soothe his anger. The compiler of the synaxarion does not decide with certainty which of these he is.

life|01-28||Όσιος Παλλάδιος||Venerable Palladius built a small cell on a mountain near the village of Immae, as Theodoret writes, from whom the synaxarion derives. Shut in there, with vigil, fasting, and unceasing prayer, he was deemed worthy by God of the gift of miracles. A certain defiled man killed a merchant who had much money and threw the corpse at the door of the venerable one's cell. When the crime came to light, the inhabitants accused him of being the murderer and broke down the door, but the venerable one prayed and raised the dead man, who revealed the real murderer, and thus the venerable one was shown to be innocent. // He worked many other miracles, but was admired more for his virtues. After leaving memorable works in the Church, he died peacefully. According to a footnote, he perhaps became bishop of Helenopolis, although Theodoret does not write this.

life|01-28||Όσιος Ιάκωβος ο Ασκητής||Venerable James left the things of the world and lived fifteen years in a cave near the town of Poruriona, with every kind of asceticism. A prostitute, urged on by licentious men, came and tried to lead him astray, but the venerable one frightened her with eternal hell and made her repent and turn to Christ. According to the text, God permitted him also to fall into great sins, so that those who seem to stand might take heed and the fallen might not despair. // A ruler with a possessed daughter brought her to the venerable one, who prayed and healed her, and the father left her in the cave with her young brother. Overcome by desire, the venerable one corrupted the girl and, fearing that it would be revealed, killed both children and threw the bodies into the river. In despair he prepared to return to the world, but he met a devout monk, heard his counsel and shut himself in a tomb, where he lived with great hardship. // When a drought came, God commanded the bishop of the city that the lack of rain would be lifted only if James prayed. The bishop and the people begged him, he prayed, and much rain came. Encouraged about his salvation, he added hardship and tears and gave up his soul to God.

life|01-29||Άγιοι Επτά Μάρτυρες οι εν Σαμοσάτοις τελειωθέντες||The seven holy martyrs, Philotheus, Hyperechius, Abibus, Julian, Romanus, James, and Paregorius, were soldiers of Christ and were martyred at Samosata. According to the text they rebuked the error of the idolaters and for this they were arrested, struck with thick rods on the hands and thighs, torn, and thrown into prison with heavy chains. Later they were brought out, torn again, hung up, and had nails driven into their heads. // According to the account they were put in the stadium before wild beasts. The saints prayed to complete their struggle there, and God received their souls, as they asked. The beasts respected the relics and did not touch them.

life|01-29||Άγιοι Σιλουανός, Λουκάς και Μώκιος οι Μάρτυρες||At the time when Numerian reigned, around 284, a persecution broke out against the Christians. Silvanus, bishop of Emesa in Coele-Syria and subject to the patriarch of Antioch, was denounced to the ruler and arrested together with the deacon Luke and the reader Mocius. After they confessed Christ as true God and anathematized those who worship the idols, the ruler became very angry. The text at this point is damaged and does not give the kind of martyrdom. // Their bodies were stolen by night by Christians, who buried them with honor and glorified God.

life|01-29||Άγιοι Σάρβηλος και Βεβαία οι Μάρτυρες οι εν Εδέσση||The holy brother and sister Sarbelus and Bebaia came from Edessa and lived in the time of Trajan, around 110. Sarbelus was a priest of the idols, handsome and glorious, with luxurious garments and a golden miter, and they honored him like a little king. Bishop Barsimaeus of Edessa often rebuked him, until once, at a feast of the idols, he was struck with compunction and believed in Christ. Both were baptized by the bishop, he himself and his sister Bebaia; Sarbelus sold his possessions, distributed them to the poor, and stayed near Barsimaeus. // The governor Lysias summoned him and, because he confessed Christ and denounced the idols, they beat him with rods and ox sinews, tore him with iron claws, burned him with torches and drove nails into his head. They put him in a mechanical device and sawed him, but according to the text he remained unharmed by the grace of Christ and all were astonished. // Bebaia, hearing this, went by herself to the governor and declared herself a Christian; they beat her with clubs and shut her in prison. Sarbelus they tortured again with wooden swords, tore his face, hung him up and burned his body, and finally flayed him. Seeing that he was still breathing, the governor commanded that the heads of both siblings be cut off, and thus they received the crowns of martyrdom. Christians secretly took the relics and buried them with honor.

life|01-29||Άγιος Βαρσιμαίος ο Ιερομάρτυρας Επίσκοπος Εδέσσης||Saint Barsimaeus was bishop of Edessa and, as the text says, became the cause of the salvation of Saint Sarbelus, whom he persuaded to believe and baptized together with his sister Bebaia. For this he was denounced to the governor of Edessa, Lysias, confessed Christ, was beaten and imprisoned. // Later royal letters came ordering the persecution to stop, and the saint was freed from prison. He returned to his metropolis and lived there pleasingly to God, and thus he died and went to the Lord.

life|01-30||Άγιος Ιππόλυτος ο Ιερομάρτυρας και οι συν αυτώ Μάρτυρες||Saints Censorinus, Sabinus, and Chryse lived under the emperor Claudius, around 269, when the vicar was Ulpian Romulus. Censorinus was first in the Senate and a magister. He was denounced as a Christian and confessed Christ boldly, was imprisoned, and because many miracles occurred, even the raising of a dead man, all the soldiers who were present believed. All twenty were beheaded. // Chryse was hung up and torn with ox-hide whips, beaten and burned with torches, had her jaws broken with stones and her back with lead balls, and finally they hung a stone from her neck and threw her into the sea. Sabinus was beaten with heavy balls at the neck, hung up and burned with torches, and giving thanks to the Lord he gave up his soul. // Hippolytus, pope of Rome, when he learned of the martyrdoms, was moved by divine zeal, went and rebuked the governor. He became angry and struck him in the face, and Hippolytus together with the presbyters and deacons who followed him passed through many tortures. Finally they bound their hands and feet and threw them into the depths of the sea, and thus they received the crowns of martyrdom.

life|01-30||Άγιος Θεόφιλος ο Νέος||Saint Theophilus lived in the years of Constantine and Irene, around 785, was born and raised in Constantinople, and was appointed strategos in the theme of the Cibyrrhaeots. He went out with the fleet of the Romans against the Saracens, together with two other strategoi who envied him. Rushing first into the fleet of the Saracens, he defeated them with skill and courage, but the two strategoi abandoned him and fled. The Saracens, who were more numerous, surrounded him and captured him alive. // They put him in prison, where he stayed four years. Then they brought him out and, while they were making sacrifices, they tried to persuade him to sacrifice and deny Christ, sometimes with flattery and sometimes with threats. Because the saint did not yield, he was beheaded and received the crown of martyrdom.

life|01-31||Άγιοι Ουϊκτωρίνος, Ουΐκτωρ, Νικηφόρος, Κλαύδιος, Διόδωρος, Σαραπίνος και Παπίας οι Μάρτυρες εν Κορίνθω||These saints came from Corinth and lived in the years of the emperor Decius, around 251. They were arrested for their confession and faith in Christ and were led to the proconsul Tertius, and after being punished with many tortures, each ended in a different way. // Victorinus, Victor, and Nicephorus were thrown together into a great mortar and crushed. Claudius died after they cut off his hands and feet. Diodorus was thrown into a furnace of fire, Serapion was beheaded with a sword, and Papias was thrown into the depths of the sea. Thus all received from the Lord the crowns of martyrdom.

life|01-31||Αγία Τρύφαινα η Μάρτυς||Saint Tryphaena came from Cyzicus on the Hellespont and was the daughter of the senator Anastasius and the Christian Socratia. She was not arrested by others, but went herself to the idolaters, mocked their idols, denounced the shameful acts by which they thought they honored their false gods, and taught them to leave vanity and turn to the faith of Christ. // By order of the governor Caesarius they threw her into a lit furnace, but she remained unharmed by the grace of Christ. They hung her up high and, when they let her go, she fell upon nails that they had fixed below. They gave her to the beasts, and most did not touch her, but a wild bull rushed and tore her with its horns, and thus she received the unfading crown of martyrdom. // According to tradition, at the spot where her blood was shed a spring of clear water appeared; women who have no milk after childbirth drink from it and acquire milk, and female animals do the same.

life|02-02||Άγιος Αγαθόδωρος ο Μάρτυρας||Agathodorus confessed that Christ is the true God and for this he was led to the ruler of Tyana in Cappadocia, a city that the Turks call Nidra or Nigde. According to the text they tore him, put him on a red-hot grill, cut out his tongue and pulled out his teeth with forceps, flayed his skin with a razor, crushed his legs and pierced his sides with a javelin. At the end they drove red-hot spits into his temples, and in the midst of these many tortures he expired and received from the Lord the unfading crown of martyrdom.
life|02-02||Άγιος Ιορδάνης ο Νεομάρτυρας||Jordan came from Trebizond. He was martyred in Constantinople in the year 1650, ending his life by the sword, as an athlete of Christ in the last times.

life|02-03||Άγιοι Αδριανός και Εύβουλος οι Μάρτυρες||Adrian and Eubulus came from Paneas and, because they longed for the confessors and martyrs of Christ, went to Caesarea of Palestine, where many were being martyred. There it was revealed that they were Christians, they were led to the ruler Firmilian and boldly confessed Christ. They were beaten on the back and sides and subjected to greater tortures, but remained steadfast. Then the ruler became angry and gave them to the beasts. Adrian contended with a lion and, because the grace of God kept him unharmed, he was beheaded. The same lion was let loose on Eubulus, who after flattery and urgings to deny Christ scorned them; he too remained unharmed and was beheaded, and thus the two received the crowns of martyrdom.

life|02-03||Άγιος Βλάσιος ο βουκόλος||Blasius came from Caesarea of Cappadocia and was the son of very rich parents; their wealth was their many animals, and from these he gave abundant alms to the poor. When a persecution by the idolaters broke out, they sought him and he, learning of it, gave himself up with joy, as if invited to a royal banquet, and hosted his persecutors. Before the governor he revealed his name, his faith, and his trade; they bound him stretched out and beat him with raw sinews, but God eased the pain and healed his wounds, and the governor called it sorcery. They put him in a cauldron of boiling water for five days, where angels encouraged him and dissolved the fire; when the soldiers found him alive, chanting with the angels, they too confessed Christ. The governor went himself, thought that the water had cooled and asked to wash with it, but was blinded and expired. Blasius baptized with that water the soldiers who had believed, went to the fold of his animals, gave instructions to his mother and relatives for their salvation and gave up his soul to God. Those present saw his soul go out like a white and shining dove; his body was buried there and his staff sprouted beside the altar and became a great tree that shaded it.

life|02-04||Άγιος Αβράμιος ο Ιερομάρτυρας Επίσκοπος Αρβήλ Περσίδος||Abramius was bishop of the city of Arbela in Persia. In the fifth year of the persecution of the Christians in Persia he was arrested by the king's chief magus, who pressed him to deny Christ and worship the sun. He answered that he could not leave the creator of the sun and of all things in order to worship a creature, and the chief magus ordered that he be stripped, thrown down, and beaten with wild rods. The saint bravely endured the torture and prayed for his torturers, saying that the sin should not be counted against them, for they know not what they do. Then the chief magus commanded that his head be cut off, and Abramius was perfected in a village called Thelman, receiving from the Lord the crown of martyrdom.
life|02-04||Άγιος Ιωσήφ ο Νεομάρτυρας του Χαλεπλή||Joseph was martyred in the year 1686 and ended his life by the sword, receiving from God an incorruptible crown.

life|02-05||Όσιος Θεοδόσιος ο εξ Αντιοχείας||Theodosius was an ascetic, different from the Cenobiarch, and came from Antioch, the son of well-known parents. Once he listened attentively to the voice of the Lord, left home, wealth, noble status, and all the pleasant things of the world and withdrew to wooded places near the sea, where he built a very small cell. He wore haircloth and underneath heavy irons on his neck, waist, and hands, occupied himself with prayer and manual work, made baskets and cultivated a few fields for the food of himself and of the strangers who visited him; his hair reached down to his feet. His fame brought many to imitate him and made the desert almost a heavenly city. When Hagarenes came to the region, they did no harm out of respect for him, but because of these raids the venerable one left the desert and went to his homeland Antioch, where he built a small hut with other brothers and taught that we must give place to wrath, as the Lord withdrew from Herod, without throwing ourselves into temptations. Living a short time longer in his homeland, he fell asleep in the Lord.

life|02-06||Άγιος Ιουλιανός ο Μάρτυρας ο εν Εμέση||Julian came from Emesa in Coele-Syria, was pious, young in age and a physician of souls and bodies. When under the emperor Numerian, in 284, the bishop of Emesa Silvanus, the deacon Luke, and the reader Mocius were arrested by the idolaters and condemned to be devoured by beasts, the young Julian was pained in heart, ran to catch up with them and kissed them. For this he too was arrested, after the others had been put to death, and they nailed his head, hands, and feet. Thus nailed he lay down in a cave and there gave up his soul to God.

life|02-06||Άγιοι Φαύστα, Ευϊλάσιος και Μάξιμος οι Μάρτυρες||Fausta lived under the emperor Maximian, in 299, came from Cyzicus and was the daughter of pious and wealthy parents, after whose death she remained the mistress of a great fortune. Neither youth nor wealth drew her away from virtue; she devoted herself to virginity, fasting, prayer, and the study of the Scriptures. Her fame reached the emperor, who sent the senator Evilasius to persuade her to sacrifice to the gods or, if she would not be persuaded, to drown her in the sea. Evilasius tortured her with every kind of torment, but she remained unharmed by the grace of God and worked various miracles, and for this Evilasius believed in Christ. Then another ruler was sent, Maximus, who bitterly tortured both Fausta and Evilasius, but seeing the miracles of her prayer he too believed, and by order of the emperor he was put into the frying pan that had been prepared for the two saints. Thus all three together received the end of martyrdom.

life|02-07||Άγιοι Χίλιοι Μάρτυρες τρείς Οικέτες, τέσσερις Προτίκτορες οι εν Νικομήδεια Μαρτυρήσαντες||These martyrs were servants of the four protectors who had arrested the hieromartyr Peter of Alexandria, who was beheaded by imperial order. After Peter's end, the four protectors believed in Christ with all their household and were martyred. Then their servants too, kindled with zeal of faith, went of their own accord to Diocletian, who was in Nicomedia, together with women and children, even infants, one thousand and three in all. They confessed that they were Christians and, because they would not be persuaded to deny Christ, they were cut down with swords by the imperial army and received the crowns of martyrdom.

life|02-08||Άγιοι Μάρθα, Μαρία και Λυκαρίων ο Οσιομάρτυρας||Martha and Mary were sisters according to the flesh, lived privately and practiced virginity. When the governor passed by their house, they leaned on the window and said that they are Christians; he grieved for the death that they would receive so young, but they answered that death for Christ is not death but life that has no end. The same was confessed by the venerable martyr Lycarion, a monk who was a boy and had been raised with them. By order of the governor all three were nailed to three crosses and finally beheaded with a sword, giving up their souls to God and receiving the crowns of martyrdom.

life|02-09||Άγιοι Μάρκελλος και Παγκράτιος ο Ιερομάρτυρας||Marcellus and Pancratius were disciples of the apostle Peter, father and son according to the flesh. Marcellus, when the Lord was still living bodily on earth and working miracles, heard of him and of his miracles, took his son Pancratius and went with him from Antioch to Jerusalem to see the Lord. Thus Pancratius became acquainted with the apostle Peter and, after the Ascension, followed him; he was ordained by him bishop of Tauromenium, a city of Sicily with an episcopal throne and a harbor, known as Taormina. He preached the name of Christ and for this was killed secretly by enemies of the faith. His father Marcellus was ordained bishop of Sicily, brought to the Lord many of the idolaters, and was perfected in peace.

life|02-09||Άγιος Φιλάγριος Επίσκοπος Κύπρου||Philagrius was also a disciple of the apostle Peter. When he became bishop of Cyprus, he taught and preached the name of the Lord, and after enduring many temptations for the true faith, he fell asleep in the Lord.

life|02-09||Όσιος Ρωμανός του Κίλικος||Romanus came from the city of Rhosus in Cilicia and carried out the struggles of virtue near Antioch. He built a small cell outside the walls of the city, at the foot of the mountain, and practiced asceticism there without lighting a fire and without the light of a lamp. His food was bread and salt, his drink the water of the spring; he wore a rough haircloth garment, his hair reached down to his feet and underneath he bore heavy irons on his neck, hands, and waist. For these struggles he received much grace from God: by his prayers he healed many from grave illnesses and granted children to many barren women. He shone with such miracles and fell asleep in peace.

life|02-10||Άγιοι Βάπτος και Πορφύριος οι Μάρτυρες και οι τρείς πιστεύσαντες γυναίκες||Porphyrius and Baptus were executioners of the hieromartyr Charalampus. When they saw the miracle with the governor, whom the saint healed after his hands had been cut off, they renounced the idols and believed in Christ. The same was done by three women who stood there and watched. The governor arrested them all, tortured them with various instruments, and beheaded them without mercy, for although he was healed in body by the saint, he remained incurable in soul.

life|02-10||Άγιοι Ενναθά, Ουαλεντίνα και Παύλος οι Παρθενομάρτυρες||Ennatha came from Gaza in Judea and was also called Constantia, and Valentina from Caesarea. When the governor Firmilian sat in the court, Ennatha appeared before him, was asked whether she denied Christ and, not being persuaded, was hung on a wooden beam and her sides were torn many times. Valentina, who could not bear to see the governor's inhumanity, also spoke boldly; she was ordered to sacrifice at an altar that was ready nearby, but she kicked it and overturned it together with its fire. The tyrant became angry and inflicted countless torments on her sides, and finally, in despair over both, he put them to death with fire. Paul followed, who was tried with various torments and remained unharmed by the grace of Christ; he was condemned to death by the sword, thanked God, prayed for those of the same faith, and was beheaded.

life|02-10||Όσιος Ζήνων ο Ταχυδρόμος||Zeno came from Caesarea of Cappadocia, the son of rich and distinguished parents, and was a courier of the emperor Valens, in 365. After the death of Valens he immediately left the military belt, found a great mountain of Antioch with many caves and settled there, cleansing his soul with the labors of asceticism. He had no lamp, chest, table, book, or mattress; his bed was a mat on stones, he wore an old cassock and fed on one loaf that a friend of his brought him every two days, while he carried the water from far away. By the labors of asceticism he received much grace from God. Although the raids of the Isaurians harmed and slaughtered many ascetics there, they could not harm him; on the contrary, they were blinded by his prayer and did not see the entrance of his cell. He did not live long after this, but from the labors of ascetic struggle below he passed to the enjoyment of rest in heaven.

life|02-12||Όσιος Αντώνιος Αρχιεπίσκοπος Κωνσταντινουπόλεως||Anthony came on his father's side from the East and on his mother's side from Europe (Rumelia), while his third homeland was Constantinople, which raised him and taught him the sacred letters. As a very small child he imitated the priests in celebrating the divine liturgy, offered bread and held a censer, prefiguring the holiness he would acquire. When he grew up he became a monk and with courage practiced practical virtue; he was ordained presbyter against his will and became abbot of the Stoudite monastery. He loved vigil, fasting, and tireless prayer, while his father too became a monk, and he gave alms "with both his hands." When the time came, by vote of the holy Synod and of the emperor he was ordained patriarch of Constantinople. Although an old man, he ran to all the churches of the city with litanies, helped the churches that had been worn down by time, gave abundantly to needy clergy and readers, and relieved the many thousands of the poor with grain and alms. He worked many great miracles and died in deep old age; his synaxis is held in his monastery.

life|02-12||Άγιος Χρήστος ο Νεομάρτυρας ο Κηπουρός||Christos was a gardener by profession. He was martyred in the year 1748 and ended his life by the sword, honored by Christ for his love for the Lord.

life|02-14||Όσιος Αβραάμης||According to the text he lived in the time of Theodosius the Great and came from the city of Cyrrhus, where he was born and raised. He exhausted his body with vigils, all-night standing, and fasting, so that for many years he remained motionless. He went to a village near Mount Lebanon, full of idolaters, who buried him in the soil and drove him away; but when tax collectors arrived and were beating the inhabitants, he took pity and paid their taxes. The inhabitants marveled at his philanthropy, became Christians, built a church, and made him a priest; he stayed three years, established them in the faith, and returned to his cell. // Later he became bishop of Carrhae in Palestine, a city full of idols, and by labors and teaching led the inhabitants to piety. Throughout his time as bishop he ate only raw herbs and drank a little water. The emperor Theodosius summoned him to Constantinople, where he lived a short while and died; his body was sent with great honor to Carrhae.

life|02-14||Άγιος Γεώργιος ο Νεομάρτυρας εκ Μυτιλήνης||According to the text he was a tailor from Mytilene and was martyred for piety in Constantinople, around 1695. The text, damaged at this point, calls him a new martyr.

life|02-15||Όσιος Ευσέβιος||Tradition does not say where he came from nor who his parents were. He became a monk in a monastery and then went up to a mountain ridge, in a village called Asina, where he built a small enclosure of dry stone, without roof or covering. He ate soaked chickpeas and broad beans, sometimes also dried figs. He remained faithful to asceticism into old age, losing most of his teeth without changing his way of life; exposed to the weather, his face wrinkled and his limbs dried up. // Because many went to see him and disturbed his stillness, he went to a hermitage nearby and made an enclosure in the corner of the wall, where he continued his struggles. It is said that in all the weeks of Great Lent he ate only fifteen dried figs, even when ill. He lived more than ninety years and died in peace.

life|02-15||Άγιος Μαΐωρ ο Μάρτυρας||He lived in the time of Diocletian and Maximian and was a soldier in the unit of the Mauri. When he was in Gaza, he was denounced as a Christian; he appeared in court, confessed Christ, and was beaten without ceasing, with such violence that thirty soldiers took turns beating him. The blood ran like a river from his body and reddened the whole ground. He bravely endured the martyrdom and gave up his soul to God, receiving the crown of martyrdom.

life|02-16||Όσιος Μαρουθάς ο Επίσκοπος και οι Άγιοι Μάρτυρες εν Περσία||Maruthas became a bishop and was sent by Theodosius the Great, around 380, to the king of the Persians. In Persia they honored him greatly for his virtue and holiness, especially because he freed the king's daughter from a demon. Having thus boldness, he asked for and received the relics of the holy martyrs who had been martyred in Persia, built a city in their name (Martyropolis) and kept them there. Later he fell asleep on exactly the same day on which he had consecrated the city, which is why his memory is celebrated together with the memory of the martyrs.

life|02-16||Όσιος Φλαβιανός||He went up to the peak of a mountain, built a small cell and shut himself in it, where he stayed sixty years without speaking to anyone and without anyone seeing him, keeping his mind in his heart. He had dug out a place, where he spread out his hands and received food from God; so that it would not be seen by those who came, he had dug it obliquely and in a circular shape. His food was soaked legumes, which he ate once a week. // God enriched him with the gift of miracles: according to the text, by his prayer he killed a huge dragon and an asp, drove a multitude of locusts from a field, freed a youth from a demon, healed the breast of a woman suffering from cancer, and raised one who had been struck by a bull and had died. After ending his life thus, he died in peace.

life|02-16||Άγιος Ρωμανός ο Οσιομάρτυρας||According to the text, which is damaged at this point, Romanus was martyred in Constantinople in 1694 and was perfected by the sword. The epigram of the day says that he ran to the tortures as if running to a wedding.

life|02-17||Αγία Μαριάμνη η Ισαπόστολος αδελφή του Αγίου Φιλίππου του Αποστόλου||After the Ascension of the Lord, the apostle Philip went together with the apostle Bartholomew and his sister Mariamne to Hierapolis of Phrygia. Because he preached the Gospel, the idolaters hung him up; when he was about to die, he prayed and, according to the text, the earth swallowed the proconsul, the ruler, and the people. Bartholomew and Mariamne, who were also hanging, begged Philip not to let them be swallowed as well; he not only did not swallow them, but brought out of the earth also those who had been swallowed, except for the proconsul and his wife Ennione. // Then Bartholomew and Mariamne left Hierapolis. Bartholomew went to India and was perfected crucified; Mariamne went to Lycaonia, preached the word of God, baptized many and died in peace.

life|02-17||Άγιος Αυξίβιος Επίσκοπος Σόλων Κύπρου||He came from old Rome and was a Greek in religion. He followed the apostle and evangelist Mark, from whom he was taught the word of truth and was baptized. He was ordained bishop of Soli in Cyprus, brought many unbelievers to Christ and worked various miracles; then he died in peace.

life|02-18||Όσιος Αγαπητός ο Ομολογητής και Θαυματουργός Επίσκοπος Σινάου||He lived in the time of Diocletian and came from Cappadocia, the son of Christian parents. As a youth he went to a monastery with up to a thousand monks and became a proven worker of the commandments of the Lord, with fasting and vigil; according to the text, for eighty whole days he ate only lupin peelings and ashes instead of bread. By his prayer he killed a dragon and healed a girl who was wasting away from illness. King Licinius, learning that he was brave, took him by force as a soldier; but he continued his asceticism there too and healed people and animals by his mere presence. When he saw the martyrs Victorinus, Dorotheus, Theodulus, and Agrippas being tortured, he wished to become a partaker in their martyrdom; after their beheading they struck him with a javelin, but he remained unharmed. // Under Constantine the Great a servant of the emperor was possessed by a demon and cried out the name of Agapetus; the emperor brought him to the palace and the demon was driven out by his prayer. The venerable one asked only to be released from military service and returned to his stillness. The bishop of the city of Synaus ordained him priest against his will and, when he died, they made him bishop by vote of the people and the priests. // As bishop he worked greater miracles and received the gift of prophecy: he told a woman everything she had done since childhood, rebuked a deacon from Heraclea in Thrace who had corrupted a virgin, and by his prayer turned elsewhere the river that was destroying the fields of Bishop Damian of Silandus. According to the text he worked more than a hundred miracles and healed incurable illnesses by the touch of his hand, his shadow, or his word. He died full of days.

life|02-19||Άγιοι Μάξιμος, Θεόδοτος, Ησύχιος και Ασκληπιοδότη οι Μάρτυρες||The saints presented themselves to the governor and, because they would not agree to deny Christ, they underwent many tortures. First they hung them on a wooden beam and tore them with iron claws, then they transported them and dragged them from city to city and threw them to the beasts to be eaten, but by divine grace they remained unharmed. Asclepiodote they threw down, stretched on a wooden beam, and then bound to a bull. In the end all together were stoned, dragged to rough wooded places and beheaded, receiving the crowns of martyrdom.

life|02-19||Όσιοι Ευγένιος και Μακάριος οι Ομολογητές||Under Julian the Apostate, around 361, the Christians hid so as not to see the sacrifices to the idols, while the idolaters forced even the Christians to take part in debaucheries. Eugenius and Macarius were arrested, confessed Christ before the Apostate and rebuked him for his apostasy. He bound them with thin straps, hung them upside down and smoked them with dung for hours, then stretched them naked on a red-hot grill and drove iron nails into all their limbs; finally he exiled them to Mauritania. They rejoiced to be exiled for Christ and sang psalms. // There, according to the text, by their prayer a thunderbolt from heaven burned a terrible dragon that lived in a cave, and seeing the miracle the local idolaters believed in Christ. The saints prayed for thirty days in the cave without food or water; a voice sent them to a rock, which cracked and brought forth abundant water, and they drank and were satisfied. On the thirty-eighth day they begged God to depart from life and he received their souls.

life|02-19||Όσιος Κόνων||He came from Cilicia and as a youth became a monk in the monastery of Penthucla, near the Jordan; he also became a presbyter and reached the summit of asceticism. Archbishop Peter of Jerusalem appointed him to baptize those who came to the Jordan, and he anointed them with the holy oil. But when he had to anoint women he was scandalized as a human being and wished to leave the cenobium; each time the Forerunner John appeared to him and told him to endure and that he would relieve him from the warfare. // One day a very beautiful girl came from Persia to be baptized and the venerable one could not anoint her, so she remained unbaptized for two days. The archbishop, learning of the elder's scandal, thought of appointing a woman for the women, but it was not possible, and Conon took his sheepskin and left, saying that he would no longer remain there. The Forerunner met him outside the cenobium and told him to return, but the elder answered angrily that many times he had promised and nothing had he done. Then the Forerunner took hold of him and sealed his body with the sign of the honorable cross, telling him that he wanted him to have a reward for this warfare; the elder returned and the next day anointed and baptized the Persian girl without thinking at all that she was a woman. He lived another twenty years, reached such dispassion that they considered him above human, and fell asleep in peace.

life|02-19||Όσιος Ραβουλάς||He lived in the time of the emperor Zeno and was born in Samosata. He was a disciple of a distinguished man, Barypsabas, and learned the Syriac language; from youth he practiced every virtue and became a monk. He withdrew from people and dwelt alone in mountains and caves, like the prophet Elijah and John the Baptist; a few years later he went to Phoenicia with some others and, because he shone with his virtues, he became known to all against his will. // With the cooperation of Zeno and John, bishop of Berytus, he built a monastery in the middle of the mountain and among the idolaters rebuked and admonished, so that almost all the Greeks there came to know God. Under Anastasius Dicorus (491) he built a monastery also in Constantinople, which took his name, and founded many other monasteries. He was attentive, sober, instructive, gentle, brotherly, and compassionate, and to the temptations of the devil he answered with passages of Scripture. He lived until the time of Justinian; when he became old, around eighty, he heard a voice from on high saying "Come unto me, all ye that labor," and a little later, after a brief illness, he died.

life|02-20||Όσιος Βησσαρίων ο Θαυματουργός||He was born in Egypt and from a young age loved God greatly. He did not defile with any sin the baptism he received as an infant; he went up to a desert place and struggled like a bodiless one, never lying down, but sleeping sitting or standing. He remained forty days and forty nights praying inside a thornbush, motionless like a pillar, with his hands and eyes raised to heaven. // According to the text, by the sign of the cross he changed the salty water of the sea into sweet and gave life to his disciple who was fainting from thirst; like Joshua son of Nun he made by his prayer the sun stand still until he finished his teaching; like Elijah he brought down rain from heaven in a time of drought, not once but many times; and he crossed the Nile on foot by the power of the cross, wetting only his feet up to the ankles. The emperor and his son Constantine, hearing of him, brought him to Constantinople and, taking hold of his feet, begged him to pray for them. He worked great miracles while alive and more after his burial, and died in deep old age.

life|02-20||Άγιος Σαδώκ ο Ιερομάρτυρας Επίσκοπος Περσίδος και οι συν αυτώ εκατόν είκοσι οκτώ τελειωθέντες||They were martyred in Persia under the king Shapur, in 330, confessing the faith in Christ, and were beheaded. It is recorded that Sadoc, before he was arrested and martyred, saw in his dream the previous hieromartyr Symeon standing on a high ladder and urging him to ascend; by this, as it seems, he was showing him the ascent through martyrdom.

life|02-20||Όσιος Αγάθων ο Θαυματουργός||He came from Italy, the son of pious parents, and lived around 650. His parents labored to teach him the whole of the God-inspired Scripture, from which he benefited so much; when they died, he gathered all their wealth and distributed it to the poor in a single day. Then he went to a monastery and became a monk, serving God night and day and praying for the world; for this he also became pope of Rome. After shining in the office of bishop, he died in peace.
