life|02-21||Όσιος Τιμόθεος ο εν Συμβόλοις||From a young age he put on the schema of the monks and with much self-restraint and intense prayer put to death the movements of the passions, so that he became dispassionate and remained to the end a virgin in body and soul. Thus he became a vessel of the Holy Spirit and received the gift of healings: he healed every illness and drove demons from people. He lived rightly and died in a good old age.

life|02-21||Άγιος Γεώργιος Επίσκοπος Αμάστριδος||He was the son of pious parents, Theodosius and Megethe, who came from Kromna, a city near Amastris. Because they were childless, they entreated God with prayer and fasting and, according to the text, learned by a divine voice that they would bear a son who would become a bishop; George was born in their old age. When he grew up, he rejected temporary goods, longed for those to come, and did not neglect divine and human learning. After being educated, he left his homeland, found an honorable elder and received from him the angelic schema of the monks. // When the bishop of Amastris died, they raised him against his will to the throne, by the vote of God and the agreement of the priests, and he was ordained in Constantinople. He took care of the order of the sacred things, the adornment of the Holy Sanctuary, the discipline of the clergy, the protection of orphans and widows, the feeding of the poor, the cancellation of debts, and above all piety and Orthodoxy. In Amastris various miracles were worked through him, and he died in peace.

life|02-22||Όσιοι Θαλάσσιος και Λιμναίος||Thalassius built a hermitage on a small mountain of a village of Cyrrhus called Tillima and surpassed all the venerable ones of that time in simplicity of character and humble-mindedness. Limnaeus, who also loved the ascetic life, went to Thalassius when he was very young and was taught by him the lessons of asceticism; later he went to Venerable Maron and, imitating his life, loved to live without roof or covering. He went up a mountain in the village of Targala and dwelt there, fencing himself in with dry stone that had the sky for a roof. // From these struggles he received grace to drive out demons and heal illnesses. Once a snake bit him, but by prayer he remained unharmed; another time, suffering from a terrible pain in his belly, he was healed by invoking the divine name. He gathered all the blind who were forced to beg, built as many cells as they were, and fed them with what he received from the Christians who visited him. After thirty-eight years of asceticism he peacefully gave up his soul to God.

life|02-22||Όσιος Αθανάσιος ο Ομολογητής ο εν Παυλοπετρίω||He was born in Constantinople of devout and very wealthy parents and from a young age wished to become a monk; he went to the regions of the strait of Nicomedia and became a monk in a monastery. He raised himself so high by his virtues and his fame spread so widely that he became known even to emperors. Under Leo the iconoclast he was accused of venerating the immaculate icons; he suffered various tortures, bitter exiles, and afflictions, but remained steadfast and preserved Orthodoxy to the end, and departed joyfully to the Lord.

life|02-22||Όσιος Βαραδάτος||He came from Antioch and, because he loved the desert and philosophical life, he first shut himself in a small cell and then went to a higher ridge, where he made from wood a box so small that it did not even fit his body, so that he was forced to stoop continually; it protected him neither from the rain nor from the sun. After many years he came out of there, persuaded by the counsels of Theodotus, patriarch of Antioch, but even then he stood unceasingly with hands stretched to heaven, glorifying God, clothed in a leather tunic that left only a small hole at the nose and mouth for breathing. He endured all these hardships although his body was weak and sick, out of divine love, and he was humble-minded. He died in peace.

life|02-23||Όσιοι Ζεβινάς, Πολυχρόνιος, Δαμιανός και Μωϋσής||Zebinas built an ascetic cell on a mountain and struggled there until his old age, surpassing the venerable ones of his time in patience in prayer; when he grew old and could not stand upright, he prayed leaning on his staff. Polychronius became his disciple and imitated the virtues of his teacher as a ring is imprinted on wax; he did not wish to wear irons, fearing that he might become proud, and instead of them he had brought to him a very heavy tree root, which he lifted at night on his shoulders and prayed, hiding it when someone knocked at his cell. According to the text, by his prayer he ended a drought and brought rain, and filled an empty oil vessel with oil. // Moses remained to the end with Zebinas, offering him obedience and service as to a father and master, and drawing his virtue from the elder as from a mirror. Damian first had Polychronius as teacher; then he went to a nearby village, Niara, found a small cell outside the village and followed there the same way of life as his teacher.

life|02-23||Όσιοι Ιωάννης, Αντίοχος, Αντωνίνος και Μωϋσής||John became a disciple and acquaintance of Venerable Limnaeus. He went to a very cold ridge, where he lived twenty-five years ascetically and without a roof, with food of bread and salt, clothed in haircloth and with his body bound with very heavy irons; he wanted no comfort, so that he ordered the cutting down of an almond tree that an acquaintance of his had planted near his bed and that had become a tree with shade, so that he would have no consolation from it. // Moses imitated the life of John and went to a peak in the village of Tama, where he carried out ascetic struggles. Antiochus, although old, practiced great asceticism, and Antoninus, also old, built an enclosure in a most desolate place and struggled like the young, with the same food (bread and salt), the same drink (water), the same haircloth garment, the same vigils and prayers. All four struggled all day and all night and neither old age nor the weakness of nature diminished their endurance; then they peacefully gave up their souls to God.

life|02-23||Όσιος Δαμιανός ο Εσφιγμενίτης||Venerable Damian practiced asceticism within the bounds of the Esphigmenou Monastery on Mount Athos and, according to the text, was perfected in peace around the year 1280. // According to tradition he had undertaken the obligation never to sleep outside his cell. Once when he found himself outside his hut and did not know which way to go, he called on God, and an angel of the Lord took him and set him in front of his hut. // After his death, so much fragrance of myrrh came from his grave that the fathers of the Esphigmenou Monastery perceived it even from a distance of a mile and more.

life|02-25||Άγιος Αλέξανδρος ο Μάρτυρας ο εν Δριζιπάρω της Θράκης||Saint Alexander lived in the time of the emperor Maximian and the governor Tiberian, around 300, and came from Carthage. // When he was arrested and urged to sacrifice to the idols, not only did he refuse but he also reviled the governor. They hung him by the tips of his hands with a heavy stone tied to his feet, and then tore him and beat him. // At Marcianopolis they burned his face with a torch. In Thrace he was beheaded and thus received the crown of martyrdom.

life|02-25||Άγιος Ρηγίνος ο Ιερομάρτυρας||Saint Rhegino came from Greece, from Livadeia, and was the son of Christian parents. For his virtuous life he was ordained bishop of Skopelos. // He was summoned to the Synod of Sardica in 347, under the brother emperors Constantius and Constans, and by his word and boldness he silenced the Arians and the Eusebians, enemies of the consubstantial. // When he returned to his see a persecution broke out against the Christians. The then ruler of Greece seized him, inflicted on him many punishments for Christ and finally beheaded him, and he received the crown of martyrdom.

life|02-26||Αγίες Φωτώ, Φώτις, Παρασκευή, Κυριακή και Ανατολή οι Μάρτυρες αδελφές της Αγίας Φωτεινής||According to the text, these five sisters of Saint Photine the Samaritan woman followed their sister to Carthage and to Rome, preaching Christ, and appeared together with her before Nero during the persecution. // They underwent the tortures together: their fingers were crushed, they were burned in a furnace, boiling lead and sulfur were poured over them, they were hung up and torn, and according to the text they remained unharmed by the grace of God. They were imprisoned and blinded, but Christ appeared and restored their sight. // In the end Nero ordered that their breasts be cut off and their skin flayed. Photis was bound to the tops of two bent trees, which when released tore her body in two. The other sisters, according to the verses, were perfected by the sword.

life|02-26||Άγιοι Ιωσής και Βίκτωρ οι Μάρτυρες υιοί της Αγίας Φωτεινής||According to the text, under Nero Victor, the eldest son of Saint Photine, had distinguished himself in a war against the Arabs and had become commander-in-chief. The emperor, not knowing that he was a Christian, sent him to Italy to punish the Christians, but he refused and declared that he would serve the heavenly king Christ. // The Lord appeared to him and renamed him Photinus, because many were enlightened through him. He arrived in Rome together with his mother, his brother Joses, and the Christians, and underwent with them the tortures of Nero. // After they cut off also their private members, according to the text they beheaded them.

life|02-26||Άγιος Σεβαστιανός ο δούκας||Sebastian was a duke in Italy and a friend of the general Victor. According to the text, he advised Victor to obey Nero, and when he refused, he was blinded and remained speechless for three days. // On the third day he cried out that the God of the Christians is one, was baptized by Victor and, according to the text, immediately regained the light of his eyes. Many Greeks who saw the miracle were baptized as well. // He was taken with the soldiers to Rome and punished together with his fellow confessors, and finally beheaded.

life|02-26||Άγιος Θεόκλητος ο Μάρτυρας ο φαρμακός||Theoclitus, who was previously called Lampadius, was a sorcerer in Rome under Nero. He was summoned to prepare a deadly drug for the saints around Saint Photine. // The saint drank it first in the name of Christ, and according to the text remained unharmed, as did all who drank with her, even from a second, stronger drug. The sorcerer then threw his magic books into the fire, believed in Christ and was baptized. // The emperor ordered that he be seized and beheaded outside the walls, and thus Theoclitus completed his martyrdom before the others.

life|02-27||Άγιος Γελάσιος ο Μάρτυρας||Gelasius was a mime, an actor. According to the verses of the synaxarion, when he was ordered to parody holy baptism, he was truly baptized and became a Christian. Afterwards he was beheaded and perfected by martyrdom.

life|02-27||Όσιος Θαλλέλαιος||Venerable Thalelaius came from Cilicia and, because he loved the ascetic life, went to the city of Gabala in Syria. On a high place a few stadia from it, where there was a temple dedicated to demons, he built a small hut. // The demons could not harm him because of his faith and the grace of God, and in anger uprooted more than five hundred trees. Because the venerable one scorned both their noises and their lit torches, they left him. // The venerable one made two wheels joined with sparse planks and lived ten years sitting or rather hanging in them, in an open space, with his face on his knees. When Theodoret asked him why he followed this new manner of asceticism, he answered that, because he is a sinner and believes in the punishments of God, he prefers to subject his body voluntarily to small afflictions in order to lighten the great punishments of the coming judgment. // According to the inhabitants of the region, by his prayer he healed people and animals. Moved, the pagan Greeks of the region abandoned their ancestral impiety and were baptized, and the venerable one tore down the temple of the demons and built in its place a church of the martyrs.

life|02-27||Όσιοι Ασκληπιός και Ιάκωβος||Venerable Asclepius and James are two ascetics mentioned in the text on the basis of Theodoret of Cyrrhus. Asclepius, according to the text, led many from error to piety and followed the ascetic and desert life, and thus was judged worthy of the crowns. // James lived shut in a small cell near a village named Nimouza, without fire or lamp. Although he was over ninety years old, he never left his cell.

life|02-28||Άγιος Νέστωρας ο Μάρτυρας||Saint Nestor lived under the emperor Decius and the governor Publius, around 250, and came from Perge in Pamphylia. Because he revered Christ, the eirenarch arrested him and led him to the governor. // He confessed before him the faith in Christ and was crucified. He thanked God and strengthened the Christians in the faith, and gave up his spirit, receiving the crown of martyrdom.

life|02-28||Οσίες Κύρα και Μαράνα||Venerable Marana and Cyra came from Beroea in the region of Antioch, of a splendid and distinguished family, and had a corresponding upbringing. Scorning the splendor of their family and the pleasures of life, they built outside the city a small enclosure, went inside and blocked the door with stones and clay. // Their maidservants wished to live a similar life, and their mistresses ordered them to build outside the enclosure a small cell and to practice asceticism there. From a small window they watched what the maidservants were doing and often urged them to prayer and to the love of God. // Marana and Cyra had neither house nor hut, neither roof nor covering, and endured the rains and snows of winter and the scorching heat of summer, considering that they enjoyed great gladness. They received their food through a small opening, through which they also conversed with others.

life|03-01||Αγία Αντωνίνα η Μάρτυς||According to the text, she came from Nicaea and lived in the years of the emperor Maximian. She appeared before him and boldly confessed Christ, whereupon she underwent various tortures and was imprisoned. Because she refused to sacrifice to the idols, they hung her up and tore her sides, while she mocked the gods of the Greeks and the error of the emperor. When the executioners went to strip her, according to the text angels came from heaven, struck and drove off the executioners and kept the saint unharmed. They then put her on a lit grill, but she again remained unharmed by the grace of Christ. Finally they put her in a sack and threw her into the lake of Nicaea, and thus she received the crown of martyrdom.

life|03-02||Άγιος Ησύχιος ο Συγκλητικός||He lived in the years of the emperor Maximian and held the office of magistrianos, first in the imperial palace and in the senate. The emperor ordered all Christian soldiers to deny Christ, or else be deprived of their belts, the sign of their rank, and live as ordinary private citizens. Many preferred to live humbly without honor rather than lose their soul, and among them was counted Hesychius. The emperor dressed him in a poor woolen garment without sleeves and forced him to associate with the women in order to humiliate him. When he asked him whether he was not ashamed to have lost his honor, the saint answered that the honor of the emperor is temporary, while the honor and glory that Christ gives are eternal. Then the emperor became enraged and threw him, with a great millstone tied to his neck, into the river Orontes in Syria, and thus the saint received the crown of martyrdom.

life|03-02||Άγιος Κοΐντος ο Μάρτυρας Ομολογητής και Θαυματουργός||He was born in Phrygia, where he also learned piety, in the years of the emperor Aurelian. He went to a village and distributed alms to the poor. The governor Rufus arrested him and ordered him to sacrifice to the idols. The saint prayed and, according to the text, freed from a demon the governor, whom it was tormenting, so he went free and even received gifts from him. By his prayer an earthquake occurred, the temple collapsed and the idols fell, and the Greeks left him. Forty days later the ruler Clearchus, a zealot of idolatry, arrested him and ordered that his legs be crushed, which according to the text immediately became healthy by the power of Christ. Then the saint wandered in various places for ten whole years, healing every illness and showing mercy to the poor, and living with such miracles and works pleasing to God he went to the Lord.

life|03-02||Αγία Ευθαλία η Παρθενομάρτυς||She was from Sicily and had a mother who suffered from hemorrhaging and was also called Euthalia. Three holy martyrs appeared in the mother's sleep and told her that, if she believed in Christ and was baptized, she would be healed. She believed and was baptized together with her daughter of the same name. The mother also had a son, Sermilian, who seized her and came close to strangling her because she had believed in Christ; she was delivered with the help of a maidservant and fled. Saint Euthalia repeatedly rebuked her brother who wished to kill their mother. When he asked her whether she too was a Christian, she answered that she was and that she was ready to die for Christ. Then her brother stripped her, beat her hard, and handed her over to one of his slaves to dishonor her, but the saint prayed and blinded the slave. Seeing this, her brother cut off her head, and thus she received the crown of martyrdom.

life|03-02||Άγιοι Νέστωρ και Τριβιμίνος οι Μάρτυρες||They came from the land of the Cibyrrhaeots, from Perge in Pamphylia, a city which according to the text later became a metropolis with fifteen bishops. In the years of the emperor Decius they were betrayed by the idolaters and struck with dry ox-hide whips. Then they were hung up and torn as far as the entrails. Because they remained steadfast in the faith of Christ, they were beheaded, and thus received the crowns of martyrdom.

life|03-03||Άγιος Θεοδώρητος ο Ιερομάρτυρας Επίσκοπος Αντιοχείας||He was a presbyter of the Church of Antioch in the years of Julian the Apostate. The emperor's uncle, also named Julian, who was a Christian and a reader of the Church of Antioch, was persuaded by his nephew, denied the faith, betrayed to the tyrant the wealth and sacred treasures of the Church and became a persecutor of the Christians. The other clergy were scattered, but Theodoret remained and preached Christ boldly. Julian the uncle arrested him, imprisoned and tortured him; they struck him on the feet and the head and hung him up and tore him for three hours. When he ordered that his sides be burned with lit torches, the executioners fell, according to the text, as if dead and believed in Christ, and the saint said that angels guard him. Those who believed were thrown into the sea and the saint guided them with words of peace. He prophesied to the uncle that he would die of a dreadful illness in his entrails and to the emperor that a spear would pierce him in the land of Persia. Julian ordered that he be beheaded, and the saint prayed joyfully and was beheaded. Christians took his relic and buried it with honors; according to the text his prophecies were fulfilled after a few days.

life|03-04||Άγιοι Παύλος και Ιουλιανή οι Μάρτυρες||They were siblings from Ptolemais, children of pious parents, in the years of the emperor Aurelian. Paul was a reader and, although young, silenced his opponents with his knowledge of the Scriptures. When the emperor came to Ptolemais, Paul encouraged his sister Julian to stand readily in the temptation and fortified himself with the sign of the cross. The idolaters denounced him as a Christian and Paul, after the vanity of the idols was exposed, was hung up and torn. Julian protested the injustice, whereupon she too was hung up and torn, and then they threw both into prison. They put them into a cauldron of boiling pitch, stretched them on a red-hot bed and struck them on the back, and according to the text an angel of the Lord freed them from the bonds and fed them in prison. The emperor ordered that Paul be bound to a stake and struck with leaden instruments, and Julian be brought to a brothel, where according to the text an angel blinded the lecherous men and she with compassion healed them. They threw them into a pit full of fire, where according to the text a miracle with a fiery cloud occurred, and finally, after burning them with lit torches, they beheaded them and they received the crowns of martyrdom.

life|03-04||Άγιοι Ακάκιος, Κοδράτος και Στρατόνικος οι Μάρτυρες||They were executioners at the martyrdom of Saints Paul and Julian in the years of the emperor Aurelian. Having compassion for the martyrs and seeing the miracles, they believed in Christ. For this they were beheaded and received the crowns of martyrdom. According to the text, the executioner Stratonicus believed especially when he felt compassion for Saint Julian, and the enraged emperor ordered that his head be cut off.

life|03-05||Όσιος Μάρκος ο Αθηναίος||He lived around the year 430 and, diligent in everything, devoted himself to the study of the divine Scriptures and reached the summit of asceticism and virtue. Proof of both are the discourses he wrote, beneficial and full of instruction, as well as the gift of miracles that was given to him. According to the text, when he was in his cell, a hyena came with her blind cub and with a humble bearing begged him to heal it; the venerable one spat on its eyes and, after praying, made them healthy. A few days later the hyena brought the skin of a large ram as thanks, but the saint accepted it only when she showed that she would never again harm the sheep of the poor. The priest of the desert swore that the venerable one never received communion from his hands, but an angel of the Lord communicated him. He bade farewell to the world at the age of forty, lived sixty years in asceticism, and went to the Lord. He was short, with a sparse beard and bald, but radiated the grace of the Holy Spirit.

life|03-06||Άγιοι Αέτιος, Βασσόης, Θεόδωρος, Θεόφιλος, Κάλλιστος, Κωνσταντίνος και άλλοι 36 Μάρτυρες||They were forty-two saints from Amorium, a city of upper Phrygia that was captured by the Hagarenes in the time of the iconoclast emperor Theophilos, who came from the same Amorium. They were generals and taxiarchs of the foremost Roman stock, and were taken captive by the Hagarenes; they were not defeated through cowardice or weakness. They remained in prison for many years and did not yield under the hardship; they bravely confessed their faith in Christ and resisted the impious Ottomans. They did not agree to deny Christ and were beheaded with joy, and so received the crowns of martyrdom.

life|03-06||Όσιος Ησύχιος ο Θαυματουργός||He was raised with piety from his infancy and, hating material cares, became a dwelling place of the Holy Spirit. He left his homeland of Andrapa in Galatia and went to the deserts, guided by God. There he settled on a mountain where, according to the text, he discerned by the clairvoyant power of the Holy Spirit that some people who were trying to dissuade him were speaking under the influence of demons, and he drove them away with the sign of the cross. He cultivated the land and, when birds ate its fruits, he rebuked them, according to the text, and they did not come again. Later, going down to a lower part of the mountain where he found water, he built a church in the name of Saint Andrew, where he lived in stillness. According to the text, he healed a girl who was tormented by a demon and prophesied that the place would become an ascetic retreat for women. He raised an ox belonging to a farmer that had fallen and had become almost like stone, making it stand up with the sign of the cross. When an angel told him that in thirty days he would go to the Lord, he gathered the brothers, admonished them, and at the hour of midnight, amid heavenly light, gave up his spirit. They buried him in a stone coffin near the gate of the church, and later, in the days of Constantine and Irene, Theophylaktos, bishop of Amaseia, transferred his relics to Amaseia, where he is venerated.

life|03-07||Άγιοι Αγαθόδωρος, Αιθέριος, Βασιλέας, Ελπίδιος, Ευγένιος, Εφραίμ και Καπίτων οι Ιερομάρτυρες||In the time of the emperor Diocletian, Hermon, Patriarch of Jerusalem, sent these seven bishops to various nations, to the land of the Tauroscythians, to preach the word of God. Ephraim was sent to Scythia and Basileus to Cherson. Basileus preached to the Greeks, but they beat him and drove him out, and he dwelt in a cave. According to the text, when the son of the city's foremost ruler died, he appeared in a dream to his family and asked that the stranger pray for him, and the son was raised; then many believed and were baptized. The rest, incited by Jews, bound the saint with ropes and dragged him through the streets, where he gave up his soul. Ephraim was beheaded because he refused to worship the idols. Eugenios, Agathodoros and Elpidios went to Cherson after the martyrdom of Basileus, preached Christ, and were bound, dragged and put to death on the sixth of March. Aetherios was later sent as bishop to Cherson; he went to Byzantium and asked Constantine the Great that the impious be punished, and the impious were driven out of the city. On his return the unbelievers threw him into the Danube. Capito was sent next as bishop and, according to the text, entered a lit furnace in his episcopal vestments and came out unharmed, whereupon the unbelievers believed and were baptized; Capito fell asleep peacefully on the twenty-second of December.

life|03-09||Άγιος Ουρπασιανός ο Μάρτυρας||When Maximian assumed the imperial rule, he tyrannized the region of Nicomedia and, convening the senate and the magistrates, announced that whoever did not return to the gods must remove his military belt and leave the palace and the city. Many Christians left, others yielded to the tortures, but those who truly loved God threw away their belts. Urpasian, before the emperor and the whole senate, cast off his cloak and his belt and declared that he served the heavenly and immortal King, Jesus Christ. // The enraged Maximian beat him with oxhide whips for many hours and shut him in a dark prison, where the saint rejoiced and prayed. Then he ordered that he be shut in an iron cage hung up high and burned with lit torches, until his flesh melted like wax and fell to the ground. According to the text, the air was filled with fragrance and the martyr ascended into heaven like a bright star, as some Christians were granted to see. The emperor commanded that the earth with his flesh and bones be gathered and scattered in the sea.

life|03-11||Άγιοι Θαλλός και Τρόφιμος οι Μάρτυρες||They lived in the time of the persecution under Diocletian and Maximian, when Asklepios was governor in Laodicea. Natives of Stratonikeia in Caria, they were arrested because they confessed Christ and were stoned for hours, but by the grace of God they remained unharmed, whereupon the governor was ashamed and set them free. // Later they were denounced again and in court confessed Christ as true God, mocked the idols and rebuked the tyrant. They were hung upside down on a wooden beam and their flesh was torn, and because they prayed and thus angered the governor all the more, they were condemned to crucifixion. As they were led to the place of punishment, many people followed them, and upon the cross they continued to pray and to teach the people. The faithful took drops of their blood, handkerchiefs and rings for blessing and protection from every affliction. After they had blessed everyone, they gave up their souls to the Lord. // Christians wrapped the relics in shrouds and buried them; the wife of Asklepios anointed them with myrrh and covered them with a precious shroud. Later Zosimos and Artemios, their fellow countrymen, took the coffin and laid it near Stratonikeia, at a distance of one mile from the city.

life|03-11||Άγιος Πιόνιος ο Μάρτυρας ο Πρεσβύτερος||He was a presbyter of the church of Smyrna in the time of the emperor Decius, about 251. He was arrested with others for his faith in Christ and was led first to the temple warden of the idols, Polemon, whom he rebuked with historical and biblical arguments for the error of his religion. According to the text, he also spoke of the miracles that had been wrought in former times by God, such as the fiery rain on Sodom and Gomorrah. // Then he was brought before the magistrate and afterwards before the proconsul Quintilian, who condemned him to be put to death by fire. Thus the saint received the incorruptible crown of martyrdom.

life|03-11||Άγιος Γεώργιος ο Νεοφανής ο εν Διϊπίω||He left his wife, children and relatives, preferred the narrow and afflicted way of the Lord, and became a monk. He wandered through cities, lands and deserts, deprived, afflicted and ill-treated. When his death was revealed to him by God, he went to Constantinople, to the church of John the Theologian in the place called Dioippion, and after staying there seven days, he fell asleep in the Lord. // When Christians came to bury him, they saw that he wore extremely heavy iron chains and that his whole body was pierced by them, and they all cried out, "Lord, have mercy." They made a marble coffin, placed the relics inside and buried them in the narthex of the church of John. According to the text, the relics poured forth healings for those who come running with faith, and some of them were still alive and affirmed it with a living voice.

life|03-11||Όσιος Γεώργιος ο Σιναΐτης||He lived in the time of Peter, Patriarch of Jerusalem, and of the emperor Justinian, around 535, as a faster and very virtuous ascetic on Mount Sinai, as Sophronios of Jerusalem writes. Once he desired to receive communion in the church of the Resurrection in Jerusalem, and according to the text he found himself there immediately, crossing in a moment a distance of twelve days, and received communion from the hands of Peter. // The patriarch invited him to the table; George answered, "Let the will of God be done," and prayed, and at once found himself again in his cell on Sinai. When the patriarch did not find him at the table, he accused him of disobedience and wrote to the fathers of Sinai, who were astonished and confessed that George had never left the mountain. Three hieromonks went to the patriarch to vindicate him, and George himself wrote that for seventy years he had not left Sinai nor entered Palestine. // He added that in six months both of them would go to meet the Lord, and the prophecy was fulfilled, since after six months both fell asleep.

life|03-14||Άγιος Αλέξανδρος ο Μάρτυρας εν Θεσσαλονίκη||He lived in the darkness of the error of idols and shone like a many-lighted star, refuting the ruinous error of the idolaters and wounding with his words, as with arrows, the devil himself. The deluded Greeks could not bear his boldness and courage and tried in various ways and with flatteries to bend his greatness of soul. Since they did not succeed, they cut off his holy head. According to the text, God rewarded him with the gift of healings, since his holy relic heals all the illnesses of those who come running with faith.

life|03-14||Άγιος Ευσχήμων ο Ομολογητής Επίσκοπος Λαμψάκου||He lived in the time of the iconoclasts. From infancy he was well brought up and became a temple of the Holy Spirit; he became a monk and rose to the dignity of the priesthood, full of the grace of God. According to the text, he raised the dead, foretold the future and spoke of distant things as if they were present; the beasts that ate the vegetables he drove away with a single command. // The iconoclasts shut him in prison because he venerated the holy icons, and by his teaching he persuaded his guards to venerate the icons. Although imprisoned and exiled, he cared for the poor and gave alms as much as he could. He ended his life peacefully and, according to the text, even after his death he benefited with countless miracles those who approached him with faith.

life|03-15||Άγιος Νίκανδρος ο Μάρτυρας ο εν Αιγύπτω||He lived in the time of Diocletian, around 293. He was devoted to piety and to love for the martyrs of Christ, and therefore made it his work to take in secret the relics of those who died for the faith and to bury them with honor and respect. Once he saw relics of holy martyrs thrown away and uncared for; he went by night, took them and reverently buried them in some place. // A pagan saw him and denounced him to the magistrate. The saint was arrested and confessed Christ boldly as true God, and they flayed him like a sheep, and so he received the crown of martyrdom.

life|03-16||Άγιος Σαβίνος ο Μάρτυρας||He came from Hermoupolis in Egypt and lived in the time of Diocletian. He hid with other Christians outside the city in a small house, and the pagans were searching for him, because the Christians honored him greatly, he was of the foremost stock, and he surpassed the others in zeal for the faith. // He was brought before the governor Arrian and confessed Christ. They hung him up and tore him so much that all his flesh fell to the ground; then they burned him with lit torches, and finally they bound him to a stone and cast him into the river Scamander, and so he received the crown of martyrdom.

life|03-16||Άγιος Πάπας ο Μάρτυρας ο εν Λυκαονία ασκήσας||Seeing the world tossed about by idolatry, he presented himself before the magistrate and put him to shame by the boldness with which he confessed Christ. They threw him to the ground and beat him with rods over his whole body and his face, then hung him up high and tore him with iron claws. Then they nailed iron shoes to his feet and forced him to walk a long way. // In the end they bound him to a barren tree, which according to the text immediately put forth leaves, flowers and fruit, and upon it he gave up his soul to God. Lycaonia has his holy relic and rejoices.

life|03-16||Όσιος Ανίνας ο Θαυματουργός||The venerable Aninas, without any education, loved stillness and meekness from a young age. At fifteen he was orphaned, left the world and went to the desert, where he lived near a monk named Maioumas, who was exceedingly without possessions. They lived in great poverty, eating once every four days. // Because he subjected the passions of the body to the mind, the wild beasts, according to the text, were also subjected to him: two lions followed him everywhere, and from one of them he removed a hard thorn from its paw and healed it. When his fame spread, crowds of people ran to him, and he healed the sick by his prayer. // According to the text, when the water of the cistern he had made for the crowd was not enough, by his prayer the cistern filled up, and another time the vessel in his hands was found full of water. Out of humility he himself tried to hide his miracles and called himself a worm. A certain bishop of Caesarea gave him a donkey, which the venerable one gave to the poor, and the bishop finally made a large jar that is preserved, according to the text, to this day. // With a prophetic spirit he wrote to the superior stylite and reconciled him with the brother who had wounded him. He also healed a woman of a grave illness, and a barbarian who wanted to rape her was tamed and became a monk near him. // He lived in his ascetic retreat for ninety-five years and a hundred and ten in all. He made many prophecies that were fulfilled, and before he died he appointed as his successor the most virtuous brother, blessed everyone and after seven days fell asleep.

life|03-17||Άγιος Μαρίνος||Saint Marinos was a Christian from parents and ancestors. Seeing the pagans offer sacrifices not only to men but also to reptiles and loathsome insects, he was fired with divine zeal and, at the time when the Greeks were celebrating before the lifeless idols, he rushed in, overturned the altar and trampled the sacrifices, calling himself a Christian. // They seized him at once, beat him with thick staves, broke his mouth and teeth with stones and dragged him by the hair. They then handed him over bound to the magistrate, who tortured him greatly, and in the end he was beheaded and received the crown of martyrdom.

life|03-18||Άγιοι Ευκαρπίων και Τρόφιμος οι Μάρτυρες και οι συν αυτοίς Μαρτυρήσαντες||Saints Trophimos and Eucarpion lived in Nicomedia in the time of the persecution under the emperor Maximian. They were strong soldiers and persecutors of the Christians, whom they arrested and imprisoned. // According to the text, as they were going to arrest Christians, they saw a fiery cloud descending from heaven and heard a voice telling them not to threaten the servants of God and to unite with them in order to gain the kingdom of heaven. They fell down in fear, the cloud opened, they saw a man dressed in white sitting in it, and heard that their sins would be forgiven if they repented. // They wept for their former error, returned, freed the imprisoned Christians and let them go. As soon as the magistrate learned of it, he was enraged, summoned them and, after hearing the vision, hung them on a wooden beam, tore them with iron claws and rubbed their wounds with hair cloths. Since they rejoiced and gave thanks to God, he ordered a furnace to be lit in the middle of Nicomedia and they were thrown in, where they gave up their souls and received the crown of martyrdom.

life|03-19||Άγιος Παγχάριος ο Μάρτυρας||Pancharios came from the land of the Thysans, from the city of Villapati, and was the son of Christian parents, tall and handsome. In the time of Diocletian and Maximian he went to Rome, became a friend of Diocletian and the first of the magistrates of the Senate, and out of excessive love for the emperor he denied the faith in Christ. // His mother and sister, learning of his fall, wrote him a letter and counseled him to remember the fear and judgment of God. Reading it, Pancharios came to himself, fell to the ground weeping and asked mercy of the Lord. When the emperor learned of it and asked him whether he was a Christian, he confessed it and declared that he would never deny Christ. // The emperor beat him with oxhide whips in the theater and then, on the advice of the Senate, sent him to the magistrate of Nicomedia with the order to put him to death. There Pancharios confessed that he wished to die for the name of Christ in order to wipe out the denial he had made. The magistrate, seeing his unshakable resolve, condemned him, and the martyr was beheaded in Nicomedia, receiving the crown of martyrdom.

life|03-19||Άγιοι Κλαύδιος, Ιλαρία, Ιάσονας και Μαύρος οι Μάρτυρες και οι συν αυτοίς Μαρτυρήσαντες||Claudius was a tribune and received from the prefect Celerinus the saints Chrysanthos and Daria in order to punish them. Seeing that they remained unharmed by the tortures and that Chrysanthos rejoiced while they were striking him, he understood that this was happening by the power of God. He fell at the feet of the saint and was baptized at once, together with his wife Hilaria, his two sons Maurus and Jason, the servants, the friends and the soldiers under his command. // When the emperor Numerian learned of it, he ordered a stone to be tied to the neck of Claudius and him to be thrown into the sea, while the soldiers were to be tortured and those who did not deny Christ to be beheaded in the theater. Thus Claudius and the soldiers received the crown of martyrdom. His sons went of their own accord, without being summoned, to martyrdom, confessed Christ before the tyrant and were beheaded. // The Christians buried their relics in a cave near the place of their execution. Hilaria took the relics of her sons and buried them separately, and often went to their tombs. She was arrested and dragged violently by soldiers; she asked them to leave her for a little, raised her hands to heaven and, praying, gave up her soul to God. The executioners, seeing the miracle, were afraid and fled, and two of her maidservants buried her relics near the tombs of her two children.

life|03-20||Άγιοι Αββάδες Μαύροι οι εν τή μονή Αγίου Σάββα αναιρεθέντες||The venerable abbas had gathered from various places and lived in stillness in the monastery of Saint Sabbas, serving God with a virtuous conduct, hardship and asceticism. The envious devil, according to the text, stirred up against them the godless Ethiopians, the so-called Blacks, who hoped to find money and wealth in the monastery. // Since they found no money, they vented their anger on the fathers: some they beheaded, some they cut to pieces, some they tore apart in the middle and some they pierced with their weapons, shedding their blood on the earth. They, giving thanks to God, gave up their souls into His hands, and received the eternal life of the kingdom of heaven, for which they had endured the former struggles of asceticism and the final torments.

life|03-20||Αγίες Αλεξανδρία, Ευφημία, Ευφρασία, Ιουλιανή, Θεοδοσία, Κλαυδία και Ματρώνη οι Μάρτυρες εν Αμινσώ||These seven holy virgins lived in the time of the emperor Maximian, when a great persecution of the Christians was taking place. In the city of Amisos in Cappadocia, where the magistrate was putting Christians to death inhumanly, they presented themselves boldly before him, confessed Christ as true God and called the magistrate inhuman and an enemy of the truth. // They stripped them and beat them with rods, then cut off their breasts with knives, hung them up and tore them so much that their entrails were exposed. Finally they threw them into a lit furnace, where they gave up their souls to God and received the crowns of struggle.

life|03-20||Άγιος Νικήτας ο Ομολογητής Επίσκοπος Απολλωνιάδος||Saint Nikitas lived in the time of the iconoclasts and became bishop of Apollonias in Bithynia, which was once subject to the metropolitan of Nicomedia. He was faithful, pious and Orthodox, also merciful and compassionate, with great knowledge of the Scriptures and still more of speech and eloquence. // The iconoclasts pressed him not to venerate the icon of Christ, of the Panagia, of the angels and of the saints, and he did not obey. He was exiled and endured unbearable trials, from which he fell gravely ill and gave up his soul to God, receiving the crown of confession.

life|03-21||Άγιοι Δομνίνος και Φιλήμων οι Μάρτυρες||Saints Philemon and Domninos were from Rome. In the time of the persecution they went about Italy preaching Christ and baptizing those who returned to the faith. For this the pagans seized them and led them to the magistrate of Italy. // Since they were neither softened by flatteries nor persuaded by promises of gifts, and confessed Christ as God, the pagans stretched them naked on the ground by the four limbs and beat them mercilessly. They threw them into prison, and then brought them out and beheaded them, and the blessed ones received the crown of martyrdom.

life|03-21||Άγιος Βήρυλλος Επίσκοπος Κατάνης||Saint Berillos came from Antioch and was a disciple of the apostle Peter. He came to the West together with the chief apostle and was ordained by him bishop of Catania in Sicily. // He shepherded his flock in a manner pleasing to God and performed many miracles. According to the text, at a spring in Catania that gave very bitter water, he changed by his prayer the bitterness into sweetness. Seeing the miracle, a Greek pagan believed in Christ, and many others believed with him. // Reaching deep old age, he fell asleep in the sleep of the righteous. His honorable relic was buried with magnificence in Catania and, according to the text, to this day it pours forth various cures for those who approach it with faith.

life|03-22||Αγία Δροσίς και οι συν αυτή πέντε Κανονικές||In the time of the emperor Trajan, five women ascetics, the Canonesses, made it their unceasing work to take the relics of the martyrs, anoint them with myrrh and bury them in their ascetic retreat. Drosis, the daughter of Trajan, went to them and asked to go with them to take the relics of a martyr. Her betrothed Hadrian advised the emperor to set guards, and so the five ascetics were arrested together with Drosis. // The emperor ordered his daughter to be guarded and the five to be thrown into a great crucible, together with bronze, so that from the mixture the bronze vessels of a new public bath might be made. According to the text, whoever approached the bath fell dead, and the priests of the idols said that the vessels were to blame. From the materials they made statues of the women in order to shame them, but the emperor saw in his sleep five pure lambs and a fearsome shepherd, Christ, saying that He had placed them in paradise, where Drosis too would come. // The emperor was enraged and ordered two ovens to be kept burning, with an inscription inviting Christians to throw themselves in. Drosis prayed to be delivered from marriage to Hadrian, went out secretly from the palace, was baptized with the water of a cistern and remained seven days, nourished, according to the text, with food that an angel brought her. On the eighth day, praying, she gave up her soul to the Lord.

life|03-24||Άγιος Αρτέμων Επίσκοπος Σελευκείας της Πισιδίας||Artemon came from Seleucia in Pisidia, where he was born and raised in the time of the holy apostles. When the apostle Paul was traveling through those parts preaching the Gospel, he made him bishop, shepherd and teacher of the city. // He shepherded his flock well, became a harbor of salvation for those in need, a protector of widows and orphans, a helper of the poor and a physician of souls and bodies. Thus he reached deep old age and died in peace.

life|03-24||Άγιος Αρτέμων ο Ιερομάρτυρας Πρεσβύτερος Λαοδικείας||In the time of Diocletian, the count Patrikios was sent to the region of Laodicea and compelled the Christians to sacrifice to the idols. Bishop Sisinios and the presbyter Artemon went by night with Christians to the temple of Artemis, shattered and burned the idols and made disappear, according to the text, the dragons of the temple. The count was enraged, but as he approached the Church, fear and a violent fever seized him, and he was brought back home sick. He wrote to Sisinios that he would believe if he were healed, and, according to the text, he was healed at once. // About three miles outside Laodicea the count met Artemon followed by two deer and six asses, which he had tamed, he said, by the word of Christ. Because Artemon confessed that he had been a Christian from a young age, the count bound him with chains. According to the text, the animals went to Sisinios and with the voice of a deer informed him of the arrest. In court the saint said that he had served sixteen years as a reader, twenty-eight as a deacon and thirty-three as a presbyter, and he refused to sacrifice. The count placed him on a heated grill, then ordered pitch to be heated in a cauldron to throw him in, but, according to the text, two angels like eagles seized the count himself and threw him into the cauldron, and his body dissolved. // Many, among them the priest of the idols Vitalios, were catechized and baptized by the saint. According to the text, a voice sent him to the coastal regions of Asia Minor, where he performed many signs and miracles, cleansed many of demons and illnesses and led many to God. In the end the pagans seized him, he was beheaded and went to the eternal dwellings.

life|03-26||Άγιοι Είκοσι Έξι Μάρτυρες οι εν Γοτθία μαρτυρήσαντες||These saints lived in the time of Jungerich, king of the Goths, and of Gratian, emperor of the Romans, around 370. Because they confessed Christ, the impious Jungerich burned the church of the Christians, and within it the twenty-six martyrs were burned, and so they received the crown of martyrdom. // At the same time, according to the text, a Christian brought an offering to the church, the pagans arrested him and, after he confessed Christ, he was burned in the fire and himself became an offering to God.

life|03-27||Άγιοι Φιλητός, Λυδία, Θεοπρέπιος, Μακεδόνας, Αμφιλόχιος και Κρονίδης οι Μάρτυρες||These saints lived in the time of the emperor Hadrian, around 125, and were Christians who worshiped God every day. Philetos was arrested together with his wife Lydia and their two children, Theoprepios and Makedon, and was brought to the emperor. He could not withstand the wisdom of the saint and sent him with his wife to Amphilochios, duke in Slavonia, who hung them on a wooden beam and ordered their bodies to be beaten with wooden swords. // Then Cronides, the commentarisios, believed in Christ, and he too was thrown into prison, where at night, while the saints were singing and praying, angels appeared and encouraged them. Amphilochios threw them into a cauldron full of oil and boiling resin, and the cauldron, according to the text, immediately grew cold. Astonished, Amphilochios himself believed and entered the cauldron, and a voice from heaven assured him that his prayer was heard. // When the emperor learned of it, he left Rome and went to Slavonia full of wrath, and ordered a cauldron of oil to be kept burning for seven days, into which the six saints were also thrown. They remained untouched again by the grace of God, and the emperor, put to shame, returned to Rome. The saints prayed, thanked God and gave up their souls, receiving the crowns of the contest.

life|03-28||Άγιος Ηρωδίων ο Απόστολος Επίσκοπος Ταρσού||Herodion was one of the seventy disciples of the Lord. He followed the holy apostles and especially Peter and became their fellow worker in the preaching of the Gospel. Afterwards he was ordained bishop of New Patras, where he taught and brought many to faith in the Lord. // For this reason Greeks and Jews seized him and beat him cruelly: some struck him in the mouth with stones and others on the head. In the end they slaughtered him, and so his martyrdom was completed and he gave up his soul into the hands of God.

life|03-29||Άγιοι Ιωνάς, Βαραχήσιος, Άβιβος, Ζανιθάς, Ηλίας, Λάζαρος, Μάρης, Μαρουθάς, Ναρσής, Σάββας και Σιμιάθος οι Μάρτυρες||These saints were from Persia, in the time of the king of the Persians Shapur and of Constantine the Great. Jonas and Barachisios were monks who left their monastery and went to a village called Marmiaboch. There they found imprisoned nine holy martyrs, Zanithas, Lazaros, Marouthas, Narses, Elias, Maris, Abibos, Simiathes and Sabbas, and encouraged them to remain steadfast in the confession of Christ to the end. The nine received the crown of martyrdom first, on the twenty-seventh of the month. // For the same reason Jonas and Barachisios were arrested and led to three magistrates, who pressed them to deny the faith in Christ and to worship the sun and water. The saints did not yield at all. Jonas was bound to a wooden beam according to the Persian custom and scourged, while Barachisios was tortured with red-hot bronze balls under the armpits and with molten lead on the eyes, nose and throat. // They cut off the fingers of Jonas's hands and feet, flayed the skin of his head and cut out his tongue. They threw him into a cauldron full of pitch, from which according to the text he came out unharmed by the grace of Christ, and in the end they cast him into a very deep pit, where he died and received the crown of martyrdom. Barachisios was dragged naked over thorns and pierced with sharp reeds. Their relics, according to the text, were buried together with those of the nine martyrs.

life|03-29||Άγιος Ευστάθιος ο Ομολογητής Επίσκοπος Κίου Βιθυνίας||Eustathios cast off the world like a heavy burden and became a monk, serving the commandments of Christ with eagerness. Later he also became a priest, after the many entreaties of the people. He was full of faith in God, love without hypocrisy, instructive, humble, compassionate and merciful, and for his virtues he became bishop of Kios in Bithynia, which he governed for many years according to the canons and traditions of the apostles. // When the heresy of the iconoclasts arose, the saint, armed with the study of Scripture, fought against them. Some denounced him to the iconoclast emperor, who at first threatened him and afterwards subjected him to insults, beatings, imprisonments and interrogations. In the end they beat him cruelly and exiled him from his bishopric, for the veneration and honor of the holy icons. // In exile he spent some years in affliction, suffering from hunger, thirst, cold and nakedness, and, giving thanks to God, he gave up his soul.

life|03-29||Άγιος Κύριλλος ο Ιερομάρτυρας και οι συν αυτώ άνδρες και γυναίκες Μάρτυρες εν Ασκαλώνι και Γάζη||The deacon Cyril lived in Phoenicia in the time of the reign of Julian the Apostate. Because he had overthrown many idols, the pagans seized him and put him to death savagely, ripping open his belly and taking out his entrails. According to the text, they even ate them, and for this they were punished by God: their teeth fell out, their tongues were cut off and their sight was ruined. // At the same time, in Gaza and Ascalon, the pagans tortured with the same cruelty virgin women and men in holy orders: they ripped open their bellies, filled them with barley and set them before swine to eat. For the martyrs of Christ these temporary torments brought eternal blessedness.

life|03-31||Άγιος Ακάκιος ο Ομολογητής Επίσκοπος Μελιτινής||Acacius lived in the time of the emperor Decius, around 251. Because he taught faith in Christ, the pagans arrested him and brought him to the consul Marcian. Asked about his preaching, he explained the whole economy of the incarnation of God the Word, spoke of the Cherubim and Seraphim and mocked the vanity of the Greek error. For this he suffered various tortures and was imprisoned. // Marcian wrote to the emperor about the saint, and he ordered him to be released without mistreatment. The saint now walked free, bearing on his body the marks and wounds of the Lord. He taught many the faith of Christ, distinguished himself by his teaching and his miracles and died peacefully.

life|04-02||Άγιοι Αιδέσιος και Αμφιανός οι Μάρτυρες||They were brothers on their mother's side and came from Lydia, and lived in the time of the emperor Maximian, around 295. After their coming to Beirut they were led to the faith of Christ and presented themselves as Christians to the magistrate Urbanos. Amphianos confessed Christ first with boldness; they struck him in the face, burned his feet smeared with oil and hung him up, and finally they threw him into the sea, where he received the crown of martyrdom. Aedesios was condemned to work in the copper mines of Egypt. When he saw there the magistrate Hierocles punishing the Christians, he took no account of his life and struck him with his own hand; he was tortured in various ways and was then thrown into the sea himself.

life|04-02||Αγία Θεοδώρα η Παρθενομάρτυς||She came from the city of Tyre and, when she was seventeen years old, presented herself to Urbanos, magistrate of Palestine. Questioned by him, she confessed the faith of Christ, and then they beat her for a long time on the sides and the breasts. Then they threw her into the sea, and so she gave up her soul into the hands of God and received the crown of martyrdom.

life|04-04||Άγιοι Θεόδουλος και Αγαθόπους οι Μάρτυρες||Theodoulos was the younger and Agathopous an elder in age, and both came from Thessaloniki. For their faith in Christ they presented themselves before the magistrate Faustinos and, because they would not agree to deny Him, they were thrown into the sea and thus completed their martyrdom. Before their end, according to the text, what they would suffer was revealed to them in a vision; they saw that they boarded a ship that was broken by the storm, all the passengers were drowned and only they were saved and climbed a mountain that reached to heaven. To Theodoulos the same was also shown by a ring, which signified the betrothal of martyrdom.

life|04-04||Αγία Φερφούθη , η αδελφή της και η δούλη αυτών οι Μάρτυρες||They lived in the time of the king of the Persians Shapur and of Constantine the Great, around 330, and were sisters of Saint Symeon who was martyred in Persia with another one thousand one hundred and fifty Christians. Because the wife of the king fell ill, some slandered them as sorceresses preparing deadly potions. They were arrested and led to the chief magus Papos, and they maintained that they were innocent and Christians, who are not permitted to do such things. Because they were accused doubly, both as sorceresses and as Christians, they were condemned to death; they were stretched on the ground and bound with stakes, then sawn in half from the head to the feet, and the pieces of their bodies were nailed to wooden beams. The queen passed between them and was healed of her illness, for, as the slanderers had assured her, only if she passed between the bodies of the saints could she be healed.

life|04-05||Οσία Θεοδώρα η εν Θεσσαλονίκη||From her youthful years she loved Christ, renounced the world and became a nun in a cenobitic monastery, where she achieved all the virtues. She showed exceeding obedience and honor to all the sisters and especially to the abbess, and kept her life pure, so that she became for the other nuns a living example of virtue. A short time after her death the abbess also died, and a crowd of people, monks and dignitaries gathered at her funeral. When they opened the tomb of Theodora, which had been there for many years, to place the relics of the abbess as well, an extraordinary miracle took place, according to the text; the dead Theodora, as if she were alive, drew herself to one side of the tomb and gave room to her spiritual mother. All those present cried out, "Lord, have mercy." From then until the time of the writer, God performed many signs through her intercession; he freed the possessed, gave sight to the blind and healed countless sick.

life|04-07||Άγιος Γεώργιος ο Σημειοφόρος Επίσκοπος Μυτιλήνης||From a young age he longed for Christ and put on the monastic habit; he achieved all the virtues, especially humility, and was very merciful. For his virtues he was ordained a hierarch and ascended the throne of Mytilene, where he excelled and with the wealth of his wisdom rebuked the iconoclasts of that time, that they might recognize their error. By his exceeding self-control, while living in a body, he rivaled the bodiless angels. God revealed his end by a divine star, both to him and to his whole flock, and he went to the Lord. According to the text, miracles pour forth from his holy relic even after his death.

life|04-09||Άγιος Βάδιμος ο Οσιομάρτυρας||He lived in the time of the king of the Persians Shapur and of Constantine the Great, around 330, and came from the city of Bethlapat, of a glorious and illustrious family. He despised the splendor of his lineage and his great wealth, and became a monk and archimandrite of a monastery. For the confession of Christ, the fire-worshipers of Persia betrayed him together with seven of his disciples and shut him in prison for four months. Then they handed him over to an executioner, Nirsan, who had been a Christian first but had denied Christ out of fear of tortures. Vadimos felt pity for him because of his denial; the executioner struck four times with a trembling hand, and so, with much pain, the saint gave up his spirit to God. Later the executioner himself was put to death with a sword, though God had chastised him before. Together with Vadimos his seven disciples were also beheaded, and all received the crowns of martyrdom.

life|04-09||Άγιος Αυδιησούς ο Μάρτυρας και οι συν αυτώ τριακόσιοι Μάρτυρες εν Περσίδι||The king of the Persians Shapur, in the fifty-third year of his reign, marched against Roman territory and took possession of a country, where he put to death the soldiers and those who could fight; the rest of the people, together with Bishop Heliodoros and the priests, he left alive. When Heliodoros died, they ordained in his place the presbyter Desan, and then the chief magus Adephar denounced to the king that these Christians blasphemed against him and his religion. All were arrested and, because they would not worship the sun and fire, they were beheaded; the text mentions four hundred Christians. Five of them were afraid and denied. One of the beheaded, Audiesous, did not receive a fatal blow and did not die, but lived and preached boldly the word of God, until an impious man rushed at him and killed him with a knife. He received the slaughter with joy, for he grieved that he had been separated from the choir of his fellow martyrs.

life|04-10||Άγιος Αφρικανός, Θεόδωρος, Μάξιμος, Πομπήιος και Τερέντιος οι Μάρτυρες και οι συν αυτοίς τριάντα εννέα Μάρτυρες||They lived in the time of Decius and of the governor Fortunian, around 251, and came from Africa. When a royal order was issued that Christians should deny Christ and that those who kept the faith be tortured, they saw that many Christians were being deceived and falling into the error of the pagans, and agreed to resist with courage of soul and body, reminding one another of the word of the Lord not to fear those who kill the body. They presented themselves before the governor, proclaimed the power of Christ and mocked the weakness of the idols, and the governor shut them in prison. Then they beat them with thorny rods and ox sinews, nailed their backs with red-hot spits, poured vinegar with salt on their wounds and rubbed them with hair cloths. Because by their prayer, according to the text, they overthrew the idols, the governor despaired and ordered them beheaded, and they received the crowns of martyrdom. Later their companions Zeno, Alexander and Theodore also presented themselves to the governor, confessed Christ and were thrown into prison bound with iron caltrops; according to the text, angels freed them and brought them heavenly food. They were handed over to the beasts, which did not touch them, and finally they too were beheaded.

life|04-10||Άγιοι Ιάκωβος και Αζάς οι Ιερομάρτυρες||They lived in the time of the king of the Persians Shapur and of Constantine the Great, around 332. The presbyter James came from one village and the deacon Azas from another. They were arrested and presented to the chief magus, and because they confessed Christ with boldness, vinegar mixed with mustard was poured into their noses, they were beaten and hung naked in an open place, where they froze from the cold of the night. Then they were taken down and, because they would not sacrifice to the sun and to fire, they were beheaded by order of the magistrate and ascended to heaven as crowned victors.

life|04-12||Οσία Ανθούσα||She was the daughter of the emperor Constantine Copronymos, who pressed her many times to marry, but she did not obey. When her father died, she distributed her property to the poor, churches, charitable institutions and monasteries, and became a mother of many orphans and a defender of widows. The Orthodox empress Irene, who reigned from 780, begged her to stay with her, and while she stayed in the palace she wore royal clothes outwardly and hair cloth within, with ascetic food, water for drink, tears in her eyes and hymns in her mouth. Later she became a nun, was tonsured by the holy Patriarch Tarasios in the monastery called that of Homonoia, and from then on did not leave the monastery. She was never absent from church, served all the sisters, adorned the church, carried water and served in the refectory, with boundless humility. She died at the age of fifty-two and went to the Lord.

life|04-13||Άγιοι Δάδας, Κυντιλλιανός και Μάξιμος οι Αναγνώστες||They were arrested in the time of the impious emperors Diocletian and Maximian, around 290, in the country of Ozovia, and handed over to the consuls Tarquinius and Gaius. They confessed Christ and were thrown into prison. There, according to the text, the devil counseled them to deny, but they rose and prayed, strengthening one another in the faith, and an angel of the Lord gave them courage and strength. In the morning, despite the pressures of the impious, they not only did not deny but proclaimed loudly Christ as true God and Creator of all; they were beaten and shut in prison again. In the end, after being examined together with others, they were beheaded and ascended to heaven.

life|04-14||Αγία Θωμαΐς η Μάρτυς||Saint Thomais was born in Alexandria, was raised with a good upbringing and married. She lived with modesty and chastity, beloved by her husband. Her father-in-law also lived in the house, and the devil led him into unclean thoughts against his daughter-in-law, when one day her husband was away. She counseled him to drive away the evil thought, but in vain, and the old man, blinded, took his son's sword and killed her. Thus Thomais became a martyr for her chastity. The old man was blinded at once, confessed the murder to Christians who came and gave himself up to the magistrate, who beheaded him. // Abba Daniel of Scetis went down to Alexandria, took her relics and placed them in the cemetery of the fathers of Scetis. According to tradition, a brother who was troubled by the passion of fornication ran to her tomb, anointed himself with oil from her lamp and in his sleep the saint appeared to him and set him free. From then on the brothers of Scetis regard her as a great helper in the battles of the flesh.

life|04-15||Άγιος Κρήσκης ο Μάρτυρας||Saint Crescens came from Myra in Lycia, of an illustrious family, and was an elder of advanced age. Seeing idolatry flourishing, he went zealously among the pagans and counseled them to leave error and turn to the God of the Christians, the creator of every breath. The governor called him an evil spirit and unfortunate, but he answered that to suffer for Christ brings happiness. To every question about his name and homeland he answered only that he was a Christian, and he did not agree to show respect to the idols even as a pretext. He was hung up and torn, then thrown into a fire that did not burn even a hair of his head, and then he gave thanks and gave up his soul to God.

life|04-16||Αγία Ειρήνη η Παρθενομάρτυς||Saint Irene was in Greece at the time of Pascha, when Saint Leonidis was martyred with the women who were with him. She glorified God with other Christians in a separate church, was revealed to the magistrate and was imprisoned. Then they brought her out of prison, cut out her tongue and pulled out her teeth, and finally beheaded her, and so she ascended to the heavens as a crown-bearer.

life|04-16||Άγιοι Φήλικας, Ιανουάριος, Σεπτεμίνος και Φουρτουνάτος οι Μάρτυρες||In the eighth year of the reign of Diocletian and Maximian an edict was issued that the books of the Christians be burned in all cities. The governor Marian, sent to the city of Biukan, brought before him Bishop Felix, the presbyter Januarius, Fortunatus and Septiminus and asked them to hand over the books. Felix answered with the word of the Gospel, not to give what is holy to the dogs nor to cast pearls before swine, and remained unmoved. They were imprisoned, bound and sent successively to the proconsul and to the prefect of the Praetorians, who threw them into a very harsh prison. After fourteen days he tried them again and bound them by the feet to horses inside a ship, and the saints were dragged for four days without food and water, giving thanks to God. On arriving in Lycaonia, the prefect freed them and urged them in a gentle voice to hand over the books and sacrifice, but they refused and were beheaded after praying.

life|04-16||Άγιοι Λεωνίδης, Βασίλισσα, Γαλήνη ή Γαληνή, Θεοδώρα, Καλλίδα, Νίκη, Νουνεχία και Χάρισσα οι Μάρτυρες||Saint Leonidis and the women who were martyred with him were from Greece, that is, the Peloponnese, and Leonidis was arrested in Troezen, where he was head of a spiritual province. He was arrested during the festal days of holy Pascha, and the holy women with him were led to Corinth to the governor Venustos. Seeing him unshakable in the faith, he ordered him to be hung up and torn, and then himself and the women to be cast into the depths of the sea. It is said that Charissa sang, like the prophetess Miriam, and the others accompanied her singing to the sea and in the ship. They bound them with stones and threw them into the sea on the day before Pascha, that is, Great Saturday, and so they received the crowns of martyrdom.

life|04-17||Άγιος Αδριανός ο Μάρτυρας ο Νέος||Adrian was one of the Christians who were arrested by the Greeks, that is, the pagans, and imprisoned. When they offered sacrifices to their false gods, they brought him out of prison and pressed him to offer incense on the altar. The brave martyr not only refused, but ran, overturned the altar, spilled the sacrifices and scattered the fire. Those present were enraged, beat him mercilessly with rods, crushed his mouth with stones and struck him on the head. Finally they lit a great furnace and threw him in, and so he completed the course of martyrdom.

life|04-18||Άγιος Κοσμάς ο Ομολογητής Επίσκοπος Χαλκηδόνος||Saint Cosmas, after being raised in asceticism and purifying himself by spiritual struggles, became a dwelling place of the Holy Spirit. He was honored with the priesthood and became shepherd of the church of Carthage, as the text says. Against those who did not venerate the icon of Christ he defended its honor and taught that it should be venerated, venerating it first himself, and for this he received the crown of confession. He kept to the end the piety he had had from childhood and fell asleep together with the wise Auxentios, with whom he had shared the ascetic struggles. His honorable relic was placed in the church of the Holy Apostles.

life|04-18||Άγιος Σάββας ο Στρατηλάτης||Sabbas lived in Gothia, near Crimea, in the time of the emperors Valentinian and Valens. From childhood he confessed the faith in Christ, mocked the pagans, refused to eat of the sacrifices to the idols and prevented others from doing so, teaching them the faith, and became a cause of salvation for many. The pagans drove him from their city and, when later they were searching for Christians, he went of his own accord and revealed that he was a Christian. At first they let him go, but then, when the leader of the Goths Athanaric came, they seized him, beat him, bound him to an axle and hung him from the beam of the house to force him to taste the sacrifices. Because he refused, they brought him to the river Mousaios and drowned him by putting a heavy piece of wood on his neck. He was thirty-eight years old.

life|04-18||Οσία Αθανασία η Θαυματουργός εξ Αιγίνης||The venerable Athanasia was born in Aegina of pious and noble parents. She learned the Psalter and the church service and wished to dedicate herself to God, but her parents married her against her will. Sixteen days after the wedding barbarians came to Aegina and killed her husband. Then she renewed her desire to become a nun, but a royal decree ordered that the widows and virgins of Aegina be married to gentiles, and so she took a second husband. She made prayers, distributed her wealth to the poor and in time persuaded her husband to become a monk, and he died a holy death. Now free, she distributed all she had and went with other women to an ascetic retreat and convent, where she became a nun. She ate only bread and water after the ninth hour and slept with her head on a stone. After four years she became abbess, but lived more humbly than all. // Later she went with the sisters and the priest Matthew to a quiet place, and then, out of necessity, to Constantinople with the eunuch presbyter Ignatios, where she stayed seven years. After a divine vision she returned to her ascetic retreat and announced to the sisters her repose twelve days beforehand. According to the text, at the time of the burial many possessed and sick were healed and afterwards many blind found their sight. She had foretold that she would receive her glory after forty days, and then two sisters saw two radiant men holding a royal garment of gold, pearls and precious stones to clothe the saint.

life|04-19||Άγιος Θεόδωρος ο Μάρτυρας και οι συν αυτώ μαρτυρήσαντες||Theodore was martyred in Perge in Pamphylia, in the time of the emperor Antoninus. He was one of the new recruits and, when the pagans made the others sacrifice, he tore up the decree and declared that he was sealed by his king Christ. They beat him and stretched him on a heated grill with pitch, sulphur and wax, but, according to the text, the earth split open, water came forth that put out the fire and he rose up unharmed. Before this the pagan priest Dioskoros believed and, after Theodore prayed for him, lay down himself on the grill and gave up his soul. They bound Theodore to a chariot, but the horses fell into a ravine and he remained untouched, and two soldiers, Socrates and Dionysios, testified that they saw a heavenly fiery chariot release him and carry him to the Praetorium. Then they threw him with his fellow martyrs into a furnace, where a dew kept them unharmed and they spoke as in a bridal chamber. // There Philippa, the mother of Theodore, who had been taken captive three years before, came from a foreign land and kissed him. The governor ordered Theodore to be crucified, the other martyrs in the furnace to be pierced with spears and Philippa to be beheaded, and so it was done. Theodore remained nailed to the cross three days alive and then died. Christians wrapped the relics with myrrh and linen cloths and buried them in a distinguished place.

life|04-19||Άγιος Γεώργιος ο Ομολογητής Επίσκοπος Πισιδίας||Saint George lived in the time of the iconoclasts and was dedicated to God from childhood. For his exceeding virtue he was ordained bishop of Pisidia. When the heresy of the iconoclasts arose in the Church and it was demanded that all hierarchs gather in Constantinople, he went too. Because he would not agree with the heretics nor deny the veneration of the holy icons, he was condemned to exile and hardship. There he spent the rest of his life and went to the Lord, to receive the crown of confession.

life|04-19||Άγιος Τρύφωνας Πατριάρχης Κωνσταντινουπόλεως||Tryphon lived in the time of the emperor Romanos, son of Constantine Porphyrogenitus, around 930. He was first a monk and became patriarch on the agreement that he would resign after a certain time, so that Theophylaktos, the emperor's son, might become patriarch. Because he did not wish to resign, he was driven from the throne by the craftiness and deceit of Theophanes of Caesarea, after being patriarch for two years and a few months. His memory is celebrated in the Great Church.

life|04-19||Όσιος Συμεών ηγούμενος της μονής Φιλοθέου Αγίου Όρους||The venerable Symeon, abbot of the monastery of Philotheou on Mount Athos, wore a single tunic and was without possessions. Later he departed from the Mountain and went to the regions of Zagora, Euripos, Attica and Larissa, preaching the word of God and bringing many to Christ. He stayed three years in a cave on a mountain of Zagora, where he gathered many brothers and built a monastery in the name of the Holy Trinity. He went to Constantinople and there fell asleep. After his repose his relics were found fragrant, and, according to the text, his skull, which is kept in the monastery of Zagora, pours forth healings for those who approach with faith.

life|04-20||Άγιοι Ακίνδυνος, Αντωνίνος, Βίκτωρ, Ζήνωνος, Ζωτικός, Θεωνάς, Καισάριος, Σεβηριανός και Χριστόφορος οι Μάρτυρες||These saints were martyred in the time of Diocletian, when the great martyr George was also arrested and tortured. Victor, Akindynos, Zotikos, Zeno and Severian saw George remain unharmed on the wheel and with one voice all five declared themselves Christians and were beheaded at once. Christopher, Theonas, Caesarius and Antoninus were bodyguards of the emperor and were present when he mercilessly tortured George and asked him to raise a dead man who had died long before by invoking Christ. When George by his prayer immediately raised the dead man, the four threw down their military belts and their arms before the emperor and in the theater and confessed Christ as true God. They were imprisoned and after a few days were hung and torn, burned with lit torches and finally thrown into the fire.

life|04-20||Όσιος Ιωάννης ο Παλαιολαυρίτης||The venerable John from a young age was wounded by longing for God and clung to Him. He left the luxury and pride of the present life, left his homeland and relatives as a stranger and took up the cross of the Lord. He reached Jerusalem, venerated the holy places and went to the monastery of the venerable Chariton, where he entered the spiritual struggles. After he had well accomplished every kind of virtue, he went to the Lord.

life|04-21||Άγιοι Ιανουάριος, Πρόκλος, Σώσσος, Φαύστος, Δησιδέριος, Ακούτιος και Ευτύχιος οι Μάρτυρες||These saints were martyred in the time of Diocletian, when in Campania in Italy the magistrate was Timothy. After various tortures they completed the course of martyrdom. The high priest Januarius was thrown into a furnace and, because he was preserved by the grace of Christ, they cut his sinews and so he finished his struggle. // Years passed and a widow, Maximina, lost her only son. Weeping, she saw above the door of the church a cloth with the icon of Saint Januarius. She remembered the prophet Elisha who raised the son of the Shunammite woman and placed the limbs of the icon upon the limbs of her son, begging the saint to have mercy on her grief. The saint, according to tradition, took pity and presented her son alive, and those who had gathered for the burial were left in amazement and glorified the Lord.

life|04-21||Αγία Αλεξάνδρα η βασίλισσα και οι θεράποντες αυτής Απολλώ, Ισαάκιος και Κοδράτος οι Μάρτυρες||Alexandra was the wife of the emperor Diocletian. She saw Saint George being tortured: he was struck in the belly with a spear without being harmed, was divided into pieces on the wheel with the iron blades and then became whole again and presented himself to the emperor, and so many believed in Christ. Seeing the miracles, Alexandra left the glory of the empire, believed in Christ and confessed herself a Christian before her husband, and was imprisoned. When the decision came that George should be beheaded and she with him, she learned of it in prison, prayed and gave up her soul to God. // Her three servants, Apollos, Isaac and Codratus, saw that she had despised the temporary kingdom and they believed too, and boldly rebuked the emperor, calling him lawless and beastly. He was enraged and imprisoned them, and in the morning ordered Codratus to be beheaded, while Apollos and Isaac were put in prison, where from hunger, after remaining many days without food and water, they gave up their souls to God.

life|04-21||Όσιος Αναστάσιος ο Ομολογητής ο Σιναΐτης||The venerable Anastasios left the world, took up his cross according to the commandment of the Lord, became a monk and followed Christ eagerly. Longing for greater struggles of virtue, he went to Jerusalem, venerated the holy places and came to Mount Sinai, where he stayed with monks who were practicing asceticism, subject to them and serving them. He became very humble-minded and received from God gifts of knowledge and wisdom, with which he wrote lives of holy fathers and composed soul-profiting discourses. He reached extreme old age and went to the Lord.

life|04-23||Άγιος Γλυκέριος ο Μάρτυρας ο γεωργός||He was a farmer and lived in the time of the emperor Diocletian.
