Saint George raised his dead ox, and Glykerios, confirmed in the faith of Christ by this miracle, confessed that he was a Christian. The unbelievers cut him to pieces with swords and so he received the crown of martyrdom.

life|04-24||Οσία Ελισάβετ η Θαυματουργός||The venerable Elizabeth entered the ascetic struggles from a very young age and, according to the text, received from the Lord the gift of healings and healed various afflictions and illnesses. She wore a single tunic and suffered from the cold and frost of winter, and never washed her body with water. She spent forty days fasting, did not taste oil for many years and did not wear shoes. For three years she kept her mind wholly fixed on God, and according to the text by her prayer she killed a huge poisonous snake. She reposed in the Lord and, according to the text, to this day she grants miracles and healings to those who run to her with faith, for even a little earth from her tomb, taken with reverence, cures every illness.

life|04-24||Άγιοι Πασικράτης και Βαλεντίων οι Μάρτυρες||They were soldiers from Dorostolon in Moesia, in a regiment of the region, and when they saw the inhabitants led astray by idolatry, they cared for the Christians who were in the prisons. For this they presented themselves publicly and declared themselves Christians, and were brought to the governor, who compelled them to sacrifice to the idols. Pasicrates spat on the idol of Apollo, and they threw them bound into prison, where he bore the chain like an ornament. When his brother Papianos begged him to sacrifice, he disowned him, stretched out his own hand over the fire and said that the flesh perishes, while the soul remains immortal. Valentio agreed with him and both were condemned to beheading. According to tradition, the mother of Pasicrates followed him and urged him to accept death willingly for Christ. Pasicrates was twenty-eight years old and Valentio thirty.

life|04-24||Άγιοι Δάναβος, Δημήτριος, Ευσέβιος, Λεόντιος, Λογγίνος, Νεστάβος, Νέων και Χριστόφορος οι Μάρτυρες||They were eight saints who, seeing the miracles of Saint George, believed in Christ and were imprisoned. Diocletian had ordered that all Christians, chiefly those in prison, sacrifice to the false gods. The eight saints did not obey; they were stripped, bound, beaten and hung up, so that their flesh fell to the ground and their entrails were exposed. In the end they were beheaded and received the crown of martyrdom. After their death, according to the text, healings pour forth for those who run to them with faith.

life|04-26||Άγιος Βασιλέας ο Ιερομάρτυρας Επίσκοπος Αμασείας||He was bishop of Amaseia in Pontus in the time of Licinius, around 317. The young Glaphyra, a maidservant of Constantia, wife of Licinius, escaped from the desire of Licinius and took refuge in Amaseia, giving Basileus her money to build a church. When Licinius learned of it, he ordered both to be arrested, but Glaphyra had already died, and so only Basileus was brought to Nicomedia. There he rebuked the false idols and despised them, and Licinius condemned him to death. They beheaded him on a ship and threw the head into the sea and the body to the other side, but, according to the text, they were joined together again and the saint was found whole by fishermen. An angel appeared to the Christian Elpidophoros, who together with the deacons Theotimos and Parthenios took the relics and brought them with honors to Amaseia.

life|04-26||Αγία Γλαφυρή||Glaphyra was a maidservant of Constantia, wife of Licinius. When she understood that Licinius desired her passionately, she revealed it to her mistress, who gave her money and sent her to the East. Wandering, she reached Amaseia, where the bishop was Saint Basileus, and gave him the money to build a church. When Licinius learned of it, he ordered both to be arrested, but Glaphyra had already died, and so only Basileus was brought before him.

life|04-27||Όσιος Ιωάννης ο Ομολογητής||The venerable John came from Eirenoupolis in the Decapolis and had Christian parents, Theodore and Gregoria, around 780. At the age of nine he became a monk in a cenobitic monastery and, because he was obedient and humble, his elder loved him, and with him he went to the Second Council of Nicaea in 783. He received the great schema and became a priest, and the emperor Nikephoros sent him as abbot of the monastery of the Katharoi, where he shepherded for more than ten years. When the persecution of the iconoclasts broke out, the emperor Leo the Armenian scattered the monks and brought him in chains to Constantinople, where the saint called him godless and was beaten with ox sinews. They imprisoned him and exiled him to the fortress of Pentadaktylos, where he remained in irons for eighteen months, and later in a prison at Kriotavros for two years. He was freed under Michael the Stammerer, but under Theophilos he was arrested again by the iconoclast patriarch, was exiled to the island of Aphousia and, after foretelling his death in three days, fell asleep in the Lord.

life|04-28||Άγιοι εννέα Μάρτυρες εν Κυζίκω||They were nine martyrs of Christ, who came from various places and were held by the pagans in Cyzicus. Questioned about their faith, they put the magistrate of Cyzicus to shame by their courage and exposed the error of the idols. They were punished with various tortures, but did not sacrifice to the idols and were beheaded with the sword. After their death, according to the text, they became a source of healings for those who approach them with faith.

life|04-28||Διήγηση γενομένου θαύματος εν Καρθαγένη Βορείου Αφρικής||In the time of the emperor Heraclius, around 625, a royal soldier of Carthage went with his wife to a suburb because of the plague and, led astray by the devil, committed adultery with the wife of his farmer. The plague struck him in the groin and he died. After three hours he began to cry out from the tomb, and when they opened it they found him alive. The pope of Africa Thalassios comforted him and after three days the man related that he had seen demons and two youths, who brought him up to heaven, where the toll houses examined his sins. At the gate of heaven the toll house of adultery overcame him and they brought him down to the place of sinners. He begged for time for repentance and his soul returned to the body. Afterwards he fasted forty days without food and water, weeping, and fell asleep again.

life|04-28||Όσιος Μέμνων ο Θαυματουργός||The venerable Memnon renounced the world for the love of God and lived in obedience and subjection, and for this he also became abbot of monks. He acquired meekness and love and became a wonderworker. According to the text, when locusts fell on the fields of the monastery, he made a prayer and drove them away, and drowned them in the river. By his prayer he brought forth water in a waterless place, which flows to this day. According to tradition, he appeared to sailors who were in danger from a storm, steered the ship and saved them. Having pleased God to the end, he went to Him.

life|04-29||Άγιοι Ιακισχόλος, Ιανουάριος, Ευφράσιος, Μάμμινος, Μαρσάλιος, Σατορνίνος και Φαυστιανός οι Μάρτυρες πρώην ληστές||They were seven chiefs of robbers who were imprisoned in Corfu when the apostles Jason and Sosipater taught them and, by their miracles, brought them to the faith of Christ, making them from wolves into sheep. Then they were thrown into heated cauldrons full of pitch, oil, wax and sulphur, and there they were perfected and received the crown of martyrdom.

life|04-29||Αγία Κέρκυρα η Μάρτυς||She was the daughter of the king Kerkyllinos. When she saw the apostles Jason and Sosipater bound in prison and learned that they were suffering for Christ, she proclaimed herself a Christian, distributed her ornaments to the poor and, despite her father's pressures, did not change her mind. They threw her into prison and handed her over to an Ethiopian to rape her, but he was torn apart by a beast as soon as he touched the door; Kerkyra healed him and taught him the faith, and he cried out that great is the God of the Christians. The soldiers lit a fire to burn her, but she remained unharmed and so brought many to the faith. In the end they hung her on a wooden beam, suffocated her with smoke and shot her with arrows; wounded by the arrows, she gave up her soul to God.

life|04-30||Άγιος Δονάτος Επίσκοπος Ευροίας||He was bishop of Euroia in Epirus in the time of Theodosius the Great, around 385. Near the city there was a spring, from which those who drank died. Donatos went there with his clergy and, according to the text, a dragon came out of the spring; the saint struck it with the rope of his donkey and killed it, and the Christians burned the beast. Then he blessed the spring and drank first of the water, and afterwards the others drank unharmed. Theodosius summoned him and the saint healed the only daughter of the emperor, who was tormented by a demon. He did not accept a reward, but asked for a place to build a church in his province. According to the text, he raised a dead man whom a creditor prevented from being buried, and when there was a drought in Constantinople, by his prayer he brought abundant rain, without being wet himself. While building the church and preparing his tomb, he fell asleep in deep old age.

life|05-01||Άγιος Βατάς ο Ιερομάρτυρας||Saint Batas came from Persia and had learned the faith in Christ from his ancestors. When he reached the age of thirty, he heard the Gospel word of the Lord that whoever does not hate father, mother, wife, children and his own life cannot be His disciple. Then he left worldly things, became a monk and surpassed everyone in fasting and self-control, guarding with care his senses and his heart. // When the Persians began a persecution against the Christians, his fellow monks withdrew, but he remained alone, for he longed for martyrdom. After thirty years of asceticism he was arrested by the fire-worshipers and brought to Yazdi, brother of Parmanavas and magistrate of the region of Vitzios. When he was ordered to worship the sun, he declared himself a Christian and ten soldiers stretched him so hard that his shoulders were dislocated; they beat him with thick staves and twenty soldiers dragged him bound along the ground. Because he remained steadfast in the faith, they put heavy stones on his belly and cut his back and the parts below his breasts with knives, and in the end they beheaded him.

life|05-01||Άγιος Φιλόσοφος ο Μάρτυρας||Saint Philosophos came from Alexandria, as Great Anthony related about him. The tyrant of the time ordered a decorated bed to be spread in a most beautiful garden of the city and they laid the saint on it on his back, with his hands and feet bound. Then they brought a prostitute, who not only with indecent words urged him to a shameful act, but embraced him and kissed him shamelessly. // He, though bound, found a way to be saved: he closed his eyes so as not to see her and bit his tongue with his teeth, so that the unbearable pain would leave the other senses of the body numb. He filled his mouth with blood and spat it on the face and clothes of the woman, who was frightened seeing the blood run like a river. Thus the saint conquered and was preserved passionless by the grace of Christ; afterwards he was beheaded and went crowned to the heavens.

life|05-03||Άγιοι Διόδωρος και Ροδοπιανός οι Μάρτυρες||Saints Diodoros and Rhodopianos lived, according to the text, in the time of the emperor Diocletian, around the year 302. For their faith in Christ they endured many painful afflictions and scourgings from their own fellow countrymen, in the city of Aphrodisias in Caria. In the end they were stoned by them and so gave up their souls to God, from whom they received the crowns of their struggle.

life|05-03||Άγιος Πέτρος Επίσκοπος Άργους||The venerable Peter was born in Constantinople of God-loving parents, who preferred that the whole family live the monastic life. Because his elder brothers, Paul and Dionysios, had first become monks, he too became a monk, together with his younger brother Plato, and surpassed his peers in the struggles of asceticism, so that the other monks also had him as a model. The then Patriarch Nicholas the Italian admired his virtue and learning and wished to honor him with the episcopate, but Peter would not accept; so the patriarch persuaded his brother Paul and ordained him archbishop of Corinth. Peter, to avoid the pressure, went with Paul to Corinth and stayed there a long time, but did not achieve his aim; when the bishop of Argos died, Christians came from Nauplion and Argos and begged Paul to ordain his brother Peter as their bishop, and he was finally compelled to accept. // As bishop he first took care for the good order of the priests and the church and opened his hand so wide in almsgiving that many times he gave to the poor even his shirt; he fed the orphans, helped the widows and freed captives from the hands of the powerful. In a time of famine in the Peloponnese he fed many thousands of people, and according to the text his jar of flour, after being emptied, was found again full in a miraculous manner. He healed a possessed girl, foretold in riddling terms a calamity that would strike the whole Peloponnese and foreknew the end of his life. He died at the age of seventy, and his holy relic, according to the text, pours forth most fragrant myrrh, drives out demons and heals illnesses.

life|05-04||Όσιος Ιλάριος ο Θαυματουργός||This venerable one from a young age took up the cross of the Lord and followed Him, subjecting the passions of the flesh to the spirit; therefore he received from God the gift of miracles. He healed many and various illnesses and drove demons out of people. Then he shut himself in a very narrow cell, where he lived far from all disturbance and noise, and, made radiant by dispassion, received the dignity of the priesthood. // According to the text, he stopped a plague of hail, drove away the animals that were destroying the crops, watered with rain the land that was dry from drought, and like Elisha and Joshua son of Nun he parted and crossed the currents of a river. He healed the withered hand of a Christian and strengthened the feet and limbs of the lame and paralyzed; and after performing many other miracles, he fell asleep in the Lord.

life|05-04||Όσιος Νικηφόρος ηγούμενος της μονής Μηδικίου||The venerable Nikephoros lived in the time of the iconoclasts. Because from infancy he loved Christ, seeing the heresy of the iconoclasts growing strong, he left the world and became a monk. He withdrew to the mountains and lived in stillness with fasts, vigils and prayer for the peace of the world. // When the heresy somewhat subsided, after many entreaties of the monks he became abbot of the monastery of Medikion, near Mountania. But the heresy flared up again under the impious Leo the Armenian, in the year 814, and the saint was exiled from his monastery, as a venerator of the holy icons and faithful to the traditions of the Apostles and of the divine Fathers. He suffered bitter exiles and was shut in a very dark prison, where, after wrestling against the heresy like a steadfast contender, he went to Christ whom he himself had longed for.

life|05-07||Άγιος Ακάκιος ο Μάρτυρας ο κεντυρίων||Saint Acacius came from Cappadocia and was a soldier, under the emperor Maximian, around the year 280. He presented himself before the magistrate of Cappadocia Firmus, confessed the name of Christ and was tortured by him with many tortures. Firmus sent him to another magistrate, Bibianos, who brought him to Byzantium together with other bound Christians; there he mauled him with harsh scourgings and twistings and threw him into prison, where, according to the text, angels of God appeared and healed him. // Then he was sent to another magistrate, Falcianos, who ordered the saint to be beheaded. His synaxis is held in his martyr's church at Heptaskalon, where the dedication of the church is also celebrated at the same time.

life|05-07||Άγιος Κοδράτος ο Μάρτυρας και οι συν αυτώ αθλήσαντες εν Νικομηδεία||Saint Codratus lived in Nicomedia in the time of Decius and Valerian, around 253. For his faith he was arrested by the pagans together with many other Christians and handed over to the proconsul Perinios, magistrate of Nicomedia. When asked about his family and homeland, he answered that he was a Christian, a servant of Christ, with the Jerusalem above as his city; the proconsul was angry and beat him with dry oxhide whips, and then threw him into prison. // At Nicaea Codratus, seeing Christians who out of fear of tortures were ready to sacrifice to the idols, reminded them of the fear of God and the day of judgment and strengthened them in the faith, while they themselves were given over to the fire. He entered the temple of the idols and shattered them, and for this they hung him and tore him. In Apameia they put him in a sack and beat him, and in Caesarea they dragged him and beat him again. In Apollonia they poured salt with vinegar on his wounds, rubbed him with hair cloths and put heated irons to his sides; then, at Roundakos and Hermoupolis, since he could not walk, they carried him in a cart. They stretched him on a heated grill with hot oil and pitch, but he said that he regarded this torture as luxury and rest, and the fire did not touch him; then the proconsul condemned him, and the saint was beheaded and received the crown of martyrdom.

life|05-07||Άγιοι Ρουφίνος και Σατορνίνος οι Μάρτυρες||Rufinus and Saturninus believed in Christ in Caesarea, at the time when the proconsul was carrying Saint Codratus about with him and tormenting him. They were hung and torn and in the end beheaded, and so received the crowns of their struggle.

life|05-07||Όσιος Ιωάννης ο Ψυχαΐτης||The blessed John from a young age imitated the life of John the Baptist and of the prophet Elijah and spent his life in hardship and asceticism. He conquered with courage the wars of the demons, was cleansed in soul by streams of tears and propitiated God with all-night vigils. With his tears, as the text says, he dried up the rivers of the heresy of the iconoclasts: he venerated and honored the icon of the Lord and of all the saints, while he loathed the opinions of the iconoclasts and ridiculed them. // In defense of the traditions of the Fathers he despised the laws of the emperors and endured with courage bitter exiles and prisons, and so struggled the same struggle as the saints and received the same crown. He had received from the Lord the gift of miracles and healings and healed the bodies and souls of the sick.

life|05-07||Άγιος Μάξιμος ο Μάρτυρας||The blessed Maximos confessed Christ boldly and led many Greeks to piety. For this reason he first endured many punishments. In the end he was stoned and, surrounded in a certain way by the stones as by a crown, he departed to the Lord to receive from Him the crown of the struggle.

life|05-09||Αγίες Ακυλίνα και Καλλινίκη οι Μάρτυρες||Aquilina and Kallinike were two beautiful but licentious women, whom the emperor Decius sent to Saint Christopher, to lead him into carnal desire and make him deny Christ. But the saint catechized them and turned them away from the worship of idols. When they presented themselves before the emperor and confessed that they were Christians, they were subjected to tortures and roasted on spits from the feet to the shoulders. After enduring this terrible martyrdom with courage, both received the crown of martyrdom.

life|05-09||Άγιοι Επίμαχος και Γορδιανός οι Μάρτυρες||Epimachos and Gordian came from Rome. Because they confessed Christ publicly, they were arrested and the magistrate tried to compel them to deny Him and sacrifice to the idols. They were not persuaded and were tortured with various tortures, and then they were beheaded and received the crown of martyrdom. Their synaxis is held in the church of the holy martyr Stratonikos.

life|05-09||Άγιος Νικόλαος ο Οσιομάρτυρας ο Νέος ο εν Βουνένοις||Nicholas came from the regions of the East and was born of noble and God-fearing parents. From youth he avoided the company of his peers and loved the company of elders and prudent people. When he grew up, he enlisted in the royal army, distinguished himself by his courage and the emperor made him duke of a province. He was sent with others to fight the rebels of Thessaly and defeated the Thessalonians, but at Larissa the Romans were defeated and he, seeing his life in danger, withdrew from the war, despised the world and went to the mountain of Vounena, where he became a monk among hesychasts. When the Avars came down to Larissa and the surrounding places and compelled the Christians to deny Christ, an angel warned the venerable one and his twelve fellow ascetics that they would soon be martyred. The Avars came to the skete, tortured and beheaded the other monks, but Nicholas, because he was handsome and prudent, they tried first to win over. Because he remained steadfast in the faith, they beat him much, bound him to a tree and shot him with arrows, pierced him with a spear and in the end put him to death. According to the text, his relics remained unburied on the mountain, kept unharmed by angels, and later were revealed by a miracle and heal to this day those who approach with faith.

life|05-10||Όσιος Ησύχιος ο Ομολογητής||Hesychios was a good and peaceful man, and like his name, so was his life quiet. He asked the Lord to show him a place to live in stillness and to please Him, and by divine revelation he received a command to go down to the coast and settle on a mountain called Maion. He stayed there many years. Then he departed and went near water, built a small church of Saint Andrew and lived the rest of his life in patience and asceticism. He performed many miracles and departed to the Lord.

life|05-11||Άγιος Μώκιος ο Ιερομάρτυρας||Mokios lived in the time of Diocletian, around 288. His parents, Euphratios and Eustathia, were noble and wealthy from old Rome. He was a priest of the Church of Amphipolis, which later was named Christoupolis, and taught constantly, preaching Christ. When the proconsul Laodikios offered sacrifice to the false god Dioskoros, Mokios went and overturned the altar. He was arrested and confessed Christ as true God. They hung him and tore his head, jaws and sides and then threw him into a furnace with pitch and tow, where the flame rose high. According to the text, the fire did not touch him even on the hairs of his head: those who stood outside saw him walking in the furnace together with three glorious men, while the flame that burst out burned the proconsul and nine of his men. // Then he was imprisoned by the governor Thalassios. When another proconsul came and could not persuade him, they bound him to two wheels, where he was crushed and torn to pieces, but was released by a miracle. They threw him to the beasts and he was kept unharmed by them, so that the people cried out that he should be set free. He was sent to the magistrate Philippesios in Perinthos of Thrace, which today is called Heraclea, and from there to Byzantium, where he was condemned and beheaded, receiving a double crown, as priest and as martyr. His relics were buried at first one mile outside the city. Later Constantine the Great built a splendid church in his name and transferred them there, where his synaxis is also held.

life|05-11||Άγιος Διόσκορος ο Νέος||Dioskoros came from the great city of Smyrna. For his faith in Christ he was brought before the magistrate and proclaimed that he was a Christian, whereupon they threw him into prison. He was questioned a second time and because he persisted in the same faith, the magistrate ordered him beheaded. Thus the blessed one received the crown of martyrdom.

life|05-13||Άγιος Λαοδίκιος ο Μάρτυρας ο δεσμοφύλακας||Laodikios was the jailer of Saint Glykeria. He saw the miracle, according to the text, when an angel of the Lord loosed the saint from her bonds and healed her head, and he was left astounded. He confessed Christ and was beheaded, receiving the crown of martyrdom.

life|05-13||Όσιος Σέργιος ο Ομολογητής||Sergios came from a glorious and great family and was great also in soul. He lived in the time of the iconoclast emperor Theophilos, around 835. Because he venerated the holy icons, they bound him by the neck with a rope, led him around the middle of the marketplace and he suffered insults and contempt. They took all his possessions, threw him into prison and then exiled him together with his wife Irene and his children. He endured with courage the afflictions of exile and, when God called him, he departed by death to receive the incorruptible crown of confession.

life|05-13||Άγιος Παυσίκακος Επίσκοπος Συνάδων||Pausikakos lived in the time of the emperor Maurice, around 585. His homeland was Apameia, which lies on the Black Sea, and his parents were noble and faithful Christians. From youth he subdued his body with exceeding fasting and prayer and became a monk. He ate a little bread and water, also practiced the art of medicine and healed bodies and souls together: he drove out demons, healed children who were born deformed and straightened those who were hunchbacked. Because of his great fame, the then Patriarch of Constantinople Kyriakos learned of him and ordained him bishop of Synada. // There he drove out the heretics, the wolves of the flock, and with the knife of teaching cut them off from the healthy body of the Christians. He went to Constantinople and healed the emperor Maurice of some affliction, and he, by a golden bull, ordered that one litra of gold be given every year to Synada. On his return, according to the text, by his prayer water gushed forth to quench the thirst of his fellow travelers. After becoming a cause of salvation for many, he passed to the other life.

life|05-14||Άγιος Θεράποντας ο Ιερομάρτυρας Επίσκοπος Κύπρου||The text acknowledges that we do not know where Therapon came from, who his parents were, nor in what time and before which governors he confessed Christ, because the records of his life were lost with time. According to the old tradition that has come down to us, he was a monk, as his icons also show, became bishop of Cyprus, came to Christ with his blood and finished with a martyr's struggle. His relics were transferred to Constantinople when the Hagarenes were planning to plunder Cyprus; then the saint appeared to those who had the relics and commanded them to transfer them there. According to the text, there where it lies it has always poured forth springs of miracles for those who approach with faith.

life|05-16||Άγιοι Αυδάς, Αυδιησούς, Βενιαμίν και άλλοι τριάντα οκτώ Μάρτυρες||Abdiesous was bishop in a city of Persia, Bethasachar. His own nephew denounced him to the king of the Persians for not obeying the doctrine of the Persians but revering Christ, and so he was brought before the king with many priests, deacons, monks and nuns. He confessed boldly Christ as true God and all were sent to Arsath, brother of the king. Because they persisted in the faith, they bound them with ropes and tightened them so hard, seven times a day, that their bones were crushed and their crackling was heard. They threw them into prison and they refused to eat the foods from the sacrifices of the idols; a God-fearing woman gave them bread and water. The bishop of the city of Bethasagar, Abdas, to whom God had revealed that he would be martyred, was also arrested. All were sent to the high priest of the Persians Maptes, before whom they affirmed their faith in Christ. They were beaten hard and beheaded, and a few days later the holy Abdiesous was also beheaded, and so all received the crown of the struggle.

life|05-17||Άγιοι Παμφαμήρ, Παμφυλών και Σολόχων οι Μάρτυρες||They were soldiers from Egypt, in the time of the emperor Maximian, around 298, and served under the tribune Campanos together with a thousand other soldiers. In Chalcedon Campanos compelled the soldiers to sacrifice to the idols and all obeyed, except the three, Solochon, Pamphamer and Pamphylon, who declared themselves Christians and that they would remain in the faith until death. They were beaten so much that their backs were split, and in the midst of the martyrdom Pamphamer and Pamphylon gave up their souls to God. Solochon was strengthened a little, called upon Christ and reproached Campanos for his ignorance. He ordered his mouth to be opened with a sword and wine from the sacrifices to be poured in; the saint bit the sword and bit off a piece of it, broke his bonds as well and, according to the text, heard a voice from heaven strengthening him. // Then they dragged him bound by the feet over rough tiles, hung him by the right hand from a beam with a heavy stone tied to the left foot, from the sixth to the tenth hour, without his denying Christ. When they cut the rope, he stood upright. In the evening Campanos, angry, thrust a reed into his ear and pushed it to the inside of his head. Christians took him on a stretcher to the house of a widow, where the saint ate a little bread, blessed those present and gave up his soul to God.

life|05-18||Άγιοι Πέτρος, Διονύσιος, Ανδρέας, Παύλος, Χριστίνα, Ηράκλειος, Παυλίνος και Βενέδιμος οι Μάρτυρες||Peter came from Lampsakos and was brought before Decius, magistrate of Abydos, who commanded him to sacrifice to Aphrodite. Because he confessed Christ, they crushed him over his whole body with chains, wood and wheels and he gave up his spirit. Paul and Andrew came from Mesopotamia and were soldiers under the same Decius, with whom they went to Athens. There Dionysios and Saint Christina were arrested and imprisoned. Paul and Andrew, seeing that Christina was a virgin and beautiful, urged her to a shameful act, but she did not yield and, instead of raping her, they were changed by her admonitions and believed in Christ. For this the three men were stoned, while Christina, falling upon them, was beheaded. // Heraclius, Paulinus and Venedimus were from Athens and preached the Gospel, urging the pagans to turn away from the error of the idols. They were arrested and handed over to the magistrate, were beaten hard and suffered many other punishments, then were thrown into a lit furnace and, because the power of God kept them unharmed, were finally beheaded and received the crown of martyrdom.

life|05-18||Αγίες Αλεξανδρία, Ευφρασία, Θεοδότη, Ιουλία, Κλαυδία, Ματρώνα, Τεκούσα και Φαεινή οι Παρθενομάρτυρες||These virgins were from Ancyra in Galatia. Saint Theodotos, who had a wife but did not neglect piety, bought wheat and loaves, offered first fruits to God and distributed them to the poor, because the magistrate of Ancyra, Theoteknos, had ordered that the foods sold to Christians be defiled with libations of the idols. He visited the prisons and strengthened in the faith the imprisoned Christians; on one visit he found the virgins, of whom Tekousa was his aunt according to the flesh. // The virgins were led before the magistrate and, because they refused to sacrifice, were given to the soldiers to be dishonored, but by the grace of Christ they remained unharmed and uncorrupted. They bound them with stones and sank them in the lake, and so they received the crown of the struggle. Christians, among them Theodotos, took their relics and buried them with honor. Theodotos was accused before the Greeks and, while they were searching for him, he presented himself of his own accord. He confessed Christ as God, they hung him up high and tore him, poured vinegar and salt on his wounds and in the end beheaded him. The magistrate also took the relics of the holy virgins out of their tombs and burned them.

life|05-19||Άγιος Ακόλουθος ο Μάρτυρας||Akolouthos lived in the time of the emperor Maximian, around 290, and came from the Thebaid of Egypt, from Hermoupolis. For his faith and confession in Christ he was brought to the governor of the region and was neither deceived by flatteries nor frightened by threats. Therefore they first hung a heavy stone from his neck and then condemned him to be put to death by fire. Thrown into it, he received the crown of martyrdom.

life|05-20||Άγιος Ασκλάς ο Μάρτυρας||Asklas came from the Thebaid of Egypt. He was accused before the governor Arrian for his faith in Christ and, after he confessed boldly, they hung him, tore his sides and threw him into prison. When the governor was crossing the Nile in a small boat, the saint prayed that he would not come ashore before confessing in writing the divinity of Christ, and, according to the text, the boat was held strangely and could not sail. The text breaks off at this point, but its title says that he was perfected by being cast into the river.

life|05-20||Όσιοι Ιωάννης, Ιωσήφ και Νικήτας||These venerable ones came from Chios and lived under the emperors Michael the Paphlagonian, Michael the Caulker and until Constantine Monomachos (around 1042). They left the world and went up to the mountain Provateion of Chios, where they practiced asceticism in a cave, eating a little bread and drinking water once a week. At night they saw a light, and when they set fire to the place, a myrtle tree remained entire and unburnt; upon it they found an icon of the Theotokos without the Infant. They took it to their cave, but the icon returned again to the myrtle, and so they built there a small church to the Theotokos. // When Constantine Monomachos was exiled in Mytilene, Nikitas and Joseph went and comforted him, foretelling that he would soon reign, and he promised to do for them whatever they asked. They asked for a church and monastery at the place of the icon; Constantine gave them his ring as a pledge, and when he became emperor, after a reminder, he built in twelve years the Nea Moni of Chios and endowed it with estates and privileges. The venerable ones died peacefully at different times and were buried in a place called Phialion; their relics are preserved to this day and, according to the text, miracles take place for those who run to them with faith.

life|05-22||Άγιος Ιωάννης ο Θαυματουργός του Βλαδιμήρου||Saint John came from a village of Bulgaria called Vladimir and was therefore named Vladimir. He was the son of Deeman, grandson of the first king of the Bulgarians Symeon, and of Anna, of the Romans, and flourished in the time of Basil the Macedonian. From childhood he was educated by Nicholas, bishop of Achrida; his parents betrothed him to the daughter of king Samuel, but he kept his virginity. After the death of his parents he became sovereign king of the Triballi (Serbs), sent preachers and teachers, built monasteries, churches, guesthouses and hospitals. // One day while hunting he saw an eagle with a shining cross on its neck, which was an angel of the Lord; in that place he built a church and prayed there seven times a day. The queen suspected him and her brother, on returning him victorious from a war, suddenly struck him with the sword. The king gave him his own sword to behead him, as he was dying for the faith. According to the text, after the beheading he took his head in his hands upon the horse, hymning God, while the murderer went mad and ate his own flesh. When he gave up his spirit, psalmody was heard and the place was filled with fragrance; many sick who kissed the relic were healed. They built a church in his name, which was later renovated by Charles, nephew of the king of the Franks, and the relic was transferred to the monastery that he himself had built, where myrrh flows and miracles take place.

life|05-24||Άγιος Μελέτιος ο στρατηλάτης και οι συν αυτώ Μάρτυρες||Saint Meletios and his companions (among them John, Stephen, Serapion, the magician Kallinikos, twelve tribunes and counts, women with their children, and in all many martyrs) were martyred in the time of the emperor Antoninus Heliogabalus and of the governor Maximus, around 218. Meletios with Christian soldiers went to the temple of the idols and by prayer overthrew them and turned them to dust; the governor arrested them and, because they would not sacrifice, beat them, nailed their feet and tortured them in many ways, without their appearing to feel pain. // In the end Meletios was hung on a pine tree and completed his martyrdom, while Stephen and John were beheaded. Serapion, who came from Egypt, believed in Christ from the miracles he saw, received from an angel ordination as bishop and was beheaded together with the magician Kallinikos, who also believed because the deadly potion he had given to Meletios did not kill him. The counts and tribunes were thrown into a lit furnace; the women Sosanna, Markiane and Palladia were cut down with clubs together with their infants, and two small children, Kyriakos and Christian, who answered that Christ is the greatest god, were beheaded. Their synaxis is held in the church of the holy martyr Plato in the forecourts of Domninos.

life|05-27||Άγιος Ελλάδιος ο Ιερομάρτυρας||Saint Helladios became a hierarch and was entrusted with the helm of the Church of Christ. As shepherd he drove from the flock the heretics and impious, and as helmsman he kept the "ship" of the Church safe from the waves and the contrary winds. When the tyrant of that time brought him before him, he confessed piety boldly and was condemned to many tortures, with his body torn. According to the text, Christ appeared to him and healed his wounds, making him more willing for the following tortures. // The tyrant was angered and threw him into a fire, where he remained unburnt by the grace of God and brought many unbelievers to the faith. Later, severely punished and beaten, he gave up his soul to God and received the crown of martyrdom.

life|05-27||Άγιος Θεράπων ο Ιερομάρτυρας||Saint Therapon became a priest in the city of Sardis because of his conduct and, because he taught the faith of Christ, the magistrate Valerian arrested him, bound him and tortured him. They brought him bound to Sinao and to Ancyra in Galatia; at the river Astelis they stretched him on his back and crushed him with rods. According to the text, the earth that was watered by his blood brought forth a great oak, which remains evergreen to this day and heals all diseases. // From there they transferred him to the region of the Thrakesians, near the river Hermos, where the bishopric of Attala is, subject to the metropolitan of Sardis. After enduring many terrible tortures, he was beheaded and received the unfading crown of martyrdom.

life|05-28||Αγία Ελικωνίς η Μάρτυς||Saint Heliconis lived in the time of the emperors Gordian and Philip (around 238) and came from Thessaloniki. She was arrested as a Christian and brought to the duke of Corinth Perinios; because she did not sacrifice to the idols but preached Christ as true God, they bound her and threw her down, melted lead, asphalt and pitch and put her in, but she came out unharmed. Then they shaved her head for shame and set fire to her whole body. // She entered the temple of the idols and by prayer overthrew the statues of Athena, Zeus and Asklepios, and for this they cut off her breasts. Before the successor of Perinios, the proconsul Justin, she did not agree to sacrifice and they threw her into a lit furnace; when the flame did not touch her, they stretched her on a heated bronze bed, where the archangels Michael and Gabriel healed her flesh. They threw her to the beasts, which did not touch her but killed one hundred and twenty servants of the proconsul; finally she was beheaded and ascended crowned to heaven.

life|05-29||Άγιος Ολβιανός ο Ιερομάρτυρας και οι μαθητές αυτού||Saint Olbianos, a bishop, lived in the time of the emperor Maximian, around 301, and for his faith in Christ was brought before the governors of Asia. When the temple wardens Agrippinos and Clement offered sacrifices to the false goddess Rhea, Olbianos was compelled to sacrifice to her; but he, with many arguments, exalted the faith of Christ and humbled the worship of idols. For this they burned his back and his inward parts with heated spits, and because he would not sacrifice even to the sun, the proconsul ordered him to be beaten without mercy with rods. // The servants lit a great fire and threw into it the athlete of Christ together with his disciples; thus he was perfected by fire and received the crown of the struggle. According to the text, he performed many miracles also in his life, and after his repose his honorable relic works miracles for those who run to it with faith.

life|06-02||Άγιος Έρασμος ο Ιερομάρτυρας και οι συν αυτώ μαρτυρήσαντες||According to the text, he came from Antioch and lived in the time of Diocletian and Maximian, around 290. From early on he lived an ascetic life and reached such perfection that, according to tradition, ravens fed him; with many gifts of God he became, against his will, a hierarch. He went about everywhere preaching the Gospel and working miracles, and in one city he raised a dead child, and baptized his father Anastasios and many others. When the emperor brought him to the temple of Zeus, the saint prayed and the bronze idol was shattered; from inside came a fearsome dragon that destroyed many people, and twenty thousand people believed and were baptized by him. // Those baptized were beheaded, but the saint was clothed in a heated bronze garment and the fire became cold like crystal; he was imprisoned and the archangel Michael freed him and brought him to Campania. There he preached and in the city of Hermelia he lived until his end, asking God for forgiveness of sins and eternal life for those who call upon him with faith. His relics are in the church of the Holy Apostles.

life|06-03||Όσιος Αθανάσιος ο Θαυματουργός||He came from the country of the Cyrrhaeans and was the son of parents of modest origin and wealth. At a mature age he became disgusted with the world and went out into the desert, following the Gospel way with a single tunic, and meeting spiritual men he gathered their virtues. A monk, a former magistrate of the imperial senate, brought him to his monastery and Athanasios by his bearing and his words brought to the fear of God the harsh monks there. Later he went to the monastery of Trajan, received the great schema and became a priest, served the liturgy, copied books in calligraphy and fasted daily until evening. // Through pure obedience and the confession of his thoughts he was freed from the passions and reached dispassion. Because the much writing harmed his eyes, he shut himself in a narrow cell and prayed to see again, promising to give to the poor whatever he earned from the books; his request was heard and he distributed to the poor all the money from the work of twenty-eight years, about nine hundred florins. He always stayed in his cell and came out only on Saturday and Sunday. // He fell asleep in deep old age, and according to the text a spiritual saint saw the apostles Andrew and John accompanying him to heaven. He had prophesied various things while he lived and, after his death, performed countless miracles.

life|06-04||Οσία Σοφία εξ Αίνου||She came from Ainos and was the daughter of pious and distinguished parents. When she came of age, her parents married her to a lawful husband, with whom she had children; and yet, amid the cares of the world, she showed by her works that these do not hinder whoever keeps the commandments of the Lord. She was not absent from church, kept vigil and prayed in her house, and when her children died she became a mother of orphans and a help of the aged. She distributed her possessions to the poor and lived ascetically, eating dry bread and drinking water. // She had great almsgiving and humility, and according to the text a vessel of wine that she distributed to the poor always remained full; but when she revealed the miracle to a relative, the vessel did not fill again and she was very grieved and increased her asceticism. She lived more than fifty-three years, thirty-four of them as an ascetic, and in the end she became a nun and died.

life|06-05||Άγιοι Απόλλων, Άρειος, Γοργίας, Ειρήνη, Λεωνίδης, Μαρκιανός, Νίκανδρος, Παμβών, Σεληνιάς και Υπερέχιος οι Μάρτυρες||These ten martyrs kept the faith in Christ and confessed Him as true God. Therefore, by order of the magistrate of Egypt, they were tortured so much by hunger, thirst and cold that they gave up their souls to God and received from Him the crowns of the athletic contest.

life|06-06||Όσιος Άτταλος ο Θαυματουργός||He left the world and all that belongs to it and became a monk, practicing asceticism with fasting, vigil and every hardship: he ate once every two or three days, often every five. He never lay on his side, but sitting or standing took a little sleep, as much as nature required. For his labors he received much grace from the Lord and was enriched with miracles, and showed great sympathy not only to people but also to animals. When the hour of his death came, he asked those present to give him the last kiss in Christ and gave up his soul to God.

life|06-06||Αγίες Βαλερία, Κυρία, Μάρθα Μαρία και Μαρκία οι Παρθενομάρτυρες||These five virgins came from Caesarea in Palestine, were taught piety by a Christian, believed in Christ and were baptized. From then on they lived quietly in a house with great reverence, devoted to fasting, prayer and vigil, and begged God that the error of the idols be extinguished and the faith of the Christians shine throughout the world. Although hidden, they were denounced to the magistrate of Caesarea and, because they would not sacrifice to the idols, they were subjected to harsh tortures and finished their martyrdom, receiving the crowns of the struggle.

life|06-06||Άγιος Γελάσιος ο Μάρτυρας||When the persecution of the pagans against the Christians broke out, he was filled with divine zeal, distributed all his possessions to the poor, put on a white garment and went to the martyrs of Christ. Seeing them tortured in various ways, he kissed their wounds, asked for their prayers and urged them to stand courageous in martyrdom. For this the pagans seized him and led him to the magistrate, before whom he confessed Christ as true God and said that the idols are deaf and insensible. The magistrate at first despised him, then struck him a little and finally ordered his head to be cut off, and so he received from the Lord the unfading crown of martyrdom.

life|06-07||Αγία Ποταμιαίνη εξ Αλεξανδρείας||In the time of Maximian she was the slave of a licentious master in Alexandria and very beautiful. Her master tried repeatedly to persuade her to a shameful act and, because he did not succeed, he became angry and handed her over to the magistrate of Alexandria, asking him to force her to yield. The magistrate tortured her in various ways, but did not persuade her, and decided to throw her into a cauldron full of boiling pitch. // The saint made him swear by the head of the emperor to lower her into the cauldron little by little and not abruptly, to see how much patience Christ would give her. So they lowered her gradually over three hours, and she prayed to God alive in the pitch, until even her head was covered; those present marveled at the power of Christ and the patience of the maiden. In this way she completed her martyrdom.

life|06-07||Άγιος Λυκαρίων ο Μάρτυρας||He came from the city of Hermoupolis in Egypt. He was arrested for faith in Christ and, brought before the magistrate, refused to renounce Him; they threw him into a dark and foul prison and after a few days brought him out, tore him with irons, nailed him to a cross and beat him and burned him in all his limbs. They threw him into a lit furnace, where he remained three days kept unharmed by the grace of God, and they forced him to drink deadly potions that remained without effect. According to the text, because of this he drew to the faith the man who had made the potions, who was beheaded and received the crown of martyrdom. They cut the sinews of the saint, put him in a lit cauldron, flayed the skin of his head and in the end beheaded him, and he too received the unfading crown.

life|06-08||Άγιοι Νίκανδρος και Μαρκιανός οι Μάρτυρες||Because they confessed the faith in Christ, they were examined by the governor Maximus and imprisoned; twenty days later they came out of prison. When they again refused to renounce Christ, they tore them with iron claws, hung them on upright beams, pierced them with irons, burned them with fire, stretched them on coals and beat them, poured vinegar on their wounds and rubbed them with tiles, and crushed their mouths and faces with stones. // The wife of Nikandros followed him and encouraged him in martyrdom, while the wife of Markianos did the opposite, weeping and showing him their child. Markianos took the child, raised his eyes to heaven and told the Lord to take care of it Himself; he kissed the child and his wife and ran on the way of martyrdom. They cut out their tongues with knives and in the end beheaded them, and so they received the crowns.

life|06-08||Αγία Καλλιόπη η Μάρτυς||She lived in the time of the emperor Decius, around 250, and excelled in beauty of soul and body. The pagans seized her and compelled her to deny the faith in Christ, but because she resisted with strength, they beat her mercilessly and cut off her breasts; according to the text, an angel of the Lord appeared and healed them. Then they dragged her over pounded tiles, burned her with fire and sprinkled salt on her burned flesh, rubbing it with hair cloths. In the end they beheaded her and the blessed one ascended victorious to heaven.

life|06-09||Αγίες Μάρθα, Μαρία, Μαριάμνη, Θέκλα και Ενναθά οι Οσιομάρτυρες||In the time of Shapur, king of the Persians, around 330, there lived near a village the priest Paul, a wealthy man, who had with him five canonesses, that is, virgin nuns adorned with virtues, and he served the liturgy and chanted with them. The devil, who could not bear their spiritual progress, urged a Persian to denounce the priest to the chief magus of the king as a wealthy Christian. The chief magus brought him with the virgins and, to take his wealth, compelled him to worship the sun and eat the blood of sacrifices; the wretched Paul, overcome by avarice, obeyed. // The chief magus then had him urge the virgins also to do the same, but they spat in his face, called him a second Judas and declared that they worship only the Lord Jesus Christ. They were beaten mercilessly for many hours and then, by decision of the chief magus, Paul himself went to behead them; they prophesied that he would lose soul and wealth and, after praying, were beheaded by him. At night the servants of the chief magus strangled Paul with a rope, he took all his money, and the prediction of the holy women was fulfilled.

life|06-10||Άγιος Νεανίσκος ο Μάρτυρας ο Σοφώτατος||When Maximus was governor in Alexandria and was persecuting the Christians, Neaniskos appeared before him, a most wise and handsome athlete of Christ, who had been betrayed by his maidservant. The governor tortured him for seven days to make him deny Christ and, seeing that he could not persuade him, issued a sentence of death. The martyr went joyfully to his martyrdom, followed by a great crowd, and with them the maidservant who had betrayed him; the saint motioned to her to come near, gave her a gold ring and told her that he thanked her, because by her betrayal she had sent him to such great blessings. At the place of condemnation he prayed and was beheaded, receiving the crown of his struggle.

life|06-10||Άγιος Τιμόθεος ο Ιερομάρτυρας Επίσκοπος Προύσης||He lived in the time of Julian the Apostate, around 361, and governed his Church well, shepherding the people. He had from God the power and grace to work miracles, and he killed a great dragon that dwelt in a cave on the public road between Prusa and the hot springs, poisoning men and animals with its breath, so that the road was impassable. A Christian queen from Apollonias of Bithynia wished to come to Prusa, and the brethren of the region sent Timothy blessings and gifts in a sacred vestment to take to her. When the dragon sprang out against him, the saint wrapped the blessings in the edge of his pallium and threw the vestment upon the dragon; on his return he found it dead and glorified God. // The miracle spread everywhere, and Julian, who learned of it, sent a man to press him to deny Christ. Timothy confessed Christ as true God, was beheaded and received the crown of martyrdom. His memory is celebrated in his church, in the hostel of Euagos, at the place called Deuteron.

life|06-10||Όσιος Κανίδης ο εκ Καππαδοκίας||He lived in the time of Theodosius the Great, around 379, the son of pious parents, Theodotos and Theophano, in the land of Cappadocia. According to the text, his mother did not eat rich foods during the nine months of her pregnancy, and when the infant was born he nursed only from the right breast and, if she ate more than she should, not even from that. After his seventh year he left everything, went to the mountain and shut himself in a small cave, where he fasted and prayed, eating a few raw vegetables without salt once a week. He lived there seventy-three whole years; because the cave sloped downward and the south winds blew into it, the hair of his head and beard fell out from the dampness. Living in this way, he died.

life|06-10||Όσιοι Θεοφάνης και Πανσέμνη||Theophanes came from Antioch, born of unbelieving parents, and soon came to the faith of Christ. At fifteen he married and lived three years with his wife, and when she died he was baptized and shut himself in a narrow cell near Antioch, purifying himself of the passions. Learning of a public prostitute, Pansemne, who was the cause of ruin for many, he prayed, left his cell, put on costly clothes and, taking ten pounds of gold from his father, went to her, promised her a chaste marriage and gave her the gold. He built another cell near his own and told her that she must become a Christian in order for them to live together. // After seven days of instruction, and hearing of the judgment to come, she was enlightened and moved to compunction; she was baptized, freed her slaves, made sacred vessels and treasures from her money and dedicated them to God, and entered the cell that Theophanes had prepared for her. She advanced so far in virtue that she cast out demons and healed illnesses by her prayer. She lived there one year and two months and died together with the venerable and wonderworking Theophanes.

life|06-12||Αγία Αντωνίνα η Μάρτυς||She came from Nicaea of Bithynia and lived in the time of the emperors Diocletian and Maximian, around 302. She was brought before the governor Priscillian for her confession of faith in Christ and was beaten on the chest. She was then imprisoned, brought again before the governor, hung on a wooden frame and burned on her sides, and they stretched her out on a red-hot grill. They pierced her hands and ankles with red-hot spits, and from her hands, according to the text, a sweet fragrance poured forth. She remained in prison, afflicted, for whole years, and finally they took her out and threw her into the sea, where she received the crown of martyrdom.

life|06-12||Όσιος Πέτρος ο εν τω Αγίω Όρει ασκήσας||He came from Constantinople, of noble and God-fearing parents, who gave him a great education, both divine and human. He was honored with a rank at the imperial court and, because the emperor admired his courage, was placed at the head of military regiments and sent to fight the Hagarenes. He was defeated, taken captive and imprisoned in chains in a dark prison. Despairing of human help, he prayed to Saint Nicholas, whom he had honored from childhood, and promised to become a monk if he were set free. Saint Nicholas, together with Symeon the God-receiver, appeared to him in a dream and loosed his bonds. Peter went to Rome, became a monk and, guided by a divine revelation, came to the southern tip of Athos, which was then uninhabited. He practiced asceticism in a cave, feeding on wild herbs, naked because his clothes had worn out, covered by the hair of his head and beard and girded with leaves. He endured many temptations from the demons, was granted visions and, according to the text, was fed with angelic bread called manna. He lived in this way fifty-three years, and at the end God revealed his accomplishments to a hunter. His life was written by Gregory Palamas.

life|06-13||Όσιος Ιάκωβος ο εξ απάτης τον αντίχριστον προσκυνήσας||He loved Christ, hated the world and renounced all his possessions. Later, however, through the working of the devil, he became so proud that he dared to say that no one else knew better than he the way of salvation. He undertook many struggles not on the counsel of the experienced but by his own will and self-satisfaction, and for this reason he was deceived by the demons. A demon transformed into an angel of light commanded him to clean his cell and light candles and incense, because Christ would come that night. Jacob did so, and when the Antichrist came with great glory and illusion, he opened the door and worshipped him. The devil struck him in the middle and left. In the morning Jacob spoke to an elder, who rebuked him severely; he wept and was broken with contrition, and the elder sent him to a coenobium. He obeyed and served in the kitchen for seven years with great humility and obedience, and afterwards stayed alone in a cell for another seven years, working with his own hands and guarding himself with exactness. Thus he learned the unerring way of God with great discernment, became a wonderworker and died in peace.

life|06-15||Άγιος Δουλάς ο Μάρτυρας||He came from the place called Zeourion Praetoriada in Cilicia. Because he confessed Christ as true God, he was led to the governor Maximus and severely beaten. When he related the Greek myth of Apollo and Daphne, he enraged the governor still more. They beat him again on the belly, laid him on his back on a red-hot grill, and on another grill they placed burning coals on his head, which had been anointed with oil. They scraped his back with iron tools, rubbed the wounds with salt and vinegar, and crushed his jaws and feet. Asked about Christ, he briefly explained the whole incarnation of the Lord. At the next examination they forced him to taste of the sacrifices to the idols; they forced a libation of wine into his mouth and he spat it out. They hung him up and tore at him so much that the bones of his face and sides appeared bare and his entrails came out. Finally they made him run up to twenty miles and, exhausted, he gave up his soul to God.

life|06-17||Άγιος Ίσαυρος ο Ιερομάρτυρας και οι συν αυτώ μαρτυρήσαντες||Isauros, a deacon of the mysteries, and his companions Basil and Innocent came from Athens and lived in the time of the emperor Numerian, around 284. They left their homeland and went to Apollonia, where by divine revelation they entered a cave and found the Christians Felix, Peregrinus and Hermeias. Isauros taught them not to love the things of this passing world, and they nourished him bodily while he nourished them spiritually. They withdrew from their relatives, who were pagans, and for this reason were denounced to the prefect of Apollonia, Tripontios. Unable to separate them from the faith, he commanded that the first three be beheaded. Isauros and Innocent were handed over to the prefect's son Apollonios, who punished them with fire and water; because, according to the text, they suffered no harm, they drew many pagans to the faith, among them the brothers Rufus and Rufinian, senators of Apollonia. In the end these too were beheaded.

life|06-17||Άγιος Φιλονίδης ο Ιερομάρτυρας Επίσκοπος Κουρίου||He lived in the time of Diocletian, around 300, and was imprisoned in Cyprus for the confession of Christ together with Aristocles, Demetrian and Athanasius the reader. When they were perfected by martyrdom, he went up to a high place, covered his face with his garment, knelt and prayed for a long time. Then he fell down standing upright, and before his body reached the ground he gave up his soul to God. At that hour two men who were walking far from the city saw him, according to the text, running naked before them, with a crown on his head, anointed with fragrant ointments and holding a palm branch, saying that he thanked Christ who had raised him from the earthly door to the gate of heaven, and then he vanished. They went to the place where the body had fallen and recognized that it was his. The pagans took the relics, put them in a sack and sank them in the sea, but it became turbulent and cast them out; then Christians found them and buried them. The martyrdom was written by Ariston, the bishop at that time, who was arrested by the pagans and later freed.

life|06-18||Άγιος Αιθέριος ο Μάρτυρας ο εν Νικομηδεία||He lived in the time of Diocletian, around 300. He was denounced as a Christian and led to the governor Eleusius, where he confessed Christ. They stretched him out and burned him with lighted torches, and burned his armpits, back and chest with red-hot iron caltrops. They put a hook in his nose and stretched him out on a red-hot iron carpet, but, according to the text, he was kept unharmed by a divine angel. In the end he was beheaded and received the crown of martyrdom.

life|06-19||Άγιος Ζώσιμος ο Μάρτυρας||He was a soldier in the time of Trajan, when Domitian was governor of Antioch of Pisidia, and he came from Apollonias of Sozopolis. He threw down his arms, took refuge in the Church and was baptized. He was brought to the governor and, because he confessed that he was a Christian, they hung him up and tore at him, stretched him out on all fours and beat him, and then laid him on a red-hot iron bed. The fire, according to the text, was turned into dew, and many pagans who were present believed in Christ. Then they nailed shoes to his feet and tied him to colts, forcing him to run behind the governor who was going to the city of the Canaanites. He ran and remained three days without food, until by the providence of God two children appeared to him, one of whom gave him bread and the other water in a vessel, and he thanked God and ate and drank. Afterwards he appeared again at the examination, was hung up again and torn, and finally was beheaded.

life|06-19||Όσιος Ζήνων||He renounced the world and became a disciple of the great elder Silvanus. Because of his great obedience, harsh asceticism and humility he became a wonderworker and miracle-worker and drove out many demons from people. He lived in this way, in struggles, for sixty-two years and fell asleep in peace.

life|06-21||Άγιοι Αντώνιος, Αναστάσιος, Κέλσιος, Βασίλισσα, είκοσι δεσμοφύλακες και επτά αδελφοί οι Μάρτυρες μετά του Αγίου Ιουλιανού μαρτυρήσαντες||Julian, from Egypt, founded a monastery in Antinoe and was abbot of ten thousand monks, in the time of Diocletian, when Marcian was governor. He was arrested and confessed Christ, while he mocked the idols. The governor commanded that the monastery be burned with all inside, and they perished by fire, both the bishop and the priests and the clergy who had taken refuge there; it is said that voices are heard at the place and miracles take place. They beat Julian and bound him with iron fetters until his bones were crushed. A certain soldier was blinded; the saint promised to give him sight if he believed in Christ, and when the priests of the idols could not heal him, a voice was heard from the temple of the idols telling them to leave the martyr alone, and the idols fell and became dust. The soldier was healed, believed and was beheaded. Urine was poured over the saint's head, but it was changed into the fragrance of balsam. Celsus, the governor's son, saw angels crowning Julian and believed, and with him twenty soldiers believed. When Julian raised a dead man by his prayer, he was baptized by the priest Antony, who was of royal descent and had seven faithful sons, and was named Anastasius. The imprisoned Julian and Celsus filled the prison with light and fragrance, and the twenty jailers were baptized. All of them were thrown into cauldrons of boiling pitch and came out unharmed; then Celsus' mother Basilissa also believed. With the sign of the cross they threw down the idols and sank the temple into the earth. Then they bound their limbs with papyrus soaked in oil and set them on fire, but they remained unharmed. They flayed the skin of the head of Julian and Celsus, put out the eyes of Antony and hung up Basilissa. They threw them to the beasts, which did not touch them, and finally beheaded them. Their blood congealed on their bodies and their relics were recognized, and the Christians buried them near a holy altar, where, according to tradition, a spring of miracles gushes forth. At the place of martyrdom an earthquake occurred which overthrew the greater part of the city and killed the governor and many pagans.

life|06-21||Άγιος Αφροδίσιος ο Μάρτυρας εκ Κιλικίας||He came from Cilicia and had revered Christ from his ancestors. He was arrested as a Christian, led to the governor Dionysius and confessed the true God. They burned him on a grill with red-hot irons and threw him into a cauldron of boiling lead; then they hung him upside down, and divine grace kept him unharmed. They let loose a lioness against him in the theater, which did not harm him, but spoke with a human voice and rebuked the cruelty of the pagans. Because of the miracle many believed in Christ and were beheaded. The tyrant commanded that a stone be split, the saint be placed in the middle and the other half be dropped on top, with the labor of fifty-five soldiers; the saint immediately gave up his soul to God.

life|06-22||Άγιοι Ζήνων και Ζηνάς οι Μάρτυρες||They came from Philadelphia of Arabia, in the time of Maximian, around 303. Zeno was a soldier and Zenas was his slave. Because Zeno wished to be martyred for Christ, he distributed all his property to the poor and freed his slaves. Learning that the governor Maximus was very fond of the idols, he went to him and, while being beaten, kicked and overturned the altar. They hung him up, beat him mercilessly and rubbed his wounds with salt and vinegar. They threw him into prison and fastened his feet in the stocks. His slave Zenas came and begged his master not to separate him from himself, and the governor, learning of it, commanded that he be shut in prison with him. Then they threw them into a pit full of fire and poured oil on top, but by the grace of God they remained unharmed, and for this reason they beheaded them. Their memory is celebrated in the church of Saint George at the place called Kyparission.

life|06-23||Άγιοι Αριστοκλής, Δημητριανός και Αθανάσιος οι Μάρτυρες εν Κύπρω αθλήσαντες||Aristocles was a Cypriot from Tamassos and a priest, and around 302, in the time of Maximian, he went up to the mountain and hid in a cave out of fear of the persecution. There, as he was praying, a light brighter than the sun appeared and a voice came from heaven urging him to go to Salamis, that is, Ammochostos, and to receive martyrdom there. He went and entered the church of the Apostle Barnabas, found the deacon Demetrian and the reader Athanasius, and after being given hospitality by them, he told them of the vision and the voice. They asked to die with him for Christ. All three came to Ammochostos and stood in a high and visible place. The governor summoned them and, learning that they were Christians, first beat and tore Aristocles and then beheaded him. Demetrian and Athanasius, who persisted in their faith, he tortured with various punishments and commanded that they be thrown into the fire; because they remained unharmed by the grace of Christ, he beheaded them too.

life|06-23||Άγιος Ευστόχιος ο Πρεσβύτερος και οι συν αυτώ||Saint Eustochius came from the city of Usara and lived in the time of Maximian, around 300. He was at first a priest of the idols, but when he saw the saints bearing witness for Christ and working extraordinary miracles, he abandoned idolatry, was baptized by Eudoxius, bishop of Antioch, and became a presbyter. // In Lystra of Lycaonia he found his nephew Gaius and his three children, Dollia, Probe and Urban, taught them the faith and baptized them together with all his relatives. // They were denounced to the governor and then to the governor of Ancyra, Agrippinus, but they would not agree to deny Christ. Dollia and Urban were torn on the cheeks, Gaius was beaten, and Eustochius was beheaded. // According to the text, Gaius and the children were bound to a bronze wheel and remained unharmed, because the wheel stopped and the fire went out. Then they tortured them in various ways, and when they persisted in confessing Christ, they were beheaded and received the crown of martyrdom.

life|06-25||Άγιοι Ορέντιος, Φαρμάκιος, Έρως, Φίρμος, Φιρμίνος, Κυριακός και Λογγίνος οι Μάρτυρες||These saints were seven brothers who lived in the time of Diocletian and Maximian, in 301. They came from the East and served as new recruits in the army, together with two hundred others, under Rhodon in Antioch, and were sent to Thrace. // When the Scythians rebelled and crossed the Danube, Maximian looked for someone to fight a duel with the brave barbarian. Orentius was chosen by all, fought the duel in the stadium, killed the Scythian and brought his head to the emperor. // The emperor marveled and offered sacrifices to the idols for the victory, but Orentius confessed that he had conquered with the help of Christ. The emperor honored him and gave him the dead man's belt, but afterwards, since he could not persuade him to deny Christ, he sent him with his brothers to Satala in Armenia, with an order to the duke there to send them back if they sacrificed, and otherwise into exile in Abkhazia and Zichia. // They were examined and remained steadfast in the faith. According to the text, Orentius was thrown into the sea from a rock, the angel Raphael brought him out and set him on a rock, where he prayed and gave up his spirit on the 24th of June. // Pharnakios went to the place Kordole and died on the 3rd of July, while Kyriakos went to the land of the Lazi and reposed on the 14th of July. Longinus, as he was sailing on a ship, prayed in the midst of a great storm and gave up his soul to God, and was buried in Pityous.

life|06-26||Όσιος Ιωάννης Επίσκοπος Γοτθίας||The venerable John came from the land of the Taurosyths, which was under the authority of the Goths, and lived in the time of the emperors of the second iconoclasm. He was the son of Leo and Photeine, was born in fulfillment of a promise and was dedicated to God from infancy. // When he came of age and his countrymen wished to raise him to the episcopal throne, they sent him to the metropolitan of Iberia, because in the Roman lands iconoclasm was dominant, and from him he received ordination. // After the death of the iconoclast emperors he went to Constantinople, spoke to the empress Irene about the Orthodox faith and returned to Gothia. When the soldiers of the Khagan rebelled and killed many Christians, he fled and ended up in Amastris, where he stayed four years. // When he heard that the Khagan had died, he said that after forty days he too would go to be judged, and so it happened: he died while teaching his flock, and his ship arrived immediately, as he had foretold. // George, the bishop of Amastris, placed the relics in a casket and carried it in procession to the ship and then to the monastery of the nuns of the Holy Apostles, where it was kept. According to the text, many miracles have been and are being worked by the relics, and while alive the saint also worked miracles, of which ten were recorded.

life|06-27||Άγιος Άνεκτος ο Μάρτυρας εν Καισαρεία της Παλαιστίνης||Saint Anectus lived in the time of Diocletian, in 298, when Urban was governor of Caesarea of Cappadocia. Because he taught the Christians not to fear tortures and to resist the pagans, he was denounced to the governor, imprisoned and brought before him. // When they pressed him to sacrifice, according to the text, he threw down the idols by his prayer. They beat him, hung him up, tore him with iron claws and tortured him with red-hot irons, lead and fire, but an angel of the Lord freed him and healed him more than once. Many pagans, seeing him healthy, believed and were baptized. // Finally he was beheaded and, according to the text, milk instead of blood ran from his neck. Tradition also says that he took his head in his hands and walked two signs before going as a victor to heaven.

life|06-28||Άγιος Παππίας ο Μάρτυρας||Saint Pappias lived in the time of Diocletian and Maximian, in 301. He believed in Christ from his ancestors and preached piety to others, and for this reason was denounced and arrested. // When he appeared before the governor and did not agree to sacrifice, but even insulted him, they stretched him out and beat him for a long time and then threw him into a cauldron full of oil and vinegar. According to the text, the martyr appeared clothed in the fire like a garment and remained in the torture seven whole days, and many unbelievers believed in Christ. // They dragged him naked over iron caltrops, tied him to wild horses, hung him upside down with a heavy stone tied to his neck and threw burning coals and stones upon him. An angel of the Lord brought him out from under the stones and made him whole, and through this miracle the executioners and a good number of the people believed, and they were beheaded and received the crown of martyrdom. // Finally the saint himself was also beheaded and went up as a victor to heaven.

life|06-28||Όσιος Σέργιος ο μάγιστρος||The venerable Sergius came from the village of Nikitia in Paphlagonia, near Amastris, and lived around 842, and for this reason his monastery was named that of Nikitiatos. He was good and the child of good parents and a relative of the empress Theodora and her son, the emperor Michael. // He was a fervent zealot of the Orthodox faith and struggled greatly for the restoration of the holy icons. // When the imperial fleet went down to Crete, he too was sent by Michael and the senate, who had only just persuaded him, to command the military regiments, because he had intelligence and ability. There he went to the Lord, and then his relics were buried in the monastery in Crete that is called to this day that of the Magistros. // Later the relics were transferred and placed in the monastery that he himself had built on the gulf of Nicomedia, between the two Emporia, of Kalos Agros and of Doskon.

life|07-02||Κατάθεσις Τιμίας Εσθήτος της Θεοτόκου||According to the text, two nobles of Constantinople, who were traveling to the Holy Places, found in Galilee a pious Jewish woman who lived in a house and prayed night and day. They learned that the Precious Robe of the Theotokos, her outer garment, was kept there in a wooden chest, and, after asking the woman's permission and keeping a vigil, they took the measurements of the chest. // In Jerusalem they made a similar chest, returned to the woman's house and secretly exchanged the two chests, sending the original to Constantinople. There they deposited the sacred treasure on their own estate, Blachernae, and built a church of the Apostles Peter and Mark, so that the matter might not become known. // Since they could not hide it for long, they revealed it to the emperor Leo, who, full of joy, built a church of the Theotokos there. The Robe, wrapped in imperial purple, is kept within the holy shrine as a safeguard of the imperial city and a protection against every illness, war and enemy. Nikephoros writes that it was woven of wool of its natural color and remained incorrupt, proclaiming the miracle of the Virgin.

life|07-02||Άγιος Κόϊντος ο Μάρτυρας||The saint was born and taught piety in Phrygia. In a village he distributed alms to the poor and healed those afflicted by unclean spirits. The governor Rufus pressed him to sacrifice to the idols and became possessed by a demon, but the saint healed him, and he rewarded him with honors and gifts and let him go free. // In Pergamon the pagans called Kymaioi arrested him and began to torture him, but an earthquake occurred, their temple collapsed and the idols were shattered, and out of fear they let him go free. Later the governor Klearchos seized him in Pergamon and broke his legs. The saint, by the grace of God, became healthy, lived ten more years and then died peacefully.

life|07-03||Άγιοι Θεόδοτος, Θεοδότη, Δολινδούχ οι Μάρτυρες και οι συν αυτοίς||These saints, who confessed Christ, were arrested by the emperor Trajan. When they did not submit to the order to deny the faith and sacrifice to the idols, they underwent various tortures and were shut in the same prison where the holy martyr Hyacinth was. // Hyacinth strengthened them in the faith, and after he was perfected in martyrdom, they were taken out of the prison and forced to eat of the sacrifices to the idols. They refused and denounced the religion of the idols. // For this reason they hung them on wooden frames and tore them, then took them down and beheaded them. Thus they went as victors to the heavens, and some Christians buried their relics with honor at the place of their martyrdom.

life|07-03||Άγιοι Μάρκος και Μωκιανός οι Μάρτυρες||The prefect Maximus forced these saints to sacrifice to the idols, but they were not persuaded and confessed the name of Christ with boldness, and were beheaded. // When Mocianus was going to the place of condemnation, his wife and children followed him weeping, and he counseled them to be silent. When Mark was beheaded, his wife was there, and with joy she took his head in her hands as a precious treasure. Thus both went as victors to the heavens.

life|07-04||Άγιος Θεόδωρος ο Ιερομάρτυρας Επίσκοπος Κυρήνης (της Λυβύης)||The saint lived in the time of Diocletian and came from Cyrene in Libya. He became an excellent calligrapher and wrote with his own hands many books, which he gave to the churches of God. For this reason his own son denounced him to the governor Dignian, because he had many books and brought many pagans to the faith, and he was imprisoned. // Seeing this, Lucius, a councillor of Cyrene, believed in Christ. The saint, according to the text, became healthy through divine grace and a little later gave up his soul to God, and a dove appeared kissing him. // The governor, learning that Lucius had believed, commanded that the three women Lucia, Aroa and Cyprilla and all the pagans who had been baptized by the saint be put to death. Lucius persuaded the governor Dignian to believe as well, and the two reached Cyprus by ship. There they found another governor who punished those who called upon Christ. Lucius gave himself up secretly to the torturers, overturned the altar of the idols and was beheaded, and Dignian buried his relics. Their memory is celebrated in the church of the martyr Theodore at Rhegium.

life|07-04||Αγίες Κυπρίλλα η Μάρτυς||The saint came from Cyrene, from the same homeland as Saint Theodore. She married and lived with her husband only two years, and remained a widow for twenty-eight years. Because she suffered from a pain in her head, she went to Saint Theodore, who was then imprisoned for the faith of Christ, and was healed. She stayed to serve him together with Lucia and Aroa. // After the martyrdom of Theodore she was accused before the governor. Because she would not agree to sacrifice, they put burning coals in her hand and incense on them to force her to burn incense to the idols.
