She said that this was not her own willing sacrifice but a satanic and involuntary one, and the executioners held her hand firmly until it was burned entirely. // Then they hung her on a wooden frame and tore her, and from her wounds, according to the text, blood came forth and from her breasts milk. Fainting under the tortures, she gave up her soul to Christ. Lucia and Aroa took her relics and buried them, singing sweet songs, and from her tomb dew welled up that healed every passion and illness.

life|07-04||Αγίες Αρόα και Λουκία οι Μάρτυρες||Lucia and Aroa served, together with Saint Cyprilla, the imprisoned Saint Theodore of Cyrene. They cut off the saint's tongue with a razor and kept it. When Cyprilla was martyred, they took her relics and buried them with sweet songs. // Later, by order of the governor, both were put to death, and now, according to the text, they dance together in the heavens with Saint Cyprilla.

life|07-05||Όσιος Λάμπαδος||The venerable one was dedicated from a young age to the ascetic life. Through self-control and prayer he put to death within his soul the mind of the flesh and shone like a bright sun, enlightening those who had been darkened by the passions and the deceit of the demons. // He worked extraordinary miracles while he lived, and after his repose miracles and healings welled up unceasingly for those who run to him with faith. The cave where his precious relics lie bears witness to this.

life|07-06||Άγιοι Λουκία η Παρθενομάρτυς και Ρήξος ο Βικάριος ο Μάρτυρας και οι συν αυτοίς μαρτυρήσαντες εν Καμπανία||This Lucia is different from Lucia of Syracuse. The vicar Rixus seized her and forced her to sacrifice to the idols and to deny Christ, but she did not obey and even brought Rixus himself to faith in Christ. He honored her greatly and settled her in a quiet house, where she lived praying and fasting. // The saint begged him to go to Campania in Italy and be martyred there for Christ. Rixus left his wife, children, wealth and all splendor and went there with her. Both were arrested, called upon Christ before the governor and confessed him as true God, and were beheaded. With them many others were also beheaded, twenty-four martyrs in all, among them Anastasius, Antoninus, Serinus, Diodorus, Dion, Apollonius and Victor.

life|07-06||Όσιος Αστίος ο Επίσκοπςο Δυρραχίου||The saint lived in the time of Trajan and the governor Agricolaus. The leading men of the city of Dyrrachium seized him, and since he would not be persuaded to sacrifice to the idols, they brought him to the governor, who scourged him with leaden thongs and ox sinews. // Because he remained steadfast in the faith of Christ, they anointed him with honey and crucified him on a wooden frame near the wall of the city, in the heat of summer. Wasps, bees and flies stung him, and so he gave up his soul to God and received the crown of martyrdom.

life|07-07||Όσιος Θωμάς ο εν Μαλεώ||In his early life the venerable one became famous for his wealth and power and set up many trophies and victories against the barbarians. Then, having come to long for Christ, he left the bitter sea of life, put on the schema of the monks and imitated the poverty of Christ. // According to the text, the prophet Elijah, whom the venerable one imitated, led him by night with a pillar of fire to a mountain called Maleon. There he shone like a bright star, and with prayers and vigils he dispelled the darkness of sin and of the demons. By his prayer a spring of water welled up, he gave sight to the blind and straightened the lame, and when he prayed he appeared from afar like a pillar of fire to those whose mind was pure. And after his repose he frees from passions and illnesses those who run with faith to his relics.

life|07-07||Άγιος Περεγρίνος ο Μάρτυρας και οι συν αυτώ Μαρτυρήσαντες||These saints came from Italy and lived in the time of Trajan. Because a persecution of the Christians was taking place, they boarded a ship and reached Dyrrachium. There they saw Saint Asteios, bishop of Dyrrachium, hanging on the cross, anointed with honey and stung by wasps and flies for the faith of Christ, and they called him blessed. For this they were arrested by the soldiers. // They confessed that they were Christians and, by order of the proconsul Agricolaus, were thrown into the Adriatic Sea and received the crown of martyrdom. The sea cast their relics onto the shore and the sand covered them. After seventy years they were revealed to the bishop of Alexandria, who took them, buried them with honor and built a small church in their name.

life|07-08||Αγίες Δώδεκα Συγκλιτικές γυναίκες οι Μάρτυρες||The twelve senatorial women believed in Christ when they saw the miracle of Saint Procopius, who by his prayer shattered the idols, which turned into water and flowed out through the door of the temple. They were arrested together with Theodosia, the saint's mother. // They were struck without mercy, their breasts were cut off and their armpits burned with red-hot iron balls. Finally they were beheaded and so received the crowns of martyrdom.

life|07-08||Άγιοι Αντίοχος και Νικόστρατος οι Μάρτυρες οι Τριβούνοι||Antiochus and Nicostratus were tribunes, officers of the two regiments of the Numeri that accompanied Saint Procopius. When they saw the miracle of the idols that turned into water after the saint's prayer, they believed in Christ and were baptized by Bishop Leontius. By order of the emperor they were beheaded and received the crowns of martyrdom.

life|07-08||Όσιος Θεόφιλος ο Μυροβλύτης ο εν Άθω ασκήσας||The venerable one practiced asceticism on Mount Athos, in the cell of Saint Basil, at the site of the holy monastery of Pantokrator, around the year 1548. After his death he exuded myrrh, and he fell asleep in peace.

life|07-10||Άγιοι Βιάνωρ και Σιλουανός οι Μάρτυρες οι εν Πισιδία||Bianor came from the province of Pisidia. For his confession of Christ he was brought before the governor of Euphratesia, Severian, and first they hung him up and struck him with wooden swords, then burned him with red-hot iron balls and removed his teeth and ears. // Silvanus, who was there and saw the courage of the saint, believed in Christ. They immediately cut out his tongue and then his head. On Bianor they pierced his ankles, put out his right eye, flayed the skin of his head and finally cut off his holy head, and so both received the crowns of the struggle.

life|07-10||Άγιος Απολλώνιος ο Μάρτυρας ο εκ Σαρδέων||The saint came from Sardis in Lydia. They brought him to the governor of Iconium, Perinius, and he confessed that he was a Christian. When they forced him to swear by the fortune of the emperor, he answered that it is not permitted for a Christian to swear by a mortal man, who does not know the Maker and Creator of all. // For these words they hung him on a cross, and there he gave up his soul to God and received the crown of martyrdom.

life|07-10||Άγιοι μύριοι Οσιομάρτυρες||These saints were ascetics and martyrs of Christ, monks who dwelt in caves and ascetic huts, and lived always in fasting, vigils and prayers. They were about ten thousand. // Saint Isidore, the first of them, had a disagreement with Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria, over ecclesiastical matters, in which Theophilus opposed him without knowing them, and he rebuked him, relying on the multitude of the monks. Theophilus did not dare to take vengeance openly on Isidore, who was known to many, and secretly sent men of like mind with him, who burned all these fathers of the skete and put them to death.

life|07-11||Άγιος Κινδέος ο Ιερομάρτυρας ο Ιερομάρτυρας ο Πρεσβύτερος||The saint came from a village named Talmenia, in the region of Side, in the time of Diocletian, with ancestors from Oumanada. When they brought him to the governor Stratonicus, he confessed Christ with boldness, and then they nailed iron shoes to his feet and made him run. // According to the text, he met a man carrying wood and, because the pagans wanted to seize it in order to burn the martyr, he gave the man thirty coins for the price of the wood. He did not let them load it on others, but loaded it himself on his shoulder. When the fire was lit, he went into it and, without being harmed, taught the pagans and urged them to the faith of Christ. // Because the air grew dark with lightning and thunder, he prayed and at once there was calm and the sky cleared, and he gave up his spirit to God. Seeing the miracle, the priest of the idols believed in Christ and persuaded his wife, who also believed. Later, according to tradition, the deacon Orestes took the saint's relics together with his precious head and carried them to his homeland, Oumanada.

life|07-12||Άγιοι Πρόκλος και Ιλάριος οι Μάρτυρες οι εν Αγκύρα||The saints lived in the time of the emperor Trajan and the governor Maximus, and came from the region of Kallippoi, near Ancyra. Proclus was arrested first, confessed Christ before the emperor and was handed over to the governor Maximus, who had him torn, burned him with lighted torches, hung him on a wooden frame and tied a heavy stone to his foot. // In the end it was decided that he be put to death with arrows. On the way he met his nephew Hilarius, who was arrested by the pagans because he greeted his uncle. Proclus, wounded by the multitude of arrows, went to the Lord. Hilarius confessed that he was a Christian, they hung him up and beat him and dragged him on the ground three miles, and then he was beheaded and buried together with his uncle Proclus. Their memory is celebrated in the monastery of Hypatia, near the place called Matrona.

life|07-12||Άγιος Σεραπίων ο Νέος ο Μάρτυρας||The saint lived in the time of the emperor Severus and was a God-fearing man, good in mind. The governor Aquila seized him, and when he asked him of what religion he was, he confessed with boldness that he believed in and revered Christ. They threw him into the fire and he received from the Lord the crown of the struggle.

life|07-14||Άγιος Ιούστος ο Μάρτυρας||The saint came from Rome and was a soldier in the regiments of the Numeri under the tribune Claudius. Returning from the war against the barbarians, he saw in ecstasy a crystal cross, and from the cross a voice came forth which taught him the mystery of piety. In Rome he distributed his belongings to the poor and rejoiced that he had gained the faith of Christ. // When the tribune Claudius learned that he had believed in Christ, he counseled him to take pity on his youth and abandon the faith. Since he did not persuade him, he sent him with letters to the governor Magnentius, who ordered that he be beaten with sinews, that a red-hot iron helmet be put on his head, red-hot balls in his armpits and iron hands on his hands, and that he be stretched out on a red-hot grill. The saint bravely endured all this, glorifying and thanking God. Finally he was thrown into a furnace, and there gave up his soul without a single hair of his being burned. His memory is celebrated at the Orphanage.

life|07-14||Όσιος Ονήσιμος ο Θαυματουργός||This venerable one is different from the Apostle Onesimus and from the martyr Onesimus. He lived in the time of Diocletian and came from Caesarea of Palestine. According to the text, his parents received holy baptism from an angel and were told the good news that they would give birth to the saint and that they should name him Onesimus. // From a young age he left his parents and went to a monastery of Ephesus, where there were eight hundred monks, and his parents, from the many tears over his departure, went blind. Because of the persecution of Diocletian the monks left the monastery, and the saint returned to his parents' house without making himself known, but wrote on paper a brief account of himself and left it at the window of the house. // Then he went to Magnesia, founded a monastery, brought his parents there and healed their eyes. After living out the rest of his life, he departed to the Lord.

life|07-16||Άγιος Φαύστος ο Μάρτυρας||Faustus lived in the time of the emperor Decius, around 250. He was arrested for his faith in Christ and confessed it with boldness. He was nailed to a cross and shot with arrows. He endured five days on the cross and gave up his soul to God, from whom he received the crown of the struggle.

life|07-16||Άγιος Αντίοχος ο Μάρτυρας ο αδελφός του Αγίου Μάρτυρος Πλάτωνα||Antiochus came from Sebasteia in Cappadocia and was a physician by profession, who went about the cities and healed the sick. As he traveled through Galatia and Cappadocia and cured every kind of illness, the governor Hadrian arrested him. They hung him on a wooden frame and tore his sides, burned him with fire, threw him into prison and the next day into a cauldron full of hot oil, where he remained seven days without suffering any harm. They also gave him to beasts, but he came out safe from them too, and by his prayer, according to the text, he destroyed all the idols and turned them to dust. Finally he was beheaded, and from his neck blood flowed together with milk. His executioner Kyriakos saw this miracle and also confessed Christ.

life|07-16||Άγιος Κυριάκος ο δήμιος||Kyriakos was the executioner who beheaded Saint Antiochus. When he saw blood flowing together with milk from the martyr's neck, he openly confessed that he was a Christian and pronounced anathema on the governor Hadrian and his idols. For this he too was beheaded and went up to the heavens, to struggle together with Antiochus.

life|07-18||Άγιος Αιμιλιανός ο Μάρτυρας||Aemilian came from Dorostolon, a city of Moesia in Thrace, and was the slave of a pagan in the time of Julian the Apostate, around 361. He believed in Christ and abhorred the idols. Once he entered the temple of the idols and broke them all with a hammer that he was holding. Because many were being arrested and beaten for this, since the culprit was not known, the saint went of his own accord and revealed that he himself had done it. They beat him mercilessly with rawhide whips and then threw him into the fire. He remained unburned and gave up his soul to God. His memory is celebrated in his church, in a place called Rhabdos.

life|07-18||Άγιοι Παύλος, Ουαλεντίνη και Θέη οι Μάρτυρες||They were siblings according to the flesh and came from Egypt. They were taken to the city of Diocaesarea, appeared before the governor Firmilian and confessed the name of Christ. They burned their right feet and blinded their right eyes. Valentina and Thea were hung on a wooden frame, torn, and put to death with fire and iron. Paul was tortured first and prayed in a loud voice for the Christians, the Jews and the Samaritans, and for the persecution to stop, so that he moved all those present. Then he was beheaded, and so all three received the crowns of martyrdom.

life|07-18||Άγιος Υάκινθος ο Μάρτυρας ο εν Αμάστριδι||He was born of pious parents, Theocletus and Theonilla, in the time of Bishop Heraclius in Amastris, a coastal city on the Black Sea. He received the name Hyacinth, according to the text, after the appearance of an angel. At the age of three he raised a dead child by calling on the name of Christ, and as he grew he worked many miracles until old age. Seeing the pagans worshipping a hollow tree called Pteleia, he was moved by divine zeal and cut it down. He was arrested and brought to the governor Castrinsius, was severely beaten and had his teeth pulled out, was dragged bound with ropes outside the city, was wounded with sharp reeds and was put in prison, where he gave up his soul. According to tradition, on his feast, as the Christians chant, a healing liquid wells up beneath his tomb, which the bishop distributes and which heals the passions of soul and body.

life|07-19||Όσιος Δίος ο Θαυματουργός||Dius lived in the time of Theodosius the Great, around 379, and came from Antioch of Syria. He practiced great asceticism and advanced in virtue, and by divine revelation went to Constantinople. At the place where he built his monastery, he cleared the ground and planted his dry staff, and by the invocation of the Holy Trinity it became a great tree, which, according to the text, bears fruit to this day. The emperor Theodosius heard of his fame, went himself to him and gave him a considerable sum of money to support the monastery. Patriarch Atticus ordained him a priest under pressure. According to the text he worked many miracles: he drew water from the depths of the earth, like Moses, and raised someone who had drowned in it. As his end drew near, he remained breathless and motionless, and those present, among them Atticus and Alexander, patriarch of Antioch, prepared his burial. Suddenly he rose as if from sleep and said that the Lord had granted him fifteen more years, and when he had completed them he fell asleep in the Lord.

life|07-21||Άγιοι Θεόφιλος και Τρόφιμος οι Μάρτυρες και οι συν αυτοίς δέκα τρείς μαρτυρίσαντες||They lived in the time of Diocletian, around 308. Because they would not agree to deny Christ, they tore their bodies and stoned them, broke their legs and threw them into the fire. They remained untouched by the fire and finally were beheaded, receiving the crowns of martyrdom.

life|07-22||Αγία Μαρκέλλα η Παρθενομάρτυς η Χιλιοπολίτιδα||According to the text, it is not known who Marcella was or where she was martyred, because no record of her survives. The inhabitants of Chios, however, built a church in her name long ago and honor her with great reverence, and according to the text many miracles take place there daily. Near the church, on the shore, there are stones that appear covered with congealed blood; the Christians scrape them, and the scrapings, placed in vessels, serve for the healing of every illness. From this blood it was known that she is a martyr, and from her appearances in sleep that she is a venerable one, for to many who run to the church for healing she appears dressed in a monastic garment and seems to come from the sea and enter her church.

life|07-23||Άγιοι Μάρτυρες οι επί Βουλγάρων τελειωθέντες||The emperor Nikephoros, in the ninth year of his reign, around 811, left Constantinople with the whole army to fight the Bulgarians, taking with him his son Staurakios and his son-in-law Michael. At first he defeated them and set up a trophy, but he became proud and gave himself up to pleasures. According to the text, the Bulgarians committed many murders without pity, even of the senate, and the emperor himself was killed by their leader Krum. The Christian soldiers who were taken alive were tortured to make them deny Christ and believe in the religion of the Scythians, but they resisted and preferred to die. They were put to death in many ways: some were beheaded with the sword, some hung or shot with arrows, and others condemned to prison, hunger and thirst. All thus received the unfading crowns of martyrdom.

life|07-23||Οσία Άννα η εν τω Λαυκαδίω||Anna lived in the time of the iconoclast Theophilos, around 829, of illustrious family and with great wealth. Her father died early and her mother raised her with piety and also died soon after. Then a Hagarene came to the Roman empire, who asked the emperor for permission to take her as wife. Anna refused, was harassed by him and begged God with tears to set her free. Her prayer was heard and the Hagarene died. Then she abandoned all worldly things, entered a church of the Theotokos and devoted herself to fasting, prayer, vigil and self-control, so that her body withered and the sinews and joints showed. She lived in this way fifty years and then, after a short illness, gave up her soul to God. Her relatives buried her in a place with many other graves. After many years, people who were tormented by unclean spirits took her body out of the tomb and found it whole, incorrupt and fragrant, while the other bodies had decayed. According to the text, through the grace of the relics demons were driven out, the blind saw and the lame walked.

life|07-25||Οσία Ευπραξία||Eupraxia was the daughter of the senator Antigonus and of Eupraxia, and lived in the time of Theodosius the Great, around 380, to whom she was related. When her father died, her mother entrusted her to the emperor, who betrothed her to a senatorial official. Afterwards Eupraxia went with her mother to the Thebaid of Egypt and entered a women's monastery with one hundred and four nuns, who lived like angels. She imitated their virtues and could no longer bear to leave the monastery, though she was then twelve years old. Her mother distributed her estates to the poor, fell ill and returned to the monastery, where she left her property to her daughter and died in the Lord. Eupraxia distributed all her paternal goods to the poor and to the churches and loved severe asceticism exceedingly. According to the text she reached such virtue that she stood motionless forty-five whole days and nights with her hands raised to heaven. She received from God the grace of miracles and freed many from passions and illnesses. Thus she lived pleasing to God and died in the Lord.

life|07-26||Αγία Ωραιοζήλη η Μάρτυς||According to the text, it is not preserved from what place Horaiozele came nor who her parents were. She was baptized and enlightened by the Apostle Andrew the First-called and devoted herself to a small church of the Archangel Michael, where she lived keeping the commandments of Christ and afflicting her body. Many pagans ran to her and through her teaching abandoned idolatry. She also acquired two virgin companions, who came to know Christ from her teaching and struggled with her in vigils, fasts and prayers. In the time of Decius, around 250, the emperor separated her from her companions and led her to the court, but she confessed Christ with courage and did not yield to flattery and threats. They beat her for many hours and Decius was blinded. The saint sent him word that he would see again if he anointed his eyes with the blood of her severed head. They beheaded her, and Decius, after anointing his eyes with her blood, regained his sight, but remained ungrateful and commanded that her relics be burned. Her synaxis is celebrated in her church, near the church of the great martyr Anastasia, where, according to the text, healings take place, among them of a paralytic and of barren women who gave birth.

life|07-27||Όσιος Σισίνιος ο Θαυματουργός||Sisinius was a hieromonk, a holy man and wonderworker, who went to the region of Mantineion in the time of the venerable Anthousa. She saw him and was moved to imitate him. He gave her a pattern and rule of monastic life and, to train her in obedience, commanded her to enter a lighted oven, and Anthousa entered and came out having suffered almost nothing. He foretold to her that she would establish a monastery with nine hundred nuns and tonsured her a nun. He appointed her to dwell on the small island of the lake near the village of Perkele. When she came and asked permission to build a church of Saint Anne, he gave her much counsel and told her plainly what would happen to her, also revealing the time when he himself would die. He died before what he had foretold was fulfilled, and Anthousa then built the other churches.

life|07-28||Άγιος Ευστάθιος ο Μάρτυρας ο εν Αγκύρα||Eustathius was a soldier. When he was led before the governor of Ancyra, Cornelius, he confessed with boldness the saving economy of the Lord Jesus Christ and they beat him severely. Then they pierced his ankles, bound him with ropes and dragged him from the city to the river Sangarios, with the governor following and watching. They put him in a case and threw him into the river, but an angel of the Lord brought the case to dry land and the saint was found inside it unharmed, chanting the psalm "He who dwells in the help of the Most High." The governor, put to shame, drew his knife and killed himself. The martyr prayed and communed of the divine Mysteries with a dove sent from heaven, according to the text, and gave up his soul to the angel who had saved him. His relics were buried in Ancyra.

life|07-28||Άγιος Ακάκιος ο Νέος ο Μάρτυρας||Acacius was young in age, in the time of Licinius, around 318. Because he confessed that he was a Christian, they hung him up and tore him and handed him over to the governor Terentius, who put him in a red-hot cauldron of pitch, oil and vinegar, but the saint remained unharmed. Then they forced him to run behind the governor who was going to Apamea and Apollonia. There he entered a temple of idols and by his prayer destroyed the idols. Next he appeared before the tribune Zelikinthius, who beat him severely and let a lion loose against him; the saint remained unharmed. They threw him into a cauldron of pitch and asphalt and, as he remained unburned, Zelikinthius thought the cauldron was cold, approached and was burned at once, becoming like dust. Afterwards Poseidonius examined him, bound him with a heavy chain and sent him to Miletus in Ionia. There, entering a temple of idols, he commanded the idols to fall and they fell and were shattered, and likewise in another temple. For this they beheaded him and milk ran from his neck instead of blood. The presbyter Leontius took his relics, anointed them with ointments and kept them in the city of Synada, together with the synaxarion of his martyrdom, in a place that was the estate of a magistrate, Dorymedon, who himself was martyred later.

life|08-01||Άγιος Ελεαζάρος ο Μάρτυρας||Eleazar was the teacher of the seven Maccabee children and lived in the time of King Antiochus, son of Seleucus, when Antiochus subjugated the Hebrews. Antiochus forced them to renounce the customs of the law and to eat pork. Eleazar, keeping the commandment of the divine law, refused. They tied his hands behind him, struck him hard and poured foul, burning liquids into his nose, and then threw him into the fire. He prayed that his blood and death might become redemption and freedom for his whole nation, and gave up his soul to God.

life|08-01||Άγιοι εννέα Μάρτυρες||According to the text, these saints, who were from Pamphylia and were called Leontius, Attus, Alexander, Kindeus, Mnesitheus, Kyriakos, Menaios, Katounos and Eukleus, lived in the time of Diocletian and the governor Flavian, around 300. They were Christians by descent, Menaios a carpenter and the others farmers. With one mind they went of their own accord to the contest of martyrdom, overthrew in one night the idols of the temple of Artemis and were arrested. They refused to deny Christ and they struck them, burned their sides, tore them with iron claws, burned their armpits with lighted torches and pierced their eyes with awls. They threw them into prison without food and water and later gave them as prey to the beasts, but the beasts did not harm them. After thunder, lightning and heavy rain, a divine voice was heard calling them to heaven, and they were beheaded, receiving the crown of martyrdom.

life|08-03||Οσία Θεοκλητώ η Θαυματουργός||The venerable Theoklito lived in the time of the iconoclast emperor Theophilos, around 829, and came from the locality of Optimata. Her parents were called Constantine and Anastasia. From childhood she was raised with piety and later, under pressure from her parents, married Zacharias, a man of the same good disposition. She gave many alms, studied the Scriptures and applied to her works what she read. She worked all day with her own hands, served the poor who came to her house and, out of great humility, the people of her household too. When the hour of her death came, she summoned her friends and foretold the day of her death, and so it happened. According to the text, after her repose many miracles were worked by her holy relics, and her relatives have the custom of lifting them each year, changing their garments and placing them again in their case.

life|08-04||Οσία Ευδοκία η Μάρτυς και η ανακομιδή των λειψάνων της||Saint Eudokia came from the East and was taken captive by the Persians. Because she was learned in the Scriptures, she taught the captives, became known and a friend to the wives of the Persians and brought many of them to the knowledge of God. For this she was denounced to the judges, beaten with rawhide whips and thrown into prison for two months. When she was tried again and confessed Christ as true God, they struck her so hard with thorny pomegranate rods that her flesh fell to the ground. Six months later they tried her a third time and wrapped her naked in reeds, which they tightened with rope so that they entered her flesh. They hung her up and broke her bones with ropes, and when they saw her half-dead and speechless, they cut off her head. Her holy relics were later translated and, according to the text, pour forth healings to those who venerate them with faith.

life|08-08||Άγιος Μύρων||Myron was born in Avrakia, a city of Crete near Knossos, and was honored as a wonderworking bishop of Crete. When he grew up, he married and cultivated the land, and from its fruits he gave alms to the poor. It is said that the more he gave, the more the produce of his fields increased. His compassion for the poor was beyond human measure. According to the tradition of the text, once he found ten men on his threshing floor stealing wheat, and they filled their sacks so full that they could neither lift them nor leave them.

life|08-08||Όσιος Θεοδόσιος ηγούμενος Ορόβων||The venerable Theodosius, from his young age, took up the cross of the Lord and lived in the mountains, in caves and in valleys. According to the text he died peacefully and was offered to God like precious myrrh and fragrant incense.

life|08-09||Άγιοι Δέκα Μάρτυρες πού μαρτύρησαν στή Χάλκη||These saints lived in the time of the iconoclast emperor Leo the Isaurian, around 716, who hated the holy icons and burned them. When the emperor attempted to tear down also the icon of Christ above the Chalke Gate of Constantinople and the ladders had already been set up, the saints (nine monks and the patrician Maria, with many others) got there first, pulled away a ladder and threw down the spatharios who was tearing down the icon, and he was killed. The enraged emperor ordered that all who were there be beheaded, while the nine monks were beaten with rods and shut in prison, where they received five hundred blows with rods a day for eight months. In the end their faces were burned with red-hot irons and they were beheaded at the place called Kynegion, together with Saint Maria the patrician, and their relics were thrown into the sea.

life|08-09||Άγιος Αντωνίνος ο Μάρτυρας από την Αλεξάνδρεια||Antoninus came from Alexandria. He was arrested by the governor of the city, hung up and torn, and then thrown into a burning furnace, where he gave up his soul to God and received the crown of martyrdom. His holy relics were found in the middle of the furnace untouched and whole, since the fire had not harmed even a hair of his head.

life|08-13||Αγία Ειρήνη η Βασίλισσα (μετονομασθείσα σε Μοναχή Ξένη)||Irene was born of fortunate parents, sovereigns of the West, and from childhood showed the virtue that she would later have. In the time of the emperor Alexios Komnenos and his wife Irene, they were seeking a beautiful and virtuous girl and found her in her, and married her to the porphyrogenitus emperor John, by whom she had eight children, four boys and four girls. She was gentle, humble, compassionate and free of anger, a protector of orphans and widows, enriched monasteries and always had the Psalms of David on her lips, living ascetically even as empress and despising the things of the throne. // Entreating the emperor with tears before the church of the Pantokrator, she obtained his promise that he would endow the monastery with treasures and estates, so that it might hold the first place among the monasteries of Constantinople. Thus she built from the foundations the monastery of the Pantokrator, as well as churches, hostels and homes for the elderly, with the help of Nikephoros, who oversaw the buildings. // According to the text, a little later she went to Bithynia and died there, as she had longed to, and her relics were buried in the monastery she had built. A little later the emperor John also died, and was buried in the same monastery of the Pantokrator.

life|08-13||Όσιος Δοσίθεος||Dositheus practiced asceticism in the coenobium of Abba Seridos, near Gaza, under the guidance of Saint Dorotheus, and died peacefully. According to the text and its note, he was an example of submission and obedience, which monks should have as a living model.

life|08-13||Όσιος Δωρόθεος||Dorotheus first practiced asceticism in the coenobium of Abba Seridos, near Gaza. Later he founded a monastery of his own, with the blessing of Abba John the prophet and the prayers of the great Barsanuphius, and died peacefully. As noted in the text, his surviving words bear witness to his great discernment.

life|08-13||Όσιος Σέριδος ηγούμενος της Μονής στή Γάζα||Seridos was abbot of the great coenobium that was near Gaza. There, according to the text, Dorotheus and Dositheus practiced asceticism, while in the region there also lived Saint Barsanuphius with his disciple John. He died peacefully.

life|08-14||Άγιος Ουρσίκιος ο Μάρτυρας||Ursicius was a soldier and lived in the time of the emperor Maximian, around 300, and came from the city of Sibento in upper Illyria, that is, Slavonia. He was denounced as a Christian and led to Maximian, who gave him to someone to judge him. They beat him on the back with rawhide whips and wounded his sides, then wrapped his hands in linen soaked in oil, put sulfur and resin on them and set them on fire. The saint said amid the punishments that his hands suffered justly, since they had delivered the tyrant. Maximian, who was accused by a certain Tertullian of being ungrateful to his benefactor, was ashamed and ordered the fire to be put out with water. A pagan, Olbianus, became angry and left, and on the road a scorpion bit him and he died in pain. Ursicius finally accepted the sentence of beheading and received the crown of martyrdom from a certain Valens, who needed three strokes of the sword on the saint's neck. His memory is celebrated in the church of the Forerunner in the place called Phorakion.

life|08-15||Κοίμησις της Υπεραγίας Θεοτόκου||According to the text, when the Lord willed to take his Mother to himself, three days earlier he revealed to her, through an angel (who according to tradition was the Archangel Gabriel), her departure from earth to heaven. The angel told her to receive the message with joy, because she was passing over to immortal life, and she rejoiced greatly. Out of longing she went up to the Mount of Olives to pray, as she was accustomed, and then, according to the text, the trees of the mountain bowed their tops and worshipped her as if they were alive. After she had prayed, she returned to her house, which shook entirely, and she lit many lamps, thanked her Son and called her female relatives and neighbors, while she cleaned and prepared her house.

life|08-15||Ανάμνηση Θαύματος Υπεραγίας Θεοτόκου||At the beginning of the reign of Leo the Isaurian, in the year 717, a multitude of Saracens with a very great number of ships (according to the text about 1,900) sailed up to take Constantinople, having first overthrown the kingdom of the Persians and deceived the Christians of Egypt and Libya. The citizens, when the enemies refused tribute, took refuge in the Theotokos, the protectress of the city. A Saracen who blasphemed Hagia Sophia fell from his horse and died, and their herald fell from a high wooden pole and was shattered. // The Bulgarians killed twenty thousand of them, the great iron chain of the city blocked their ships, some were broken up by the storm and others were burned by the Romans. The Saracens reached such hunger that, according to the text, they ate human flesh and unclean animals. Many of them went over to the Romans, and the rest left with nothing accomplished a year later, on the 15th of August. // According to tradition, their leader Suleiman could not enter the city because his horse reared on its hind legs. When he raised his eyes, he saw at the gate a mosaic icon of the Theotokos with Christ in her arms, got down and entered on foot, accusing himself of his earlier blasphemy. The author regards the deliverance of the city as a saving act of the Theotokos.

life|08-17||Άγιοι Παύλος και Ιουλιανή οι Μάρτυρες και οι συν αυτών Μαρτυρήσαντες (δήμιοι)||Paul and Juliana were siblings, of noble parents, and lived in Ptolemais in the time of the emperor Aurelian, around 270. Paul studied the Scriptures and silenced his opponents, and when the emperor arrived, he encouraged his sister to stand with courage. They confessed Christ and were hung up, torn and thrown into a cauldron of boiling pitch, from which they came out unharmed, and then onto a red-hot iron bed, where they rejoiced. The executioners Quadratus and Acacius took pity on them and were beheaded for it. // In prison an angel of the Lord loosed them from their chains and gave them bread. The executioner Stratonicus felt pity for Juliana and the emperor beheaded him. The saints were thrown to poisonous serpents without being harmed, Paul was struck on the jaws with lead and with thorny rods, and Juliana was led to a brothel, where an angel blinded those who approached and she later healed them with water. Then they were thrown into a pit of fire, and a cloud rained fiery rain upon the emperor, who was afraid and brought them out. Finally they were bound to a wooden frame, burned with torches and beheaded.

life|08-17||Άγιοι Στράτων, Φίλιππος, Ευτυχιανός και Κυπριανός οι Μάρτυρες||The four saints lived in Nicomedia and often went up to the theater to instruct the pagan people, to turn them away from idolatry and bring them to the faith of Christ. One day the governor of Nicomedia found the theater empty and learned that the people, taught by the saints, had abandoned their amusements and were following a new way of life. He ordered them to be brought before him. // They confessed that they have faith in Christ and teach it to others as well. They were led to the theater and handed over to the beasts, from which they remained unharmed. They were tortured in various ways and in the end were thrown into the fire, where they completed their martyric struggle.

life|08-18||Άγιο Πλήθος των Πενήτων (Φτωχών)||According to the text, these poor were those to whom the saints Florus and Laurus distributed the money they had received from Licinius to build a temple of idols. With their help they tied the idols by the neck with ropes and pulled them down to the ground, and then dedicated the temple to Christ. // When Licinius learned of it, he ordered a furnace to be lit and the poor who had taken the money and had shattered the idols to be thrown into it. Thus the blessed ones gave up their souls to God and received the crowns of martyrdom.

life|08-18||Άγιοι Έρμος (ή Ερμής), Σεραπίων και Πολύαινος οι Μάρτυρες||These saints came from Rome. Some unbelievers denounced them for revering Christ and hating the idols, and they appeared before the prefect of Rome, where they confessed their faith with boldness. They were first imprisoned in a dark and foul-smelling prison. // When they came out and would not agree to sacrifice to the idols, they were dragged over rocky and impassable places, and in this martyrdom they gave up their souls to God, from whom they received the unfading crowns of the struggle.

life|08-19||Άγιοι Τιμόθεος, Αγάπιος και Θέκλα οι Μάρτυρες||Timothy came from Palestine and, because he was perfect in word and life, became a teacher of piety. He was arrested and appeared before the governor of Gaza, Urban, where he confessed that he was a Christian and set out theologically the whole economy of Christ's incarnation. He was severely beaten and tested with every kind of torture, but remained immovable, and finally was thrown into the fire, where he gave up his spirit to God. // In the same city of Gaza were also Agapius and Thecla, who came from Bizye. They were severely tortured for the faith in Christ and, because they remained even more steadfast, were handed over to the beasts, by which they were put to death and received the crown of martyrdom.

life|08-20||Άγιοι Ηλιόδωρος και Δοσάς (ή Δοσαί ή Σοδάς) οι Μάρτυρες||According to the text, in the fifty-third year of his reign, Sabor, king of the Persians, marched with many armies against a Roman fortress and began to tear down the churches of the Christians, to shatter the holy icons and to burn the relics of the saints. Then Heliodorus, who was ninety-five years old, and Dosas appeared with courage before the king, rebuked his impiety and proclaimed the true faith of Christ. // They endured many and various tortures, their noses were cut off and finally they were beheaded. The saints thanked God, gave up their souls and went up crowned to the heavens.

life|08-20||Άγιοι Σέβηρος και Μέμνων ο Κεντυρίων||Severus came from Side in Pamphylia, the son of the Thracian Petronius and of Mygdonia. When he came to Philippopolis and saw the thirty-seven martyrs contending for Christ, he too confessed his faith with boldness. He was severely torn, red-hot iron rings were put on his fingers, he was stretched on four stakes and sawn, a red-hot iron belt was girded on him and finally he was beheaded. // Memnon, who was also called Centurion, was first stretched between two columns and three strips of skin were removed from his head to his feet. Then his feet were cut off and he was thrown into a furnace, where he gave up his soul to God and received the unfading crown of the struggle.

life|08-20||Άγιος Λούκιος ο βουλευτής||Lucius lived in the time of Diocletian, around 290. He came from Cyrene in Libya, was a leading man of the city and stood out for his stature, and at first was attached to idolatry. When the hieromartyr Theodore, bishop of Cyrene, was martyred bravely, Lucius was moved by the grace of Christ, believed and was baptized. He also persuaded the governor Dignian to believe and took him with him to Cyprus. // There, seeing that Christians were being arrested and put to death, he gave himself up to the torturers. He kicked and overturned the altar, scattering the sacrifices that were on it, and the governor ordered that he be beheaded. Thus his soul went up victorious to the heavens.

life|08-21||Αγία Βάσσα η Μάρτυς και τα τέκνα αυτής||Bassa lived in the time of Maximian and came from Edessa. She married a priest of the idols and bore him three sons, Theognius, Agapius and Pistus, whom she raised with piety, since she herself was a Christian from her ancestors. She was denounced by her own husband and appeared with her three sons before the proconsul, where she confessed that she was a Christian. // Theognius was hung up and torn, and Agapius was beaten and the skin of his head was flayed down to the chest, while his mother encouraged him and he said that nothing is as sweet as suffering for Christ. The third son, Pistus, was also tortured, and all three were beheaded. Bassa was thrown into prison, where she received food from the hand of an angel. Later she was arrested again, and because she would not agree to sacrifice to the idols, they tied her hands behind her, crushed her limbs and finally cut off her head, and so she received the crown of martyrdom.

life|08-22||Οσία Ανθούσα και συν αυτή||Anthousa lived in the time of Valerian and came from Seleucia in Syria, the daughter of Antonius and Maria, rich people attached to the idols. She believed secretly in Christ and wished to be baptized and to see Bishop Athanasius, who was preaching in Tarsus of Cilicia. She persuaded her mother to give her two mules and, taking her two servants, Charisimus and Neophytus, pretended to go to her nurse. // According to the text, Athanasius was carried by angels onto the road and stood before her, and where there was no water a spring welled up and two angels gave her white garments. She was baptized, and so were the two servants, and she gave the bishop her precious gold-woven dress to sell and distribute the price to the poor. The nurse drove her away and her mother grieved, and so Anthousa left, was made a nun by Athanasius, put on a hair garment and went into the desert, where she lived twenty years among the beasts, enduring many temptations from the demons. She died peacefully on the rock where she used to sleep. // Charisimus and Neophytus, after the martyric death of Athanasius, confessed Christ before Valerian and the duke Apellian, were hung up and torn for three hours, were beaten and beheaded.

life|08-22||Όσιος Αθανάσιος ο Ιερομάρτυρας||Athanasius was a bishop who preached the word of God in Tarsus of Cilicia. According to the text, when Anthousa asked to meet him in order to be baptized, he was carried miraculously by holy angels onto her road and, after he prayed and a spring welled up, he baptized her together with her two servants. Later he received her as a nun and gave her a hair garment. // He was arrested by the pagans, appeared before the emperor Valerian, was severely beaten with rods and finally beheaded.

life|08-22||Άγιοι Ειρηναίος, Ώρ και Ορόψις οι Μάρτυρες||Irenaeus was a deacon of the Church and preached with boldness Christ as true God. He was arrested by the pagans and appeared before the governor, together with the Christians Horus and Oropsis. All three confessed their faith in Christ and were thrown into the fire, but a sudden rain put it out and they remained unharmed. // They were then handed over to the beasts and these did not harm them either, and they were hung on a wooden frame and severely torn. In the end they were beheaded and received the crowns of the struggle.

life|08-23||Όσιος Καλλίνικος||Callinicus was at first a presbyter and sacristan of the church of the Theotokos of Blachernae. For his virtues he was ordained Patriarch of Constantinople, in the time of the emperor Justinian II the Slit-Nosed (685). // The emperor, as he was thinking of ways to harm the church of the Theotokos of the Metropoleis, asked the saint to give a prayer for it to be demolished. The saint answered that a prayer is not given for demolition, but for building and support, since God made the world to stand and to endure. // According to the text, Justinian later lost his throne, had his nose cut off and was exiled to Cherson. He returned with the help of the Bulgarians, entered Constantinople by deceit and filled the city with murders. Then Callinicus was arrested, falsely accused as a conspirator and exiled to Rome, where they shut him in the foundations of a wall and plastered it over on the outside. // After forty days the wall opened and the saint was found alive. Four days later he died and was buried in the church of the holy Apostles Peter and Paul, where the apostles had appeared to the Pope and asked him to place him there.

life|08-24||Άγιος Ευτυχής ο Ιερομάρτυρας μαθητής του Αγίου Ιωάννη Θεολόγου||Eutychus followed the Apostle Paul and was full of the grace of the Holy Spirit. He preached the Gospel with courage and overthrew many temples of the idols, and for this he endured beatings, bonds and many years of suffering in prison, where, according to the text, he received heavenly bread. // He was thrown into fire and then to the beasts, and one of them spoke with a human voice, causing astonishment in those who heard it. He remained unharmed by all the punishments and went to his homeland, Sebaste. // An angel of the Lord went before him and strengthened him. There the saint completed his life and died peacefully, in deep old age.

life|08-24||Άγιος Τατίων ο Μάρτυρας||Tatian came from the place Mantinaion, which belonged to the metropolis of Claudiopolis of Erdelia, in the province of Honorias. The pagans arrested him because he revered Christ and brought him before the governor Urban, where he confessed that he was a Christian and was imprisoned. // When he was questioned again and remained steadfast in the faith, they struck him with sticks and tore him with iron claws. Then they dragged him on the ground and, as he reached the gate of the city, he sealed himself with the form of the precious cross. He heard from on high a divine voice proclaiming the good things being prepared for him in the heavens, and so he gave up his soul to God and received the crowns of martyrdom.

life|08-24||Όσιος Γεώργιος ο Ομολογητής ο Λιμνιώτης||George loved the monastic life from a young age and stayed in the mountains of Olympus. After undertaking many struggles, he confessed piety and Orthodoxy with boldness in the time of Leo the Isaurian, who destroyed the holy icons and burned the relics of the saints (716). // He rebuked the tyrant's impiety and preached the veneration of the holy icons, and suffered many torments in his deep old age, since he was ninety-five years old. In the end they cut off his nose and burned his honored head, and the saint endured it with courage. Giving thanks and praying to God, he gave up his soul.

life|08-27||Αγία Ανθούσα η νέα||According to the synaxarion, the holy martyr Anthousa the Younger tied a great weight, a stone, to her neck and threw herself into a well, where she completed her martyrdom.

life|08-27||Όσιος Ποιμήν||The venerable Poemen came from Egypt. He left his homeland with his brothers and together they became monks. When their mother, out of longing, came to see them, they shut the door of their cell so as not to look upon her. She wept, and Poemen said to her through the door whether she wished to see them in this world or in the other, and the mother left with joy without seeing them. // Once the ruler of the place put the venerable one's nephew in prison and sent word that he would release him if his uncle came to see him. Poemen did not go, not even when his sister begged him with tears. He sent word to her that the ruler should examine the young man according to the laws, and the ruler, marveling at the exactness of his way of life, released the nephew. // He was once asked whether he should cover his brother's sin, and he answered that if we cover our brother's sin, God will cover ours. He practiced every virtue to such a degree that all the fathers and ascetics of Egypt and the Thebaid were regulated and corrected by him. After living out his life in this way and becoming an elder full of days, he fell asleep in the Lord.

life|08-30||Άγιοι Φήλιξ, Φουρτουνάτος, Σεπτιμίνος και Ιανουάριος οι Μάρτυρες||The four saints, the hieromartyr Felix, Fortunianus, Septiminus and Januarius, were brave soldiers of Christ. With zeal for the faith they fought bravely against the error of idolatry and, remaining faithful to the commandments of Christ, scorned the questions of the pagans who urged them to deny piety. // Because they were not persuaded, they endured persecutions, bonds, tortures of the body and many transfers from place to place, and in the end were condemned to beheading. According to the text, then a fearful miracle occurred, for the sun and the moon, unable to bear the unjust slaughter, were turned to blood. The martyrs, beheaded, received from the Lord the unfading crowns of the struggle.

life|08-30||Όσιος Φαντίνος ο Θαυματουργός||Fantinus came from Calabria in Italy and was the son of George and Bryaine. He was dedicated to God almost from his swaddling clothes and, when he reached a suitable age, was given to a monastery, where he practiced every virtue. // He became a tried worker of the commandments of God and was granted divine revelations. He went without food twenty whole days and went naked for four years, and suffered many hardships and dangers when the Saracens invaded Italy as raiders. // After sixty years of such temptations he took his two disciples, Vitalius and Nikephoros, and went to the Peloponnese. He stayed a long time in Corinth and became a cause of salvation for many. Then he went to Athens, where he venerated the church of the Theotokos, and afterwards to Larissa, to the tomb of Saint Achillius. // Next he went to Thessaloniki and stayed eight years near the miracles of Saint Demetrius, keeping his usual rule of self-control. He ended his life in good old age and went to the Lord whom he longed for.

life|08-31||Κατάθεσις Τιμίας Ζώνης της Θεοτόκου||According to the text, the emperor Arcadius, son of Theodosius the Great, brought from Jerusalem to Constantinople the precious Belt of the Theotokos, which was kept there together with the precious Robe by a virgin woman, and placed it in a splendid case that he named the holy Shrine. The text notes in a footnote another tradition, according to which the Belt was brought in the time of Justinian from Zela in Cappadocia. // After about four hundred and ten years, Leo the Wise opened the holy Shrine for his wife Zoe, who was afflicted by an unclean spirit. The empress had seen in a vision that she would be freed if the precious Belt were placed upon her. // The Belt was found radiant, the patriarch spread it over the empress and at once she was freed from the demon. All glorified God and thanked his Mother, and the Belt was placed again in the holy Shrine.

life|08-31||Ανακαίνιση του Ναού της Θεοτόκου εν τω Νεωρίω||In the time of Michael and Theodora (842), the patrician Antonius had a house in Constantinople, in the court of the Neorion, and a church of the Theotokos that the iconoclasts had deprived of holy icons. He renovated the church and built beneath it a small bath, while above there was always doxology. Healings began to take place in the church, and some Christians asked that bathing take place in the bath once a week, and the sick were healed. // When he died, the patrician left the church and the bath to God-loving Christians. Because they were poor, in time they neglected them, and the bath almost disappeared, while the church was left with one priest. // When the emperor Romanos needed materials for his palace and thought of demolishing the church, the Theotokos appeared at night to the overseer Raiktor and to a relative of his and threatened them not to tear it down. The emperor learned of it and gave orders that the church be renovated and the bath enlarged, where Romanos, Constantine and Christopher bathed. // They decreed that every year an imperial procession should go out to the bath and they gave it to the monastery of Raiktor. The text also relates miracles of healing of women and of a monk Antonius in the church.

life|09-01||Άγιοι Εύοδος, Καλλίστη, Αγαθοκλεία και Ερμογένης οι Μάρτυρες||Evodus, Callista and Hermogenes were siblings according to the flesh and pagans by descent. In the years when the Apostles were preaching they believed in Christ and were baptized. // They were denounced as Christians to the local governor and, when they appeared before him, they confessed Christ with courage. They were condemned to death by the sword, and so they completed the struggle of martyrdom and went to the heavens crowned.

life|09-01||Άγιος Αγγελής ο Νεομάρτυρας||Angelis was martyred in Constantinople in more recent times. According to the text, he completed his martyrdom by the sword, that is, he was beheaded. // The verses of the Synaxaristes play on his name: he was a man, but in essence an angel, and by the stroke of the sword he appeared as an angel among the angels. His martyrdom is referred to the New Martyrologion.

life|09-01||Όσιος Μελέτιος ο νέος||The venerable Meletius the Younger practiced asceticism on the mountain of Myoupolis and ended his life in peace. // According to the footnote of the Synaxaristes, which relies on Meletius, he lived in the time of Alexios Komnenos, around 1081. He came from Cappadocia, from a village called Moutalaske, and came to Greece, where he enlightened many by his God-pleasing deeds. He spent his life in the holy monastery honored in the name of the Archangels, known as the monastery of Symbolon, and his life was written by Nicholas, bishop of Methone. This monastery was later honored in the name of Saint Meletius himself.

life|09-02||Άγιοι Αειθαλάς και Άμμων (ή Αμμούν) οι Μάρτυρες||Aeithalas and Ammon were brought as Christians before Babdos, governor of Adrianople in Thrace. When he asked them about their family and profession, they answered that they were Christians, and he ordered them to sacrifice to the idols. // Because they were not persuaded, they were whipped with ox sinews so much that in the midst of the beating they gave up their souls into the hands of God.

life|09-02||Άγιοι Ελεάζαρ και Φινεές οι Δίκαιοι Ιερείς||Eleazar was the son of Aaron and Phinehas the son of Eleazar and grandson of Aaron. Eleazar was overseer of the tabernacle of witness, responsible for the oil of the light, the incense and the sacrifice. // Phinehas, out of zeal for God, killed Zimri and Cozbi the Midianite woman, who, committing fornication openly, were insulting Moses and the congregation of Israel, and pierced them both with a spear. For this zeal he received, according to the words of God, an everlasting covenant of priesthood for himself and his descendants.

life|09-02||Άγιος Διομήδης ο Μάρτυρας||Saint Diomedes completed his martyrdom by death by the sword. // According to the verses of the Synaxaristes, he bravely endured the executioners, like iron that withstands iron.
life|09-02||Άγιος Ιουλιανός ο Μάρτυρας||Saint Julian was martyred with his head crushed by a piece of wood. // The verses of the Synaxaristes say that he kept his mind toward God sound to the end.

life|09-02||Άγιος Φίλιππος (ή Θεόδοτος ή Θεόδωρος) ο Μάρτυρας||Saint Philip was martyred by the sword, that is, by beheading. // The verses of the Synaxaristes say that the swift cut of the blade brought him quickly to the Master whom he loved.

life|09-02||Άγιος Ευτυχιανός ο Μάρτυρας||Saint Eutychian completed his martyrdom burning on a grill over a fire. // The verses of the Synaxaristes say that in this way he passed into the blessed lot of the martyrs.
life|09-02||Άγιος Ησύχιος ο Μάρτυρας||Saint Hesychius was martyred by hanging. // According to the verses of the Synaxaristes, out of longing for the Master he accepted the noose quietly.
life|09-02||Άγιος Λεωνίδης ο Μάρτυρας||Saint Leonides was martyred in fire. // The verses of the Synaxaristes say that his longing for God made him endure even the flame with ease.

life|09-02||Άγιος Ευτύχιος ο Μάρτυρας||Saint Eutychius completed his martyrdom by crucifixion. // The verses of the Synaxaristes say that, following in the footsteps of the Lord, he too endured the passion of the cross.

life|09-02||Άγιος Φιλάδελφος ο Μάρτυρας||Saint Philadelphus was martyred with a stone weighing down his neck. // The verses of the Synaxaristes say that, leaving behind the weight of the flesh with the weight of the stone, he went up light to heaven.
life|09-02||Άγιος Μελάνιππος ο Μάρτυρας||Saint Melanippus completed his martyrdom by fire. // The verses of the Synaxaristes say that he found purification when cast into the fire.

life|09-02||Αγία Παρθαγάπη η Μάρτυς||Saint Parthagape completed her martyrdom in the sea, in its waters. // The verses of the Synaxaristes say that in this way she found above in heaven the sea of God's gifts.

life|09-03||Αγία Βασίλισσα||In the time when Alexander was governor of Nicomedia and a persecution of the Christians was taking place, Saint Basilissa was denounced as a Christian. She confessed her faith with boldness and underwent harsh tortures: she was struck in the face, stripped and beaten with rods, the skin of her feet was flayed, her ankles were pierced with iron spikes and she was hung upside down over the smoke of sulfur, pitch, asphalt and lead. // According to the text, she remained unharmed in a blazing furnace and between two great lions. Alexander was moved, fell at her feet and asked forgiveness, and she led him to Antonius, bishop of Nicomedia, who baptized him. Alexander died a little later, glorifying God. // Basilissa buried the governor together with the bishop and went outside the city, about three signs away. There she prayed upon a rock and, according to the text, water welled up from the rock. She drank of it, thanked God and gave up her spirit. The bishop buried her relics near the rock, from which the water flows, as the text says, to this day.

life|09-03||Άγιος Αριστίων ο Ιερομάρτυρας Επίσκοπος Αλεξανδρείας||Aristion was bishop of Alexandria. Because he taught the word of the Gospel with boldness, he was arrested by the governor of Alexandria and confessed before him that Christ is true God. // They threw him into fire and so he received the desired end of martyrdom.

life|09-03||Άγιος Αρχοντίων ο Μάρτυρας||Saint Archontion completed his martyrdom by famine, that is, by hunger. // The verses of the Synaxaristes say that in this way he conquered the ruler of the world, the devil, who is compared there to a lamia, a predatory beast.

life|09-03||Άγιος Ζήνων ο Μάρτυρας||Saint Zeno was martyred cast into boiling lead. // The verses of the Synaxaristes say that, aflame with divine longing for God, he passed joyfully through the hot lead.

life|09-03||Άγιος Κωνσταντίνος ο Βασιλιάς, ο Νέος ο εν τοις Αγίοις Αποστόλοις||Constantine was an emperor, and according to the verses of the Synaxaristes Christ crowned him in the heavens, as a pious man, with a becoming crown. // According to the footnote, which relies on Meletius, it appears that he was the son of Heraclius, in 611, and Orthodox in faith. He lived as emperor only a few months and was put to death by poison.

life|09-03||Άγιος Πολύδωρος ο Νεομάρτυρας||Polydorus was martyred in new Ephesus, in more recent times, and completed his martyrdom by hanging. // The verses of the Synaxaristes present him as a gift of God, precious and new, in keeping with his name, Polydorus. His martyrdom is referred to the New Martyrologion.

life|09-03||Άγιος Χαρίτων ο Μάρτυρας||Saint Chariton completed his martyrdom cast into a pit of quicklime. // The verses of the Synaxaristes say that, entering the pit of quicklime, he found incorruptible and indestructible light in heaven.

life|09-03||Όσιος Θεόκτιστος συνασκητής του Μεγάλου Ευθυμίου||Theoctistus loved God from childhood, left his homeland and relatives and went to the holy places of Jerusalem. He came to the lavra of Pharan, six miles from Jerusalem, found a cell and shut himself in there, struggling against the passions and the demons. // Then Great Euthymius also came and stayed with him. The two venerable ones were united by a bond of love and ascetic fellowship: they had the same mind and did the same works. After the second day of Theophany they would withdraw into the deeper desert and return to their cells on the feast of Palms. // After five years they found a large cave on the northern cliff of a dry river and lived there on wild herbs, until their virtue became known. Many brethren ran to them and it became a coenobium, of which Theoctistus was superior until the end of his life. Euthymius built a lavra nearby and sent to the coenobium of Theoctistus those who wished to become monks, among them, many years later, the young Sabbas. // Theoctistus, in deep old age, fell gravely ill and died. Venerable men buried him, among them Euthymius, then ninety years old, and the patriarch of Jerusalem Anastasius, on the third of the month, in the year 451.

life|09-04||Αγία Ερμιόνη||Hermione was one of the four virgin prophetess daughters of the Apostle Philip, one of the seven deacons. Together with Eutychis she went to Asia to find John the Theologian and, because God had translated him, she found Petronius, a disciple of Paul, and was taught by him. Hermione practiced the art of medicine and crowds of people were healed by the invocation of the name of Christ. // Under Trajan she was denounced as a Christian. The emperor tried to persuade her and ordered her to be slapped, but she saw Christ sitting in the court in the form of Petronius and he strengthened her. Trajan let her go free and the saint opened an inn in Asia, where she cared for strangers in soul and body. // Under Hadrian, in 117, she was brought again and beaten. According to the text, when they throw her into a cauldron of pitch, sulfur, asphalt and lead, after she was sealed with the sign of the cross, the fire went out and she remained untouched. On a red-hot frying pan an angel scattered the fire and burned those who were near. Hadrian sent her to a pagan temple and, as she prayed, thunder was heard and all the idols fell in pieces. // He then ordered her to be beheaded outside the city, but the hands of the executioners Theodulus and Theotimus withered, and they believed in Christ, were healed and died through her prayer. Afterwards the saint also fell asleep in the same place, and Christians buried their relics in Ephesus.

life|09-04||Άγιοι 3.608 (κατ' άλλους 3.628) Μάρτυρες πού μαρτύρησαν στή Νικομήδεια||These saints were found hidden in the mountains and caves of Nicomedia, around the year 290. The emperor Maximian first tortured them with various torments and finally put them to death. // Thus they received the crowns of martyrdom.

life|09-04||Άγιοι Θαθουήλ και Βεβαία||Thathuel and his sister Bebaia lived in the time of the emperor Hadrian, around 117. Thathuel was a priest of idolatrous error, but he was instructed by a bishop and came to faith in Christ. // For this reason the local governor Augarus had him beaten with rods and his eyes burned. Then they bound his hands behind him and struck him on the belly, hung him by one hand, scraped him and burned him from beneath with fire, and finally sawed him with a device, starting from the head. He completed his martyrdom by the sword, together with his sister Bebaia.

life|09-04||Άγιοι Θεότιμος (ή Τιμόθεος) και Θεόδουλος||Theotimus and Theodulus were executioners. According to the text, when they took Saint Hermione outside the city to behead her, before she could pray their hands withered. // They fell at her feet, believed wholeheartedly in the Lord Jesus Christ and were healed. They asked her to pray for them too and, giving up their souls in her presence, departed with a blessed end. Their relics were buried in Ephesus together with those of the saint.

life|09-04||Άγιοι Κεντυρίων, Θεόδωρος, Αμμιανός, Ιουλιανός και Ωκεανός οι Μάρτυρες||Centurion, Theodore, Ammianus and Julian came from the same village. For their confession of Christ they were first tortured with various torments by the emperor Maximian, around 288. // Then they were put into a heated bath, and according to the text an angel of God kept them unharmed. Their feet were cut off with axes and they were thrown into a fire, where they ended their lives in the Lord.

life|09-04||Άγιος Σαρβήλος (ή Ζάρβηλος) ο Μάρτυρας||Sarbelus was martyred by stoning. // According to the verses of the Synaxarion, because he did not honor the impious worship, the hands of impious men pelted him with stones.

life|09-04||Άγιος Βαβύλας ο Ιερομάρτυρας και οι συν αυτώ||Babylas was bishop of Antioch, successor of Zebinus, in the time of the emperor Numerian. When he learned that Numerian had inhumanly slaughtered the son of the king of the Persians, whom he held as a hostage for peace, and that he sacrificed to idols and sought to enter the church, he stood at the doors. He broke through the bodyguards, put his hand on the emperor's chest, rebuked him and drove him out of the church. // The emperor was silent at that moment, but the next day he summoned the saint and, since he could not bend him either with flattery or with threats, bound him with iron chains at the neck and feet and cast him into prison. Three children followed him, brothers according to the flesh, young in age but elders in knowledge. The emperor questioned them and found them unyielding, as he did their mother, and he commanded that the mother be struck on the face and that the children be given as many blows with rods as they had years. Then he ordered that Babylas be hung up together with the children and torn with iron claws. // Finally he decided that they should be put to death by the sword. Babylas placed the children before him and, when he saw them beheaded first, he said the words of Isaiah: "Behold, I and the children whom God has given me." Then he himself was beheaded, around 283. The Christians buried him with the chains on his neck and feet, as he had instructed while he lived.

life|09-04||Άγιος Βαβύλας ο Μάρτυρας ο διδάσκαλος στή και οι 84 Μαθητές του οι Μάρτυρες||At the time when the emperor Maximian was in Nicomedia and proclaiming a persecution, around 298, a pagan informed him that in a hidden chamber sat an old man, Babylas, who taught the children of the Christians to revere the Crucified One and to turn away from the gods. They brought him before the emperor together with his students, who numbered eighty-four. // The saint answered that the gods of the nations are demons, whereas their own God made the heavens. The emperor ordered that he be struck with stones on the nape of the neck, on the ribs and on the shins; his joints were broken, they loaded him with heavy chains and shut him in prison. Among the children, who refused to sacrifice, ten stood out in particular, and Ammonius and Charitus said that they were faithful Christians. All the children cried out, "We are Christians and we do not sacrifice," and the tyrant ordered them to be beaten and imprisoned without food. // In the end he ordered that both the children and their teacher be put to death by the sword. On the way to the place of execution, the saint sang with them, "Behold, I and the children whom God has given me." Babylas was beheaded first, and then the children. Christians took the relics by night, carried them by boat to Constantinople and buried them in three coffins outside the northern wall, where the Chora monastery stands.

life|09-05||Άγιος Αβδαίος ο Επίσκοπος||Abdaeus lived in the time of Theodosius the Younger and of Yazdegerd, king of the Persians, around 412. The chief magus arrested him and tried to force him to worship the sun and fire. // Since he was not persuaded, they struck him over his whole body with pomegranate rods full of thorns, so much that he became like a dead man. The executioners brought him to his house and, after a short while, he gave up his soul to God.

life|09-05||Άγιοι Μέδιμνος, Ουρβανός, Θεόδωρος και 80 Ιερείς και Διάκονοι||These saints were persecuted from the Church by the evil-minded Arian emperor Valens. They suffered many torments and punishments and in the end were put on a boat without ballast, which was left to drift out at sea. // When it reached the gulf called Astacene, the Arians sent some of their like-minded men by skiff, who set fire to the ship. The saints, struggling with the fire and the sea, were burned together with the ship, sank, and so were perfected in the Lord.

life|09-07||Άγιοι Εύοδος και Ονησιφόρος οι Απόστολοι||Evodus was one of the seventy apostles and became bishop of great Antioch, after the apostle Peter. Having preached the Gospel with power and shone in every virtue, he passed to the Lord. // Onesiphorus is the one whom the apostle Paul mentions in the second epistle to Timothy, wishing mercy upon his household because he often refreshed him and was not ashamed of his chains. He became bishop of Colophon, later called Sugandzikion, in Asia Minor; he proved able in speech and courageous, and he strengthened the faith of Christ even unto blood, and so departed to the heavens.

life|09-07||Άγιος Ευψύχιος ο Μάρτυρας||Eupsychius came from Caesarea. When his father died, he was baptized and received the faith in Christ, distributed all his possessions to the poor and preached Christ to all the unbelievers. For this reason the governor of Cappadocia arrested him in the time of the emperor Hadrian. They scraped his sides and threw him into prison, where, according to the text, an angel of the Lord healed him. They hung him up again and scraped him harshly, and in the end they beheaded him, and according to tradition, from his severed neck milk and water flowed instead of blood. Thus he received from the Lord the crown of martyrdom.

life|09-08||Άγιοι Ρούφος και Ρουφιανός οι Μάρτυρες||Rufus and Rufinianus were martyrs of Christ who completed their martyrdom by the sword, being beheaded. The synaxarion preserves only this memory of the manner of their death, namely that one followed the other into martyrdom.

life|09-08||Άγιος Αθανάσιος ο Νεομάρτυρας||Athanasius was martyred in Thessaloniki and completed his martyrdom by hanging, that is, suspended. The synaxarion notes in a verse that his gallows appeared as a ladder that raised him up to heaven.
life|09-08||Άγιος Αρτεμίδωρος ο Μάρτυρας||Artemidorus completed his martyrdom in fire, burning for his faith in Christ. The synaxarion preserves no other details about his life.

life|09-08||Άγιος Σέβηρος ο Μάρτυρας||Severus was a martyr of Christ who was ready to endure every pain and completed his martyrdom by the sword, being beheaded. The synaxarion mentions no other details about his life.

life|09-08||Γέννησις της Υπεραγίας Θεοτόκου||The father of the Theotokos, Joachim, came from the royal tribe of David and, because he had no child and was reproached for it, he did not cease to offer double gifts to God, since he was wealthy and devoted to God. Her mother, Anna, also came from the royal line of David and was most noble in body and soul. // Both grieved over the reproach of childlessness: Joachim went to the mountain and Anna entered the garden, and they besought God with tears to grant them the fruit of the womb. They were heard and begot the Theotokos Mary, the holiest of all the saints, and so they obtained an incomparable offspring. From their daughter, the ever-virgin Mariam, the Son of God deigned to be born. // The text also explains the ancestry of Anna: from Matthan, who took as wife Mary of the tribe of Judah, were born Jacob, the father of Joseph the betrothed, and three daughters, Mary, Sobe and Anna. Mary bore Salome, Sobe bore Elizabeth and Anna bore the Theotokos, so that Salome, Elizabeth and the Theotokos were first cousins to one another.

life|09-09||Άγιος Σεβηριανός ο Μεγαλομάρτυρας||Severian lived in Sebasteia in the time of the king Licinius and the duke Lysias, in the year 315, and was known everywhere for his virtue and his faith in Christ, while belonging to the senatorial order. When Lysias, who had also put to death the holy Forty Martyrs, came to Sebasteia, they denounced him for teaching many Greeks to become Christians, for having inspired by his teaching the courage of the forty martyrs and for tending, as a wealthy man, the imprisoned Christians. // The saint anticipated the envoys, presented himself alone before Lysias and confessed the faith with boldness. They beat him with sinews, hung him up and scraped him with iron claws, and the governor marveled at his patience. They shut him in prison, and five days later summoned him again: they broke his mouth with a stone and again hung him up and scraped him. // In the end they brought him up onto a high wall, tied two heavy stones to him, one at the neck and one at the feet, and hung him. Hanging there he showed marvelous courage and gave up his soul to God. // The Christians took the relic and carried it with honor to Sebasteia. According to the text, as the Christians were going out to receive it, a servant of the martyr died. His wife, who could not go out, spoke to her dead husband as to a living man and called him to rise and go to meet their master, and the dead man rose, cast off the shroud, ran and met the relic. He lived another fifteen years and a little more, and then died again. // The relic was buried in a place revealed later by God: according to the text, an eagle appeared holding a crown woven of fragrant flowers and dropped it upon the spot, and the Christians, understanding the sign, dug and found the relic.

life|09-09||Άγιος Χαρίτων ο Μάρτυρας||Chariton was a martyr of Christ and completed his martyrdom by the sword, having been beheaded for his faith. The synaxarion preserves no other details about his life.

life|09-09||Όσιος Θεοφάνης ο Ομολογητής||Theophanes lived in the time of the emperors Carus and Carinus, in the year 283, and was born of Greek parents. He believed in Christ in a marvelous way when he was very young: he saw a child in danger of dying from the cold, took off his clothes and clothed him. When his father asked him where his clothes were, he answered that he had put them on Christ, and when his father asked him who Christ is, since they worship Hermes and Apollo, the saint disowned his father as godless. // According to the text, an angel of the Lord took him to Mount Diabenon and handed him over to an ascetic who had practiced asceticism for seventy-five years. The latter taught him the ascetic life and the sacred letters, and both were fed by an angel. Five years later the ascetic died and Theophanes remained to practice asceticism for another fifty-eight years. // Guided by an angel, he came out of the cave and, seated upon a lion, went about proclaiming to all the faith in Christ. The emperors Carus and Carinus arrested him, gave him a hundred blows and tortured him with various punishments. But because many Greeks believed and were baptized through his miracles, they were put to shame and set him free. The saint returned to the cave, lived another seventeen years and died, having lived seventy-five years in all.

life|09-10||Αγία Πουλχερία η βασίλισσα||Pulcheria was the sister of the king Theodosius the Younger. After succeeding to the throne of her brother, she married the most pious Marcian, who was an old man, so that he might govern the state well, and she kept her virginity incorrupt and pure to the end. // She lived a pious and God-pleasing life, built many churches and hospitals and convened at Chalcedon the holy and ecumenical Fourth Council. Having shone with many accomplishments, she fell asleep in peace and went to Christ the heavenly Bridegroom. // According to a comment in the text, she was very learned in the Greek and Latin languages, taught her brother Theodosius how to conduct himself and to be pious, and fought the heresy of Nestorius and Eutyches, for which reason Leo, the pope of Rome, also loved her.

life|09-10||Άγιοι Απελλής, Λουκάς και Κλήμης οι Απόστολοι||This Apelles is different from the Apelles who became bishop of Heraclea in Thrace. The apostle Paul mentions him in the epistle to the Romans as approved in Christ. According to the text he became chief shepherd of Smyrna, served Christ piously and departed to him. // Luke is different from the evangelist. Paul mentions him in the first epistle to Timothy. He became the first bishop of Laodicea in Syria, shepherded well his rational flock and went to the Lord. // Clement is different from the bishop of Rome. Paul mentions him in the epistle to the Philippians as his fellow-laborer in the Gospel. He became bishop of Sardis and, bearing in his body the marks of Christ, departed to him.

life|09-10||Άγιος Βαρυψάβας ο Μάρτυρας||Barypsabas received from a hermit the precious blood that had flowed, according to the text, from the side of the Lord Jesus Christ, or according to others from the icon of Christ. With this blood he performed many healings. For this reason he was killed by unbelievers with clubs, and the precious blood remained preserved by the disciple of the saint.

life|09-10||Όσιος Πέτρος Επίσκοπος Νικαίας||Peter was bishop of Nicaea. The synaxarion notes that he ended his life in peace and, as his verse says, after death became a fellow-assessor of the fishermen, that is, of the apostles. It preserves no other details about his life.
