life|09-11||Άγιος Ευφρόσυνος ο μάγειρας||Euphrosynus was born of rustic parents and grew up with a private upbringing. Later he went to a monastery, became a monk and a servant of the monks, and always worked in the kitchen. Because he was rustic, everyone despised him and mocked him, but he bore everything with courage of heart and a calm mind. // In the monastery there was also a priest, a friend of God, who begged that God reveal to him the good things that those who love him will enjoy. One night, as he slept, he saw in his sleep that he found himself in a garden full of marvelous good things and saw there in the midst Euphrosynus the cook enjoying them. When he asked him what garden it was, he answered that it is the dwelling of God's elect and that God had permitted him to be there. The priest asked for something of these things, and Euphrosynus put some apples into his cloak. // When the semantron sounded, the priest woke up and really found the apples in his cloak. He asked Euphrosynus where he had been that night, and he at first denied it, as one humble-minded. In the end he confessed that the Lord had worked through this lowly man to inform the priest. // The priest related the vision to all the brothers, who marveled and were stirred to zeal for virtue. Euphrosynus, avoiding the glory of men, left the monastery secretly and remained completely unknown. Many sick people who ate of those apples were healed, according to the text.

life|09-11||Άγιοι Διόδωρος, Διομήδης και Δίδυμος||These saints were from Laodicea in Syria. The ruler of the place arrested them and, because they confessed with boldness that they were Christians, they were scourged so harshly that from the great beating they gave up their souls to God and received from him the crowns of martyrdom.

life|09-12||Άγιοι Μακεδόνιος, Θεόδουλος και Τατιανός οι Μάρτυρες||The holy Macedonius, Theodulus and Tatian were martyrs of Christ and completed their martyrdom by the sword, being beheaded for the love of Christ. The synaxarion preserves no other details about their lives.

life|09-12||Άγιος Θεόδωρος ο Ιερομάρτυρας Επίσκοπος Αλεξανδρείας||Theodore was bishop of Alexandria. Because he preached Christ with boldness, the Alexandrians seized him and, inflamed with anger, crowned him with thorns and struck his face. They led him bound around the whole city and threw him into the sea. Because he remained unharmed through all this by divine grace, in the end, by order of the governor, he was beheaded and went as a victor to the heavens.

life|09-12||Άγιος Κουρνούτος ο Ιερομάρτυρας Επίσκοπος Ικονίου||Cornutus was born and raised in the city of Iconium and later became its bishop. Once, while he was in the village called Sursuru and was teaching the faith to unbelievers, the persecutors seized him and brought him to the governor Perinius. After he courageously endured all his savagery, they cut off his head and he received the crown of martyrdom.
life|09-12||Άγιος Ωκεανός ο Μάρτυρας||Oceanus was a martyr of Christ and completed his martyrdom in fire, burning for his faith. The synaxarion mentions no other details about his life.
life|09-12||Όσιος Δανιήλ ο Θάσιος||Daniel is the venerable one associated with Thasos, and the synaxarion notes that he ended his life in peace. It preserves no other details about his life.

life|09-13||Άγιοι Κρονίδης, Λεόντιος, Σεραπίων, Γορδιανός, Σέλευκος, Μακρόβιος, Ουαλέριος (ή Ουαλεριανός), Λουκιανός, Ζωτικός και Ηλεί οι Μάρτυρες||Cronides shone as a deacon in Alexandria, and Leontius and Serapion became his disciples. Because they learned piety from him, the unbelievers seized them together with their teacher and, after they had tried many and various torments, bound their hands and feet and threw them into the sea. According to the text, angels brought their relics out of the sea and by visions commanded certain Christians to bury them. // Seleucus, Gordian the Cappadocian and Macrobius from Paphlagonia were tortured with various punishments in the province of Galatia, with fire and with racks, and in the end were given as prey to the wild beasts. Their friend Valerius, lamenting and weeping over the tombs of his beloved martyrs, died from the longing he had for them. // Zoticus, Elias and Lucian, in the city of Tomi, by order of the governor Maximus suffered many torments and were then beheaded. All these martyrs completed their martyrdom in the time of the tyrant Licinius, in the year 315.

life|09-13||Άγιος Στράτων ο Μάρτυρας||Straton was a wonderful martyr in Bithynia. The governor of the place seized him and tortured him with various punishments. Then they tied his hands to the branches of two cedars, which they bent down with great force, and afterward let them spring back to their place, and so they divided him into two pieces. The saint gave up his soul to God and received his martyr's end in the time of the tyrant Licinius, in the year 315.

life|09-13||Όσιος Ιερόθεος ο Νέος||Hierotheus the New, the Iberian, was born, according to the synaxarion, in the year 1686 and ended his life in peace. The verse that accompanies him says that he put the passions to death through self-restraint and pains and became a friend to God. No other details are preserved in the text.

life|09-13||Όσιος Πέτρος ο εν τω Ατρώα (κατ’ άλλους "ο εν τή Αγρέα")||The venerable Peter, who is known as the one in Agrea, ended his life in peace. His verse says that, just as Peter loosed the bond of the flesh, so he went to God, the unshakable rock. No other details are preserved in the text.
life|09-14||Άγιος Θεοκλής ο Μάρτυρας||Theocles was a martyr of Christ and completed his martyrdom by the sword, being beheaded for his faith. The synaxarion preserves no other details about his life.

life|09-14||Άγιος Βαλεριανός το νήπιο||Valerian was a small child, an infant, and was beheaded with a sword for his faith in Christ. The verse of the synaxarion says that God gave him in heaven a most great crown. No other details are preserved.

life|09-14||Άγιος Μακάριος ο Οσιομάρτυρας ο Νέος||Macarius was martyred in Thessaloniki, according to the synaxarion at the beginning of the 16th century, and was a disciple of Saint Niphon of Constantinople. He completed his martyrdom by the sword, being beheaded, and became a venerable martyr.

life|09-14||Άγιος Πάπας ο Μάρτυρας||Papas lived in the time of the king Maximian and the governor Magnus, in the city of Laranda in the province of Lycaonia. His martyrdom was varied: he received blows on the jaws, was hung up and torn with iron claws, iron shoes were nailed on him and he was forced to run in them. Thus, after such torments, the blessed one gave up his soul to God.

life|09-14||Ύψωσις του Τιμίου και Ζωοποιού Σταυρού||Constantine the Great, equal to the apostles, was the first of the emperors of old Rome to accept Christianity. While he was at war and saw that the enemy army was larger than his own, he was in perplexity and fear. Then at midday there appeared in the sky the form of a cross made of stars, and around it letters that said, "By this, conquer." He immediately made a similar cross and commanded that it go before the army, and he defeated the enemies utterly. Thus he understood the power of the Crucified One, believed and was baptized together with his mother. // He sent his mother Helen to Jerusalem, to venerate the Tomb of the Lord and the other holy places and to find the precious Cross. After searching with zeal, she found it hidden, together with the other two crosses of the thieves and with the nails. Since she did not know which of the three was the Lord's, she recognized it by the miracle: a dead widow was raised as soon as she touched the cross of the Lord, while the other two did nothing. // Helen and the senate that was with her venerated the precious Cross with great reverence. Since the people also asked to venerate it and, because of the crowd, this was not possible, they asked to see it at least. Then Macarius, patriarch of Jerusalem, went up to the ambo and lifted it with his two hands, showing it to all, and the people cried out from the heart, Lord, have mercy. From then on the holy fathers decreed that Christians celebrate on this day the venerable and universal Exaltation of the Cross.

life|09-15||Άγιος Βησσαρίων Αρχιεπίσκοπος Λαρίσης||Bessarion was born in 1550, according to the text, of Orthodox parents, in a village of Megales Pyles, at the edge of Macedonia or rather in Thessaly. At the age of ten he longed for the monastic life and went to Mark, metropolitan of Larissa, with whom he passed regularly through the ranks, from reader to priest, and later was ordained bishop of Domenikos and Elassona. But the people did not receive him, out of contentiousness, and the saint paid no heed to the contempt, but stayed with Mark, serving and tending in word and deed the sick and poor of Larissa. // When the see of Stagoi became widowed, its people asked him to shepherd them, and he remained there six years, enduring many afflictions and exiles from a certain malicious man, Dometius. When Mark died, at the request of the bishops, the clergy and the people, he became metropolitan of Larissa by the appointment of Patriarch Jeremias. // The text mentions the freeing of slaves and the help given to those in need, as well as the bridges he built, among them the bridge over the river that descends from Pindus toward Aetolia and is called Leukopotamos, which no one before him had managed to build. He was the first to found and build from the foundations the Monastery of Christ the Savior, called Lousikon, near his village, which was later renovated by his nephew Neophytus and others. // Having governed his flock in a God-pleasing manner, he departed to the Lord at about fifty years of age. His holy skull, after his death, gushes forth miracles and healings and drives away, according to the text, plague and pestilence from those who run to it with faith.

life|09-15||Άγιος Ιωάννης ο Νεομάρτυρας||John was from Crete and was martyred, according to the synaxarion, at the beginning of the 19th century. He became a new martyr for his faith in Christ. Other details of his martyrdom are not preserved in the text.

life|09-15||Άγιος Μάξιμος ο Μάρτυρας||Maximus was a martyr of Christ who completed his martyrdom by the sword, being beheaded. His verse says that, seeing Christ offer him a crown, he offered his head to the sword. Other details are not preserved.

life|09-15||Όσιος Γεράσιμος κτήτορας της Ιεράς Μονής Αγίας Τριάδος Σουρβίας||Gerasimus was the founder of the Holy Monastery of the Holy Trinity, called Sourvia, which is located near Makrinitsa in Zagora. He ended his life in peace. His holy skull is kept, according to the synaxarion, in the monastery. No other details are preserved.

life|09-15||Όσιος Φιλόθεος ο Πρεσβύτερος και θαυματουργός||Philotheus came from the village of Myrmis in the theme of the Opsikion. His mother was called Theophila, a name similar to his own. He married, had children and, as a devout and prudent man, was ordained a priest. From then on he devoted himself to fasting and prayer and was granted by God the gift of miracles. // To many hungry people he marvelously gave bread, he changed the water of a river into wine and moved a great rock to another place by his word alone, and he performed other such miracles while he lived. // When he died and was buried, a year later they transferred his relic to another place. According to the text, as the two priests wished to move it, the saint stretched out his hands like a living man, took them by the shoulders, rose, walked three steps and was placed in the spot where he lies to this day, gushing forth inexhaustible myrrh.

life|09-16||Αγία Μελιτίνη η Μάρτυς||She came from Marcianopolis in Thrace and lived in the time of the emperor Antoninus and the governor Antiochus, around the year 100. Because she did not deny the faith in Christ, she suffered many torments and was handed over to the wife of the governor so that she might be softened by flattery. But not only was she not deceived, she also made the governor's wife a Christian. By her prayer she cast down and ground to dust the idols of Apollo and Heracles and performed other miracles, leading many unbelievers to the faith. For this she was beheaded and received the crown of martyrdom. // Her relic remained unburied, until a Christian from Macedonia, Acacius, asked for it from the governor and took it, to carry it to his homeland. Acacius fell ill and died on the journey, and when the ship reached a headland of Lemnos, the relic of the saint was buried there and beside her was also buried Acacius, the lover of martyrs. Her relic, according to the text, is found whole in the Patriarchate of Constantinople.

life|09-17||Αγία Αγαθόκλεια||She was the slave of a Christian, Nicholas, but his wife was unbelieving and impious. For eight whole years this woman tormented her, to bring her to impiety: at times she struck her on the neck with large hard stones, at times she forced her to run barefoot over difficult places, she crushed her ribs with an iron hammer and burned her tongue. Since she could not persuade her, she set fire to her neck, and so the saint departed from the body and went to the heavens.

life|09-17||Άγιοι Μάξιμος, Θεόδοτος και Ασκληπιοδότη οι Μάρτυρες||There was a woman, Asclepiodote, and two young men, Maximus and Theodotus. For their confession of Christ the unbelievers beat them, cut off the extremities of their bodies and threw them into a dark prison. In the end they were beheaded and together received the crowns of martyrdom.

life|09-17||Άγιοι Λουκία και Γεμινιανός||Lucia was a widow and Geminianus her son. Both were martyred for Christ. Geminianus, full of courage, endured with fortitude the cut of the sword, while Lucia, according to the verse of the synaxarion, ended her life peacefully.

life|09-17||Αγία Θεοδότη η Μάρτυς||In the time of the emperor Severus Alexander, around 222, the governor Simplicius was sent to Cappadocia to persecute the Christians. Theodote, a wealthy woman from the regions of the Black Sea, was denounced and, because she did not deny Christ, was hung up and scraped on the sides for many hours, yet without appearing to feel pain. In prison, according to the text, the doors opened by themselves and the next day she appeared completely healthy, without a mark of a wound. They put her into a furnace, from which the flame came out and burned about seventy men, while she came out unharmed, singing psalms. Simplicius dragged her bound with him to Ancyra and Nicaea, where in the temple of the idols, as soon as she prayed, the idols fell and were shattered. They wished to saw her, but the saw twisted and the executioners grew weary, and then the governor ordered that she be beheaded, and so she received the crown of martyrdom.

life|09-17||Άγιοι Πηλέας και Νείλος οι Ιερομάρτυρες και Επίσκοποι||They were two bishops from Egypt, who were arrested in the time of the persecution of the Christians by the idolaters. Together with the glorious officials Patermuthius and Elias and with others from Egypt and Palestine, they underwent martyrdom by fire, and received their crowns from the Lord.

life|09-17||Άγιοι Πατερμούθιος και Ηλίας οι ένδοξοι||They were two glorious officials of Egypt, who were arrested in the persecution of the idolaters against the Christians. Together with the bishops Peleus and Nilus and with fifty martyrs from Palestine, they completed their martyrdom by fire and received their crowns from the Lord.

life|09-17||Άγιοι 100 Μάρτυρες οι Αιγύπτιοι||They were arrested in the same persecution against the Christians, together with the bishops Peleus and Nilus and the officials Patermuthius and Elias. First the pagans blinded them by putting out their eyes and cut the tendons of their left feet, and then handed them over to labor in the mines. In the end they were beheaded and received from the Lord the crowns of the struggle.

life|09-17||Άγιοι Χαράλαμπος και Παντολέων και η συνοδεία τους||The synaxarion preserves here only their memory, together with the verse that Charalampus went joyfully to the slaughter and Pantoleon to the knife with the courage of a lion. Their memory belongs also to their company, that is, to the martyrs who were martyred with them.

life|09-18||Αγίες Σοφία και Ειρήνη οι Μάρτυρες||Their synaxarion is limited to a brief mention: the holy martyrs Sophia and Irene were perfected by the sword, their heads having been cut off. According to the verse, through this death they saw the peace that surpasses all understanding.

life|09-18||Αγία Αριάδνη||She lived in the time of the emperors Hadrian and Antoninus, from the year 117 to 139, as the slave of an official, Tertyllus, the foremost man of the city of Promissus in Phrygia Salutaris. Her master forced her to celebrate with him in the temple of the idols the birthday of his child, but she did not obey and they struck her hard. When the governor pursued her again, she approached a rock and prayed to be saved from her persecutors. According to the text, the rock split open at a divine nod and received her within itself, while the persecutors were destroyed by fearsome angels who appeared mounted on horses and with spears.

life|09-20||Άγιοι Υπάτιος και Ανδρέας οι Ομολογητές||They came from Lydia and as children went to school, where by their fasting, vigils, pure life, humility and love they surpassed all the students. Hypatius loved the monastic life and Andrew took up service in the church. When the bishop of Ephesus learned of their virtuous conduct, he summoned them and ordained Hypatius a bishop and Andrew a presbyter. The iconoclast Leo brought them before him, because they preached the truth and taught reverence for the holy icons. He imprisoned them, they were dragged along the ground, their heads were flayed, he burned holy icons upon them, smeared their beards with pitch and dragged them through the city, and finally slaughtered them at the place called Xerolophos. After their death he did not allow them to be buried, but threw them to the dogs.

life|09-20||Άγιοι Μάξιμος, Ευπρέπιος, Αναστάσιος, Θεόδωρος και Αναστάσιος (άλλος) οι Ομολογητές||Maximus and his three disciples, Anastasius, Theodore and Euprepius, together with the other Anastasius, were confessors of Orthodoxy. According to the text, Maximus convened a synod in Rome in the year 645 and anathematized the heresy of Constans, grandson of Heraclius, who taught that Christ has one will. The emperor brought them from Rome, exiled them to Thrace, and when he saw them unafraid, he cut off the right hands and the tongues of Maximus and of the elder Anastasius and exiled them to the land of Lazica together with the other disciples. Maximus lived three years in exile and fell asleep full of days, the elder Anastasius ended his life after twenty years of exile, the younger Anastasius ended his life in a fortress of Thrace, Theodore died after twenty years of exile and Euprepius after one year. Thus all received the crowns of confession.

life|09-20||Άγιοι Αρτεμίδωρος και Θαλός οι Μάρτυρες||Their synaxarion is very brief. They were beheaded with the sword, because they did not worship Artemis, the goddess of the pagans who kills strangers.

life|09-20||Άγιος Ιλαρίων ο Οσιομάρτυρας ο νέος από την Κρήτη||He was a Cretan and was martyred in Constantinople, where he was perfected by the sword. According to the verse of the synaxarion, he received a double crown, as a venerable one and as an athlete of the Lord. His martyrdom is referred to a more recent martyrology.

life|09-20||Όσιος Μελέτιος Επίσκοπος Κύπρου||He became bishop of the Church of Cyprus and was devout and God-fearing. His ceaseless work was to teach the people the divine words of Christ and to distribute his possessions to the poor. Thus he lived all his life and fell asleep in peace.

life|09-20||Άγιος Ιωάννης ο Αιγύπτιος και οι 40 συν αυτώ Μάρτυρες||John the venerable martyr and the forty martyrs who were with him, because they did not obey an impious and lawless emperor (Maximian), died by the sword in the year 295. Thus all received the crowns of martyrdom.

life|09-21||Άγιος Ευσέβιος ο Μάρτυρας||Of his own accord he presented himself to the governor of Phoenicia and told him that he was doing a foolish work in persecuting the flock of Christ. The governor grew angry and ordered that he be hung up and torn, and that his wounded limbs be rubbed with hair cloths and salt. But the martyr rejoiced as if someone else were suffering. The governor, at a loss what to do, ordered that he be beheaded, and so the blessed one went up to the heavens to receive the crown of martyrdom.

life|09-21||Άγιοι Ευσέβιος, Νέσταβος, Ζήνων, Νέστωρ και Βούσιρις οι Μάρτυρες||According to the synaxarion, Eusebius, Nestabus and Zeno were brothers and died as martyrs by stoning, because of their right faith. Sozomen describes their martyrdom.

life|09-21||Όσιος Ισαάκιος (ή Ακάκιος) Επίσκοπος Κύπρου||He became bishop of the Church of Cyprus and was devout and God-fearing. His ceaseless work was to teach the people the divine words of Christ and to distribute his possessions to the poor. Thus he lived all his life and in the end was put to death by unbelievers with the sword, and went to the Lord whom he longed for.

life|09-21||Άγιος Πρίσκος ο Μάρτυρας||His synaxarion is very brief: Priscus was martyred by fire. According to the verse, he had living water in his heart and therefore did not fear the burning of the body.

life|09-22||Άγιοι Ισαάκ και Μαρτίνος οι Μάρτυρες||Isaac and Martin were martyrs who were perfected by the sword. According to the verse of the synaxarion, Isaac, as a young man, completed by being slain what was lacking from the sacrifice of the patriarch Abraham, while Martin hastened toward the sword with courage from Christ. The main narrative of their martyrdom is not preserved here.

life|09-22||Όσιος Κοσμάς ο Ζωγραφίτης||He was a venerable ascetic of Mount Athos, of the Zographou monastery, whose ascetic life is placed at a date that cannot be read clearly in the text. According to the verse, he closed the eyes of the body and saw on high the face of the Lord.

life|09-23||Σύλληψις του Τιμίου Προδρόμου και Βαπτιστού Ιωάννη||When the Lord was about to come down from the heavens and be conceived without seed in the virginal womb of the Theotokos, he wished to confirm his seedless conception by another marvelous wonder. So he sent the archangel Gabriel to the prophet and high priest Zechariah, who was in the temple, offering incense and praying for the people, and announced to him the marvelous conception of the Forerunner in the womb of his barren and aged wife Elizabeth, which we celebrate today. Because Zechariah did not believe the message, he was punished with speechlessness and silence, until he should see the message of the archangel fulfilled. According to the notes, the event is placed on the tenth day of the seventh month, and the conception took place, according to Sebastos of Trebizond, on a Sunday.

life|09-23||Άγιος Ανδρέας ο Μάρτυρας||He lived at the time when Basil the Macedonian reigned, in the year 867, when in Africa the Hagarenes held sway and their ruler was the cruel Abrahim. Andrew was already an old man when he presented himself before Abrahim and confessed with courage the faith in Christ. They threw him into prison, where he remained many years, until he was worn out by hunger, thirst and hardships. Finally, because he would not renounce piety, the governor mounted a horse and struck him first in the chest and then in the back with a javelin, and the saint, while giving thanks to God, fell to the ground. Then he was beheaded and gave up his soul into the hands of God.

life|09-23||Αγία Ραΐς η παρθένος||She came from a country of Egypt called Bata (or Tamman), was the daughter of a certain Peter and put on the monastic habit at the age of twelve. Once, going with other virgins to the spring to fetch water, she saw a crowd of virgins, men, presbyters, deacons and monks, whom the governor Lucian held bound. When she learned that they were bound for Christ, she took courage in her soul. The commentariensis (the jailer) advised her to take care of her life and not to die prematurely with the others, but she was not only not persuaded but presented herself to the governor, mocked his gods and, when he derided the faith of the Christians, spat in his face. They tortured her greatly and in the end she was beheaded, receiving from the Lord the crown of martyrdom.

life|09-23||Άγιος Νικόλαος ο Νεομάρτυρας ο παντοπώλης εκ Καρπενησιου||He was a grocer in Constantinople and there he was martyred, perfected by the sword. According to the verse of the synaxarion, he sold on earth all his wares but bought Christ in the heavens, with the sword. His martyrdom is referred to the New Martyrology.

life|09-24||Όσιος Κόπρις||He was born on a dunghill outside the monastery of the cenobiarch Theodosius, because his mother, pursued by the Hagarenes, fled toward Saint Theodosius and was seized by the pains of childbirth. The monks found the infant, by order of Theodosius took him and named him Copris, and fed him with the milk of a goat, which came down by itself from the mountain at the hours of nursing. When he grew up, he was loved by Theodosius and, because he kept the image unblemished, he received the grace to subdue wild beasts. According to the text, he seized a bear that was eating the lettuces of the garden and drove it away, and later, when a bear wounded the monastery's donkey, he made it carry the wood in its place. It was also, according to the text, that he put his bare hand into the boiling cauldron, and the boiling stopped without his suffering anything. After the death of Theodosius he was granted to see him and to chant with him, and Theodosius called him to rest, whereupon Copris, after bidding farewell to all the fathers and brothers, went to the Lord.

life|09-25||Όσιος Παφνούτιος||He was the father of Venerable Euphrosyne. When his daughter left the house secretly and became a monk under the name Smaragdus, he sought her for years in the mountains and ravines. On the day Euphrosyne died she was revealed to him, said only one word to him and Pafnutius, having been granted to see his daughter after thirty-eight years, left homeland and world, became a monk himself and succeeded his daughter in the place and way of life of the monastery. He fell asleep in peace, rejoicing and glad.

life|09-25||Άγιος Παφνούτιος ο Οσιομάρτυρας και αναχωρητής και οι συν αυτώ 546 μαρτυρήσαντες||The synaxarion states only that the venerable martyr Pafnutius was martyred by crucifixion. According to the verse, the friends of the world crucified him, who was already crucified to the world. The narrative of his life is referred to the Neon Eklogion.

life|09-25||Άγιοι Παύλος, Ταττή και τα παιδιά τους||Paul and Tatta, husband and wife, and their four children, Sabinian, Maximus, Rufus and Eugene, came from Damascus. They were denounced as Christians, their feet were secured in the stocks and they were bound with chains. After the trial, they were struck hard and the members of their bodies were racked, and so they gave up their souls to God and received the crowns of martyrdom.

life|09-26||Μετάστασις Αγίου Ιωάννου του Θεολόγου||He came from Bethsaida of Galilee, son of the poor fisherman Zebedee and of Salome. He helped his father with fishing together with his brother James, and when the Lord called him, he left father and boat and followed Christ. He became the beloved disciple, a virgin, who went up Tabor, sat beside the Lord at the mystic supper and followed Christ at the arrest and at the cross, where the Lord entrusted his Mother to him. He was the first, together with Peter, to see the burial wrappings in the tomb, he saw the ascended Lord and received the Holy Spirit at Pentecost. He stayed in Jerusalem until the dormition of the Theotokos, until by the lot of the apostles it fell to him to preach in Asia Minor. According to the text, together with his disciple Prochorus he suffered a storm and shipwreck, they reached Ephesus and there, after he raised Domnus and the father of Dioscorides and dispelled the demon of the bath, he baptized Romana and many others. At the festival of Artemis he destroyed her idol by prayer, an earthquake occurred that killed two hundred people, whom he raised, and the Ephesians believed and were baptized.

life|09-26||Μετάστασις Αγίου Ιωάννου του Θεολόγου||The apostle and evangelist John was preaching in Ephesus, where, according to the text, after his prayer the temple of Artemis collapsed and the demon who dwelt there was driven out. Under Domitian he was exiled to Patmos together with his disciple Prochorus; on the way, according to the text, he raised a soldier, calmed the storm and healed one of his escorts who was suffering from dysentery, so that the escorts believed. In Patmos, according to the text, he freed Apollonides from the spirit of Python and defeated the magician Kynops, whom they worshiped as a god and who sank into the sea; a multitude of people believed and were baptized, among them the proconsul of the island. // When he was recalled from exile under Trajan, the Christians of Patmos asked him to leave his word in writing; John fasted three days, went up the mountain with Prochorus and, amid thunder and lightning, heard a voice saying "In the beginning was the Word," whereupon he dictated the Gospel to Prochorus and handed it to the Christians. Then he returned to Ephesus, where, according to the text, he turned back a young man who had become the leader of robbers, baptized a Jew who believed on seeing a Christian survive poison by the sign of the cross, and gave gold to a poor Christian. // He lived in all one hundred and five years and seven months: he preached nine years before the exile, stayed fifteen in Patmos and lived twenty-six more after his return. In the end he went out from the house of Domnus, whom he had raised, with seven of his disciples, prayed and asked them to dig a grave in the shape of a cross. He lay down inside, they covered him with earth weeping and, at sunrise, he gave up his spirit; when the brothers opened the grave again, they found nothing. The compiler cites testimonies of the Fathers that he indeed died and notes that from his tomb a fine dust comes forth that heals many illnesses.

life|09-26||Αγία Χήρα η Μάρτυς||The holy martyr Chera, according to the four-line verse of the text, was put to death by slaughter for her faith in Christ. The text gives no other details of her life and says only that with her blood she signed her commitment to the Word, her bridegroom.

life|09-26||Αγίες Θέκλα, Μαριάμνη, Μάρθα, Μαρία και Ενναθά οι Παρθενομάρτυρες και Μονάστριες||The text mentions five holy virgins and nuns, who loved Christ and were put to death by their father Paul, who was excessively fond of money. Nikodemos notes that in his opinion these are the same five virgins mentioned in the Synaxarion of 9 June, because there too there are five and there too their murderer is called Paul and fond of money; in the case where he is called their presbyter there, perhaps a spiritual and not a fleshly father is meant.

life|09-27||Αγία Ακυλίνα||The holy Aquilina, according to the text, was a new martyr and was perfected by death after they beat her with rods until she was crushed. The verse of the Synaxarion presents her as a woman by nature who appeared a courageous man before the torments. The text gives no more details about her origin or time.

life|09-27||Αγία Γαϊανή||The holy martyr Gaiane, according to the text, completed her martyrdom after they burned her back. The verse of the Synaxarion says that she offered her back to be burned, in order to see the sword of flame surround her. The text mentions no other details of her life.

life|09-27||Αγία Επίχαρις η Μάρτυς||The holy Epicharis lived in Rome in the time of Diocletian, around 298. She was arrested as a Christian by the prefect Caesarius and, after she confessed with boldness the name of Christ, they hung her up and tore her, and four soldiers crushed her limbs with a lead ball. Because she prayed, according to the text angels came and killed her four torturers. Finally she was condemned to beheading; when she reached the place of execution and stood on a rock, according to the text the rock gushed water. She was beheaded and gave up her soul to God.

life|09-27||Άγιοι Φουρτουνιανός και Φιλήμων ο Επίσκοπος||The holy martyrs Philemon, who was a bishop, and Fortunian are commemorated together on 27 September. According to the verses of the text, Philemon, who loved Christ and was loved by him, was martyred together with Fortunian. The text gives no other details about the place, time or manner of their martyrdom.

life|09-27||Όσιος Ιγνάτιος του Βαθέος Ρύακος||The venerable Ignatius came from the second province of the Cappadocians and lived in the time of Nikephoros Phokas and John Tzimiskes, around 963. From a young age he dedicated himself to God and went to the monastery of Bathys Ryax, where he learned ascetic strictness from the venerable Basil, abbot and founder of the monastery. He was gradually ordained reader, subdeacon, deacon and presbyter and became abbot of the monastery, which he increased in income and buildings, building churches of the Archangel Michael, of the prophet Elijah and of the Holy Apostles, as well as a strong enclosure for the nuns of the area. // He rebuked the rulers with boldness and courage and, after he had made sacred treasures, a signon and a Gospel book covered in silver, he sent them to his monastery. He fell ill with dysentery in Constantinople and, while hastening to reach his monastery, he ended his life in Amorium, where they buried him in a venerable house. A year later the fathers of the monastery opened the tomb and found his relic incorrupt, whole and full of spiritual fragrance; they carried it to the monastery and kept it in the narthex of the church.

life|09-28||Άγιοι Καλλίνικος και Ευστάθιος ο Ρωμαίος οι Μάρτυρες||The holy martyr Eustathius the Roman, according to the verse of the Synaxarion, struggled bravely and was perfected by the sword. The text notes that in the printed Synaxaristes Callinicus is also added, but without verses and without other details. No more details are given about their life and martyrdom.

life|09-28||Άγιοι Μάρκος ο ποιμένας, Αλέξανδρος, Αλφειός και Ζώσιμος τα αδέλφια, Νίκων, Νέων, Ηλιόδωρος και λοιπές Παρθένες και Παιδιά οι Μάρτυρες||These saints lived in the time of Diocletian, when Magnus was governor in Pessinus, around 290. Mark was a shepherd of sheep, with white hair that reached to his heels. When it was revealed that he was a Christian, they hung him up and tore him and sent him to Claudiopolis, where they summoned three smiths from the village of Katalyton, the brothers Alexander, Alpheus and Zosimus, to make iron fetters. According to the text, as soon as they began to strike the iron, it ran like water and their hands became numb; they heard a voice urging them to be martyred together with Mark and confessed at once that they were Christians. // The three brothers were tortured on racks, received molten lead in their mouths and were nailed to a rock, and so gave up their souls. Mark put on iron shoes, was beaten, pierced with spits, had his tongue cut out and was nailed to a rock, and in the end was beheaded. Nikon, Neon and Heliodorus were arrested together with many children and virgins and were beheaded at the place called Moromilion; thus all received the incorruptible crowns of the struggle.

life|09-28||Άγιος Αλέξανδρος και οι συν αυτώ 30 Μάρτυρες||The holy martyr Alexander and thirty other martyrs who were martyred with him are commemorated in the Synaxarion as men who were perfected by the sword. The verse of the text stresses that Alexander was outstanding and that three decades of men were numbered with him. The text gives no other details about the place or time.

life|09-29||Αγία Γουδελία (ή Γοβδελία)||The holy martyr Gudelia was perfected by the sword, according to the verse of the Synaxarion, which says that she offered to Christ her head, as the head of all, by beheading. The text gives no other details about her origin, time or the circumstances of her martyrdom.

life|09-29||Αγία Πετρωνία η Μάρτυς||The holy martyr Petronia was perfected by the sword, having bowed her neck to be beheaded. The verse of the Synaxarion says that, after her death, her gaze opens toward the divine rock, that is, toward Christ. The text mentions no more details of her life.

life|09-29||Άγιοι 150 οι Μάρτυρες||The Synaxarion commemorates one hundred and fifty martyrs of Palestine, who, according to the verse of the text, struggled together, like fifteen decades, and together receive the heavenly crown. The text gives no other information about the time or manner of their martyrdom.

life|09-29||Άγιοι Γοβδελαάς, Δάδας, Κάσδοος και Κασδόα||In the time of Shapur, king of the Persians, around 330, Dadas was Persian by race and Christian by faith, a relative of the king, and revealed his piety. They threw him into a heated furnace, which, according to the text, was extinguished by the sign of the cross and gave forth water. The king's son, Gobdelaas, asked Dadas who had taught him these things and, after he saw a second furnace extinguished by the invocation of Christ, he believed. The king gave him to Gargalus, who tortured him with ox-hide whips, rods, spits, heated irons, a cauldron of pitch, crucifixion and arrows. According to the text, Gobdelaas was continually healed by an angel and the arrows turned back; Gargalus and another Gargalus, a magician, the foremost among the torturers, believed. // He was baptized, according to the text, by a cloud that rained water and oil, and said that amid the tortures his soul had been strengthened in the faith. In the end he was pierced with reeds and gave up his soul to God; his body was dragged by horses and torn, and the pieces were bought by two priests, Dadias and Lydias, who buried them with aromatic spices. Dadas was tortured in various ways and finally cut limb from limb; his members were buried by pious Christians. // Gobdelaas' sister Kasdoa, the king's daughter, also believed, was beaten and imprisoned and died in prison. According to the text, Gobdelaas appeared by night to the priests and asked that his sister be baptized and receive communion; Dadias baptized her and gave her communion in the company of an angel and she gave up her soul. Another relative of the king, Kasdoos, was struck with a wooden sword for the name of Christ and was perfected. The queen anointed the relic of Kasdoa with myrrh, wrapped it in royal purple and placed it together with the relic of Gobdelaas.

life|09-29||Άγιοι Τρύφων, Τρόφιμος και Δορυμέδων||The holy martyrs Tryphon, Trophimus and Dorymedon are commemorated on 29 September together with the one hundred and fifty martyrs of Palestine. The verse of the Synaxarion says that Trophimus and Dorymedon found, together with Tryphon, the heavenly place, that is, the crown of glory. The text gives no more details about the time or manner of their martyrdom.

life|09-30||Αγίες Ριψιμία (η Ριψίμη), Γαϊανή και Άλλες 32 Παρθενομάρτυρες||These holy women were virgins and nuns in the time of Diocletian, around 292, and their superior was Gaiane. When Diocletian was preparing to marry, he learned that Rhipsime was exceedingly beautiful and sent her proposals of marriage. She loved virginity and fled secretly with Gaiane and seventy other virgins toward the city of Ararat in Armenia, where they hid in winepresses. Diocletian wrote to the king of Armenia, Tiridates, to send Rhipsime to him or to take her himself as wife; Tiridates, when he learned of her beauty, fell in love with her too. // According to the text, a thunderclap and a divine voice were heard that strengthened the virgins, while many of the envoys were left speechless or were killed. Tiridates brought her by force to the palace, but she did not yield and remained untouched by the power of Christ. Gaiane, when called to persuade her, encouraged her to resist and for this they broke her teeth with stones and exiled her. The king sent his chief cook, who seized Rhipsime, cut out her tongue, burned her with torches, opened her belly, put out her eyes and cut her to pieces; together with her seventy Christian men were killed. // The thirty-two fellow virgins who went to gather her relics were beheaded with the sword, while Gaiane and two other virgins were tortured with syringes, their skin was flayed, their tongues and bellies were cut, and in the end they were beheaded. In their honor Gregory of Greater Armenia later built three churches, and other churches were built in various parts of Armenia.

life|09-30||Άγιοι 1000 Μάρτυρες||The thousand holy martyrs, according to the text, were beheaded with the sword. The verse of the Synaxarion presents them as a phalanx of a thousand beheaded, who found countless crowns in the struggle. The text gives no other information about the place or time.

life|09-30||Άγιος Μαρδόνιος ο Μάρτυρας||The holy martyr Mardonius was perfected, according to the text, after they placed burning coals on his navel. The verse of the Synaxarion says that Mardonius bears on his navel, as a mark of the passion, the seal of the burning. The text gives no other details.

life|09-30||Άγιος Στρατόνικος ο Μάρτυρας||The holy martyr Stratonicus was perfected by the sword. The verse of the Synaxarion says that he alone defeated a whole army of demons. The text gives no more information about his origin or time.

life|10-02||Όσιος Θεόφιλος ο Ομολογητής||The venerable Theophilus was a monk in the time of the emperor Leo the Isaurian, around 716. Seeing the impiety of the tyrant and the war he waged against the holy icons, he presented himself before him and rebuked him with great boldness, calling him godless, lawless and forerunner of the antichrist. The emperor was enraged, beat him harshly, threw him into prison and left him for some time hungry and thirsty. Then they sent him into exile, and there, giving thanks to God, he fell asleep in the Lord.

life|10-04||Άγιος Πέτρος ο Ιερομάρτυρας εκ Καπιτωλίων||The holy Peter was born and raised in the city of Capitolias and was very wise, prudent and discerning. He had married and had three children, but later became a monk and the bishop of the metropolis of Bostra ordained him a priest by force. He was denounced to the ruler of the Hagarenes as a teacher of the Christians, and because he spoke before him with courage about the faith in Christ, they cut off his right hand and both feet, put out his eyes and nailed him to a cross. In the end they beheaded him, and his martyric body they burned and threw into the river.

life|10-04||Αγία Δομνίνη η Μάρτυς και οι θυγατέρες αυτής Βερνίκη και Προσδόκη||Domnina and her daughters Bernice and Prosdoce, wounded by divine zeal and love for God, left their homes and relatives and went to the city of Edessa. There the husband of Bernice and her father, who were idolaters, arrived suddenly with soldiers, and they arrested them and took them toward Hierapolis, near which a river flows. When the soldiers ate and got drunk, the saints escaped secretly, prayed to God, entered the river and let themselves go with the currents, and so ended their lives drowned. According to Chrysostom, the mother took her daughters by the hand and plunged them into the water so that their virginity might not be ruined by the soldiers, and she herself also sank with them, leaving their shoes outside the river.

life|10-04||Άγιοι Φαύστος, Γάϊος, Ευσέβιος και Χαιρήμων (ή Χαρήμων) οι Διάκονοι||These saints were disciples of the great Dionysius and deacons of the Lord. Gaius and Faustus were exiled together with their teacher and, after suffering much, reached the end of martyrdom. Eusebius and Chaeremon, after the exile of their teacher, visited the martyrs who were in the prisons and buried their precious relics. They lived until the time of the emperor Decius, around 250, and after enduring many trials for the confession of Christ, they were beheaded and received the crowns of martyrdom.

life|10-04||Άγιος Αύδακτος (ή Άδαυκτος) ο Μάρτυρας και η θυγατέρα του Καλλισθένη||Audactus came from Ephesus and was honored by Maximinus, so that he became duke and prefect around 235, because he surpassed others in wealth and prudence. When Maximinus asked for his daughter Callisthene in marriage, Audactus refused to give her to a man alien to the faith of the Christians. For this they seized his property, exiled him to Melitene and there beheaded him. Callisthene cut her hair, put on men's clothes and hid in Nicomedia. Eight years later she went to Thrace and healed the girl of a woman who had diseased eyes, and when the parents asked that she marry the girl, she revealed that she was a woman and made them glorify God. After the death of Maximinus, under Licinius, she presented herself to his wife, the Christian Constantia, sister of Constantine the Great, who made her a mother to her son. With her help she recovered her father's property, transferred his relic from Melitene to Ephesus, built a church in his name and kept it there. Having lived the rest of her life in an apostolic manner, she fell asleep in the Lord.

life|10-04||Όσιος Αμμούν ο Αιγύπτιος||The venerable Ammoun was Egyptian by birth and was left an orphan. After the death of his parents his uncle forced him to marry, and he agreed with his wife to keep virginity. He always worked in the balsam grove, that is, the garden with the balsam plant, with much toil, and after eighteen years he left and went to the great Anthony. Anthony marveled at his virtuous life, and Ammoun became a benefit to many by his virtue and by the many miracles he performed. According to the text, when he died, the great Anthony saw his soul ascending to the heavens, carried by holy angels.

life|10-05||Αγία Μαμελχθή||Mamelchtha came from Persia and was a servant of the temple of Artemis, while she had a Christian sister. She saw in her dream an angel of God showing her and teaching her the mysteries of the Christians, woke up frightened and told it to her sister, who took her to the bishop and he baptized her. As soon as the idolaters learned of it, they were angry and killed her with stones, while she was still wearing the white garments of holy baptism, and threw her into a very deep pit, from which the Christians with difficulty brought out her holy relic. Then the bishop went to the king of the Persians and obtained permission to tear down the temple of Artemis and to build in its place a church of the holy martyr, where he also kept her precious relic.

life|10-07||Άγιοι Ιουλιανός ο πρεσβύτερος και Καισάριος ο διάκονος||Under Claudius Caesar, when the Christians were being persecuted mercilessly, Caesarius came from Africa to Tarracina and, seeing the sacrifices of the idolaters, spat on them and trampled them. He was arrested, remained three days hungry in prison and was led bound before the consul. According to the text, when he prayed inside the temple of Apollo, the temple collapsed and crushed the high priest of the idols and many others. The consul Leontius believed and was baptized, and the presbyter Julian gave him holy communion, whereupon he gave up his soul to God. // The governor Loxorius put the presbyter Julian and the deacon Caesarius into hair sacks and threw them into the sea. The saints warned him that he would die badly from a snake, and indeed two days later a great snake coiled around him on the shore and left him at death's door; a little later he died. The sea cast the bodies of the saints onto the shore, and the priest Eusebius with a certain Felix, guided by a divine vision, took them and buried them near the city.

life|10-07||Άγιοι Λεόντιος ο Υπατικός, Ευσέβιος ο Πρεσβύτερος και Φήλιξ||Leontius was a consul and saw the miracle of Saint Caesarius, when the temple of Apollo fell. He believed in Christ, was baptized openly before all and, after receiving communion from the presbyter Julian, died peacefully, exactly as he had asked of the saint. // The priest Eusebius and Felix, guided by a divine vision, took from the shore the bodies of the martyrs Julian and Caesarius and buried them. But the son of the consul Leontius arrested them and beheaded them and threw their heads into the river. Thus the two were perfected by the sword. The presbyter Quartus from Italy, guided by an angel, took their relics and buried them in a distinguished and honorable place.

life|10-07||Άγιος Πολυχρόνιος ο Ιερομάρτυρας||According to the text, Polychronius came from a province of the East and his father, Bardanius, was a farmer. From childhood he sent him to learn the sacred letters and he showed great prudence and self-restraint. According to tradition, by his prayer a spring of water gushed forth near his father's house, so that his fellow citizens would not labor to bring water from afar. At a mature age he went to Constantinople and worked in the vineyards, eating once every two or three days; the owner of the vineyard marveled at his virtue, gave him money and sent him back to his homeland. // With the money he built a church and lived in it. He took part in the First Ecumenical Council of Nicaea and was a defender of the right faith, having become a reader, then a deacon and presbyter. After the death of Constantine the Great, who gave freedom to the heresy of Arius, he worked to strengthen piety. The Arians, out of envy, found him one day serving the liturgy at the Holy Table and slaughtered him with swords, mixing his blood with the blood of the Lord.

life|10-08||Αγία Ταϊσία||Thaisia, urged by her mother from childhood, became an instrument of the devil and lived dissolutely. Later the venerable Pafnutius taught her and she was persuaded that there is repentance and forgiveness of sins from the Lord. She distributed to the poor all her property, which was worth four hundred pounds of gold, and shut herself in a cell, groaning from the depth of her heart, "You who formed me, have mercy on me." She stayed so for three years and then came out of the cell by order of the abba and superior there; fifteen days later she died in the Lord.

life|10-09||Οσία Ποπλία η Ομολογήτρια||Publia lived under Julian the Apostate, around 361. She married and stayed a short time in marriage, bore a son, John, and offered him to God; out of humility he many times avoided his election as bishop of Antioch and remained a presbyter. She herself became abbess of a monastery of virgins. When Julian passed through Antioch demanding that people worship the idols, Publia sang loudly with the nuns the psalm, "The idols of the nations are silver and gold, the works of the hands of men." The emperor ordered that she be struck on the face so hard that the blood stained the ground. But he did not put her to death, because he was preparing for Persia; there he was killed and the saint remained free, lived a short time in peace and ended her life.

life|10-09||Όσιος Πέτρος ο «από στρατιωτών»||Peter lived in the time of the king Theophilus, around 829. He came from Galatia, the son of Theophilus and Eudokia, and was called Leo. Because he was handsome and strong, the king made him a count, and for many years he showed courage in the wars. Then he despised everything and became a monk, with the name Peter instead of Leo. He went to Olympus, from there to Jerusalem, Laodicea and Attalia, endured the toils of the journey and the fierce wrath of the Ishmaelites and finally returned to Olympus. When the fame of his virtue reached the emperors, Basil the Macedonian, in 867, persuaded him to settle in a monastery. There he fought many struggles and peacefully gave up his soul to the Lord.

life|10-10||Άγιοι 200 Μάρτυρες||According to the text, these two hundred were Greeks (pagans) who saw the miracles in the martyrdom of Saint Eulampius and his sister Eulampia, under Maximian, in Nicomedia. Eulampius had commanded the idol of Ares to fall and it was shattered, and together with his sister they were thrown into a boiling cauldron without being harmed. From this miracle the two hundred Greeks believed in Christ. They were all beheaded together with Eulampius and Eulampia and received the crowns of martyrdom.

life|10-10||Άγιος Βασιανός||The venerable Bassian came from the East, from the land of the Syrians, and came to Constantinople under the pious king Marcian, around 450. He was so distinguished in virtues and miracles that Marcian built a church in his name, which survives to the days of the author. His disciples reached three hundred, and Saint Matrona was his disciple. By his life he led many to salvation, healed various illnesses and performed countless miracles. He died in deep old age and was buried in the church that bears his name.

life|10-10||Άγιος Θεόφιλος ο Ομολογητής||Theophilus was born near Tiberioupolis (present-day Strumica) of pious parents and was baptized at the age of three. At thirteen he went to the venerable Stephen on Mount Silentium, saying that he heard his voice calling him to take up his cross and follow him. Stephen received him, taught him asceticism for three years and then handed him over to the abbot of the Lavra there, who made him a monk. His parents looked for him and, when they found him, the abbot did not wish to let him go; then, according to the text, a voice from on high within the church commanded that he be let go. His parents built a monastery nearby, where he practiced asceticism. // When Leo the Isaurian declared war on the icons, around 716, he summoned Theophilus, who confessed that the holy icons must be venerated, and they beat him with raw sinews. They bound him and led him by force to Nicaea together with the venerable Longinus the stylite. There they stretched him in the form of a cross on two pillars and flayed him with dry sinews, so that the blood stained the earth, and forced him to run in red-hot iron shoes. // The one called the consul was ashamed because of his virtue and, after they discussed from the Scriptures the honor of the icons, he was persuaded and promised to try to persuade the king. He set him free and Theophilus returned to the monastery to the joy of the brothers and neighbors. A little later he understood that his end was approaching, arranged the affairs of the monastery, taught and bade farewell to the brothers and fell asleep.

life|10-11||Αγίες Ζηναΐδα και Φιλονίλλα||The two sisters came from Tarsus of Cilicia and were relatives of the apostle Paul. They left their homeland and their possessions and, according to the text, practiced the art of medicine in appearance, while they fasted, kept vigil and served every illness with much patience and without payment. By their miracles they brought many unbelievers to the faith of Christ and finally died peacefully.

life|10-12||Αγία Αναστασία η Παρθένος||Anastasia lived under Decius and Valerian, around 250, came from Rome and practiced asceticism in a monastery together with other virgins. She was denounced as a Christian and presented before the governor with an iron chain. They struck her on the face, stripped her and burned her with fire, sprinkling her with pitch, oil and sulfur. They hung her on a wooden beam and cut off her breasts, pulled out her nails and teeth, cut off her hands and feet and in the end beheaded her. Thus she received the crown of martyrdom.

life|10-12||Αγία Δομνίνη η Μάρτυς||Domnina lived under Diocletian, around 286. She presented herself to the governor of the metropolis of the Anazarbeans, Lysias, and confessed Christ. They beat her first with raw sinews and burned her feet with red-hot irons, then broke her bones with rods, dislocating the joints of her limbs, and threw her into prison. There the blessed one gave up her soul to God.

life|10-13||Άγιος Βενιαμήν ο Ιερομάρτυρας ο Διάκονος||Benjamin was a deacon of the Church in Persia, in the time of Yazdegerd, king of the Persians, and Theodosius the Younger, around 412. By his teaching he brought many Greeks and Persians to the knowledge of God, for which reason they accused him to the king as an evildoer. After a beating he was imprisoned for two whole years, until the envoy of Theodosius intervened and the king promised to free him if he stopped teaching the magi. Benjamin answered that it was not possible for him not to impart the light he had received, and he was freed. He continued to teach for a year, and the king summoned him again and commanded him to deny Christ. The saint replied that, if whoever despises a mortal king deserves death, much more does whoever despises the Creator and worships a creature deserve hell. In anger the king commanded that reeds be driven under the twenty nails of his hands and feet and, since the saint considered it a game, that a sharp reed also be put in his private parts, so that he would suffer unbearable pains.

life|10-13||Άγιος Διόσκορος ο Μάρτυρας||Dioscorus was martyred under Diocletian, around 288. He came from the so-called Skenopolitans and was a councillor. He regarded all worldly things as refuse, in order to gain Christ, and presented himself boldly before the governor Lucian, whom he astonished and mocked, without regard for his threats and flatteries. The governor showed fire and instruments of torture, but all remained powerless before the courage of the martyr, and in the end he beheaded him with the sword. Thus Dioscorus received the crown of martyrdom.

life|10-13||Άγιος Φλωρέντιος ο Μάρτυρας||Florentius came from Thessaloniki and was a Christian, zealous for piety and virtue. He openly reviled the gods of the Greeks and strengthened the Christians in the faith, leading them to the fulfillment of the commandments of God. He was arrested by the governor of Thessaloniki and confessed before all Christ as the God before the ages and creator of all things, while he mocked the gods of the Greeks as wood, stones, metals and lifeless idols. They beat him hard, hung him on a beam and tore him and in the end threw him into a lit fire. In it he died rejoicing, praying and giving thanks to God.

life|10-13||Όσιος Νικήτας ο Ομολογητής και Πατρίκιος||Nicetas was born in Paphlagonia of pious parents, who are said to have been relatives of the empress Theodora. He studied the sacred letters and at seventeen went to Constantinople, where the empress Irene, around 780, learning that he had been made a eunuch by his parents as an infant, took him into the palace. He soon became the foremost of her people, reached the dignity of patrician and was appointed general of Sicily. From youth he wished to become a monk, but the emperors prevented him, until under Michael he obtained permission to become a monk in Constantinople, in a monastery near the Golden Gate. He was fifty years old. // When the iconoclast Leo the Armenian ruled, Nicetas, seeing the insults against the icons, left for a dependency he had donated. Slanderers told the emperor that he had an icon of Christ from Rome and venerated it, and an envoy threw it away with contempt. Later they asked him to commune with the iconoclast patriarch Anthony, but he refused and was exiled. He wandered to various dependencies and places (Panteichion, Eriboulos, Zoulousa) and finally built a church of the Archangels in Katisia, where he lived several years with brothers. In the end he went to a monastery near the sea, foresaw his death and fell asleep at the age of seventy-five, after teaching the monks. According to the text, after his death he performed many miracles.

life|10-13||Αγία Χρυσή η Παρθενομάρτυς||The holy new martyr Chryse struggled in a village of the province of Moglena called Slatena, in the year 1795. According to the text, she completed her martyrdom hacked to pieces, cut piece by piece. Her detailed martyrdom is referred to the New Martyrology.

life|10-14||Άγιοι Ναζάριος, Προτάσιος, Γερβάσιος και Κέλσιος οι Μάρτυρες||The saints lived in the time of the emperor Nero, around 57, and were led to the faith of Christ by Peter, the chief of the apostles. Nazarius, when he was twenty years old, went about the cities of Italy and preached Christ. After ten years he reached Placentia, where he found Protasius and Gervasius imprisoned by the governor Anulinus for their faith. Driven out of the city, he went to Cimelia, found Celsus, a child of three years, and took him from his mother; then the governor Dinovaus imprisoned him. After he was freed, he preached together with Celsus, was arrested by Nero, bound and thrown to the wild beasts, from which he remained unharmed. He returned to Placentia, where he found Gervasius and Protasius still alive, and afterward was beheaded in Mediolanum together with his three fellow athletes, and the four received the crown of martyrdom.

life|10-14||Άγιος Πέτρος ο Αυσελάμου||The saint came from the region of Eleutheropolis, from a village called Ania (or Anea). He was brave in soul and strong in body, and after being tried in many struggles for piety and despising all earthly things, he became in the end a sacrifice and whole burnt offering to Christ. In the sixth year of the reign of Diocletian he received the crown of martyrdom by fire, after first undergoing various torments.

life|10-14||Όσιος Σιλβανός ο Ιερομάρτυρας ο Γέρων||The saint came from Gaza in Palestine, which was also named Constantia. He was a gentle and guileless man, elderly, first a soldier and later, for his lofty and pure life, a presbyter of the Church of Gaza. He presented himself to the unbelieving people of Caesarea and rebuked them for their impiety, and for this he was beaten harshly and his sides were torn. He was condemned to work in the copper mines at the place called Zoorrys, where he became a bishop at the request of the people. A little later, exhausted by the mine and by illness, he was beheaded by the idolaters, and together with him forty other martyrs were beheaded, some from Egypt and some from Palestine.

life|10-15||Όσιος Βάρσος||Saint Barsus the Venerable, Bishop of Edessa and confessor, shone like another star through his virtue and miracles, not only in Edessa but also in Phoenicia, Egypt and the Thebaid, and his fame spread throughout all these provinces. When Emperor Valentinian (in the year 364) learned of his fame, he exiled him to the island of Arandus. Because crowds gathered there to hear his teaching, he moved him to the city of Oxyrhynchus in Egypt, and, because everyone from the surrounding area came there too, he exiled him to a distant fortress near the barbarians. There the saint died, having boldness before the Lord. According to tradition, his bed is still preserved on the island of Arandus and is honored by the locals, because the sick who lie on it with faith immediately regain their health.

life|10-16||Όσιος Μαλός||Saint Malus the Venerable left the world, wealth and relatives and went to deserted and uninhabited places, where he practiced asceticism with fasting, vigils and other hardships. His face was cheerful, and in the name of Christ he worked miracles: he cleansed lepers, drove out demons and granted sight to the blind. After his death his honored body became a source of healings, for it received the grace to flow with myrrh, in order to drive away every passion and to heal incurable diseases.

life|10-17||Άγιος Ανδρέας ο Οσιομάρτυρας||Andrew lived in the days of Emperor Constantine Copronymus, around 741, and came from Crete, the son of pious and virtuous parents. Seeing Christ's flock being corrupted by the heresy of iconoclasm, he went to Constantinople, presented himself before the emperor, rebuked him for his impiety and spoke boldly that the holy icons must be venerated. The emperor threw him down together with those present, and they beat him, and when the saint continued to rebuke him, he ordered that he be stripped, stretched with ropes and beaten, so that the ground was stained red with his blood. They beat him again, dug into his ribs, crushed his mouth and threw him into prison; the next day, because he resisted again, they tore his flesh apart. In the end they bound him by the feet and dragged him through the marketplace to throw him into the place of the criminals. There, as they were dragging him, a fisherman, urged on by a demon, seized a butcher's knife and struck him in the middle of the leg, and so the saint gave up his soul. His relic was thrown into the place of the criminals, but twelve demoniacs from various parts of Constantinople took it and buried it in a holy place called Krisis, and as a reward they were freed from the demons.

life|10-17||Άγιοι Κοσμάς, Δαμιανός, Λεόντιος, Άνθιμος και Ευπρέπιος οι Ανάργυροι και οι συν αυτών 15 Ανάργυροι||According to the text, there are three pairs of holy unmercenaries named Cosmas and Damian, and all of them practiced medicine. Those commemorated today were from Arabia and traveled through every city and country, healing the sick without payment and, using medicine as an occasion, preaching the faith of Christ to unbelievers. In the days of Diocletian and Maximian they went to Aegae in Lycia together with their three brothers, Leontius, Anthimus and Euprepius. They appeared before the governor Lysias, confessed Christ and were beaten without any mercy, and were cast into the depths of the sea, but they did not drown and were found safe on dry land by the grace of God. They were then thrown into a blazing furnace, from which they again remained unharmed, and they were hung on a cross. Finally all five brothers were beheaded together and received the crown of martyrdom.

life|10-18||Όσιος Ιουλιανός ο εν τω Ευφράτη ποταμώ||Saint Julian the Venerable renounced the world and went to the banks of the river Euphrates, where he found a cave and lived a solitary life. Many imitated him, built huts near him, reached the number of one hundred and ate the same foods as he did. According to the text, he killed a dragon with the sign of the cross, and he also went to Mount Sinai, where he built a church near the rock on which Moses saw God, and it is preserved to this day. When the impious Julian went to Persia, frightened Christians asked for the help of his prayers; he prayed for ten days and heard a divine voice saying that at that very hour the impious emperor was being slain. Later, as he was going to Antioch, he saved by a miracle a seven-year-old child who had fallen into a well, and in Antioch, despite a high fever, he rose up through prayer to bless the crowd of Christians. On the road to Constantinople a bedridden man who touched his cassock was healed in body and soul. On the return journey, in the city of Cyrrhus, Christians begged him to help them against the heretic Asterius; after a night of prayer Asterius died from a blow sent by God, and the saint returned to his disciples and died in peace.

life|10-19||Άγιος Ούαρος ο Μάρτυρας||Uar lived in the days of Maximian, in 304, and served in the imperial army of Egypt, in the legion of the Tyanians; he was renowned in lineage and incomparable in bodily strength, and the emperor loved him. He was secretly a Christian, cared for those imprisoned for the faith and begged God that he himself might be counted worthy to suffer. When seven hermit ascetics were imprisoned for the faith and one of them died in prison, Uar was counted with the others in his place. He was immediately hung up and beaten with thick rods, then with raw leather thongs, four soldiers dragged him, and, hung up again, he was torn with iron claws, losing most of his flesh. After five hours of torments he gave up his soul to Christ. A noble and wealthy woman, Cleopatra, took his relic by night and carried it to her homeland, Palestine, where she built a church in his name.

life|10-19||Άγιοι Έξι Οσιομάρτυρες οι ερημίτες||These six hermits practiced asceticism in the desert and were martyred together with Saint Uar. According to the text, seven ascetics had been imprisoned for the faith, and when one died before the martyrdom, Uar presented himself in his place. The remaining six, who had lived ascetically, were perfected together by the sword.

life|10-19||Οσία Κλεοπάτρα||Cleopatra was a noble and wealthy woman from Palestine. She took the relic of the martyr Uar by night and, with her only son, built a church in his name. At the dedication of the church, having bought a royal office for her son and having placed the chlamys and the belt upon the relic so that they might be blessed, she feasted all who were present. Her son grew tired, fell into a fever and died; she took him on her shoulders, laid him at the martyr's tomb and begged the saint either to raise him up or to take her with him. She fell asleep and saw in her sleep Uar with her son, both in radiant garments and crowns, and she woke up full of joy. She placed her son's body beside the martyr's, distributed her wealth to the poor and lived seven years beside the tomb in fasting, prayers and tears, seeing the martyr and her son every Sunday. She died in peace and was buried near her son's tomb.

life|10-19||Όσιος Ιωάννης ο Θαυματουργός ο ασκητής||Saint John the Venerable was born in the village of Skrino, near Sofia, to pious Bulgarian parents, in the days of Peter, king of the Bulgarians. From childhood he was devout, and while some envious people called him a hypocrite, he distributed his belongings to the poor and became a monk. After a divine vision he went up a mountain and lived in stillness in a small hut, feeding on wild herbs and wearing a garment of skin. His nephew Luke took refuge with him as a child, but the boy's father snatched him back; then the saint prayed and the child died from a snake bite, while the venerable one glorified God who had saved him from eternal death. One night demons struck him in the form of robbers and drove him away, and he went to the inner wilderness of Mount Rila, where he dwelt in the hollow of a great tree. By divine providence chickpeas grew there, which nourished him, and he healed a demoniac through prayer. Later, to avoid glory, he went to an unknown cave on a high rock, and according to the text an angel of the Lord brought him food every day. King Peter went to see him but could not advance in the difficult place, and he sent two servants to him and afterwards gold and fruit with a letter; the venerable one accepted the fruit and the letter but not the gold.

life|10-20||Οσία Ματρώνα η Θαυματουργός η Χιοπολίτιδα||Matrona came from the village of Volissos on Chios. Her parents, Leo and Anna, were pious and wealthy. From childhood she loved God, left her homeland and her family and distributed part of her inheritance to widows and orphans, while with the rest she built a church in the name of Christ the Savior and a bath for sick strangers. According to the text, when they dug the foundations a treasure was found, but she prayed that it would vanish, and the treasure was changed into extinguished coals. She lived in prayer, psalmody and tears and so wasted her body that she appeared almost without flesh. According to the text, when barbarians seized the island, one of them tried to abuse a nun and was found dead; the venerable one raised him up by her prayer and advised him not to do such things again. The miracle made the other barbarians gentle, so that when they came again they harmed no one. After her repose her relic became a source of miracles and healings, and the people of Chios call her Saint Kyra (the Lady), because she gained lordship over the passions.

life|10-20||Όσιος Γεράσιμος ο νέος ασκητής, ο Πελοποννήσιος (Μνήμη ανακομιδής ιερών λειψάνων του)||Gerasimos came from Trikala in the Peloponnese and his parents, Demetrios and Kale, were named Notaras. He learned letters and when he grew up he left his homeland and traveled through Zakynthos, Greece, Thessaly, the Black Sea, Constantinople and Chalcedon. He went to Mount Athos, where he gathered from the ascetics the flowers of virtue, and then to Jerusalem, where he was ordained subdeacon, deacon and presbyter by Patriarch Germanos. He served for one year as lamp-lighter at the Holy Sepulchre and for twelve years served the patriarch, fasted forty days at the Jordan, and visited Sinai, Alexandria, Antioch, Damascus, Egypt and Crete. He returned to Zakynthos and lived five years in a cave in strict asceticism, eating only boiled pumpkins without salt and soaked legumes, without bread. Then he went to Cephalonia, where he stayed in a place called Spilaia and afterwards at Omala, renovated an old church, built cells and founded a women's monastery, the New Jerusalem, with twenty-five nuns. In deep old age he foretold his end, taught the nuns and fell asleep on August 15, 1579. Because that day is the feast of the Dormition of the Theotokos, his commemoration was moved to October 20, when the translation of his relic also took place, which was found intact, fragrant and the color of saffron. According to the text, the saint appeared and held a woman who fell at night into a well of the monastery, so that she would not sink into the water.

life|10-21||Άγιοι Γάϊος, Δάσιος και Ζωτικός οι Μάρτυρες||The three saints were in Nicomedia and, full of divine zeal, they tore down the idols that stood in the temples of the pagans. When their act was discovered, they endured every kind of torture. They were hung on wooden posts and their flesh was scraped with cloths made of goat hair. Then stones were tied to their necks and they were thrown into the sea, where they received the crowns of martyrdom.

life|10-21||Άγιοι Θεοδότη και Σωκράτης ο Πρεσβύτερος||Theodote lived in the time of Emperor Alexander Severus, around 222, the daughter of noble parents from a country of the Black Sea region, and she lived in stillness in an ascetic dwelling. When it was revealed that she was a Christian, the governor of Cappadocia seized her and she confessed her faith in Christ. They hung her up and tore her, and threw her into a heated oven, where she was kept unharmed by the grace of Christ. They led her to Byzantium and from there to Ancyra, where the presbyter Socrates was. While the pagans were celebrating a public festival and worshiping the idols, he was filled with divine zeal, went and tore down the altar and the sacrifices upon it, and for this he was beheaded. Theodote was compelled to sacrifice to the idols, but she did not obey and was perfected by the sword.
life|10-21||Άγιος Ιωάννης ο Νεομάρτυρας||John came from Monemvasia. He was perfected in martyrdom through tortures in Thessaloniki, having kept the rules of fasting until the end of them.

life|10-22||Άγιοι Αλέξανδρος, Θεοδότη, Γλυκερία, Άννα καίΕλισάβετ οι Μάρτυρες||Alexander was a bishop and by his teaching turned many pagans to faith in Christ and baptized them. The governor arrested him, subjected him to many tortures, tore him and compelled him to sacrifice to the idols, but he did not obey. Seeing his courage and patience, the soldier Heraclius believed in Christ, was tortured and was finally beheaded. Because Alexander worked a miracle and was kept unharmed from his wounds by the grace of the Lord, he drew to the faith four women, Theodote, Glykeria, Anna and Elizabeth. They spoke out against the error of the idols and were beheaded. Last of all Alexander was also struck with the sword and received from the Lord the crown of victory.

life|10-23||Άγιος Ιγνάτιος||Ignatius, Patriarch of Constantinople, was the son of Michael Rhangabe, who reigned shortly before Leo the Armenian, and a grandson of Emperor Nikephoros. Leo the Armenian made him a eunuch, and he became a monk and abbot of the monastery of the Archangel. Later he became Patriarch of Constantinople and governed the Church for eleven years and five months. Michael, the son of Theophilos, drove him from the throne and proposed Photios in his place. When Emperor Basil the Macedonian deposed Photios, Ignatius was restored and remained on the throne for another eleven years. He was driven out again and in his place Stephen, the son of Basil, became patriarch. Ignatius returned to his first monastery and reposed there in the Lord, having lived seventy-nine years.

life|10-23||Όσιος Μακάριος ο Ρωμαίος||According to the text, three venerable elders from the monastery of Saint Asclepius in Mesopotamia of Syria decided to travel the earth to its ends and, after many labors and dangers, reached a cave. There they met Macarius the Roman, with white hair, a hardened body and very long nails and beard. He received them, after first assuring himself through prayer that they were Christians, and told them his life. He was the son of a Roman senator, and on the day of his wedding, to which his parents had betrothed him against his will, he fled in secret and followed an old man. This old man was the archangel Raphael, who led him toward the desert. In the cave he found a dead lion and raised its two cubs; the lions later kissed the feet of visitors. One day the devil appeared to him as a beautiful woman and tempted him, and Macarius, repentant, fasted forty days. After this he saw the cave filled with light and a man with a crown singing a heavenly ode and ascending to heaven with lightning, thunder and earthquakes, and he remained speechless for seventy days. The three elders bade him farewell, the lions accompanied them for three days, and with the help of angels they returned to their monastery, where they told what they had seen and heard.

life|10-24||Άγιοι Γυναίκα και το Βρέφος της||According to the text, a pious woman with a five-year-old boy went, when Saint Arethas was beheaded, to his relic and anointed herself and her child with the martyr's blood. Then she cursed and reviled the Jewish tyrant, whereupon the soldiers seized her, lit a fire and threw her in. The child was tormented by the separation from his mother and cried out her name. He was brought before the king, who sat him on his knees and asked whom he loved. The child answered that he loved his mother and had come to obtain permission to go with her to martyrdom, that is, to die for Christ and live again with Him. When he realized that the king was a Jew, he refused to accept anything from him and asked to be let go to his mother. Seeing his mother thrown into the fire, he bit the king hard on the thigh, the king flung him from his knees, and the child ran to the furnace and leaped in, where together with his mother he inherited the crown of martyrdom.

life|10-24||Αγία Σεβαστιανή η Μάρτυς||Sebastiane lived in the reign of Emperor Domitian, around 82, and preached Christ. She was denounced to the governor Sergius as a Christian and confessed that she had been taught and baptized by the Apostle Paul and that she was ready to die for Christ. They beat her with leaden balls and put her in prison, where the Apostle Paul appeared to her and told her not to grieve. After seven days they threw her into a greatly heated furnace, from which she came out unharmed, and during her prayer hail fell that put out the fire, so that the governor fled in fear. They learned that she was from Heraclea and sent her bound to the governor there. They hung her on a rack and tore her body for three hours, and her flesh was fragrant like myrrh, while she prayed silently. They threw her to the wild beasts, but a lion took on a human voice and praised her, and a lioness stood beside her, gentle as lambs. They beheaded her outside the city and from her body, instead of blood, milk flowed.
