They put her body and head in a sack with three hundred pounds of lead and threw it into the sea, but an angel of the Lord tore open the sack and the relic came out onto the shore. A senator's wife, Ammia, wrapped it in shrouds, anointed it with myrrh and buried it.

life|10-25||Άγιοι Μαρκιανός και Μαρτύριος οι νοτάριοι||Marcian and Martyrius were notaries and scribes of Paul the Confessor, Patriarch of Constantinople, in the time of Constantius, around 337. They read the sacred books to the people and were distinguished for their piety, modesty and orthodoxy. When Paul was exiled to Armenia and died there, strangled by the Arians, they boldly rebuked the impious and preached that the Son is consubstantial with the Father. They did not yield before flattery and promises of gifts nor before threats of wounds and tortures, and for this they were put to death by the sword. They were buried at the gate of Constantinople called Melandesia.

life|10-25||Άγιος Αναστάσιος ο Μάρτυρας||Anastasius went by himself to the tyrants and boldly confessed Christ as true God and creator of all things, and everyone was astonished. By his words and his courage he showed that his mind was unshakable, and for this he was beheaded and thrown into the sea. A devout woman took his relic, which the sea cast up, wrapped it in shrouds and myrrh and built a church in the name of the martyr, where she buried it. According to the text, many extraordinary healings took place through the relic.

life|10-27||Αγίες Καπετωλίνα και Ερωτηΐδα||The two saints lived in the time of Emperor Diocletian, when Zilikinthios was governor of Cappadocia, in the year 289. Capitolina was noble and wealthy and Erotheis was her servant. Capitolina distributed her property to the poor, freed her slaves and boldly presented herself to the governor, proclaiming Christ as true God; she was imprisoned and the next day beheaded. Erotheis threw stones at the governor and for this they struck her with rods, but she remained unharmed by the grace of Christ, and finally her head was cut off with the sword. So both received the crown of martyrdom.

life|10-27||Διήγηση γιά τους Ίβηρες||In the time of Emperor Constantine the Great, around 332, a pious woman, trained in the ascetic life, was taken captive by the Iberians (the present-day Georgians) and continued her ascetic struggles there also. Because the Iberians had no medical art, a mother brought her sick child to her; she laid it on her bed, prayed to the Lord and the child was healed. Her fame reached the queen, who suffered from a difficult illness; the captive healed her through prayer and refused gifts, asking as her reward that the queen believe in Christ and that a church be built in His name. The king at first was unwilling, but on a hunt he was blinded and was released from the darkness when he called upon the God of the servant; then he built the church following her instructions. To have the church consecrated, the king asked Constantine for a teacher of the faith, and he sent a virtuous high priest with gifts. By miracles and teaching, this man led the whole nation to Christ, baptized it, built churches, ordained priests and died in peace.

life|10-28||Άγιοι Τερέντιος και Νεονίλλη και τα τέκνα αυτών||Terentius and Neonilla, with their children, lived all together like one family in one house and secretly worshiped God. They were denounced to the governor and presented themselves in court; when they confessed Christ as true God and mocked the idols, they were hung up and torn, and their wounds were sprinkled with very sharp vinegar and salt, while a fire was burned beneath them. They prayed and with silent voice encouraged one another in martyrdom; according to the text, angels invisibly freed them from their bonds and healed their wounds, and the unbelievers were afraid. Then they were beaten with clubs, bound to wheels, thrown to the wild beasts and put into cauldrons of boiling pitch, but they remained unharmed; the boiling of the pitch, says the text, was changed into water. In the end they were beheaded with the sword and received the crowns of martyrdom.

life|10-28||Άγιοι Τερέντιος, Αφρικανός, Μάξιμος, Πομπηΐος, Φωκάς και άλλοι 36 Αφρικανοί Μάρτυρες||These saints were from Africa and lived in the time of Emperor Decius and the governor Fortunatus, in the year 250. They were arrested as Christians and were beaten first with raw sinews and then with rods; afterwards their backs were burned with heated spits and their wounds were rubbed with hair cloths, salt and vinegar. When they were questioned again and did not deny Christ, they were bound with chains and dragged naked, and they were also tortured with heated instruments and with claws. So all of them together received the crowns of martyrdom.

life|10-28||Όσιοι Φιρμιλιανός και Μελχίων||Firmilian was Archbishop of Caesarea and Melchion a sophist and presbyter of Antioch; the two of them deposed Paul of Samosata. According to a note in the text, Firmilian convened a synod at Iconium, where it was decreed that the Novatians, and in general all schismatics who came to the Catholic Church, were to be baptized. Both died in peace.

life|10-28||Άγιος Κυριακός ο Ιερομάρτυρας||Kyriakos is the one who revealed the Honorable Cross together with Saint Helena; after he believed in Christ and was baptized, he became Bishop of Jerusalem. He lived until the time of Julian the Apostate, in 361, who on his campaign against the Persians passed through Palestine, arrested him and pressed him to sacrifice to the idols. The saint rebuked him and Julian commanded that his right hand be cut off, saying that with it he had written many letters and had caused many to deny the gods; then they poured lead into his mouth and stretched him on a heated bronze bed. Finally they threw him into a cauldron of boiling oil and also struck him with a javelin, and the athlete of Christ gave up his spirit.

life|10-28||Αγία Άννα μητέρα του Αγίου Κυριακού||When Anna heard of the tortures of her son, Saint Kyriakos, she came to see him; for this she herself was arrested. They hung her by the hair and burned her with lighted torches, and so she gave up her soul into the hands of God.

life|10-29||Όσιος Αβράμιος και Μαρία η ανεψιά του||Abraham was the son of Christian parents; he married against his will, but left everything out of longing for Christ and withdrew into the desert, shut in a small hut where he practiced asceticism with great strictness. After fifty years of asceticism he was ordained a priest and then, against his will, bishop of a village called Tainia, near Lampsacus, where with many labors and temptations he led its pagan inhabitants to the faith. Afterwards he left secretly for his old place of stillness. When his brother died, he took his orphaned daughter, Mary, seven years old, gave her a cell near his own and taught her asceticism from the window. At the age of twenty Mary fell into sin, despaired and took refuge in a brothel; Abraham dressed as a soldier, went unrecognized on horseback, found her and brought her back to her cell. She repented so much that after a few years she also worked great miracles. The venerable one fell asleep in peace and after a short time his niece also reposed.

life|10-29||Οσία Άννα||Saint Anna the Venerable was born in Byzantium to a devout married deacon of the church of Blachernae, in the time of Leo the Isaurian, around 716. When her parents died, her grandmother married her to a very devout man. Her paternal uncle, an ascetic of Olympus, prophesied to her that if she did not cover her husband in the grave she would not give birth to the child she was carrying; indeed her husband died after the sixth month and she, after giving birth, handed the child over to another uncle of hers. When the uncle came again and foretold that her two children would die soon, she thanked him, received his blessing and began to distribute her property to the poor; when the children died, she wept for them and distributed whatever was left to her. She dressed as a man, went to Olympus, was tonsured a monk by a monk and, under the name Euphemianos, entered a cenobium, where by her humility she became an example for all. Her servant found her at the end and followed the monk to another monastery, where the venerable one worked many miracles; because the place was too narrow for the many who wished to become monks, the abbot asked Patriarch Tarasios and obtained a place, where he built the monastery of the Abramites, and there he ordered the venerable one to spend the rest of her life. A wicked monk slandered her as a eunuch and tried to throw her down a precipice in order to reveal her sex; he saw nothing and was paralyzed on one side, and later he was arrested for murder and hanged. The venerable one, to avoid scandals, went to Stenon with two monks, Eustathios and Leophytos, and later to Byzantium near Sigma, where she lived a holy life, worked miracles and healings and died in peace.

life|10-29||Αγία Μελιτίνη η Μάρτυς||Saint Melitene the Martyr was denounced to the local governor as a Christian. In court they struck her in the face and stripped her, and she stood for many hours in the middle of the tribunal, disgraced for Christ. Even naked she mocked the governor and his idols, considering the dishonor an honor for the sake of Christ. They tortured her with many tortures, she remained unharmed, and in the end they killed her with a sword, and she gave her soul to God.

life|10-30||Άγιος Μαρκιανός ο Ιερομάρτυρας||Marcian was ordained by the Apostle Peter and sent as bishop to Syracuse in Sicily. By the miracles and signs he performed he astonished everyone, and by his prayer alone he tore down the altars of the idols; he brought the inhabitants to the knowledge of God and to holy baptism. The Jews, out of envy and because they could not bear his boldness, killed him by a violent death, and so he received the unfading crown of martyrdom.

life|10-30||Άγιοι Αστέριος, Κλαύδιος, Νέων και Νεονίλλη τα αδέλφια||The four siblings were Christians and lived together, with considerable property, in the time of Diocletian, when Lysias was governor of Cilicia, in 288. Their stepmother, in order to keep unjustly the inheritance of their parents, denounced them as Christians, and the governor agreed with her so as to take a share himself. Claudius was hung up, torn, his feet were burned and he was thrown into prison; the other brothers, Asterius and Neon, were also cruelly tortured and remained steadfast in their confession. Neonilla was beaten, hung by the hair, her head was shaved for dishonor and burning coals were placed on her chest, and so she gave up her spirit; her body was put into a sack and sunk in the sea. The three brothers were beheaded outside the city and their bodies were thrown to the wild beasts and birds of prey.

life|10-30||Αγία Ευτροπία η Μάρτυς||Eutropia was denounced in Alexandria to the governor Apellian as a Christian who visited the imprisoned saints in the prisons. She fearlessly confessed Christ; they hung her up and tore her and then burned her with lighted torches. She regarded the flame as cool water and assured everyone present that she saw a awesome man who was refreshing her, whom the soldiers also saw. They tortured her even more cruelly and threw her into prison; the next day she mocked the governor and his idols, and then they cut out her tongue and then her head, and she received the crown of martyrdom.

life|10-31||Άγιος Επίμαχος ο Αιγύπτιος||Epimachus came from Egypt and lived on the mountain of Pelusium, afflicting himself with many hardships. When the inhuman judge Apellian came to Alexandria and furiously pursued the Christians, Epimachus, moved by divine zeal, went down to the city and tore down an altar of the idols. Then he rushed at the tyrant, and only the bodyguards prevented his wrath. They hung him on a wooden post and tore him with iron claws and rubbed him with rough stones; in prison he encouraged the imprisoned Christians to stand bravely in the struggles. According to the text, a piece of the martyr's flesh, as it was flung into the air, dripped blood onto the blind eye of a girl who was watching in the theater and weeping over his sufferings, and her eye saw again. Finally they beheaded him with the sword; the Christians buried his body with honor, and years later his relic was transferred to Constantinople on March 10.

life|10-31||Άγιος Ιάκωβος Επίσκοπος Μυγδονίας||James became bishop of Antioch of Mygdonia, which is also called Nisibis, and because of his great virtue he became a great wonderworker; he raised a dead man by the power of Christ and brought many from idolatry to the knowledge of God, while many Christians who had denied Christ out of fear he restored to the faith. He also wrote a very beneficial book, from which Theodoret, Bishop of Cyrrhus, quotes excerpts. He was tested by pagan emperors but did not bend. He lived until the time of Constantine the Great and at the First Ecumenical Council in 325 he was one of the 318 Fathers; afterwards he went to Constantinople, met with Metrophanes, returned to his throne and shortly afterwards, shining with signs and miracles, fell asleep in the Lord.

life|11-02||Άγιοι Ευδόξιος, Αγάπιος και οι συν αυτών οκτώ Μάρτυρες||These saints were soldiers in Sebaste in the time of Emperor Licinius. They were interrogated by Auxanios, the governor of Sebaste, by the duke Marcellus and by Marcus Agricolaus, and were tortured in various ways. In the end they were thrown into the fire and so gave their souls to God, receiving from Him the crowns of martyrdom.

life|11-02||Άγιοι Συγκλητικοί||These saints were soldiers in Sebaste in the time of King Licinius, around the year 315. They were interrogated by Auxanios, governor of Sebaste, by Marcellus the Duke and by Marcus Agricolaus and were tortured in various ways. Finally they were thrown into the fire, thus gave their souls into the hands of God and received the crowns of martyrdom.

life|11-02||Όσιος Μαρκιανός||Saint Marcian the Venerable came from the city of Cyrrhus. He left his homeland and the splendor of his family and went to the middle of the desert, where he built a cell so small that it barely covered his body, and shut himself in wearing hair garments. All his food each evening was twenty-four drams of bread, and he drank only as little water as he needed to live. Soon he acquired disciples, Eusebius, who inherited his hut, and Agapetus. // When his sister brought food, the venerable one accepted only his nephew and sent him back with what they had brought, saying that they had brought it out of kinship and not out of love for God. According to the text, a great dragon that threatened the ascetics fell apart in pieces when the venerable one sealed it with the sign of the cross and blew upon it; also, a divine light shone upon him at night and enabled him to read his psalter. // Flavian of Antioch, the bishop of Cyrrhus and other bishops begged him to come out of his cell for the benefit of the brethren, but he remained shut in. He brought back to the Orthodox faith many from various heresies. Because he learned that many were quarreling over his body and had prepared shrines and churches in his name, he made Eusebius swear that he would hide it after his death in a remote place, and then he died.

life|11-03||Όσιος Ακεψιμάς||Saint Acepsimas the Venerable lived in the time of Theodosius the Great, around the year 382. He shut himself in a dug-out space, made with turns like the tendril of a vine, and stayed there sixty years without anyone seeing him and without speaking to any human being. He turned his mind to the heart and beheld God noetically, from whom he received every consolation. // His food was barley soaked in water; he came out twice a week and took water from a nearby spring, without anyone seeing him. He worked many miracles, received the priesthood under compulsion and fell asleep in peace in the Lord.

life|11-03||Άγιος Αχαιμενίδης||Achaemenides was the son of the prefect of the city in Persia, in the time of King Yazdegerd and Theodosius the Younger. He left the religion of his father and believed in Christ. When the king learned of it, he tried hard to make him return to his old faith, and when he did not succeed, he stripped him of his wealth, clothes and offices and sent him to wander naked, with only a loincloth, among the camels of the army. // After many days the king saw him from the window, burned by the sun and covered with dust, took pity on him and ordered that a shirt be put on him. Thinking that he had softened, he asked him to deny the son of the carpenter, that is, Christ. The saint was filled with zeal, tore the shirt, threw it at the king and told him to keep it together with his impiety. The king drove him naked from the palace, and he lived the rest of his life piously and fell asleep in peace, receiving the crown of confession.

life|11-04||Άγιοι Νίκανδρος και Ερμαίος||Nicander was Bishop of Myra and Hermaeus a presbyter, both ordained by the Apostle Titus. Because they drew many Greeks away from the idols and brought them to faith in Christ, they were denounced to the count of the city, Libanius. He tied them to horses and made them run, so that their flesh was torn and the ground was stained red with their blood. // Then they hung them up high and struck them with a wooden sword, threw them into a furnace of fire, from which they came out unharmed by the power of God, and finally he ordered that nails be driven into their hearts, heads and bowels and, while still alive, that they be shut in a tomb. There, from the cruel violence, they gave their souls into the hands of God.

life|11-05||Άγιοι Δομνίνος, Τιμόθεος, Θεόφιλος, Θεότιμος, Δωρόθεος ο Πρεσβύτερος, Ευψύχιος, Καρτέριος, Σιλβάνος, Πάμφιλος, Φιλόθεος, Νέαρχος και άλλοι Άγιοι Μάρτυρες άνδρες||These saints were martyred in the time of Emperor Maximian, when Urbanus was governor of Palestine, around the year 298. Domninus was martyred first; he was greatly tortured and ended in the fire. Timothy, Theotimus and Theophilus, who were young and handsome, the tyrant condemned to be put to death by blows of the fist, while Dorotheus, a venerable presbyter, he gave as food to the wild beasts. // Eupsychius and Karterius, who were mature in age, he ordered to be castrated, and Silvanus he condemned to suffer in the mines in the place called Phaeno. Three virgins he handed over to the licentious, while other maidens he put in prison, and all this he did within one hour. Pamphilus, who was adorned with every wisdom and virtue, they wounded in the sides twice and threw into prison together with other confessors, and so the martyrdom of all was completed.

life|11-05||Όσιος Γρηγόριος||Saint Gregory the Venerable loved Christ from a young age and was adorned with all the virtues. After the death of his predecessor he became, by divine providence, Bishop of Alexandria, by the vote of the bishops of the city and with the agreement of the Christ-loving people, and became an exact teacher of orthodoxy and of the virtuous life. He taught more by deeds than by word, for he was meek, humble, merciful, prudent, a father of orphans, a defender of widows, a guide of the erring, a physician of the sick and a comfort of the sorrowful. // The devil put the iconoclast opinion into Emperor Leo, who reigned in 813, and persuaded him to bring the saint bound in irons from Alexandria to Constantinople. Before the Senate and the officials the saint rebuked him and called him a heretic and impious. The emperor ordered that he be torn with whips, and the saint endured the beating with joy, saying that for the holy icon of Christ he was ready to be cut in all his members. They exiled him, and after three whole years in exile he gave his soul to God, receiving the crown of confession.

life|11-07||Άγιοι Μελάσιππος, Κασσίνη και Αντώνιος||The saints were martyred in Ancyra in the time of Julian the Apostate, around 361, and were Christians from their ancestors. Antony was thrown into prison, while Melasippus and Kassine were hung up, torn and burned with fire; Melasippus had his legs cut off at the knees and Kassine her breasts, and both gave their souls to God on the instrument of torture. // Antony, who spat in Julian's face and called his parents blessed, that is, Melasippus and Kassine, was hung up and torn, his ankles were pierced and heavy stones were hung from his feet, they sat him on a red-hot iron throne and led him around the city shaved and with a stone on his neck, for shame. The duke Agrippinus put him in a lighted oven and then threw him to the wild beasts, from which the saint came out unharmed by divine grace and brought forty children to the faith, who were beheaded immediately. Then they stretched him on a heated bed and struck him with rods, cut off his hands and threw him into a furnace, where he again remained unharmed and led many to the faith, and finally he was beheaded.

life|11-07||Άγιοι Αύκτος, Ταυρίων και Θεσσαλονίκη οι Μάρτυρες||The saints were martyred in Amphipolis in Macedonia. Thessalonike was the daughter of a rich and arrogant priest of the idols, Cleon, and neither the wealth nor the glory of her father, nor his entreaties, could make her deny Christ. They stripped her, four men struck her with raw hides, they broke her ribs, took away her possessions and exiled her, and in exile, still confessing Christ, she gave her soul into His hands. // Auctus and Taurion, after sharply accusing that barbarous and cruel man, were denounced as Christians to the consul Thorybius. They stripped them, struck them with stones, threw them into a heated furnace, from which they came out unharmed, shot arrows at them many times without their being wounded and threw them into a nearby lake, from which again they came out unharmed by divine grace. The tyrant, bewildered, ordered that they be beheaded, and so they received the crowns of martyrdom.

life|11-07||Άγιος Αλέξανδρος ο Μάρτυρας από την Θεσσαλονίκη||Alexander lived in the time of Emperor Maximian, around 298, and came from Thessaloniki. He presented himself at the tyrant's tribunal, kicked the altar with his foot and scattered the libations and the sacrifices to the demons that were upon it. For this he was beheaded and received the crown of martyrdom.

life|11-09||Άγιοι Ονησιφόρος και Πορφύριος οι Μάρτυρες||These saints lived in the time of the persecution of the Christians under the emperors Diocletian and Maximian, around 290. They were accused as Christians before the governors and, when they were led to court, they confessed with great courage Christ as true God and creator of heaven and earth. For this they underwent various tortures over the whole body and were stretched on red-hot gridirons, where they rejoiced and thanked God, because through the pains they saw the enjoyment of eternal goods. The tyrants grew still angrier, tied their feet to wild horses and ran them for hours through thorns and rough places, so that the flesh of the athletes was torn apart and scattered and their souls ascended to the Lord. Some Christians secretly took their holy relics and buried them in a village called Pangeanon.

life|11-09||Οσία Ματρώνα||According to the text, she lived in the time of King Marcian and Leo the Great and came from Perge in Pamphylia. She married, bore a daughter and went up to Constantinople with her husband, where she became a friend of a virgin, Eugenia, and, imitating her asceticism, she stayed continually in the churches with fasting and vigils. Her longing for God was kindled; she entrusted her daughter to a woman she knew and, dressed in men's clothes, went to the monastery of Saint Bassianos, where she stayed for some time in the guise of a eunuch. When Bassianos learned the truth by revelation, he sent her to a women's monastery in Emesa. From there she went to Jerusalem, to Mount Sinai and to Berytus, where by prayer she caused water to come forth in a waterless place. After many attacks and temptations from the demons she returned to Constantinople, revealed herself to Bassianos and was permitted to remain in the monastery, which to this day is called that of Matrona. She lived nearly one hundred years and died peacefully.

life|11-09||Αγίες Ευσταλία και Σωπάτρα||Eustolia lived in the time of King Maurice, around 584, and was the daughter of pious parents who lived in Rome. From childhood she was given to a monastery, where she practiced asceticism with fasting and vigils, and, burning with divine love, she left Rome and went to Constantinople. After visiting the churches of the city, in the church of the Theotokos at Blachernae she found Sopatra, the daughter of King Maurice, who begged her to become her spiritual mother. Sopatra left the kingdom of her father and its glories and pleasures, put on the monastic habit and, after asking her father for a suitable place, built a church together with Eustolia. Many devout women and virgins went there and shared in their strict monastic life. Eustolia struggled for many years, became a cause of salvation for many and died peacefully, leaving Sopatra as successor of her struggles, who also reached the summit of virtue and fell asleep peacefully.

life|11-09||Άγιος Αντώνιος ο Μάρτυρας||He came from the land of the Syrians and his trade was stonecutter. Seeing the Greeks sacrificing in the temple of the idols, he advised them to abandon the error, and because they did not listen to him he withdrew to a desert place. There he found an ascetic, a servant of God, Timothy, and lived with him for three years. Then he received his blessing and returned to his village, where he found the pagans celebrating; he entered their temple and shattered all the idols, and for this they seized him and beat him severely. Afterwards he went to Apamea in Syria and asked Bishop Hosius for permission to build a church in the name of the Holy Trinity. When he began to build, his Greek acquaintances learned of it, went by night and killed him mercilessly with clubs, and so he gave up his soul into the hands of God.

life|11-10||Άγιος Ορέστης ο Μάρτυρας||He lived in the time of King Diocletian, around 289, and came from the city of Tyana in Cappadocia. Because he confessed Christ as true God, the governor Maximus arrested him and, since he would not deny Him, beat him with rods so hard that his bowels were cut and could be seen from outside. They brought him to the temple of the idols, and the martyr blew upon the idols, which immediately fell and became dust, and then they threw him into prison. After seven days he was presented again to the governor and, because again he would not sacrifice, they pierced his ankles with long nails and tied him with chains to a wild horse. The horse, driven on, ran with great force for a distance of about twenty miles, and so the athlete of Christ gave up his spirit to God.

life|11-11||Άγιος Βίκτωρ ο Μεγαλομάρτυρας||He was martyred under King Antoninus, around 160, and the duke Sebastian in Italy. Because he was compelled to deny Christ and was not persuaded, first they crushed his fingers and then put him into a lighted furnace, where he stayed three days and came out unharmed. Then they forced him to drink deadly poisons, which did not harm him, and for this reason the apothecary who had prepared them believed in Christ. Next they pulled out his sinews and burned him with boiling oil, forced him to drink powder mixed with vinegar, put out his eyes and hung him upside down for three days. Finally they flayed his skin, and with such torments the brave contender gave up his soul to God.

life|11-11||Άγιος Βικέντιος ο Μάρτυρας||He was a hieromartyr in the reign of Maximian and under the governor Datian. As a deacon in Augustopolis in Spain he taught the people of God together with Bishop Valerius. Both were arrested and led before Datian, who put iron chains on them and sent them to Valentia, where he imprisoned them in a dark and foul prison. After some days he brought out Vincent and commanded that he be torn; they nailed him to a cross and beat him on all his limbs, took him down from the nails and distorted his limbs, burned his sides, laid heated iron rods on his chest and pierced him with red-hot spits. Because he remained unharmed, they threw him into prison, where he was granted help and a visit from God and, after he prayed, he gave up his spirit and received the crown of martyrdom. His relic was buried there by devout Christians.

life|11-12||Άγιοι Αντώνιος, Ζεβίνας, Γερμανός, Νικηφόρος και Μαραθώ οι Μάρτυρες||These saints were martyred in the time of Emperor Maximian. Antony was an old man, while Nikephoros, Zebinas and Germanus were young. They were arrested in Caesarea, boldly confessed Christ as true God and were beheaded. Maratho was a virgin from Scythopolis in Coele-Syria, a city also called Nysa or Methora, which was honored with a metropolitan throne. She too was arrested for her piety, was led naked around the whole city and was then handed over to the fire, where she was perfected in martyrdom.

life|11-12||Όσιος Μαρτίνος||Martin, who was called wonderworker and became bishop in Gaul (Francia), was at first an official with the title of count and then a commander-in-chief, sent to war against barbarians. He feared the great multitude of the enemies, but a dream with a divine vision promised him victory and indeed he won. Before the war he had had compassion on a poor man: he gave him part of his chlamys and fed him and gave him drink, and in the dream the Lord told him that to Him he had offered all this. After he then abandoned the world and practiced asceticism for seven years as a monk, studying the Scriptures, he became bishop of the city of Constantine in Gaul. According to the text he raised the dead, killed dragons and changed a living dove into gold to help a poor man and then restored it to its form. After working many other miracles, he fell asleep peacefully.

life|11-15||Άγιοι Ελπίδιος, Μάρκελλος και Ευστόχιος οι Μάρτυρες||Elpidius was a member of the senate and a confidant of the apostate Emperor Julian, but when he was writing laws it became evident that he was a Christian. Because he refused to renounce Christ, they clothed him in a rough garment of hair full of iron thorns and smeared with boiling pitch and beat him; then they threw him into a cauldron of boiling water, made him drink extremely harsh drinks with sulfur and asphalt and handed him over, together with Eustochius and Marcellus, to wild horses and bulls, which, however, stood motionless by divine power. Their limbs were crushed with rods and they were thrown into the fire, where they gave up their souls. According to tradition, their bodies were buried on Mount Carmel, Christ appeared there with angels and feasted them, transferred Eustochius and Marcellus to another place and raised Elpidius for a second contest. Julian had him pulled apart in four directions, beat him, poured vinegar and salt on his wounds, stretched him on burning coals and struck his head with an iron hook, while he remained unharmed and brought many unbelievers to Christ. Finally they threw him into a lighted furnace and he gave up his spirit to God.

life|11-15||Άγιος Δημήτριος ο Μάρτυρας||This saint was arrested in the time of Emperor Maximian and the governor Publius. He endured many tortures for his faith in Christ and was finally beheaded with the sword, thus receiving the crown of martyrdom.

life|11-17||Άγιοι Γεννάδιος και Μάξιμος Πατριάρχες Κωνσταντινουπόλεως||Gennadius was the first patriarch elected after the fall of Constantinople, a very learned and virtuous man. At the founding of the patriarchal school, the so-called Great School of the Nation, the text mentions him as its first founder. Concerning Maximus, the text notes that in the list of patriarchs there are two Maximuses and that it is not clear which of the two is commemorated today. One was a monk and was on the throne only six months under Theodore Lascaris (in the year 1206). The other ascended the throne in 1450, was renowned for his virtue and taught his flock every Sunday in the church.

life|11-17||Όσιοι Ζαχαρίας και Ιωάννης||John was a glorious and wealthy man who became a monk and lived humbly, keeping vigil one night in the Great Church, the Hagia Sophia of Constantinople. There he saw a luminous man, Zacharias, open with the sign of the cross the closed doors of the church, pray and go out, while the doors closed again by themselves. John followed him to his little house near the stairs of Saint Julian and, falling at his feet, begged him with tears to reveal his way of life to him. Zacharias, who was a shoemaker and leather-worker, said that he lived with his wife Maria in virginity, concealing it by saying that she was barren. He divided his daily wage into two equal parts: one he gave to the poor and the other he spent on the needs of the household. John marveled and glorified God, while Zacharias, to avoid human glory, left the house and vanished unknown.

life|11-17||Όσιος Γεννάδιος ο Βατοπαιδινός||Saint Gennadius the Venerable practiced asceticism in the monastery of Vatopedi and was its cellarer. According to the text, through a miracle of the Theotokos he was granted to see an empty jar overflowing with oil. He died peacefully.

life|11-18||Άγιο Νήπιο||This holy child was present when the prefect asked the martyr Romanus in which God he believed. He too was asked in which God he believed and answered that he believed in the God of the Christians. They beat him in the presence of his mother, who was pious, and when he was thirsty and asked for water she told him not to drink the perishable water, but to endure so as to drink the living water of blessedness. Because the child continued to rebuke the tyrant, they struck him a second time and in the end he was beheaded with the sword.

life|11-18||Άγιος Πλάτωνας||Plato came from Ancyra in Galatia and was the brother of the martyr Antiochus. He boldly confessed Christ before everyone and was led to the governor Agrippinus. Ten soldiers struck him, they stretched him on a heated bronze bed and beat him, and with red-hot iron balls they burned him in the armpits and sides. They cut his scalp into strips, and tore his flesh and ribs so much that his face changed and was not recognizable. Finally they beheaded him, and so he received the crown of martyrdom.

life|11-19||Αγίες Μάνα και Θυγατέρα||These saints were the wife and daughter of the prefect Aquilinus. They believed in Christ when they saw Saint Azes remain unharmed by the fire, since the flame they had lit beneath him went out. The prefect commanded that the one hundred and fifty soldiers who had believed be beheaded first together with his wife and daughter, and so these also received the crown of martyrdom by the sword.

life|11-19||Άγιοι 150 Μάρτυρες Στρατιώτες||The one hundred and fifty soldiers were sent by the prefect Aquilinus to arrest Saint Azes, but they themselves also believed in Christ. The cause was the miracle the saint performed on the road: when the soldiers were thirsty, he brought forth water and gave them to drink. The prefect ordered that they be beheaded first, and so they were perfected in martyrdom.

life|11-19||Άγιος Άζης||Azes came from the region of the Isaurians and was a soldier. He left military life and lived in solitary places, where he performed many healings and miracles. He was denounced by hunters and led to Diocletian, where he confessed his faith in Christ, and he was handed over to the prefect Aquilinus together with one hundred and fifty soldiers who had been sent to arrest him and who believed on the road, when they saw the miracle of the water he brought forth to quench their thirst. The prefect tortured him with many wounds, hung him on a log and lit a fire beneath him, but the flame went out and the saint remained unharmed. Thus the wife and daughter of the prefect believed. The prefect commanded that first the soldiers and the two women be beheaded and then that the saint also be beaten severely and beheaded.

life|11-19||Άγιος Βαρλαάμ||Barlaam came from Antioch in Syria and was an old man in age. He was brought before the governor of Antioch because he confessed Christ and, because he would not sacrifice to the idols, they beat him with whips and tore out his nails. They led him to an altar and ordered him to stretch out his right hand, on which they put burning coals and incense, so that if he shook it off it would appear that he had offered sacrifice. He remained unshaken, without moving his hand, until the fire consumed the flesh and pierced through the hand and the coals fell off by themselves. In this torture he gave up his soul to God. Basil the Great and John Chrysostom honored him with panegyrics.

life|11-19||Άγιος Ηλιόδωρος ο Μάρτυρας||Heliodorus lived in the city of Magydus in Pamphylia in the time of Emperor Aurelian and preached Christ boldly, and for this he was denounced to the governor. Because he would not sacrifice to the idols, they hung him up, scraped him and burned him with lighted torches, but as he asked help from Christ a voice was heard from heaven which reassured him. The soldiers holding the torches heard the voice, saw four angels and believed, and they were thrown into the sea. The martyr they put into a heated bronze ox, which became cold, and he sang psalms inside; according to the text, the idols of the temple of the Pantheon also fell down when he bowed there. They hung him up and drove heated nails into his head, but, calling upon God, he was relieved of the pain, and then they made him stand in a heated pan, where he prayed and urged those present to enter, and those who entered remained unharmed and believed. Finally the governor Aetius ordered that his tongue be cut out, that he be hung up and beaten for two hours with a wooden sword, and they dragged him outside the city. There he prayed and was beheaded, receiving the crown of martyrdom.

life|11-19||Προφήτης Αβδίας ή Οβδιού ή Αβδιού||The Prophet Obadiah, whose name means servant of the Lord or confessing, came from Shechem, from the village of Bethanaram, and lived around 1800 BC according to the text. He served first King Ahab and then Ahaziah, who sent to the Prophet Elijah two captains of fifty, who were burned with their soldiers by fire that fell from heaven. The third captain of fifty was sent by Ahaziah, Obadiah, and he approached with humility, fell at Elijah's feet and begged him not to burn him but to go down to the king, and so it happened. From then on Obadiah left the king and followed Elijah as his disciple, prophesied much and when he died they buried him in the tomb of his fathers.

life|11-20||Άγιος Δάσιος ο Μάρτυρας||Dasius was a soldier at Durostorum, a city near the Danube, in the time of Maximian, around 298. In the city the pagans had the custom, thirty days before the feast of the god Cronus, of choosing a young and handsome soldier, dressing him in royal garments, allowing him every desire and in the end sacrificing him on the altar. The lot fell on Dasius, and he reasoned that, since he had to die, it was better to die as a Christian for Christ. He presented himself to the rulers and openly confessed his faith, and Diocletian and Maximian tortured him greatly and in the end beheaded him with the sword.

life|11-20||Άγιοι Νιρσάς και Ιωσήφ||Nersas and Joseph were bishops in Persia, old men, the first about eighty and the second eighty-nine years old. Together with them other bishops, priests and laymen were martyred, as well as virgins and women ascetics. The Persians tortured them with various punishments, but they did not deny their faith and were beheaded.

life|11-20||Άγιοι Ευστάθιος, Θεσπέσιος και Ανατόλιος οι Μάρτυρες||They lived in the time of Maximian, around 300, from Gangra in Galatia, sons of Philotheus and Eusebia. Eustathius studied letters, while Thespesius and Anatolius practiced the trade of their father, who sold clothes. On a journey of theirs to Nicomedia, the father and Anatolius were taught the faith by the presbyter Lucian and were baptized, and later the other two were also baptized by Anthimus, Bishop of Nicomedia. The father became a presbyter and Eustathius a deacon. After the death of their parents they were denounced to Maximian as Christians; they were beaten with rods and imprisoned, and an angel released them from their bonds. Thrown to the wild beasts they remained unharmed, and the count Antony tortured them in Nicaea by hanging and iron claws, so that the earth reddened with blood. An angel healed them again in prison, and when their beheading was ordered, they themselves gave up their souls on the way to the place of execution; the executioners, out of fear of the tyrant, nevertheless cut off the heads of the dead bodies.
life|11-20||Άγιος Θεόκτιστος ο Ομολογητής||According to the text Theoktistos was a patrician and eunuch in the time of the empress Theodora. The Synaxarion honors him as a confessor.

life|11-22||Άγιοι Μάρκος, Στέφανος και Μάρκος οι Μάρτυρες||They lived in the time of Diocletian and the governor Magnus, around 290, from Antioch in Pisidia. They were arrested and openly confessed Christ. They first underwent many tortures and, because they would not deny Him, they were beheaded.

life|11-22||Άγιος Προκόπιος ο Παλαιστίνιος||Procopius devoted his life to asceticism. He came from Aelia, that is Jerusalem, and lived in Scythopolis, where he served in the church as reader, as translator from the Syriac language and as exorcist of demons. When his deeds became known, they led him to Caesarea, and the governor pressed him to sacrifice to the idols and to obey the four emperors. He answered with the verse of Homer that the rule of many is not good, let there be one ruler, one king and one God, the creator of all things. The angered governor condemned him to death by the sword.

life|11-22||Άγιος Μένιγνος ο κναφέας||Meniguos lived in the time of Decius, around 251, from Parium on the Hellespont, and had the trade of fuller, that is, a bleacher of cloth. When the governor of Asia was throwing the Christians of the coastal regions into prison, the prisoners prayed during the night, and according to the text the Lord appeared, loosed their bonds, opened the prison and sent them out to preach. When Meniguos heard this, he was filled with faith and longing for martyrdom, and twice, as he was washing in the river, he heard a voice calling him. Then he gave back the clothes he had, which belonged to others, and when the governor came and was reading the imperial decrees against the Christians, Meniguos rushed forward, snatched the letters from him, tore them up and trampled them in the name of Jesus Christ. They beat him, hung him up and tore his flesh with iron claws, and when they ordered that the fingers that had torn the decrees be cut off, according to the text milk ran instead of blood. The next day he confessed Christ again before everyone and was condemned to beheading. At the place of execution he taught the people, entrusted his wife to the guardians he had appointed and was beheaded; those present saw a white turtledove come out of his mouth and fly into the sky. His brothers secretly took the relic, and according to the tradition in the text they later found his head, which had been left behind, thanks to a star that shone over it, and buried it where he himself had indicated to them.

life|11-22||Όσιος Αββάς||Saint Abbas the Venerable came from the race of the Ishmaelites. He left parents and homeland, followed a monk and put on the monastic habit, and together they came to Saint Eusebius the Venerable to become his disciples. When the monk who accompanied him died, Abbas stayed in the place of the great Eusebius and lived there thirty-eight years, always advancing in virtue. He never wore shoes, ate only as much as was needed to stay alive, was girded with a heavy iron and spent most of the day and night standing or kneeling in prayer, and no one ever saw him lying down. He became abbot of the monks there and was a model for all, and after a long life he fell asleep in peace.

life|11-23||Όσιος Σισίνιος ο Ομολογητής||Sisinius lived in the time of Diocletian, around 300, and came from Cyzicus. He was denounced to the governor Alexander as a Christian and they tied him to wild horses, forcing him to run. They beat him mercilessly, poured sharp vinegar into his nose and he endured other tortures also, while also working miracles, and they threw him into prison. According to the text, when he was present at the First Ecumenical Council of 325 against Arius, he silenced Arius with the arguments of his right doctrines, proclaiming that the Son is consubstantial with the Father. He lived well and in a manner pleasing to God and died in peace.

life|11-24||Άγιος Θεόδωρος ο Μάρτυρας||Theodore was in Antioch in the time of Julian the Apostate, around 361. When Julian ordered the relics of Saint Babylas to be moved from Daphne, the Christians who were carrying them sang the verse of the psalm "Let all who worship carved images be put to shame." Julian was angered and ordered that one of the singers be arrested, the zealous young man Theodore, whom they seized from the marketplace. They hung him on a post, scourged his back and pierced his sides with claws from morning until evening, and then they bound him with chains and threw him into prison. The next day Julian, learning of his courage and that the death of martyrs is a victory for them, let him go free. When they asked him whether he had been in pain, he said that at first he had a little pain, but afterwards a man appeared who wiped his sweat with a soft cloth and gave him courage, and that he was sorry when the tortures stopped, because the heavenly consolation ceased also. Julian died a bitter death in Persia, while Theodore rests in the heavens.

life|11-25||Άγιοι 150 Ρήτορες||They were the one hundred and fifty rhetoricians who believed in Christ through the teaching and wisdom of Saint Catherine, together with many other Greeks. According to the text they were perfected by fire.
life|11-25||Αγία Βασίλισσα||Saint Basilissa was the wife of King Maxentius. She was beheaded with the sword for her faith in Christ.

life|11-25||Άγιος Πορφυρίων (ή Πορφύριος) ο Στρατηλάτης και οι 200 Στρατιώτες του||Porphyrios was a general and was martyred together with two hundred of his soldiers; all of them were perfected by the sword.
life|11-25||Άγιοι 670 Μάρτυρες||They were six hundred and seventy martyrs who were perfected by the sword.

life|11-25||Όσιος Πέτρος ο Ησυχαστής||Peter was born of pious parents near the Black Sea. He lived with his parents only the first seven years and devoted the whole rest of his life to philosophy and asceticism. He went first to Galatia and then to Palestine, where he venerated the holy places, and went down to Antioch, where he shut himself in a cell and lived in prayer, eating a little measured bread and drinking a little water every two days. For his virtues he received from God authority over the demons: he freed a certain Daniel from a demon, taught him and made him his fellow ascetic, healed the blind and other illnesses, and other deeds of his remain in writing or oral tradition. He became famous throughout Antioch and its environs and died at the age of ninety-nine.

life|11-26||Όσιος Ακάκιος ο εν τή Κλίμακι||Acacius was a monk in a monastery in Asia and practiced asceticism from childhood. He had as overseer and elder a very negligent and harsh monk, who treated him so badly that Acacius often had a bruised eye or neck or a wounded head. // After spending nine years under his obedience, he died and was buried in the cemetery of the fathers. According to tradition, when his elder and a discerning father went to the tomb and asked him whether he had died, he answered that a laborer of obedience cannot die. His former elder was afraid, fell down in tears and made a cell beside the tomb, where he lived in repentance. // The relic of Acacius, according to the text, was preserved intact for many years. When a certain monk put a dead brother also in his tomb and the dead man was found twice thrown out, the monk scolded the saint for disobedience. The next day the dead man was in the tomb, but Acacius was not found, and the tomb appears empty to this day with his name. Saint John of the Ladder also wrote about the venerable one.

life|11-26||Όσιος Ιάκωβος ο Αναχωρητής||James first shut himself in a small house and practiced remembrance of the name of God. When he grew stronger, he went up a mountain thirty stadia from the city of Cyrrhus and stayed there without a cave, hut or any covering, with only the sky as roof, visible to all. // He wore heavy irons and chains at his waist, neck and elbows, and fed on soaked lentils in the evening. He fell gravely ill, and his patience was well known, even when crowds gathered to take his relic. According to the accounts he stayed buried in the snow for three days and nights praying, and his neighbors dug him out. // By his blessing fevers were extinguished, demons departed and the water he blessed became medicine. According to the text he raised a child, whom his father had vowed to God if he lived and who died at the age of four. The saint prayed and the child came to life. He also related the assaults of the demons, who tried to make him die of thirst, but he overcame them. After his good struggle he died and went to the Lord.

life|11-28||Άγιος Ειρήναρχος||Eirenarchos came from Sebaste and was young when he became an executioner, that is, a punisher of those condemned, and served in the tortures of Christians. Under Diocletian the governor Maximus was torturing seven Christian women, and Eirenarchos, seeing how bravely they endured, was enlightened by the grace of God and openly confessed Christ. // According to the account he was first thrown into the lake and came out alive, then into a lighted furnace and was preserved unharmed. Finally he was beheaded with the sword together with the presbyter Acacius, who had baptized him, and so both received the crown of martyrdom. On the same day the seven women are also honored.

life|11-28||Άγιοι Βασίλειος, Στέφανος, Ιωάννης ο από Λεγαταρίων ή Λεγατοκρίων, δύο Γρηγόριοι και άλλοι Μάρτυρες||Many soldiers of Emperor Constantine Copronymus, who were Orthodox, renounced the world and became monks, and the lawless emperor punished them. Basil he blinded and, because he would not agree to deny the veneration of the holy icons, he kicked him in the belly and his bowels burst, whereupon he gave up his soul to God. // Another he imprisoned, cut off his nose and exiled him to Cherson, and he went away to Khazaria, became bishop there and died. Another Stephen was exiled to Sougdaia and died after benefiting many. Two Gregories with many others were exiled and fell asleep in the Lord. John of Legatarioi was exiled to Lafnousia and, being often beaten at the emperor's command, ended his life. All these, fellow martyrs of Saint Stephen the Younger, received the crown of martyrdom for the holy icons.

life|11-28||Άγιοι Τιμόθεος, Θεόδωρος, Πέτρος, Ιωάννης, Σέργιος, Θεόδωρος, Νικηφόρος, Βασίλειος, Θωμάς, Ιερόθεος, Δανιήλ, Χαρίτων, Σωκράτης, Κομάσιος, Ευσέβιος και Ετιμάσιος||Under Julian the Apostate, around 361, the commentariensis of Nicaea ordered the Christians to sacrifice to the idols or be tortured. Many refused, others died in the tortures and others were scattered. Among them were Timothy, Comasius, Etimasius, Eusebius and Theodore, who reached Tiberiopolis (the present-day Strumica). Timothy later became its bishop, and Theodore also became a bishop, one of the fathers of the First Ecumenical Council. Comasius, a former soldier, and Eusebius became monks and preached the Gospel. // To these five came also the priests Peter, John, Sergius, Theodore and Nikephoros, the deacons Basil and Thomas and the monks Hierotheus, Daniel, Chariton and Socrates, and all together they enlightened and healed people, asking as their reward that they believe in Christ. // The governors Valis and Philip arrested them in Strumica and, because they confessed Christ and despised the idols, they condemned them to beheading by the sword. They went to the place of execution with joy and received the crown of martyrdom. The priest Peter, who rebuked the governors, was beaten and his hands were burned before he was beheaded. According to the text a woman blind from birth took his right hand and, as she touched it to her eyes, she saw the light, and she placed it in the church of Saint Anastasia in Thessaloniki. The Christians buried the relics with honors in Tiberiopolis, and their miracles caused many Greeks to believe.

life|12-03||Άγιος Γαβριήλ ο Ιερομάρτυρας Πατριάρχης Κωνσταντινουπόλεως||Gabriel was first a bishop and later was martyred in Prusa, around 1659. The Synaxarion honors him as a hieromartyr, because he received a double crown, of the high priesthood and of martyrdom.

life|12-04||Άγιος Σεραφείμ ο Νέος Ιερομάρτυρας||Seraphim was Bishop of Phanarion and was martyred in 1601. According to the Synaxarion he was perfected by being pierced through, and his blood flowed like rivers. It calls him a new hieromartyr.

life|12-04||Όσιος Ιωάννης ο Θαυματουργός Επίσκοπος Πολυβότου||From a young age John hated the pleasures of the body and adorned his life with fasting and chastity. After passing through all the ecclesiastical ranks, that is, reader, subdeacon, deacon and presbyter, he was ordained Bishop of Polybotus. // When Leo the Isaurian became emperor in 716 and began to blaspheme the holy icons, John rebuked him vehemently, taught his flock the Orthodox faith and assured them that he would remain in it even after death. // According to the text, he received from God such wonderworking power that by a divine chastisement he persuaded the Hagarenes who lived around Amorium in Phrygia to hand over the Christian captives they held. // After living in a manner pleasing to God and reaching deep old age, he died. His honored relic was preserved incorrupt and whole until the time of the text. The Christians of the place raise it upright on the day of Pentecost, clothe it in hierarchical vestments and support it on the Holy Table and later on the holy synthronon, where two priests hold it throughout the liturgy. The author adds that the saint every day frees the possessed and heals illnesses.

life|12-05||Άγιος Αναστάσιος ο Μάρτυρας||Anastasius was a Christian and, seeing the holy martyrs being tortured and cut to pieces by the pagans, he became zealous for martyrdom and longed for it himself. // At the age of sixteen he marked his body with the sign of the cross, went of his own accord to the court and cried out in a loud voice the words of the Prophet Isaiah. He declared that he was a Christian and believed in Jesus Christ, while he anathematized the idols and their worshipers. // The pagans beat him severely and told him that if he persisted they would cut off his head. In the end they beheaded him, took him in a small boat a little way from the shore and threw his body into the sea.

life|12-05||Άγιοι Οσιομάρτυρες του Αγίου Όρους||These venerable ones practiced asceticism in the cells of Mount Athos and rebuked the Latin-minded, that is, the emperor Michael and the patriarch Beccus. According to the Synaxarion, the first of them was hanged, while the rest were perfected by the sword.

life|12-07||Άγιος Αθηνόδωρος ο Μάρτυρας||Athenodorus lived in the days of Emperor Diocletian and came from Syria in Mesopotamia. From a young age he became a monk. // He was denounced as a Christian to the governor Eleusius and confessed Christ. They stretched him between two pillars and burned all his limbs with lighted torches, burned his armpits with heated irons and hung him by iron hooks from his nose. They also stretched him on a heated bronze carpet, which according to the text the saint miraculously turned from burning to cold. They also put him in a heated bronze bull, from which he was kept unharmed by an angel. // By his miracles he drew to faith in Christ fifty Greek men and then thirty others. Finally he was condemned to beheading, but the executioner was paralyzed and fell as if dead with his sword and no one else dared to approach. So the saint prayed, gave up his soul into the hands of God and received the crown of martyrdom.

life|12-07||Άγιοι 300 Μάρτυρες πού μαρτύρησαν στήν Αφρική||These saints lived in the days of Emperor Zeno, when the Arian Honorich was ruler of Africa, successor of his father Gizerich. The Arian bishops Cyril and Vilinardes persuaded him to raise a great persecution against the Orthodox, so terrible that it surpassed the persecutions of Diocletian and Maximian. // Honorich ordered that the priests of fifteen cities of Africa be persecuted and that the sacred vestments and treasures of the Orthodox be taken away. Any Christian who was not rebaptized in the heretical baptism of the Arians was to be put to death at once. Some Orthodox could not endure the tortures and fled, leaving homelands and houses, while those who were firm in the faith gave themselves up willingly to martyrdom. // Thus three hundred Orthodox were put to death in Africa by the Vandals, because they confessed the Son consubstantial with the Father.

life|12-07||Άγιοι Ορθόδοξοι Μάρτυρες πού κάηκαν μέσα σέ Ναό||In the persecution of the Arian Honorich in Africa, the Orthodox had taken possession of a single church, where they gathered and celebrated the divine liturgy. When the Arians learned of it, they surrounded the church, lit wood and dry brush around it and burned together both the church and all the Christians who were praying inside. Honorich praised the audacity of the barbarians.

life|12-07||Αγία Ορθόδοξη Γυναίκα η Μάρτυς||This woman was Orthodox and lived in Rome, in the years when the wife of Odoacer, the Arian Sunilda, was forcing her to be baptized a second time in the baptism of the Arians. Sunilda was not able to persuade her and commanded that she be baptized by the Arian bishop of Milan. // The Orthodox woman came out of the font, asked her maidservant for two obols and gave them to the bishop, telling him to take his payment for the common bath that had washed her, thus ridiculing the Arian baptism. As soon as Sunilda learned of it, she commanded and they burned the blessed woman. // Her husband feared the punishment of fire, went of his own accord and was baptized a second time in the baptism of Arius, but later, as he was going to an oratory outside the city, he was burned up by a thunderbolt that fell from heaven.

life|12-07||Όσιος Παύλος ο Υποτακτικός||Paul came from parents who were neither glorious and rich nor poor, and they educated him in the sacred letters. When he grew up, he left the world and went to a monastery, where he put on the angelic habit and strove to attain all the virtues, surpassing the other monks. // According to the text, once the abbot together with the most devout brothers prayed with hardship for many days that God would show to what degree of virtue Paul had attained. One night the brothers were caught up into a wonderful garden, where they saw Paul, who told them that the garden had been made for their sake and gave each of them a flower, branch or herb. On waking, they found them in their hands. // On another occasion, when pitch was boiling in a bronze vessel and overflowed and there was no wood to stir it, Paul put his hand in and stirred it, and his hand remained whole and did not even turn black. He used to call himself earth and a fool for Christ. // Later he went to Jerusalem and venerated the holy places, passed over to Cyprus and stayed a few years on a high mountain. Then he went to regions near Constantinople, where he heard a voice from on high telling him to go up the mountain and be perfected. He went up the hill called Paregoria, and after a short time he fell asleep in the Lord.

life|12-08||Άγιοι Σωσθένης, Κήφας, Απολλώς, Τυχικός, Καίσαρ και Επαφρόδιτος οι Απόστολοι εκ των 70||These saints were among the seventy apostles, and Paul mentions most of them in his epistles. Sosthenes became Bishop of Colophon in Ionia, Apollos Bishop of Caesarea and Epaphroditus Bishop of Colophon after Sosthenes, while according to another manuscript he became a bishop in Cyprus. Caesar became Bishop of Corone in the Peloponnese. // All lived rightly and shepherded in holiness the flock of Christ in the churches entrusted to them. They also endured many temptations from the pagans for faith in Christ and were perfected by giving up their souls into the hands of God.

life|12-08||Όσιοι Σωφρόνιος και Δαμιανός Επίσκοποι Κύπρου||Sophronius came from Cyprus, the son of Christian and devout parents, and was very learned, because he read and studied day and night the Scriptures and the words of the Lord. He became so virtuous that he received great gifts from God and worked miracles. // After the death of the most holy Bishop of Cyprus Damian, he was ordained Archbishop of Cyprus by the bishops, with the agreement of all the people. He became the wealth of the poor, the feeder of the hungry, a helper of orphans, a protector of widows, a redeemer of the oppressed and a covering of the naked. Thus he lived pleasing to God and fell asleep in peace.

life|12-09||Όσιος Στέφανος ο νεολαμπής ο εν τω Αγίω Αντίπα κειμένου||Stephen lived in the days of Theophilos, in 829, and was born in Constantinople to parents Zacharias and Theophano, who were virtuous and wise and lived in the district of Zeugma, near the church of the Protomartyr Stephen. According to the text, his mother carried him while fasting, on bread, water and greens, and when he was born a luminous cross appeared on his chest. As an infant, when his mother ate more, he refused to nurse, and so she was compelled to practice self-restraint. // He was baptized, educated in the sacred letters and, when Methodios became patriarch, his father was ordained presbyter and Stephen was tonsured a reader. At fourteen his father died and Stephen shut himself in the oratory of Saint Peter, where he prayed eating only cabbages. The Apostle Peter appeared to him and then the hieromartyr Antipas, and from then on his prayer and fasting increased even more and he was ordained presbyter, working many miracles. // In 879, under Basil the Macedonian, a great earthquake occurred in Constantinople and the church of Saint Antipas was split. Stephen entered a pit like a tomb, where he stayed twelve years, and from the dampness his hair and beard fell out and his body became almost entirely paralyzed. He came out deadened and put on the monastic habit with even harsher asceticism, tasting only one dried fig on the feasts of the Lord. After fifty-five years of ascetic struggles, at the age of seventy, he gave up his soul to God.

life|12-09||Σύλληψις Αγίας Άννης||The Lord, wishing to prepare for Himself a living temple, sent an angel to the righteous Joachim and Anna, from whom He was pleased that His Mother according to the flesh should be born, and announced to them beforehand that Anna, barren and advanced in years, would conceive. By the conception of the barren woman God confirmed the seedless conception and incorrupt birth of Christ from the Virgin. // The holy Theotokos was conceived in the womb of Anna from the seed of Joachim and was born, not after seven months as some say, but beyond the laws of nature, because of Anna's barrenness and old age. Only the Lord Jesus Christ was conceived and born without the seed of man. // The Church celebrates this conception in remembrance of the divine oracles and the joyful tidings that the angel gave to the righteous ones. God moved the barren womb of Anna to bear fruit and was pleased that the prudent parents should bear the daughter who had been predestined and chosen before the ages. The synaxis is held in the venerable house of the Theotokos, near the Great Church.

life|12-10||Άγιος Γέμελλος ο Μάρτυρας||Gemellus lived in the days of Emperor Julian, in 361, and came from Ancyra, from the parish called Klimakene. When Julian passed through the city, the saint stood before him and wounded him with inspired words like arrows. The angered emperor commanded that he be girded with a red-hot iron belt, which burned him so much that the fluid of his flesh covered the ground. // Then he ordered him to follow him on the road. In the small town where they arrived, the saint was stretched out and beaten with clubs, pierced with heated irons, hung up and torn. Because he despised the torments and reviled the impious emperor, they put him in a heated pan filled with oil, resin and fat and struck him with iron rods. According to the text, a violent rain fell that put out the fire and the martyr remained unharmed. // Gemellus was still unbaptized. By the economy of God he was baptized by a certain priest and came out of the font healthy, without a wound on his body, and heard a voice from heaven telling him that he was blessed, because he had labored much. The transgressor then nailed him to a cross by the hands and feet and the saint, praying, gave up his spirit to the Lord. Some Christians secretly took his body from the cross and buried it in a notable place.

life|12-10||Όσιος Θωμάς ο Δεφουρκινός||Thomas came from the foothills of Mount Kyminas, from simple parents who lived self-sufficiently. When he reached the prime of his age, he despised worldly things, became zealous for the life of the monks and became a monk. Later a glorious official of Constantinople, Galokeiktes, built a monastery near the river Sangarius and the local bishop proposed Thomas to him as abbot. He governed the monastery wisely for several years. // But because many ran to him and disturbed his stillness, he made the most virtuous monk abbot and withdrew to the foothills of a mountain, without roof or covering. The brothers found him and with difficulty persuaded him to accept a small cell. There he also received two devout laymen as monks, whom he named Peter and John. // The devil attacked him first with mosquitoes for three years, then with flies and ants, and finally with snakes, which tormented him for eleven whole years. The venerable one endured, thanking God. According to the text, once at the time of the liturgy a fearsome dragon appeared and the saint, after praying that he might tread upon it, saw it fall into a ravine, while the snakes of the cell departed and were devoured. // From then on he was freed from temptations and received from God the gift of healings and prophecies. He left his disciple John as abbot and withdrew to more desolate mountains. Emperor Leo the Wise sent him a sealed letter containing a thought of his heart, and the venerable one, having foreknowledge, had already written the answer and gave it to the messenger before receiving the letter. The emperor tried to see him, but the humble Thomas avoided it. After many years, in deep old age, he gave up his soul to God.

life|12-11||Όσιος Λουκάς ο Νέος Στυλίτης||Luke lived in the days of Emperor Romanos Lekapenos and Constantine Porphyrogennetos, under Patriarch Theophylact, the son of Romanos. He came from the East and was the son of Christopher and Kale. // When the war against the Bulgarians began, the order of the emperors compelled him to go also. Many thousands of men fell in the war, but he was saved by divine providence and became a monk. He advanced in asceticism and was ordained presbyter, wore heavy irons to subdue the body and fasted the six days of the week, eating only the prosphora and raw greens. // He climbed a pillar and stayed three years. Then he heard a divine voice calling him and went to Olympus, where he put a stone in his mouth like a bridle so as not to speak. From there he returned to Constantinople and went to Chalcedon, where he climbed another pillar and worked countless miracles. After staying on the pillar forty-five years, he fell asleep in the Lord.

life|12-11||Άγιοι Αειθαλάς και Ακεψέης οι Μάρτυρες||These saints came from Persia, from the city of Arbela. Aeithalas was a priest of the idols and came to know the faith in Christ as follows: as soon as he thought of going to the bishop of the Christians, he was immediately healed of the hemorrhage that afflicted him. After being catechized by the bishop, he returned to his city to teach piety to others also. // He was denounced as a Christian to the governor of the city, confessed Christ, had his ear cut off and was thrown into prison. Akepsees was a deacon, was arrested and confessed the faith, whereupon they beat him mercilessly and sent him together with Aeithalas to the chief cook of the king, a great office among the Persians. // He presented them to the king, before whom both preached Christ and were beheaded, receiving the crowns of martyrdom.

life|12-11||Άγιος Μείραξ||Meirax was a Christian, the son of pious parents, who through lightness of mind was deceived by the devil and denied the faith in Christ before the Amira, trampling the cross and declaring that he was a Hagarene. His parents did not cease to beseech God to change his mind, and God heard their entreaty. // Meirax came to his senses, repented and, on the advice and with the blessing of his parents, went to the synagogue of the Hagarenes, made the sign of the cross before the Amira and confessed Christ again, anathematizing their religion. He was imprisoned and spent three days without food and water, and then they interrogated him and scourged him repeatedly, but he remained steadfast. // In the end he was condemned to death. The servants led him by ship out to sea, let him pray, cut off his head and threw it to the bottom. His body did not appear, while the honored head came out of the sea and was taken by Christians, who paid one hundred florins to the Amira in order to keep it freely. They placed it in a silver case, and according to the text from then until today it has flowed with fragrant myrrh and worked many and various healings.

life|12-11||Άγιος Βαρσαβάς ο Μάρτυρας||Barsabas boldly confessed in Persia Christ as true God. For this reason the governor of Persia ordered that his head be cut off and so he received the crown of martyrdom.

life|12-12||Άγιος Συνετός ο Μάρτυρας||Synetos lived in the time of Emperor Aurelian, around 270, and was a reader of the church of Rome. When he saw Aurelian sacrificing to the idols, he spoke to him and, in jest, promised that he too would sacrifice, but it became evident that he said it only to mock him. For this they beat him with rods so much that the ground was stained with his blood, and threw him into prison. // The next day they stretched him on a heated iron gridiron, but he heard a divine voice from on high that strengthened him, a heavy rain came and put out the fire, and he remained unharmed. Then, by order of the emperor, they dug a deep pit filled with sharp stakes and nails and threw him in, where almost all his limbs were cut. By divine providence, however, he became healthy again. // They shut him in the so-called Pantheon and from there, after he came out, they beheaded him, and so he received the crown of martyrdom.

life|12-13||Όσιος Αρσένιος ο Ασκητής πού ασκήτευσε στό Λάτριο όρος||Arsenius came from Constantinople, from pious, wealthy and distinguished parents. The emperor made him general and patrician of the province of the Kibyrrhaiotai, and once he took command of an imperial fleet. Because of a great storm the ships were sunk and only he was saved and came ashore. // Then he obtained leave and became a monk, as he had long desired. He afflicted his body with fasts, vigils, sleeping on the ground and heavy irons, wore hair garments and ate very little. He lived first opposite the place called Hieron, and then on Mount Latros in Asia Minor, where according to the text, by the cross and his prayer, he killed an asp (snake) that was poisoning the waters. // He was for a short time abbot in the monastery of the Kellibaroi and urged many to virtue. He withdrew again into stillness, shut himself in a hole that was the lair of wild beasts, and by his prayer drove the beasts away. Later he returned to the monastery but lived shut in a narrow cell, speaking and eating only on Sunday, and according to the text he was fed by an angel. With his staff he made bitter waters sweet. // Before he died, he gathered the monks around him and taught them about renunciation of the world, patience, brotherly love, humility and prayer, and with tears gave up his soul to God. After death, according to the text, he healed a demoniac who had tried to dig through his tomb and had been paralyzed, and a monk with dropsy who venerated at the tomb.

life|12-14||Άγιοι Φιλήμων, Απολλώνιος, Αρριανός και οι τέσσερις Προτεκτοράτοι||They lived in the time of Diocletian and the governor Arrianus in the Thebaid of Egypt, around 290. Thirty-seven Christians were arrested and led to the governor. One of them, Apollonius, a reader of the church, was afraid of the tortures and gave four florins and his clothes to the flute-player Philemon, so that he might put them on and sacrifice to the idols in his place. // But Philemon, putting on the clothes of Apollonius, put on mentally also faith in Christ and, when commanded to sacrifice, confessed Christ. When the governor reproached him that he was not baptized, Philemon prayed and rain fell only upon him, which according to the text became his baptism by God; then he prayed and fire from heaven burned the flute and the florins in the hands of Apollonius. // Apollonius, who had become the cause of Philemon's believing, presented himself to the governor and preached faith in Christ, and they cut the tendons of his feet and dragged him through the whole city. Philemon was hung on an olive tree and they shot arrows at him, but the arrows did not touch him and one turned back and blinded the governor, whom the saint healed. He had told him that after his martyrdom, if he put earth from his tomb on his eye, he would be well. // When Philemon and Apollonius were beheaded, Arrianus went to the tomb, took earth and became healthy, and believed in Christ together with four Protectors (bodyguards), and all were baptized. Diocletian brought him to trial, bound him with irons, hung a stone around his neck and lowered him into a chasm, where they covered him with earth. According to the text, that same evening Diocletian found him alive in his own bed with the irons and the stone, and he told him that he was Arrianus. // Then Diocletian threw him into the sea together with the four Protectors, shut in five sacks of sand. A great dolphin brought the sacks to the shore of Alexandria, where the slaves of Arrianus found them, and the relics were carried by ship on the Nile and buried with honors in the metropolis of the Antinoites, as a divine voice directed.

life|12-15||Αγία Ανθία η Μάρτυς||Anthia was the mother of Saint Eleutherius and had been taught the faith in Christ by the Apostle Paul. When her son was put to death by the sword, she embraced and kissed his dead relic and was herself put to death by the sword, receiving together with her son the crown of martyrdom.

life|12-15||Άγιος Κοράμων ο Μάρτυρας ο Έπαρχος||Koramon was a prefect and, according to the text, proposed to Emperor Hadrian that an oven with sharp spits be constructed to torture Saint Eleutherius. But he himself first entered the oven, full of the Holy Spirit, confessed Christ as God and came out unharmed. Afterwards he was beheaded and received the crown of martyrdom.

life|12-15||Αγία Σωσάννη||Susanna lived in the time of Maximian, around 300, came from Palestine and had a Greek father and a Jewish mother. She escaped the impiety of both, was baptized by Bishop Silvanus and, when her parents died, distributed her property to the poor and freed her slaves. She dressed as a man, cut her hair and entered a men's monastery in Jerusalem under the name John, and because of her virtues she became archimandrite of the monastery. // After twenty years she was slandered by an ascetic woman, who, thinking she was a man, had urged her to sin and, because she refused, accused her of supposedly having tried to rape her. Susanna accepted the slander joyfully, until the abbot wished to depose her. Then, of necessity, she asked for two virgins and two deaconesses and assured them by the facts that she was a woman. The Bishop of Eleutheropolis was astonished and ordained her deacon, and from then on, according to the text, she worked many miracles. // When the governor Alexander went to Eleutheropolis and sacrificed to the idols, the saint went of her own accord and by her prayer overthrew the idols, and confessed Christ. They cut off her breasts, which according to the text became healthy again, and the executioners who saw it believed and were beheaded. They poured molten lead into her mouth with a funnel, but divine grace protected her, until she was scourged and thrown into the fire, where she gave up her soul to God.

life|12-15||Άγιος Βάκχος ο Νέος||Bacchus came from Palestine and lived in the time of Constantine and Irene, around 780. His parents were Christians, but his father, carried away by vanity, denied the faith and went over to the religion of the Hagarenes, and raised seven children in it. The third son, Dachak, who had remained unmarried, after the death of his father revealed to his mother, a faithful Christian, his intention to become a Christian and she encouraged him. // He went to Jerusalem and, led by a monk, reached the Lavra of Saint Sabbas, where he was baptized with the name Bacchus and became a monk. The abbot, fearing lest it become known to the Hagarenes, who then ruled Jerusalem, sent him outside the monastery. In Jerusalem he found his mother and told her everything, and she and his other brothers believed and became Christians. // Only one brother remained unbelieving and denounced Bacchus to the Hagarenes. They arrested him and led him to the Amira of Jerusalem, who sent him to the general and the judges. There Bacchus confessed Christ as true God and mocked the faith of the Hagarenes as false. He was beheaded and received the crown of martyrdom.

life|12-15||Όσιος Παύλος ο νέος ο ασκητής||Paul was born in 912 at Elaia, near Pergamon, to pious parents, Antiochus and Eudokia, who descended from the family of Saint Joannikios the Great. He was left an orphan, became a swineherd to live, and his elder brother Basil, a monk on Mount Latros, called him to himself after a divine revelation. The inhabitants of the place hindered him twice, but the third time he succeeded in reaching his brother, who handed him over to the ascetic elder Peter. // Paul served the elder with obedience and humility. Once when he grew drowsy at the service, the elder slapped him and from then on he was never again negligent. After the elder's death, the other monks wanted to make him abbot, but he refused and went to higher and more inaccessible parts of Latros, eating raw acorns and devoted to prayer, vigils and fasts, while he rendered the temptations of the demons ineffective. // Later he came down to the lower parts of the mountain, where he built a church to the Holy Trinity. According to the text God gave him the gift of miracles: he brought forth water in a waterless place, received fire from heaven and his fingers were illuminated in prayer, while an angel lived with him and served him. At his name demons and diseases departed. // He was short in stature, bald, with a broad beard and a yellow face, but with wondrous grace.
