He was described as a prophet and beholder of many visions, and when he reached the end of his life he fell asleep. After death, according to the text, he was glorified by miracles and by myrrh that flowed from his tomb.

life|12-16||Άγιος Μαρίνος ο Μάρτυρας||Marinus lived under Emperor Carinus, around 283. He was Roman by race and from a young age took part in the council and had honors from the Senate. When he was denounced as a Christian and was unwilling to sacrifice to the idols, they hung him up and struck him with wooden swords. // Then they stretched him on a heated gridiron, threw him into a lighted pan and a cauldron of boiling water, but he remained unharmed, since the fire miraculously became coolness. They also threw him to the wild beasts, which did not touch him. Then he deceived the emperor, saying that he would go to the temple of the idols to sacrifice, entered and by his prayer overthrew the idols. For this he was beheaded and received the crown of martyrdom, while his father and mother accompanied him to the place of condemnation and called him blessed.

life|12-17||Άγιοι Πατερμούθιος, Κόπρις και Αλέξανδρος οι Οσιομάρτυρες||These saints were martyred in the days of Julian the Apostate, in 361, after having first spent their lives in stillness in the desert of Egypt. Julian, as he was going to fight the Persians, learned about them and brought them before him. He first asked Patermuthios how old he was and, when he heard that he was forty-five, sent him out; then he took Copres and by various devices and flatteries persuaded him to deny Christ. But Patermuthios reminded him of the fasts, prayers and struggles of asceticism and brought him back to the faith. Then the tyrant commanded that Copres's tongue be cut out and that he be put on a red-hot gridiron; Copres grew fearful seeing the sparks, but, strengthened by Patermuthios, he went up onto the gridiron with him and, by the grace of God, both remained unharmed. Then they were thrown into a lighted furnace, where the monk Alexander also entered with them, who boldly confessed Christ; all three came out unharmed and for this, by order of the tyrant, they were beheaded and received the crown of martyrdom.

life|12-17||Όσιος Στέφανος ο Ομολογητής||He was the ruler of an island near Gades in Spain, which some called Libertis and others Berroe. He had great wealth and had been raised in the pious faith, but he regarded all the things of the world as refuse, left the rule to his sons and went to Rome, where he put on the monastic habit. From there he went to Constantinople and met the emperors Constantine and Romanos Porphyrogennetos in 919, who sent him to Jerusalem, as he himself had asked. There he received the great and angelic habit from Patriarch Christodoulos and from Dounales was renamed Stephen. He received many insults and beatings from the Saracens, because his beard was cut all around; from Jerusalem he went to Egypt, where he was imprisoned together with the two priests who followed him and was afflicted for months by hunger and thirst. They sent him to the emir of Egypt, who bound him with heavy fetters and tried to force him to deny Christ; he resisted steadfastly and confessed the Lord, and for this was punished with still more wounds and tortures. From these he fell ill and, after God revealed to him that his repose was near, he gave up his soul.

life|12-18||Άγιοι Νικόστρατος, Ζωή η σύζυγός του, Τραγκυλίνος και η σύζυγός του Μαρκία, Κλαύδιος, Τιβούρτιος, Κάστωρ, Καστούλος, Μάρκος και Μαρκελλίνος οι Μάρτυρες||According to the text, Sebastian, a senator from Milan, brought many to the faith in the days of Diocletian and Maximian, and strengthened the twin brothers Marcus and Marcellinus, sons of Tranquillinus and Marcia, who held first place in family and wealth. Through them he led to the knowledge of God also their father Tranquillinus, who catechized the prefect Chromatius, and Chromatius, healed of his illness, believed, destroyed the idols of his house and was baptized. Bishop Gaius ordained the two brothers deacons, Tranquillinus presbyter and Sebastian defender of the Church. When the persecution broke out, they were arrested separately: Nicostratus, the husband of Zoe, Claudius, Castor, Tiburtius the son of Chromatius, Castulus in whose house the saints stayed, and Zoe, and after various tortures they ended their lives. Marcus and Marcellinus remained a long time in prison and underwent various tortures; their parents and relatives were ready to persuade them by entreaties to deny, but Sebastian prevented them. According to the verses of the text, Zoe and Tiburtius died by the sword, Tranquillinus by stoning, Claudius was thrown into the sea and Marcus and Marcellinus were wounded with lances. Sebastian boldly confessed Christ before Diocletian, was condemned to be bound to a stake and shot with dense arrows, and his body became like a hedgehog. Afterwards they beat him to pieces with thick rods and, cut to pieces, he gave up his soul to God.

life|12-18||Άγιος Ευβίωτος||He lived in the days of Emperor Maximian, in 298, and came from the village of Ptoketon in the province of Opsikion, where he was born, grew up and died. Because he lived a life pleasing to God and practiced every virtue, he suffered much from the pagans, who bound and beat him as he went from place to place. They were especially embittered because he worked many miracles and by them turned many unbelievers to faith in Christ. Once they crushed him with clubs and stones and threw him into the fire, but he remained unharmed by the grace of Christ, and many, seeing the miracle, believed and were baptized in the Church there, which the Apostles Paul and Silas had inaugurated. The governor of Cyzicus, Leontius, brought him bound, beat him with stones, hung him up and tore his body with whips, gave him to the wild beasts and threw him into prison, but the saint remained unharmed and many Greeks believed. The gladiators who were ordered to slay him fell into a frenzy and killed one another. After twenty-two days news came that Constantine the Great was advancing from the West to fight Maximian, and the frightened Maximian ordered that the Christians be freed. Eubiotus returned to his cell, lived five more years working many miracles and peacefully gave up his soul to the Lord.

life|12-18||Όσιος Φλώρος||He was Bishop of Amisus in Cappadocia and lived in the days of the emperors Justin, Tiberius and Maurice, that is, around 584. He was the son of Florus and Euphemia and became skilled in every learning, both the outer learning of the Greeks and the inner learning of the Divine Scriptures. First he became a royal secretary and then rose to the dignity of patrician; he married and had children, but his children and his wife died in an epidemic. Then he became a monk and lived in stillness on an estate he had in the place called Anaplos. For his virtue he was ordained Bishop of Amisus, governed well the flock entrusted to him and, after also working miracles, died and went to the Lord.

life|12-19||Άγιοι Ηλίας, Πρόβος και Άρης οι Μάρτυρες||These saints were from Egypt and were Christians. They were going to Cilicia to serve and to visit the Christians who were suffering martyrdom there. When they reached Ascalon, they were arrested and brought before the judge Firmilian; they confessed that they were Christians and endured various tortures. Aris ended his martyrdom by fire, while Probus and Elias were beheaded. Their synaxis and feast is celebrated at the martyrion of Saint Philemon, in the place called Strategion.

life|12-19||Άγιοι Τιμόθεος και Πολύευκτος οι Μάρτυρες||Timothy was arrested and confessed Christ, and after many tortures he ended his martyrdom by fire in Mauretania in Africa. Polyeuctus was first tortured with various punishments in Caesarea and was finally thrown into the fire, where he ended his martyrdom. Thus both received their crowns from the Lord.

life|12-20||Όσιος Φιλογόνιος||From childhood Philogonius was given to the study of the sacred letters and from the beginning became a dedication to God. He learned all the sciences with great accuracy, in keeping with his keen intelligence, and lived a distinguished life, although he had a wife and children, as a lawyer and judge who defended the wronged and helped the oppressed. Because of the purity of his life he was found worthy also of inner ecclesiastical authority, and from the outer tribunal of the judges he ascended to the sacred sanctuary of the Church and of the bishops; he became Patriarch of Antioch. At that time the persecutions of the tyrants had only just ceased, but their remnants still remained, and there was great turmoil caused by the heretics, which had begun in his days; all this was hindered and quelled by the wisdom and governance of the saint, as Saint Chrysostom relates at greater length. Having shepherded his flock in a manner pleasing to God and lived an angelic life, he departed to the Lord.

life|12-21||Αγίες 130 Γυναίκες||According to the text, these hundred and thirty women believed in Christ through Saint Juliana, who had remained unharmed in the burning furnace. For their faith they were beheaded with the sword, together with five hundred men who had believed in the same way.

life|12-21||Άγιοι 500 Μάρτυρες||According to the text, these five hundred men believed in Christ when they saw Saint Juliana remain unharmed in the burning furnace, which was extinguished. They were immediately beheaded with the sword, together with a hundred and thirty women who had believed in the same way.

life|12-21||Άγιος Θεμιστοκλής ο Μάρτυρας||He lived in the days of Decius, in the year 250, and came from Myra in Lycia, where he was a shepherd of sheep. The governor Asclepius had begun a persecution against the Christians and was searching for the martyr Dioscorides, who had fled and hidden in the mountain. The searchers found Themistocles pasturing his sheep and questioned him; he hid Dioscorides, saying that he did not know where he was, and handed himself over, confessing that he was a Christian. He stood before the governor, proclaimed Christ with boldness, and they beat him on the belly so much that his belly burst. Then they hung him on a wooden frame and dragged him over sharp iron nails, by which he was torn to pieces in all the members of his body, and he gave up his holy soul to God, receiving the crown of martyrdom.

life|12-22||Αγία Θεοδότη η Μάρτυς και τα τρία παιδιά της||Theodote came from Nicaea in Bithynia and, as a Christian, practiced the commandments of the Lord and raised her three children in the knowledge of God. When she heard of the good works of Saint Anastasia the Deliverer from Potions, she went and lived with her, she and her children. The governor Leucadius had asked for her in marriage, and the emperor Diocletian gave her to him, thinking that in this way she would be drawn away from the faith; but she was not persuaded, and asked Leucadius to wait a little. In the meantime she went with Anastasia to the prisons, visited the imprisoned Christians and encouraged them to endure the sufferings for Christ. When Leucadius realized that he was attempting something impossible, he sent the saint bound, together with her sons, to the proconsul Nicetius, governor of Bithynia, who became angry with her eldest son, Evodus, lit a great furnace and commanded that the saint and her children be thrown into it. Thus they completed their martyrdom, and their synaxis is celebrated in their martyrs' church, in the place called Campus.

life|12-22||Άγιος Χρυσόγονος||Chrysogonus came from Rome in the days of Diocletian, in the year 290, was a God-fearing man and became the teacher of Saint Anastasia the Deliverer from Potions, both in the faith of Christ and in the sacred letters. When a persecution against the Christians broke out under Diocletian and Maximian, he was arrested and imprisoned; then his disciple wrote to him to pray for her and for her husband. Diocletian, who was in Nicaea, learned that in the prisons of Rome there was a great multitude of Christians who would not deny the faith, because they had Chrysogonus as their inspirer to martyrdom, and he commanded that the others be put to death if they would not deny, and that Chrysogonus be sent to him in chains. Before the tyrant the saint was neither persuaded by flattery nor softened by threats, but preached Christ as the only God and the gods of the idols as a delusion of men. The tyrant grew angry and commanded that he be taken to a deserted place and beheaded, and so the saint received the crown of martyrdom.

life|12-23||Άγιος Πομπίος||He was one of the ten saints who were martyred in Crete in the days of Decius, in the year 250, and he came from Heraklion, together with Euarestus. The saints were handed over by the unbelievers to the governor of Crete, who ordered the executioner to lead them around the altars of the idols and, if they refused to sacrifice, to punish them with various punishments. For thirty whole days the pagans pursued them, mocked them, bound them, stoned them, slapped them, spat on them and dragged them over dung heaps. Then the governor interrogated them and, seeing their steadfast faith, ordered that their limbs be twisted and that after many tortures they be beheaded, and so they received the crowns of martyrdom. Their synaxis is celebrated at the martyrs' church of Saint Stephen, near the place called Plakidia.
life|12-24||Αγία Βασίλα η Μάρτυς||Saint Basilla was a martyr who suffered martyrdom together with Saint Eugenia. According to the text, she completed her struggle by beheading, with the sword.
life|12-24||Άγιος Φίλιππος ο Μάρτυρας||Saint Philip was the father of Saint Eugenia. According to the text, he ended his life as a martyr, killed with a knife.

life|12-24||Άγιοι Πρώτα και Υάκινθος οι Μάρτυρες||The saints Protus and Hyacinth were eunuchs and fellow ascetics of Saint Eugenia. According to the text, they were beheaded with the sword and so received the crown of martyrdom.

life|12-24||Όσιος Νικόλαος «ο από στρατιωτών»||Venerable Nicholas was a soldier in the time of the emperor Nicephorus, around 802, when the army was marching against the Bulgarians. One evening he stayed at an inn, and the innkeeper's daughter, seized by passion, came to him three times to seduce him. He drove her away all three times with stern words, reminding her that the devil was troubling her and that he himself was going to war and bloodshed. // At night he saw a vision: a fearsome judge who showed him the battle, where the Bulgarians were cutting down the Romans. Among the dead bodies there appeared a lush green space the size of a bed, and the judge told him that it was his own place, from which he had escaped because he had conquered licentiousness. He further promised him that a natural death would not overtake him if he served God genuinely. // Nicholas went up a mountain and prayed for the army. The Bulgarians attacked by night the Romans, who were sleeping unguarded, and killed them all, together with the emperor Nicephorus. Then he remembered the vision, thanked God, and went to a monastery where he became a monk. He served God for many years and became very discerning and a great spiritual father.

life|12-24||Όσιος Αντίοχος||According to a note by the editor of the text, this Antiochus seems to be the well-known monk of Palestine, from the lavra of Saint Sabbas, who lived in the time of the emperor Heraclius, around 610. He became famous for his virtue and holiness and mourned the capture and burning of Jerusalem by the Persians and the carrying off of the Precious Cross to Persia. // He wrote a letter to Abbot Eustathius of the monastery of Attalea in Ancyra of Galatia and composed the work Pandectes, in one hundred and thirty chapters, as well as many prayers to the Lord. He also mourned the venerable fathers of the lavra of Saint Sabbas who were killed by the Ishmaelites. According to the text, he also spoke the well-known saying that the proud monk is like a vine that is fruitless and without root, and that the prayer of the humble bends God, while the supplication of the proud provokes him to anger.

life|12-26||Όσιος Ευάρεστος||Venerable Euarestus was born in the province of Galatia of renowned parents, in the time of the iconoclast Leo the Armenian, around 815, and in the days of his successor Michael the Stammerer. He was raised with an education in the sacred letters and was obedient to his parents, dear to his friends, kind to strangers and truly pleasing to all. Since a longing for the monastic life won him over, he went to Constantinople with his father, where they were hosted by their relative Bryennius, later a patrician. // When Bryennius was sent by the empress Theodora as ambassador to the Bulgarians and took Euarestus with him, he met in a place called Skopelos an elderly monk. There he cut his hair and became a monk, and reading a book of Venerable Ephraim the Syrian, he was moved to compunction and tried to live by what it taught. The elder provided him with blessings and letters of recommendation and sent him to the monastery of Stoudios, where he entered zealously into the spiritual struggles. // He ate once a week a little bread of barley flour and vegetable broth, and had his waist and neck bound with two heavy iron chains, which were connected to others on his shoulders and chest. He lived seventy-nine years and died with trust in the Lord, and his relics were buried in the monastery called that of Kokkorovion.

life|12-26||Όσιος Κωνσταντίνος ο εξ Ιουδαίων||Venerable Constantine came from Synada in Phrygia and was a Hebrew by birth. When he was a child and was following his mother, he saw a Christian who was yawning form with his hand the sign of the cross over his mouth, and from then on he imitated it and followed with warm faith the other works of the Christians as well. His face was illumined and, after a fast of a few days, he was taught by God the doctrines of the Christians. According to the text, a Jewish girl who approached him indecently fell dead when he made the sign of the cross, and afterwards he raised her. // Guided by a cloud he reached a monastery called Psoubution. When the abbot had him venerate the cross, the cross inclined of itself onto his head and engraved its image, which remained indelible until his death. He was baptized and took the name Constantine, and on the stone where he stood coming out of the font the prints of his feet were marvelously impressed. // He practiced harsh asceticism and worked at the trade of the Apostle Paul, sewing skins and making tents. According to tradition, when he prayed the place was filled with fragrance, the doors of the church opened by themselves when he arrived, and he discerned the hidden thoughts of the brothers. // Later he went to Olympus, to Myra in Lycia, to Cyprus and to Attalia, where, according to the text, he crossed a deep river on foot. On Olympus he stayed forty days buried up to his waist in a pit and fasting. He received the presbyteral ordination against his will and went to Atroa, continuing his ascetic struggles. He foresaw his death eight years earlier and, when the hour came, he died peacefully, having clearly revealed beforehand everything about his repose.

life|12-27||Άγιος Θεόδωρος ο Α’ Αρχιεπίσκοπος Κωνσταντινουπόλεως||Saint Theodore was born and raised in Constantinople, in the time of the emperor Constantine the Bearded, and was a man of great piety. He was ordained a presbyter of the Great Church and became syncellus and skeuophylax. // When the then patriarch Constantine died, Theodore was pressed by the emperor, the senate and all the hierarchs and was ordained Patriarch of Constantinople. He governed the Church in a manner pleasing to God for two years and three months and withdrew from the throne in 678. Afterwards he spent the rest of his life well and died peacefully, and the Great Church celebrates his memory on a Sunday.

life|12-27||Άγιος Μαυρίκιος ο Μάρτυρας και οι συν αυτώ||The saints Maurice and his companions were soldiers of the emperor, coming from Apamea, in the time of Maximian, around 297. When the emperor passed through the city, they were denounced as Christians, confessed their faith with boldness, had their belts taken from them and were imprisoned. Three days later, because they remained steadfast, they were beaten hard, thrown into the fire and hung on a wooden frame while their sides were torn. // To grieve Maurice more, who was the first among them, Maximian commanded that his son Photinus be beheaded. Then he sent the saints to a marshy place between two rivers and a lake, full of wasps, flies and mosquitoes. There the soldiers stripped them, tied them to stakes and smeared them with honey, and threw before Maurice the body of his son. The saints bravely endured the torment for ten whole days and nights and then, after praying to God, gave up their souls.

life|12-28||Αγία Δόμνα η Μάρτυς||Saint Domna lived in the time of Maximian and came from Nicomedia. She was a priestess in the temple of the palace, which was called the Dodekatheon because it held idols of twelve gods. She found the Acts of the Apostles and the epistles of Paul, was enlightened and was baptized by Cyril, bishop of Nicomedia, together with the eunuch Indes. The salary she received from the palace she distributed to the poor, and when the chief eunuch discovered that she was a Christian, she pretended to be mad. She was sent to the bishop of the Christians to be cured and stayed in an ascetic community of virgins. // When Maximian returned victorious from the campaign against the Ethiopians and asked for her, Domna left secretly in men's clothing, while he was destroying the ascetic communities. Hearing of the martyrdom of the twenty thousand Christians, she rejoiced and wished to imitate them. She went down to the sea and, together with clergy, took the relics of the saints Indes, Gorgonius and Peter, which fishermen had washed ashore, and hid them within the walls of Nicomedia. She was denounced to Maximian and, by his order, was beheaded and afterwards her body was burned.

life|12-29||Όσιος Μάρκελλος||Venerable Marcellus lived in the time of the emperor Leo the Great and of Patriarch Gennadius, and came from Apamea in Syria Secunda, from a glorious and distinguished family. He received a complete education in letters and, leaving his studies and his family, went to Ephesus, where he was hosted and practiced asceticism in one of the monasteries. // Then he went to Saint Alexander at the monastery of the Akoimetoi, having heard of his divine and lofty way of life, and there, through his daily progress in virtue, he surpassed all the brothers. After the repose of Alexander and of his successor Jacob he became abbot of the same monastery. He received power and grace from God and performed many miracles, and in the end fell asleep peacefully.

life|12-29||Όσιος Θαδδαίος ο Ομολογητής||Venerable Thaddaeus was a barbarian by race and at first a slave of the most venerable Theodore, who took the monastery of Stoudios with imperial authority and made it a coenobium. Later he was freed and became a monk at the monastery of Stoudios, and everyone loved him for his God-pleasing conduct: he occupied himself with fasting and vigils, guarded his tongue, paid attention to the divine words and kept obedience and non-possession. // In the time of the iconoclast emperors Michael the Stammerer and Theophilus, many pious bishops and abbots were imprisoned or exiled. Thaddaeus went with his abbot to the palace and, out of divine zeal, rebuked the impious emperor before the officials. The emperor commanded that the icon of the Savior be brought there, thrown on the ground, and that the venerable man be stood upon it, held by strong men, so that he would trample it even against his will. The venerable man answered that this was a device of the emperor's cunning and that he venerates the icon of Christ and prefers to die for it. // The tyrant grew angry, especially because a coarse Scythian by race insulted him, and they beat him with thick rods so much that everyone thought he had died. They dragged him by the feet through the marketplace and threw him near the wall, beside the spring. Thaddaeus endured all this bravely and gladly, lived three days longer and then went to the Lord.

life|12-30||Οσία Θεοδώρα η από Καισαρίδος||Venerable Theodora lived in the time of Leo the Isaurian, father of Constantine Copronymus, and came from a distinguished and illustrious family. She was the daughter of the patrician Theophilus and of Theodora, who was barren for many years and entreated God and the Theotokos, and received the child through Saint Anna. When she grew up, she was dedicated to the monastery of Saint Anna, called Phigidion. // Leo the Isaurian, who was seeking a bride for his son, took her by force from the monastery and brought her to Constantinople, where everything was prepared for the wedding. Suddenly, however, armies of Scythians came into Europe, the bridegroom was sent to face them and was killed in the first attack. Then Theodora took gold, silver, pearls and precious garments, left the palace secretly by ship and returned to her monastery. // When her flight was discovered, Leo's second son went to find her, saw her as a nun with shorn hair in old tattered clothes and did not trouble her. From then on Theodora practiced harsh asceticism: she ate a piece of bread every two or three days, wore a single hair garment, slept on stones and wore irons that wounded her body. Thus she struggled for many years, distinguished herself in every virtue and went to the ageless life.

life|12-30||Άγιος Φιλέταιρος||Saint Philetaerus was born and raised in Nicomedia, the son of a prefect and a Christian, and was denounced by pagans to Diocletian, in 286. He was tall and handsome, with hair and beard that shone like gold, and the emperor, dazzled, flattered him, seeking to draw him away from the faith. When Diocletian blasphemed Christ, the saint prayed and a terrible thunder and earthquake followed. They threw him into a fiery furnace, but according to the text he extinguished the fire by prayer and came out unharmed, and the emperor set him free. // Under Maximian he confessed Christ again. They beat him with rods, hung him up and tore him, gave him to the beasts, which became tame at his feet, and by his prayer the idols were shattered. When the executioners who were to behead him were left with a paralyzed hand, they bound him with irons and exiled him to Proconnesus. In exile, and all along the road, he performed miracles: he drove out demons, cleansed lepers, healed illnesses and overthrew idols. In Nicaea, as soon as he approached a famous temple, all the idols fell and were shattered, and many believed, among them the count of the city and six of his soldiers. // At Sigriane in Media, led by an angel, he met his fellow martyr Eubiotus and they went up together to his cell. After seven days Philetaerus fell asleep there, giving up his soul to Christ. The count and the six soldiers died peacefully eleven days later and were buried beside his tomb.

life|12-31||Όσιος Γελάσιος||According to the text, Venerable Gelasius had a book containing the Old and the New Testament, worth eighteen coins, which was kept in the church for the brothers to read. A stranger brother stole it, and Gelasius realized it but did not pursue him. The thief went to sell it in the city, and whoever wished to buy it showed it to Abba Gelasius himself, who pretended to know nothing and told the buyer that it was good and that he should take it at the price asked. // When the buyer told the thief that he had shown it to the elder, the thief asked whether he had said nothing else, and learned that he had not. Moved by the elder's forbearance, he no longer sold the book but took it to Gelasius and begged him to accept it. The venerable man did not want to, but when the other said that he would find no peace, he said that since he had no peace he would take it. Thus the thief was benefited by the elder's deed and remained a brother until the end of his life.

life|02-01||Αγία Περπέτουα η Μάρτυς και οι συν αυτή||Saint Perpetua suffered a martyr's death in Carthage, at the beginning of the 3rd century, under the emperor Septimius Severus. She was a young woman with an infant and, together with the martyrs with her, was condemned to be thrown to the beasts of the amphitheater. // According to tradition, she herself recorded in prison what she experienced, a text that has been preserved as a precious martyrdom account of the ancient Church. The Church honors her memory on the 1st of February.

life|02-07||Όσιος Λουκάς ο εν Στειρίω της Ελλάδος||Venerable Luke of Stiris in Greece is the well-known Venerable Luke, who practiced asceticism at Stiris in Phocis, in Central Greece, in the 10th century. According to tradition, he lived a strictly ascetic life and was granted the gifts of foresight and of working miracles. // The renowned monastery of Venerable Luke near Distomo is dedicated to his name. The Church honors him on the 7th of February.

life|04-03||Όσιος Ιωσήφ ο Υμνογράφος||Venerable Joseph the Hymnographer was born in Sicily at the beginning of the 9th century and lived as a monk in the years of iconoclasm. He became one of the best-known poets of ecclesiastical hymnography: he wrote a multitude of canons and hymns, many of which are still sung in the services of the Menaion. He fell asleep around 886, and the Church honors his memory on the 3rd of April.

life|04-10||Αγία Όλδα η Προφήτης||Huldah was a prophetess of the Old Testament, who lived in Jerusalem in the days of King Josiah. When the book of the Law was found in the Temple, the king sent to ask her for the word of God. Huldah prophesied that calamity would come upon Jerusalem because of the people's unfaithfulness, but that Josiah, because he humbled himself before God, would die in peace. The account is found in 4 Kingdoms and in 2 Chronicles, and the Church honors her memory on the 10th of April.

life|04-18||Άγιος Κύριλλος ο ΣΤ’ ο Ιερομάρτυρας||Cyril VI served as Ecumenical Patriarch at the beginning of the 19th century and, after his resignation, lived in exile. In the years of the Greek Revolution of 1821 the Ottomans put him to death, and for this reason the Church honors him as a hieromartyr. His memory is celebrated on the 18th of April.

life|04-29||Άγιοι Ιάσονας και Σωσίπατρος οι Απόστολοι||According to tradition, Jason and Sosipater are numbered among the Seventy Apostles and were collaborators of the Apostle Paul. Jason hosted Paul in Thessaloniki (Acts 17), while Sosipater is mentioned as a kinsman of Paul in the Epistle to the Romans (16:21). According to tradition, Jason became bishop of Tarsus and Sosipater of Iconium, and they preached the Gospel in Corfu, where they also fell asleep. The Church honors their memory on the 29th of April.

life|05-05||Άγιος Εφραίμ ο Ιερομάρτυρας ο εν Νέα Μάκρη Αττικής||Saint Ephraim was a clergyman who was martyred, according to tradition, in the years of Turkish rule, in the area of Nea Makri in Attica. // His veneration spread widely in the 20th century, after the discovery of his relics, and the Church honors his memory on the 5th of May.

life|05-11||Άγιοι Κλήμης, Σάββας, Αγγελάριος, Γοράσδος και Ναούμ οι Θαυματουργοί Ισαπόστολοι||According to tradition, these saints were disciples of the saints Cyril and Methodius, the enlighteners of the Slavs, and labored for the spread of the Christian faith and of the Slavonic written word in the Slavic world, chiefly in the Balkans, in the 9th and 10th centuries. // The Church honors them as equal-to-the-apostles on the 11th of May.

life|05-12||Όσιος Νεκτάριος της Όπτινα||Venerable Nectarius of Optina was a Russian monk and elder of the monastery of Optina, known for its spiritual tradition, and he died at the beginning of the 20th century, after the dissolution of the monastery by the new authorities. // Many had recourse to the elder for counsel, and the Church honors him as a venerable father on the 12th of May.

life|05-16||Άγιος Γεώργιος ο Ομολογητής Επίσκοπος Μυτιλήνης||Saint George was bishop of Mytilene and is honored as a confessor of the faith, according to tradition for defending the veneration of the holy icons in the time of iconoclasm. // The Church honors his memory on the 16th of May.

life|05-23||Άγιος Δεσιδέριος ο Ιερομάρτυρας Επίσκοπος Βιέννης||Saint Desiderius was bishop of Vienne in Gaul (present-day France) at the beginning of the 7th century. According to tradition, he was martyred because he defended the truth and Christian morals against the powerful of his time. // The Church honors his memory on the 23rd of May.

life|05-24||Άγιοι 318 Πατέρες της Α’ Οικουμενικής Συνόδου||The 318 holy Fathers were the bishops who gathered in 325 at Nicaea in Bithynia, under the emperor Constantine the Great, in the First Ecumenical Council. // The Council condemned the heresy of Arius, who taught that the Son is a creature, set forth the consubstantiality of the Son with the Father and established the first articles of the Creed. // The Church honors their memory on the 24th of May.

life|05-27||Άγιος Φίλιππος Α’ Μητροπολίτης Μόσχας||Saint Philip was Metropolitan of Moscow in the 16th century, under Ivan the Terrible. He opposed with boldness the violence and arbitrary acts of the time and, according to tradition, was put to death in 1569 by order of the ruler. // The Church honors him as a hierarch and martyr for the truth on the 27th of May.

life|05-29||Άγιος Αλέξανδρος Πατριάρχης Αλεξανδρείας||Saint Alexander was Patriarch of Alexandria at the beginning of the 4th century. He confronted the heresy of Arius, who was a presbyter of his Church, and took part in the First Ecumenical Council of Nicaea in 325, where Arianism was condemned. // Athanasius the Great was ordained as his successor, and the Church honors Alexander as a champion of the right faith.

life|05-29||Άγιος Ανδρέας ο Νεομάρτυρας ο Αργέντης||Saint Andrew came from Chios and was martyred there in 1465, in the first years after the Fall of Constantinople, because he refused to change his faith. // The Church honors him as a new martyr on the 29th of May.

life|05-29||Άγιος Λουκάς Αρχιεπίσκοπος Κριμαίας||Saint Luke was born in 1877 in Crimea and in the world was named Valentin Voino-Yasenetsky. He was a distinguished surgeon and author of medical works and at the same time a clergyman, and later Archbishop of Simferopol and Crimea. // He endured imprisonments and exiles under the Soviet regime and died in 1961. The Church honors him as a saint and as a physician of souls and bodies.

life|06-02||Άγιος Ιωάννης ο Μεγαλομάρτυρας ο Νέος ο Τραπεζούντιος||Saint John the New was a merchant from Trebizond and lived, according to tradition, in the 14th century in Asprokastro (Cetatea Albă), at the mouth of the Dniester. He was denounced as a Christian and, because he refused to renounce his faith, suffered a martyr's death. // His relics were later transferred to Suceava in Moldavia, where he is especially venerated, and the Church celebrates his memory on the 2nd of June.

life|06-03||Άγιος Γρηγόριος ο Ιερομάρτυρας Μητροπολίτης Δέρκων||Saint Gregory was Metropolitan of Derkoi and lived in the years of Ottoman rule. In 1821, in the climate of reprisals that followed the outbreak of the Greek Revolution, he was put to death by the Ottoman authorities. // The Church honors him as a hieromartyr.

life|06-03||Άγιος Δωρόθεος ο Ιερομάρτυρας Μητροπολίτης Αδριανουπόλεως||Saint Dorotheus was Metropolitan of Adrianople. In 1821, in the climate of reprisals that followed the outbreak of the Greek Revolution, he was put to death by the Ottoman authorities, and the Church honors him as a hieromartyr.

life|06-03||Άγιος Ιωσήφ ο Ιερομάρτυρας Μητροπολίτης Θεσσαλονίκης||Saint Joseph was Metropolitan of Thessaloniki in the years of Ottoman rule. In 1821, in the climate of reprisals after the outbreak of the Greek Revolution, he was put to death by the Ottoman authorities, and the Church honors him as a hieromartyr.

life|06-04||Αγίες Μάρθα και Μαρία αδελφές του Αγίου Λαζάρου||Martha and Mary were sisters of Lazarus and lived in Bethany. The Gospel relates that they received the Lord in their house, where Martha served with eagerness, while Mary sat at the feet of Jesus listening to his word. // They believed in Christ and witnessed the resurrection of their brother Lazarus. The Church honors the two sisters as models of hospitality and of faith.

life|06-04||Άγιος Ανδρόνικος ο Ιερομάρτυρας Αρχιεπίσκοπος Περμίας||Saint Andronicus was Archbishop of Perm in Russia. During the persecution by the Bolsheviks, in 1918, he was arrested and put to death, and the Church honors him as a hieromartyr and one of the New Martyrs of Russia.

life|06-08||Άγιος Κλοδούλφος Επίσκοπος Μέτζ||Saint Chlodulf was bishop of Metz in France in the 7th century. He was the son of Saint Arnulf, bishop of the same city, and continued the pastoral work of his father. // The Church commemorates him on the 8th of June.

life|06-08||Άγιος Μεδάρδος ο Θαυματουργός Επίσκοπος Νογυόν Γαλλίας||Saint Medard was born in northern France in the 5th century and served as bishop of Noyon and Tournai in the days of the Merovingians. He was renowned for his charity, piety and miracles and fell asleep around the middle of the 6th century. // The Church honors him on the 8th of June.

life|06-10||Άγιος Ιωάννης Μητροπολίτης Τομπόλσκ και πάσης Σιβηρίας||Saint John, Metropolitan of Tobolsk and of all Siberia, lived at the end of the 17th and the beginning of the 18th century and carried out missionary and pastoral work in Siberia. He fell asleep in 1715, and the Russian Church honors him as a saint.

life|06-10||Άγιος Φιλόθεος Μητροπολίτης Τομπόλσκ Ρωσίας||Saint Philotheus, Metropolitan of Tobolsk, lived at the end of the 17th and the beginning of the 18th century. He developed great missionary activity in Siberia and baptized many of the natives. He fell asleep in 1727, and the Russian Church honors him as a saint.

life|06-12||Άγιος Ιωάννης ο Μεγαλομάρτυρας ο Νέος εκ Τραπεζούντος και εν Ασπροκάστρω||Saint John the New, who came from Trebizond, was according to tradition a merchant who was martyred at Asprokastro (Cetatea Albă) in Moldavia, in the 14th century, because he did not deny Christ. // His relics are kept at Suceava, where the people honor him with reverence as the protector of the region.

life|06-13||Οσία Αλέξανδρα η Ηγουμένη και θεμελιώτρια της Μονής Ντιβέεβο||Venerable Alexandra was a noble widow who became a nun and founded the monastery of Diveyevo in Russia in the 18th century. The monastery later grew under the spiritual care of Venerable Seraphim of Sarov. The Church honors the Venerable one as abbess and founder of the monastery.

life|06-14||Άγιος Κύριλλος ο Ιερομάρτυρας Επίσκοπος Γορτύνης||Saint Cyril was bishop of Gortyna in Crete in the 3rd century. According to tradition, in the persecutions of the emperor Decius he confessed Christ with courage and was martyred. // The Cretans honor him as one of the ancient saints of the island, and the Church celebrates his memory on the 14th of June.

life|06-15||Άγιοι Αχαϊκός, Στεφανάς και Φουρτουνάτος οι Απόστολοι εκ των Εβδομήκοντα||Achaicus, Stephanas and Fortunatus are mentioned by the Apostle Paul in the first epistle to the Corinthians, where they are praised because they made up for the absence of the Corinthians in his company and comforted him. // Tradition numbers them among the seventy Apostles and regards them as collaborators of Paul in Corinth. The Church honors their memory on the 15th of June.

life|06-15||Άγιος Λάζαρος ο Μάρτυρας πρίγκιπας των Σέρβων||Saint Lazar was ruler of the Serbs in the 14th century. He resisted the advance of the Ottomans and fell in the battle of Kosovo in 1389, where, according to tradition, he preferred death for the faith and the fatherland to submission. // The Serbian Church honors him as a holy martyr, and his relics were kept at Ravanica.

life|06-15||Άγιος Μιχαήλ ο πρώτος Μητροπολίτης Κιέβου και πάσης Ρωσίας||Saint Michael was the first Metropolitan of Kiev and of all Rus, sent from Constantinople in the days of Prince Vladimir, after the Christianization of the Rus, around 988. According to tradition he organized the first ecclesiastical structures of the country. // The Church honors him on the 15th of June.

life|06-17||Όσιος Υπάτιος ο εν Ρουφιαναίς||Venerable Hypatius was abbot of a monastery at Rufinianae, near Chalcedon, in the 5th century. He had a reputation as an ascetic and wonderworker and, according to tradition, supported the Orthodox faith in the time of the dispute over Nestorius. // The Church honors him as a venerable father on the 17th of June.

life|06-19||Άγιος Ασύγκριτος ο Ιερομάρτυρας||Saint Asyncritus is mentioned by the Apostle Paul in the epistle to the Romans. According to tradition he is numbered among the seventy Apostles and was a bishop, who was martyred for his faith in Christ. // The Church honors him as a hieromartyr on the 19th of June.

life|06-20||Άγιος Σιλβέριος ο Ιερομάρτυρας Επίσκοπος Ρώμης||Saint Silverius was bishop of Rome in the days of the emperor Justinian (536-537). He was driven from his throne amid the political and ecclesiastical disputes of the time and exiled to an island in the Tyrrhenian Sea, where he died of hardships. // The Church honors him as a hieromartyr for his sufferings and for his steadfastness.

life|06-21||Άγιος Λουαρσάβος ο Μάρτυρας βασιλέας της Γεωργίας||Saint Luarsab II was king of Kartli, in Eastern Georgia, at the beginning of the 17th century. He was taken captive by the Persian shah Abbas and, according to tradition, was imprisoned and put to death in 1622, because he refused to change his faith. // The Church of Georgia honors him as a martyr.

life|06-24||Άγιος Νικήτας Επίσκοπος Ρεμεσιάνας της Ρουμανίας||Saint Niketas was bishop of Remesiana, a city in present-day Serbia, at the end of the 4th and the beginning of the 5th century. He carried out missionary activity among the peoples of the Danube region, especially the Dacians, and is known for his theological and hymnographic writings. // The Church celebrates his memory on the 24th of June.

life|06-24||Γενέσιον του Τιμίου ενδόξου Προφήτου, Προδρόμου και Βαπτιστού Ιωάννου||John the Forerunner was born to the priest Zechariah and Elizabeth, in the old age of his parents, after an angelic announcement, as the Gospel according to Luke relates. The Lord named him the greatest among those born of women. // He preached repentance in the wilderness of the Jordan, baptized Jesus and prepared the work of the Messiah. The Church celebrates his birth on the 24th of June, six months before Christmas.

life|06-26||Άγιος Διονύσιος Αρχιεπίσκοπος Σουζδαλίας||Saint Dionysius lived in the 14th century and served as Archbishop of Suzdal. He served in the difficult years of Russian history and is honored as a saint of the Russian Church. His memory is celebrated on the 26th of June.

life|06-30||Όσιος Γεώργιος ο Αγιορείτης εξ Ιβηρίας||Venerable George was born in 1009 in Georgia and became a monk at the Iviron Monastery on Mount Athos, of which he became abbot. He distinguished himself as a translator, having translated into Georgian many Greek patristic and liturgical texts. // He fell asleep in 1065, according to tradition in Constantinople, and is honored as one of the great saints of the Georgians.

life|06-30||Όσιος Μαρτιάλιος Επίσκοπος Λιμόζ Γαλλίας||Saint Martial is regarded as the first bishop of Limoges in France. According to the tradition of Gregory of Tours, he came from Rome in the middle of the 3rd century, as one of the seven bishops sent to preach the Gospel in Gaul. // His memory is especially honored at Limoges.

life|07-01||Άγιοι Ιούλιος, Ααρών οι Μάρτυρες και οι συν αυτοίς Μαρτυρήσαντες εν Βρεττανία||The saints Julius and Aaron were martyred in Britain, according to tradition in the city of Caerleon in Wales, in the time of the persecutions of Diocletian, at the beginning of the 4th century. Together with them is honored also the number of the other Christians who gave their witness in the same place. // The Church honors them as the first known martyrs of Britain, together with Saint Alban.

life|07-01||Άγιος Επάρχιος ο Έγκλειστος ο εν Γαλατία||Saint Eparchius lived in the 6th century in Gaul, in the region of Angoulême, and is also known by the name Cybard. According to tradition he lived as an enclosed ascetic in a cell, devoted to prayer, and disciples gathered around him. // The Church honors him as a venerable ascetic of the West.

life|07-03||Άγιος Ανατόλιος ο Επίσκοπος Λαοδικείας||Saint Anatolius was born in Alexandria in the 3rd century and distinguished himself by his education in philosophy and the natural sciences. He was ordained bishop of Laodicea in Syria, where he shepherded his flock with prudence and wrote treatises. // The Church honors him as a God-enlightened shepherd of his time.

life|07-04||Οσία Μάρθα η μητέρα του Αγίου Συμεών του εν τω Θαυμαστώ όρει ασκήσας||Venerable Martha was the mother of Saint Symeon the Younger, who practiced asceticism on the Wondrous Mountain near Antioch, in the 6th century. According to tradition, after her life as a mother she herself also followed the monastic life, near her son. // The Church commemorates her as a venerable mother who is honored together with her son.

life|07-05||Όσιος Προκόπιος του Σάζαβα||Venerable Procopius was born in Bohemia around 970 and became a priest and monk. He founded the monastery of Sázava in Bohemia, where they celebrated also in the Slavonic language. He died in 1053. // The Church honors him as a venerable father and abbot of Bohemia.

life|07-06||Όσιος Δανιήλ ο Εικονογράφος||Venerable Daniel the icon painter lived in Russia at the end of the 14th and the beginning of the 15th century. He was a monk and a painter of icons and worked with the monk and icon painter Andrei Rublev in the painting of churches. He died around 1428. // The Church honors him as a venerable father who served God through the art of iconography.

life|07-07||Άγιος Παλλάδιος ο Επίσκοπος Ιρλανδίας||Saint Palladius was a deacon in Rome. In 431 Pope Celestine sent him as the first bishop to the Irish who already believed in Christ. // His work is connected with the beginnings of the organized Church in Ireland, before the wider mission of Saint Patrick.

life|07-07||Άγιος Φήλιξ ο Επίσκοπος Νάντης||Saint Felix lived in Gaul in the 6th century and was ordained bishop of Nantes, around 549. He died in 582 and the Church honors him as a shepherd who cared for his flock. // The sources of the West remember him for his building care for the church of the city.

life|07-07||Άγιος Χέδδας ο Επίσκοπος Δυτικής Σαξωνίας||Saint Hædde was bishop of the West Saxons in England. He took up the office at the end of the 7th century and died in 705. // Bede the Venerable mentions him as a man of prudence and piety, and the Church honors him as a shepherd of Britain.

life|07-10||Αγίες Ρουφίνη και Σεκούνδη οι Μάρτυρες||The saints Rufina and Secunda were sisters and, according to tradition, were martyred in Rome in the 3rd century, in the persecutions of the time, because they did not deny Christ. // The Church honors them as virgin martyrs, and their memory is among the oldest in Rome.

life|07-12||Άγιοι Θεόδωρος και Ιωάννης ο υιός του οι Πρωτομάρτυρες Κιέβου||Theodore and his son John were Varangian Christians who lived in Kiev. In 983, when the crowd demanded John as a sacrifice to the pagan gods, his father refused to hand him over and the mob killed them both. // They are regarded as the first martyrs of Russia, a few years before the Christianization of the people.

life|07-12||Άγιος Παυλίνος ο Ιερομάρτυρας ο Επίσκοπος Λούκκας και οι συν αυτώ μαρτυρήσαντες||According to tradition, Saint Paulinus lived in the 1st century and was a disciple of the Apostle Peter, who sent him to preach the Gospel in Lucca in Tuscany. He became the first bishop of the city and was martyred there together with other Christians. // The Church honors him as a hieromartyr.

life|07-12||Άγιος Σεραπίων ο Επίσκοπος Βλαντιμίρ||Saint Serapion was bishop of Vladimir in Russia in the 13th century, during the period of the Mongol invasions, and died in 1275. Tradition remembers him for his teaching and for his support of the people in the trial of the age. // The Church honors him as a holy shepherd.

life|07-13||Αγία Γολινδούχ η Περσίδα πού μετονομάσθηκε Μαρία||Saint Golinduch was born in Persia into a family of magi and, after a vision, believed in Christ and was baptized with the name Maria. Because of her faith she was imprisoned and put to death in 591 under King Chosroes II. // The Church honors her as a martyr who gave her confession with courage.

life|07-15||Άγιος Αθανάσιος ο Επίσκοπος Νεαπόλεως||Saint Athanasius was bishop of Neapolis, present-day Naples, in the middle of the 9th century. He died in 872. // The Church honors him as a shepherd of the city, who lived in a time of difficult raids.

life|07-16||Αγία Ιουλία η Μάρτυς η εν Κορσική||According to tradition, Saint Julia came from Carthage and was taken as a slave to Corsica, where she was tortured and martyred because she did not deny Christ. // The Church honors her as a martyr and protectress of the island.

life|07-17||Αγίες Βεστία, Δονάτα, Σεκούνδη, Βερονίκη και Ιανουαρία οι Μάρτυρες οι εν Σίλη Καρθαγένης||The saints Vestia, Donata, Secunda, Veronica and Januaria were Christians from Scilli in the region of Carthage, in North Africa. They were condemned and beheaded on the 17th of July in the year 180 by the proconsul Saturninus, because they did not deny Christ. // Together with their companions, they are among the well-known martyrs of Scilli, whom the records of their trial mention.

life|07-17||Άγιοι Κύριλλος και Μεθόδιος οι Ισαπόστολοι και Θαυματουργοί||The saints Cyril and Methodius were brothers from Thessaloniki, of the 9th century. Cyril created the Slavonic alphabet and, together with Methodius, they translated into the Slavonic language the Scripture and the services of the Church, in their mission to Moravia. // The Church honors them as equal-to-the-apostles and enlighteners of the Slavs.

life|07-17||Άγιοι Σπεράτος, Νάρταλος, Κυττίνος, Βεντούριος, Λετάντιος, Φήλιξ και Ακουϊλίνος οι Μάρτυρες εν Σίλη Καρθαγένης||The saints Speratus, Nartzalus, Cittinus, Veturius, Laetantius, Felix and Aquilinus were Christians from Scilli in the region of Carthage. They were arrested under the emperor Marcus Aurelius and, because they did not deny Christ, were beheaded on the 17th of July in the year 180 by the proconsul Saturninus. // The records of their trial are among the oldest Christian texts of Africa in Latin.

life|07-21||Άγιος Βίκτωρ ο Μάρτυρας ο εν Μασσαλία αθλήσας και οι συν αυτών μαρτυρίσαντες||Saint Victor served in the Roman army and, according to tradition, was martyred at Marseilles around 290, under Maximian, because he did not deny Christ. Together with him his fellow soldiers were also martyred. // The Church honors him as a martyr, and his memory is preserved in Gaul.

life|07-25||Κοίμησις της Αγίας Άννης Μητρός της Υπεραγίας Θεοτόκου||According to the tradition preserved in the Protoevangelium of James, Saint Anna was the wife of Joachim and the mother of the Most Holy Theotokos. Their marriage was childless for many years, until by divine intervention Mary was born. // The Church honors her dormition on the 25th of July and regards her as a model of patience and faith.

life|07-26||Όσιος Μωϋσής ο Ούγγρος||Venerable Moses the Hungarian was Hungarian by origin and a servant of Saint Boris in Kiev. After the murder of Boris in 1015 he was taken captive and suffered much, but he took refuge in Kiev and became a monk at the Kiev Caves Lavra. He died around 1043. // The Church honors him as a venerable father who endured trials with patience.

life|07-27||Άγιος Εκκλέσιος ο Επίσκοπος Ραβέννας||Saint Ecclesius was bishop of Ravenna from 521 to 532, in the time of the Ostrogoths. He began the building of the church of Saint Vitalis, which was completed after his death. // The Church honors him as a shepherd who took care for the rebuilding of the city.

life|07-27||Οσία Ανθούσα η Ομολογήτρια||Venerable Anthusa was abbess of the monastery of Mantineon and lived in the 8th century, in the period of iconoclasm. According to tradition, she defended the holy icons and suffered exiles and persecutions from the emperor Constantine V. // The Church honors her as a confessor of the faith.

life|07-28||Άγιος Πιτιρίμ ο Θαυματουργός ο Επίσκοπος Ταμπώφ||Saint Pitirim lived in Russia in the 17th century and was bishop of Tambov. He died in 1698, and tradition remembers him for his charitable work and for miracles attributed to his intercessions. // The Church honors him as a wonderworking shepherd.

life|07-28||Οσία Ειρήνη εκ Καππαδοκίας κειμένη εν τή μονή Χρυσοβαλάντου||Venerable Irene came from Cappadocia and lived in the 9th century in Constantinople, where she became abbess of the monastery of Chrysobalanton. According to tradition, she was distinguished for her asceticism and her gifts. // The Church honors her as a venerable mother.

life|07-30||Αγία Ιουλίττη η Μάρτυς η εκ Καισαρείας||Saint Julitta lived in Caesarea in Cappadocia and, according to tradition, was a widow with property. When she faced injustice from a ruler, she confessed her faith in Christ and was martyred under Diocletian, around 303. // The Church honors her as a martyr, and Saint Basil the Great refers to her memory.

life|08-02||Άγιος Βασίλειος ο διά Χριστόν Σαλός και θαυματουργός εν Μόσχα (Ρώσος)||Saint Basil was a Russian ascetic who lived in Moscow in the 16th century and followed the difficult path of foolishness for Christ, that is, of deliberate contempt for the world out of love for Christ. The people honored him as a wonderworker. The famous church on Red Square in Moscow has taken his name. The Church honors him on the 2nd of August.

life|09-02||Άγιοι Ελεάζαρ και Φινεές οι Δίκαιοι Ιερείς||The saints Eleazar and Phinehas are righteous priests of the Old Testament, the son and grandson of Aaron respectively, according to Scripture. Eleazar succeeded Aaron in the priesthood and Phinehas became known for his zeal for God and for His people. The Church honors their memory on the 2nd of September.

life|09-02||Άγιος Ιουλιανός ο Μάρτυρας||Saint Julian is a Martyr of Christ, whom the Church honors on the 2nd of September. Because there are many saints with the same name, it cannot be determined with certainty from our sources who exactly he is and what he did, so no details are given.

life|09-02||Άγιος Φίλιππος (ή Θεόδοτος ή Θεόδωρος) ο Μάρτυρας||Saint Philip, who in some sources is also called Theodotus or Theodore, is a Martyr of the Church with a commemoration on the 2nd of September. The difference in names shows that the information about him is not firm, and for this reason no further details are given.

life|09-03||Άγιος Ιωάννης ο διά Χριστόν Σαλός του Ρώστωφ||Saint John the Fool for Christ of Rostov is a Russian saint who chose the form of asceticism of "foolishness," that is, of a voluntary humble and apparently irrational life out of love for Christ. According to tradition he lived in Rostov. The Church honors him on the 3rd of September.

life|09-07||Άγιοι Εύοδος και Ονησιφόρος οι Απόστολοι||The saints Evodus and Onesiphorus are honored as Apostles, among those whom tradition mentions in the circle of the seventy. Onesiphorus is mentioned by the Apostle Paul in the Second Epistle to Timothy for his hospitality and his love. According to tradition Evodus served as bishop of Antioch. Their memory is celebrated on the 7th of September.

life|09-10||Αγία Πουλχερία η βασίλισσα||Saint Pulcheria the empress was the empress of Byzantium in the 5th century, sister of Theodosius II, who governed the state with piety. Together with her husband Marcian she supported the Church and the Fourth Ecumenical Council of Chalcedon in 451. Her memory is celebrated on the 10th of September.

life|09-15||Άγιος Βησσαρίων Αρχιεπίσκοπος Λαρίσης||Saint Bessarion, Archbishop of Larissa, lived in the 16th century and is honored as a hierarch and founder of the Holy Monastery of Dousiko in Thessaly. Tradition also connects him with the stone bridge of Pyli. He died in 1540 and the Church honors his memory on the 15th of September.

life|09-26||Μετάστασις Αγίου Ιωάννου του Θεολόγου||Saint John the Theologian is the Apostle and Evangelist, the beloved disciple of the Lord, who wrote the Gospel, three epistles and, according to tradition, the Apocalypse on Patmos. According to tradition he lived his last years in Ephesus and died at a very advanced age. On the 26th of September the Church celebrates his repose.

life|10-02||Άγιος Θεόδωρος ο Μεγαλομάρτυρας ο Γαβράς||Theodore Gabras was a Byzantine governor of the region of Trebizond at the end of the 11th century and fought the Seljuk Turks who threatened Pontus. // According to tradition, he died in captivity without renouncing his faith, and for this reason the Church honors him as a great martyr on the 2nd of October, especially in Pontus.

life|10-04||Άγιος Edwin (Άγγλος)||Edwin was king of Northumbria in England in the 7th century. He was baptized a Christian in 627 by Bishop Paulinus and supported the work of evangelizing his people. // He was killed in battle in 633, and the Church honors him as a saint on the 4th of October.

life|10-05||Άγιοι Πέτρος, Αλέξιος και Ιωνάς οι Θαυματουργοί Μητροπολίτες Μόσχας και πάσης Ρωσίας||Peter († 1326), Alexis († 1378) and Jonah († 1461) served as metropolitans of Moscow and of all Rus. // Peter transferred the seat of the metropolis from Vladimir to Moscow, Alexis governed the Church and supported the young prince Dimitri, and Jonah led the Russian Church in the years before its autocephaly. The Russian Church honors them as wonderworking saints and commemorates them on the 5th of October.

life|10-09||Όσιοι Ανδρόνικος και Αθανασία η συμβία του||Andronicus and Athanasia were a married couple who lived in Alexandria. // According to tradition, after they lost their children, they distributed their property and devoted their lives to the monastic life, and the Church honors them as venerable ones on the 9th of October.

life|10-10||Άγιος Ανδρέας ο διά Χριστόν Σαλός εκ Τότμα (Ρώσος)||Andrew lived in Totma in northern Russia in the 17th century and practiced asceticism as a fool for Christ, that is, he deliberately adopted the appearance of madness for the sake of humility. // The Russian Church honors him as a saint on the 10th of October.

life|10-11||Άγιος Φιλόθεος ο Κόκκινος, Πατριάρχης Κωνσταντινούπολης||Philotheus Kokkinos lived in the 14th century and was a monk and abbot at the Great Lavra on Mount Athos, metropolitan of Heraclea and twice Patriarch of Constantinople (1353-1354 and 1364-1376). // He was a fervent supporter of hesychasm and of Gregory Palamas, whose life he wrote, and he wrote other ecclesiastical works as well. The Church honors him as a saint on the 11th of October.

life|10-11||Όσιος Θεοφάνης ο Ομολογητής ο Γραπτός, Επίσκοπος Νίκαιας||Theophanes the Inscribed was a monk from Palestine, brother of Theodore the Inscribed, and suffered persecutions together with him during iconoclasm. Under the emperor Theophilus the two brothers confessed their faith and verses were engraved on their faces, whence the epithet "Inscribed." // Later he became bishop of Nicaea, died around 845 and is also known as a hymnographer. The Church honors him as a venerable father and confessor on the 11th of October.

life|10-15||Άγιος Λουκιανός ο Ιερομάρτυρας Πρεσβύτερος της Εκκλησίας της Αντιοχείας||Lucian was a presbyter and scholar in Antioch, known for his careful correction of the texts of the Holy Scripture and for his school. // During the persecution of Maximinus Daia he was taken to Nicomedia, where, after confessing his faith, he was martyred in 312. The Church honors him as a hieromartyr on the 15th of October.

life|10-19||Αγία Frideswide (Αγγλίδα)||Frideswide was an English abbess of the 8th century († around 727) and founder of a monastery in Oxford, where she is honored as protectress of the city and of the university. // The tradition about her life also contains many legendary elements, which are not set out here. The Church commemorates her on the 19th of October.

life|10-19||Άγιος Σαδώθ (ή Σαδώκ ή Σαδώχ) ο Επίσκοπος και οι 120 Μάρτυρες από την Περσία||Sadoth was a bishop in Persia and was martyred in the 4th century, during the persecution of the Christians by King Shapur II, together with about 120 other Christians. // The Church honors them as martyrs on the 19th of October.

life|10-28||Άγιος Αρσένιος Αρχιεπίσκοπος Σερβίας||Arsenius I was the second archbishop of the Serbs and successor of Saint Sava, and directed the Church of Serbia in the middle of the 13th century. // The Serbian Church honors him as a saint on the 28th of October.

life|11-01||Άγιος Ερμινίγγελδος ο Μάρτυρας||According to tradition, Saint Hermenegild was a prince of the Visigoths of Spain, son of King Leovigild, and embraced the Orthodox faith from an originally Arian family, through the teaching of Leander of Seville. Because he refused to return to the heresy, he was imprisoned and, according to tradition, was put to death around 585. The Church honors him as a Martyr.

life|11-04||Άγιος Πορφύριος ο Μίμος||According to tradition, Saint Porphyrius the Mime was an actor of Roman times. While he was mocking on stage the baptism of the Christians, he is said to have truly believed in Christ and to have confessed his faith before the audience, as a result of which he was put to death as a martyr. The Church honors his memory on this day.

life|11-10||Όσιος Αρσένιος ο Καππαδόκης||Venerable Arsenios the Cappadocian was born around 1840 in Farasa in Cappadocia and as a priest served the Christians of his region, and, according to tradition, baptized the later Venerable Paisios the Athonite. With the exchange of populations in 1924 he followed his flock to Greece and died the same year. The Church honors him as a venerable father and wonderworker, and his memory is kept on this day.

life|11-26||Όσιος Νίκων ο «Μετανοείτε»||According to tradition, Venerable Nikon "Metanoeite" lived in the 10th century. A monk of Pontic origin, he traveled through Crete and mainland Greece and preached everywhere with the phrase "Repent" (Metanoeite), whence he took his epithet. He was active especially in Sparta, where he also fell asleep, and the Church honors him as a venerable father and wonderworker on this day.

life|11-29||Άγιος Brendan (Ιρλανδός)||Saint Brendan the Irishman lived, according to tradition, in the 6th century and was abbot and founder of monasteries in Ireland, among them Clonfert. Medieval tradition attributes to him a sea voyage to an "Island of the Blessed." The Church honors him as a saint on this day.

life|12-28||Άγιοι Δισμύριοι (20.000) Μάρτυρες οι εν Νικομηδεία καέντες||According to tradition, the twenty thousand Christians of Nicomedia gathered in a church to celebrate the Nativity of Christ, in the days of the emperor Diocletian (beginning of the 4th century). // The emperor ordered the doors to be shut and fire to be set, and so they were all martyred by burning. The Church honors their memory on the 28th of December.
